nodes.summary: This text is an introduction to the historical background of periodontology. It traces knowledge and treatment of periodontal disease from ancient times through the nineteenth century, covering early civilizations, the classical world, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It highlights key figures and their contributions, including Hippocrates, Celsus, Paul of Aegina, Albucasis, Avicenna, Sabuncuoglu, Paracelsus, Vesalius, Eustachius, Paré, Leeuwenhoek, Fauchard, Hunter, Berdmore, Koecker, Parmly, Riggs, and Horace Wells. Major themes include the recognition of calculus as a cause, development of scaling instruments and surgical techniques, oral hygiene recommendations, early classification of periodontal diseases, the emergence of periodontics as a specialty, and the discovery of anesthesia.

nodes.title: The Eighteenth Century
nodes.summary: This text is an introduction to the historical background of periodontology. It covers early illustrations and antiplaque experiments, the rise of modern dentistry in 18th-century Europe with Pierre Fauchard’s comprehensive book and instruments, John Hunter’s anatomical work, and Thomas Berdmore’s writings on periodontal problems. In the 19th century, it discusses Leonard Koecker’s oral hygiene advice and focal infection views, Levi Spear Parmly’s role as father of oral hygiene and inventor of dental floss, and John W. Riggs, who became the first periodontics specialist and promoted conservative treatment and prevention. It also mentions Riggs’s followers, the lasting use of Younger’s instruments, and the beginning of modern medicine/dentistry with Horace Wells’s discovery of anesthesia.

nodes.title: The Nineteenth Century
nodes.summary: The text provides a historical overview of periodontology, covering early antiplaque experiments, key figures from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (Fauchard, Hunter, Berdmore, Koecker, Parmly, Riggs), major medical advances (anesthesia, germ theory, antisepsis, radiographs, inflammation pathology), the development of concepts such as nonspecific plaque hypothesis and gingivectomy, the history of necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, and the influential Vienna and Berlin schools of the early twentieth century that shaped modern periodontics.

nodes.title: The Twentieth Century
Vienna
nodes.summary: The text covers historical aspects of periodontology, including Moritz Karolyi's occlusal correction methods; the history of necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis from Xenophon through Hunter, Vincent, and Plaut; and the major contributions of the Vienna and Berlin schools in the early twentieth century. It highlights key figures such as Gottlieb, Orban, Kronfeld, Weinmann, Sicher, Weski, and Neumann, and their roles in developing histopathologic concepts, surgical approaches, and terminology of the periodontium.

nodes.title: Berlin
nodes.summary: The text covers the historical background of periodontology, including early recognition and descriptions of necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, the rise of periodontics in Vienna and Berlin with key figures such as Gottlieb, Orban, Weski, and Neumann, contributions from the United States and other countries, the history and decline of the focal infection theory, and early evidence of dental implants in ancient civilizations.

nodes.title: Historical Periodontology: Flap Surgery, Focal Infection, and Dental Implants

It also includes figures of Robert Neumann and his surgical procedure.

nodes.title: Dental Implants
key_items: The United States and Other Countries

nodes.title: After World War II
nodes.summary: The text covers the historical background of periodontology, beginning with early dental implant attempts from the 19th and early 20th centuries, including materials such as gold, porcelain, cobalt-chromium, tantalum, and titanium, culminating in Bränemark's successful titanium implants and the concept of osseointegration. It then describes postwar periodontal research leadership in the US and Scandinavia, highlighting major researchers and clinicians, the shift toward studying microorganisms and host response, and key workshops and conferences. It also discusses periodontal organizations and journals, the evolution of periodontal education in the United States, and the history of the book itself, including its authors and editions. A list of historical references is included.

The section covers the twentieth-century history of periodontology: the Vienna and Berlin schools, key figures such as Gottlieb, Orban, Kronfeld, Weinmann, Sicher, Weski, and Neumann, Moritz Karolyi's occlusal corrections, and the history of necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis; early flap surgery and its controversies; contributions from US and international clinicians, including the surgical pack and dental hygienist training; the focal infection theory's rise, harmful extraction practices, decline, and 1990s revival; dental implants from ancient attempts to Bränemark's osseointegration; postwar US and Scandinavian research leadership, the shift to studying microorganisms and host response, and key workshops and conferences; the development of periodontal societies, journals, education, and specialty training; and the book's own history, authors, editions, and historical references.

structure.title: 1 Evidence-Based Practice

nodes.title: 1 Evidence-Based Decision Making
Evidence-Based Decision Making: Background, Definition, and Principles
nodes.summary: This page opens Part 1 on evidence-based practice with Chapter 1, presenting authors and the chapter outline. It emphasizes the importance of using the best scientific evidence in dental care and developing skills to find, evaluate, and apply information. It provides the background of evidence-based medicine at McMaster University, defines evidence, evidence-based medicine, and evidence-based dentistry, and describes new methods and tools for generating, synthesizing, accessing, and applying evidence. The text explains evidence-based decision making as a formal process combining research evidence with clinician experience, patient preferences, and clinical circumstances, and notes that evidence adds to, rather than replaces, clinical expertise and patient input.

nodes.title: KEY DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: The text introduces evidence-based decision making (EBDM) in dentistry, covering its background, definitions, principles, and process. It explains the origin of evidence-based medicine at McMaster University, the need for clinicians to find, evaluate, and apply scientific evidence, and the integration of evidence with clinical expertise and patient values. It also lists key concepts such as systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical practice guidelines, and the new tools that distinguish modern evidence-based practice.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
1.e1
CHAPTER 1 Evidence-Based decision Making
Abstract
Informing decisions with the best available evidence brings clinical research findings to the realities of practice. Clinicians who learn and practice evidence-based methodology will be able to find, efficiently filter, interpret, and apply research findings to improve patient care.
Key Words levels of evidence internal validity external validity generalizability randomized clinical trial (RCT) primary evidence secondary evidence clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) systematic reviews (SRs) meta-analyses (MAs) evidence-based decision making (EBDM)

nodes.title: Key Words
nodes.summary: This chapter covers evidence-based decision making (EBDM), including its definition, principles, required skills, and contrasts with traditional decision making. It discusses evidence-based dentistry as defined by the ADA, its incorporation into dental education accreditation standards, and the role of technology in accessing evidence. The PICO framework for formulating clinical questions is explained and demonstrated through a trauma-related dental case scenario comparing early versus late pulp extirpation.

nodes.title: Evidence-Based Decision-Making Process and Skills
Asking Good Questions: The PICO Process
nodes.summary: The text covers the evidence-based decision-making (EBDM) process, including required skills, underlying principles, and the PICO framework for formulating clinical questions. It discusses evidence-based dentistry as defined by the ADA and its integration into dental education. It also explains how technology supports evidence access, gives clinical examples using PICO, and highlights the importance of understanding research methodologies and levels of evidence.

nodes.title: Becoming a Competent Consumer of the Evidence
4 PART 1 EvidEnCE-BAsEd PRACTiCE
nodes.summary: The text covers a clinical case of dental trauma managed through evidence-based decision making, including replantation, splinting, and follow-up; the clinician’s PICO questions about splinting duration and pulp extirpation timing; a decision pathway from injury to resolution; tables linking question types to study methodologies and evidence levels; and an explanation of evidence-based practice concepts such as primary versus secondary sources, challenges in using evidence, and available sources of secondary evidence from organizations and databases.

nodes.title: Sources of Evidence
nodes.summary: This text covers evidence-based decision making, including the types of clinical questions and corresponding research methodologies and levels of evidence, the distinction between primary and secondary evidence sources, useful databases and websites, and the hierarchy of evidence. It explains challenges in applying EBDM, the role of clinical practice guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, how the highest level of evidence varies by question type, and the importance of staying current with evolving evidence and using evidence-based filters in literature searching.

nodes.title: Levels of Evidence
nodes.summary: The text describes evidence-based practice in dentistry, focusing on the hierarchy of clinical evidence, the role of clinical practice guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, and how to search for and appraise evidence. It explains that CPGs are top-level evidence, should be based on MAs/SRs, and change as evidence evolves, using the American Heart Association endocarditis guideline as an example. It details the levels of evidence from CPGs down to expert opinion, noting that the highest level depends on the clinical question (e.g., therapy vs. prognosis). It also covers using PubMed, MeSH terms, PICO questions, Boolean operators, filters, and multiple databases to find evidence, including example searches for tooth avulsion and replantation. Finally, it addresses critical appraisal of retrieved evidence using structured checklists and appraisal forms.

The section explains how to become a competent consumer of evidence in evidence-based dental practice. It illustrates evidence-based decision making with a clinical case of dental trauma, including PICO questions, a decision pathway, and tables linking question types to study methodologies and evidence levels. It covers sources of evidence (primary vs. secondary), databases and websites, and the hierarchy of evidence from clinical practice guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses to expert opinion. It also describes searching PubMed with MeSH terms, PICO, Boolean operators, and filters; using multiple databases; and critically appraising evidence with checklists, while emphasizing that the highest level of evidence varies by question and that evidence evolves over time.

nodes.title: Searching for and Acquiring the Evidence
nodes.summary: The text discusses evidence-based decision making in dentistry, focusing on searching and appraising evidence for two PICO questions related to tooth avulsion and replantation. It describes the use of PubMed, MeSH terms, Clinical Queries, and additional databases, along with specific search strategies and their results. Inclusion criteria for selecting studies are outlined, and the importance of critical appraisal using structured checklists is emphasized. Table 1.3 and Table 1.4 are referenced for search terms and appraisal guides, respectively.

nodes.title: Appraising the Evidence
key_items: Common Ways Used to Report Results
nodes.summary: The text describes the evidence-based decision making (EBDM) process in dentistry, using a tooth avulsion and replantation case. It explains how PICO questions guided literature searches using PubMed/MEDLINE, MeSH terms, Clinical Queries, and specialty databases, with Boolean operators and filters to find guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. Search results and inclusion criteria are detailed. It covers critical appraisal tools such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and CASP, and result reporting measures like ARR, RRR, and NNT. The appraised evidence supported pulp extirpation within 10–14 days and splinting durations of 1 week for avulsion and 2–4 weeks for lateral luxation. The clinician applied these findings successfully, and the chapter discusses evaluating patient outcomes and self-performance, along with highlights and conclusion emphasizing that EBDM requires practice but improves clinical care and closes the gap between research and practice.

nodes.title: Applying and Evaluating Evidence-Based Dentistry in Practice
key_items: Applying the Evidence: Evidence-Based Dentistry in Action
nodes.summary: The page covers key tools for critical appraisal, such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and CASP, and explains result-reporting measures like CER, EER, ARR, RRR, and NNT. It demonstrates the EBDM process through a dental trauma case, appraising systematic reviews and guidelines on pulp extirpation timing and splinting duration, then applying this evidence to patient care. The text also describes evaluating clinical outcomes and self-performance in EBDM, and concludes with highlights emphasizing that EBDM helps clinicians find, filter, interpret, and apply research findings to improve patient care.

The section covers the evidence-based decision-making (EBDM) process in dentistry, including required skills, principles, and the PICO framework for asking clinical questions. It defines evidence-based dentistry per the ADA, discusses its role in dental education, and explains how technology aids evidence access. Using a tooth avulsion and replantation case, it demonstrates forming PICO questions, searching PubMed/MEDLINE with MeSH terms, Boolean operators, filters, and specialty databases, and selecting studies with inclusion criteria. The section addresses becoming a competent consumer of evidence by understanding primary and secondary sources, the hierarchy of evidence, and critical appraisal tools such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and CASP, along with reporting measures like ARR, RRR, and NNT. It shows how appraised evidence supports pulp extirpation within 10–14 days and specific splinting durations, then applying this evidence in practice. Finally, it emphasizes evaluating patient outcomes and self-performance, noting that EBDM requires practice, improves clinical care, and bridges the gap between research and practice.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text covers evidence-based practice in dentistry, including critical appraisal tools (CONSORT, PRISMA, CASP), common outcome measures (CER, EER, ARR, RRR, NNT), and a clinical case applying EBDM to dental trauma. It describes using evidence from systematic reviews and clinical guidelines for pulp extirpation timing and splinting duration, combining evidence with clinical experience and patient preferences, evaluating outcomes and self-performance, and concludes with the importance of EBDM for bridging research and practice.

nodes.summary: The text includes the heading and full references for Chapter 1 on evidence-based decision making. It then presents the beginning of Chapter 2 on critical thinking and assessing evidence, which introduces twelve tools for evaluating causality. The key content covers the importance of skepticism in clinical evidence, illustrated by the beta-carotene example where initial beliefs in protective effects were overturned by randomized trials showing harm. It also discusses why much chronic disease evidence is unreliable, including the rarity of effective treatments, complexity of disease causes, poor methodology, and the failure of presumed protective interventions. These concerns are applied to periodontics, suggesting that periodontal diseases are complex and the abundance of claimed treatments may reflect a lack of truly effective therapies.

The section opens Part 1 on evidence-based practice with Chapter 1, introducing the authors, outline, and the importance of using the best scientific evidence in dental care. It provides the background of evidence-based medicine at McMaster University and defines evidence, evidence-based medicine, evidence-based dentistry, and evidence-based decision making as a formal process that integrates research evidence with clinician experience, patient preferences, and clinical circumstances. It lists key concepts such as systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical practice guidelines, levels of evidence, validity, generalizability, RCTs, and primary/secondary evidence, and highlights new tools for generating, synthesizing, accessing, and applying evidence. The chapter also covers the ADA definition of evidence-based dentistry, its place in dental education, and how technology supports evidence access. The PICO framework is explained and illustrated through dental trauma cases, with demonstrations of searching PubMed/MEDLINE using MeSH terms, Boolean operators, filters, specialty databases, and study selection. It details the skills needed to become a competent consumer of evidence, including understanding the evidence hierarchy and using critical appraisal tools such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and CASP, as well as outcome measures like CER, EER, ARR, RRR, and NNT. The section applies appraised evidence to decisions such as pulp extirpation timing and splinting duration, stresses combining evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences, and emphasizes evaluating outcomes and self-performance. It concludes that EBDM requires practice, improves care, and bridges research and practice. The references list supports the chapter and includes a radiographic healing figure. A final subsection references Chapter 1 and transitions to Chapter 2 on critical thinking and assessing evidence, covering twelve causality tools, the beta-carotene example, why much chronic disease evidence is unreliable, and implications for periodontics.

nodes.title: 2 Critical Thinking
Critical Thinking: Assessing Evidence with Twelve Skeptical Tools
nodes.summary: This page from Chapter 2, 'Critical Thinking: Assessing Evidence,' discusses the need to critically evaluate clinical evidence rather than rely on authority. It introduces 12 tools for assessing evidence, with the first tool being skepticism. The beta-carotene example demonstrates how observational evidence can be overturned by randomized trials. The text also outlines four reasons why much medical evidence is misleading, including low treatment success rates, complexity of chronic diseases, poor methodology, and the lack of magic bullets for lifestyle-related harms. These concerns are applied to periodontics, where the abundance of purported treatments may actually signal the absence of truly effective therapies and the complexity of periodontal diseases.

nodes.title: Twelve Tools for Assessing Evidence Be Skeptical
nodes.summary: The chapter emphasizes the need for critical thinking and skepticism when assessing clinical evidence, especially in periodontics. It introduces twelve tools for evaluating causality, beginning with skepticism, and uses examples such as beta-carotene to show how promising evidence can later prove harmful. It explains why much chronic disease evidence is unreliable, cites four contributing factors, and suggests that the abundance of periodontal treatments may reflect a complex, challenging disease rather than true effectiveness. The abstract and keywords reinforce the need for evidence-based dentistry and better use of higher-level evidence like randomized trials.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
10.e1
CHAPTER 2 Critical Thinking
Abstract
Dentistry is still largely based on the principle of the inverted evidence pyramid. Case series and biologic plausibility, the lowest levels of evidence, often rule the day. Randomized trials, the highest level of evidence, frequently remain ignored. This chapter offers some critical thinking guidelines on how to evaluate information so that the best evidence can guide your clinical decision making.
Keywords epidemiology biostatistics evidence-based dentistry evidence-based medicine controlled trials case-control studies temporality cohort studies

nodes.title: Keywords
Do Not Trust Biologic Plausibility
nodes.summary: The text discusses the low scientific quality of periodontal research and warns against relying on biologic plausibility or causal chain reasoning in medicine and dentistry. It gives examples where biologically plausible treatments failed to help patients and notes such reasoning is only level 5 evidence. It mentions the removal of flossing recommendations from Dietary Guidelines due to insufficient evidence and critiques the weak evidence base for periodontitis management. The text then describes three systematic study designs used in clinical research—RCTs, cohort studies, and case-control studies—explaining their methods, levels of evidence, and challenges, with RCTs as the gold standard.

nodes.title: What Level of Controlled Evidence Is Available?
nodes.summary: The text critiques the overreliance on biologic plausibility and deductive reasoning in medicine and periodontology, arguing that such reasoning has led to ineffective or harmful treatments and weak evidence for practices like flossing. It then describes the hierarchy of controlled evidence—RCTs, cohort studies, and case-control studies—and emphasizes that establishing causality requires careful attention to temporality, prespecified hypotheses, and avoiding post hoc data-driven modifications. Overall, it calls for a shift toward higher-level evidence and rigorous scientific methods to place periodontics on a firmer footing.

nodes.title: Did the Cause Precede the Effect?
nodes.summary: The text discusses challenges in evidence-based medicine, emphasizing that controlled studies only show exposure–endpoint associations with uncertainty, not absolute causality. It stresses temporality as essential for causal claims, using examples from prayer, Alzheimer's disease, obesity, and periodontitis. It also critiques poor adherence to pre-specified hypotheses and data-generated findings, describing harmful post-trial modifications of sample, exposure, and endpoint definitions, with relevant examples from cardiovascular, HIV, oncology, and periodontal research.

nodes.title: No Betting on the Horse After the Race Is Over
key_items: Did the Cause Precede the Effect?
nodes.summary: The text covers evidence-based practice and critical appraisal of clinical research. It contrasts levels of evidence, notes case-control studies are lowest, and frames studies as examining exposure→endpoint associations. Causality assessment relies on temporality, pre-specified hypotheses, association strength, and is inherently uncertain. Temporality—cause preceding effect—is essential but often unclear in chronic diseases (Alzheimer's, obesity, periodontitis) and is illustrated by a retroactive prayer example. The text stresses that hypotheses must predict observations before data analysis; post hoc/subgroup/exposure/endpoint modifications produce unreliable data-generated ideas, leading to data-torturing (opportunistic vs Procrustean). Clinically relevant pretrial hypotheses require a clinically relevant true endpoint (versus surrogate), unbiased/relevant comparisons, representative real-world study samples, and small type I and type II error rates. It defines type I/type II errors and power, notes false results depend on true effectiveness, and concludes that larger association sizes, such as hepatitis B and liver cancer, are more readily accepted as causal than smaller associations such as electromagnetic radiation and childhood leukemia or periodontitis and coronary heart disease.

nodes.title: What Is a Clinically Relevant Pretrial Hypothesis?
key_items: Clinically Relevant Endpoint; Common and Relevant Comparisons; Representative Study Sample; Small Type I and Type II Error Rates
Small Type I and Type II Error Rates
nodes.summary: The text covers persistent clinical research problems such as ambiguous primary endpoints, flexible outcome definitions, post hoc endpoint changes, and statistical trickery/data torturing, distinguishing opportunistic (hypothesis-generating) from Procrustean (hypothesis-proving) data torturing. It then defines clinically relevant pretrial hypotheses using four characteristics: true clinically relevant endpoints, relevant comparisons without comparator bias, representative real-world samples, and small type I/II error rates. It contrasts true vs surrogate endpoints, emphasizes appropriate control groups and generalizable samples, explains error rates and power, and concludes that larger observed associations are more readily judged causal, as illustrated by hepatitis B, electromagnetic radiation, and periodontitis examples.

nodes.title: Size Does Matter
key_items: What Is a Clinically Relevant Pretrial Hypothesis?
Clinically Relevant Endpoint; Common and Relevant Comparisons; Representative Study Sample
Small Type I and Type II Error Rates
nodes.summary: The text discusses problems in clinical research such as endpoint changes and data torturing, then defines the four components of a clinically relevant pretrial hypothesis: clinically relevant true endpoints, relevant comparisons, representative samples, and low error rates. It explains true versus surrogate endpoints, comparator bias, sample representativeness, and type I/II errors. It then covers measures of association, focusing on odds ratios, confidence intervals, and the importance of association size for causal inference, including expert thresholds for observational studies. Finally, it emphasizes evaluating alternative explanations and confounding, illustrated by beta-carotene and periodontitis examples where observational findings conflicted with randomized trial results.

nodes.title: Is a Better Alternative Explanation Available?
nodes.summary: The text covers interpretation of odds ratios and confidence intervals, using a chronic periodontitis-fatal MI table and examples such as penciclovir, including statistical significance and expert thresholds for judging causal associations. It discusses the unreliability of observational epidemiology, the need to explore alternative explanations, criteria for confounding, crude vs adjusted associations, residual confounding, and modeling issues, with beta-carotene and periodontitis-low-birth-weight examples. It then addresses randomization quality, healthy user bias, and bias from excluding noncompliant patients, and includes clinical correlations on periodontitis in pregnancy and periodontal maintenance compliance.

nodes.title: Was the Study Properly Randomized?
nodes.summary: The text covers confounding in epidemiology, including criteria for confounding, crude versus adjusted associations, measurement and residual confounding, modeling issues, and the role of randomization. It discusses problems with improper randomization, healthy user bias, biases from excluding noncompliant patients, and the essential elements of proper randomization. It also addresses the limitations of nonrandomized evidence, using the hormone replacement therapy example and ethical, sample size, and political barriers to RCTs. Finally, it describes placebo and nocebo effects, sham surgical controls, quantified placebo effects, and examples such as fluoride trials and pain studies.

nodes.title: When to Rely on Nonrandomized Evidence
nodes.summary: The text discusses the complexity and potential biases of randomized controlled trials. Proper randomization must include pre-randomization enrollment with baseline data, independent and auditable treatment assignment, concealment of the allocation process, and analysis according to assigned treatment rather than treatment received, with imputation for missing data. It then argues that nonrandomized evidence can be unreliable, using hormone replacement therapy as an example: strong epidemiologic support was contradicted by a randomized trial showing serious harms. RCTs may be limited by ethical principles, very large sample sizes for rare events, and political or economic factors. The text also covers placebo and nocebo effects, explaining how sham surgery helps distinguish true treatment effects from these effects. It quantifies placebo responses and emphasizes that randomized placebo versus no-treatment comparisons are needed for reliable estimates, illustrating this with a fluoride trial systematic review in which the choice of control group affected the estimated treatment effect.

nodes.title: Did the Investigators Take Into Account the Placebo or Nocebo Effects?
key_items: When to Rely on Nonrandomized Evidence
nodes.summary: The text discusses critical thinking in evidence-based practice, covering the importance of proper randomization and its components, the limitations and challenges of nonrandomized evidence, ethical and practical barriers to RCTs, the impact of placebo and nocebo effects, and the threat of conflicts of interest in clinical research. It also highlights how these issues apply to periodontal and dental research and calls for integrating evidence-based thinking into clinical practice while reducing bias in guidelines.

nodes.title: Was Protection in Place Against Conflict of Interest?
nodes.summary: The text discusses evidence-based practice, beginning with the reality and possible mechanisms of placebo effects. It then focuses on conflicts of interest in clinical research, explaining how financial and other secondary interests can distort evidence, suppress negative findings, influence study design, and limit translation of research into practice. It describes protections such as trial registration and monitoring boards, notes the prevalence of conflict in dental research, and concludes with lessons for periodontal research, including reducing reliance on biologic plausibility, using controlled clinical observations, and possibly excluding experts from guideline development. References are listed on a companion website.

This chapter promotes critical thinking in dentistry and periodontics by encouraging reliance on higher levels of controlled evidence rather than biologic plausibility or low-level case series. It critiques causal-chain reasoning, explains the hierarchy among RCTs, cohort studies, and case-control studies, and emphasizes that controlled studies show associations rather than absolute causality. Key topics include the necessity of temporality, pre-specified hypotheses, clinically relevant true endpoints, unbiased comparisons, representative samples, and low error rates; interpretation of association size, odds ratios, and confidence intervals; and evaluation of confounding and alternative explanations. The chapter also covers proper randomization, the unreliability of nonrandomized evidence, limitations of RCTs, placebo/nocebo effects, and conflicts of interest, concluding with lessons for periodontal research and evidence-based clinical practice.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text discusses placebo effects and conflicts of interest in evidence-based medicine. It notes that placebo effects can be measurable and may influence outcomes like caries through autonomic nervous system changes. It then addresses why ineffective procedures remain in practice, defines conflict of interest, and gives examples of how financial and other secondary interests can bias research through suppression of evidence, unpublished negative trials, distorted analyses, and misallocated resources. It highlights industry influence and protective measures, then applies these issues to dental and periodontal research, emphasizing the need for evidence-based practice, better conflict-of-interest policies, and reduced reliance on biologic plausibility. References are available on a companion website.

It then focuses on conflicts of interest in evidence-based medicine, explaining how financial and other secondary interests can bias research evidence through suppressed data, unpublished negative trials, distorted study designs, and industry influence. It highlights examples from ineffective surgical procedures and dental research, and describes protections such as trial registration and monitoring boards. The conclusion urges the integration of evidence-based thinking into periodontal research and clinical practice, less reliance on biologic plausibility, and adherence to Institute of Medicine recommendations about expert involvement in guidelines.

It describes the four components of the periodontium (gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, alveolar bone), the three zones of oral mucosa, clinical features of gingiva, the marginal gingiva, and the gingival sulcus and its depth in health.

Chapter 2 advocates critical thinking and evidence-based dentistry, especially in periodontics. It critiques reliance on low-level evidence such as case series and biologic plausibility, describing the inverted evidence pyramid and urging greater use of randomized trials. It introduces twelve skeptical tools for assessing evidence, starting with skepticism, and uses the beta-carotene example to illustrate how observational findings can be overturned by randomized trials. The chapter explains why much medical evidence is misleading, citing low treatment success rates, the complexity of chronic diseases, poor methodology, and the lack of magic bullets for lifestyle-related harms. It applies these issues to periodontics, where the abundance of treatments may reflect disease complexity rather than true effectiveness. It also covers the evidence hierarchy, causal appraisal concepts such as temporality, pre-specified hypotheses, true endpoints, unbiased comparisons, representative samples, error rates, odds ratios, confidence intervals, confounding, randomization, limitations of RCTs, and placebo/nocebo effects. Conflicts of interest and their impact on research are discussed, along with protections like trial registration and monitoring boards. The section concludes by urging evidence-based practice, less reliance on biologic plausibility, and improved conflict-of-interest policies. structure.title: 2 Biologic Basis of Periodontology

3 Anatomy, Structure, and Function of the Periodontium
Normal Periodontium: Anatomy, Oral Mucosa, Gingiva, and Sulcus
nodes.summary: This page from Chapter 3 on the normal periodontium introduces the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, emphasizing its four components—gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone—and their integrated function. It outlines the oral mucosa's three zones, describes the clinical features and divisions of the gingiva, details the marginal gingiva's anatomic characteristics, and discusses the gingival sulcus and its depths in healthy and ideal conditions.

nodes.title: Gingival Sulcus
nodes.summary: This chapter covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the normal periodontium, which comprises gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. It describes the three zones of the oral mucosa, the clinical features and subdivisions of the gingiva, and the characteristics of the marginal gingiva and gingival sulcus, including variations in sulcus depth. It also notes that periodontal components interact and that pathologic changes in one can affect others, with additional online content on gingival epithelium, alveolar process, and attachment apparatus, as well as coverage of development, vascularization, innervation, and functions.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
19.e1
CHAPTER 3 Anatomy, structure, and function of the Periodontium
Abstract
The normal periodontium provides the support necessary to maintain teeth in function. It consists of four principal components: gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. Each of these periodontal components is distinct in its location, tissue architecture, biochemical composition, and chemical composition, but all of these components function together as a single unit. Research has revealed that the extracellular matrix components of one periodontal compart- ment can influence the cellular activities of adjacent structures. Therefore the pathologic changes that occur in one periodontal component may have significant ramifications for the maintenance, repair, or regeneration of other components of the periodontium.
Key Words gingiva alveolar bone cementum periodontal ligament

nodes.title: Key Words
Attached Gingiva
nodes.summary: The text describes normal gingival anatomy, including the gingival sulcus and probing depth, the attached gingiva and its width variations, and the interdental gingiva. It covers clinical landmarks, measurement considerations, regional differences, and shapes of interdental gingiva.

nodes.title: Interdental Gingiva
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the gingiva, including normal clinical landmarks, sulcus probing depth and influencing factors, characteristics and width of attached gingiva, variations in interdental gingiva and papillae, microscopic composition of epithelium and connective tissue, and the epithelium's active role in innate host defense.

nodes.title: Microscopic Features
Gingival Epithelium
General Aspects of Gingival Epithelium Biology
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, microscopic structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on the gingiva. It describes normal interdental gingival variations, microscopic composition, the biology of gingival epithelium including its active role in host defense, three epithelial compartments (oral, sulcular, junctional), keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, keratinization types, keratin and envelope proteins, cell junctions, metabolic gradients, nonkeratinocyte cells (melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells), basal lamina structure, and regional variations in epithelial structure and keratinization.

nodes.title: Structural and Metabolic Characteristics of Different Areas of Gingival Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text describes the ultrastructural features of the gingival basement membrane, including the basal lamina, hemidesmosomes, lamina lucida/densa, anchoring fibrils, permeability, and barrier function. It then covers regional variations in gingival epithelium—oral, sulcular, and junctional—highlighting their functions, metabolic activity of epithelial cells, factors affecting keratinization, and the relative keratinization of different oral mucosa areas. The oral epithelium is described in detail: its location, thickness, keratinization types, and four cellular layers. The passage also refers to histochemical and histological figures illustrating the basement membrane and epithelial variations.

nodes.title: Oral (Outer) Epithelium
key_items: Structural and Metabolic Characteristics of Different Areas of Gingival Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text describes the microscopic structure and function of gingival epithelium. It details the basal lamina and its components, then compares the three epithelial regions: oral, sulcular, and junctional epithelium. The oral epithelium is keratinized or parakeratinized with characteristic layers and keratin expression. The sulcular epithelium lines the sulcus, is nonkeratinized but can keratinize under certain conditions, and is semipermeable. The junctional epithelium is a unique nonkeratinized collar attached to the tooth by hemidesmosomes and internal basal lamina, with distinct structural features, formation, and roles in adhesion and protection against bacterial colonization. Regional keratinization patterns, metabolic activity, and age-related changes are also covered.

nodes.title: Sulcular Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text describes the anatomy, structure, and function of the sulcular and junctional epithelia of the periodontium. It covers the sulcular epithelium's location, nonkeratinized morphology, keratinization potential, and role as a semipermeable barrier. It then details the junctional epithelium's structure, layers, dimensions, formation, attachment to the tooth via basal laminae and hemidesmosomes, biochemical features such as laminin production, its association with gingival fibers as the dentogingival unit, and its protective function against bacterial colonization.

nodes.title: Junctional Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text details the anatomy, structure, and function of the sulcular and junctional epithelia of the periodontium, as well as the development of the gingival sulcus. It describes sulcular epithelium as a thin nonkeratinized layer lining the sulcus, its keratinization potential, permeability, and histological/cytokeratin profile. It also covers junctional epithelium's structure, attachment via basal laminae and hemidesmosomes, unique cytokeratins, role in the dentogingival unit, and defensive functions. Finally, it explains how the gingival sulcus forms during tooth eruption from reduced enamel epithelium and oral epithelium, with ongoing renewal and coronal migration of junctional epithelial cells.

nodes.title: Development of Gingival Sulcus
nodes.summary: The text covers the structure and function of the periodontium, focusing on the junctional epithelium, gingival sulcus development, gingival epithelial renewal, cuticular structures on teeth, gingival fluid, gingival connective tissue, and gingival fibers. It describes the roles of the junctional epithelium in barrier function and host defense, the formation and self-renewal of the junctional epithelium and sulcus during tooth eruption, the circadian and inflammatory influences on epithelial mitosis, the classification and nature of tooth cuticles, the composition and diagnostic potential of gingival fluid, the components and organization of gingival connective tissue, and the arrangement and functions of gingival fiber groups.

nodes.title: The Periodontium: Epithelial Renewal, Cuticular Structures, Gingival Fluid, Connective Tissue, Fibers
nodes.summary: The page covers key structural and functional aspects of the periodontium, including renewal of the gingival epithelium, cuticular structures on the tooth, gingival fluid, gingival connective tissue, and gingival fibers. The oral epithelium continuously renews by balancing cell formation and shedding; mitotic activity varies with time, keratinization, and inflammation, and shedding removes bacteria. Tooth cuticles are thin acellular structures classified into acquired and developmental coatings, including the reduced enamel epithelium, coronal cementum, and dental cuticle. Gingival fluid acts as a transudate/exudate with biomarker potential and functions in cleansing, adhesion, antimicrobial defense, and antibody activity. The gingival connective tissue, or lamina propria, consists of cells, fibers, vessels, nerves, and ground substance, with collagen and elastic fiber systems and a connective tissue attachment that limits epithelial migration. Gingival fibers are type I collagen bundles arranged as gingivodental, circular, and transseptal groups that brace, support, and unite the gingiva.

This section provides a comprehensive overview of the gingival epithelium and associated periodontal structures. It covers the general biology of gingival epithelium, including its three compartments (oral, sulcular, and junctional), keratinocyte behavior, keratinization, cell junctions, nonkeratinocyte cells, and basal lamina. It describes the ultrastructural features of the basement membrane and the structural/metabolic characteristics of different epithelial regions. Detailed attention is given to the oral, sulcular, and junctional epithelia, their morphology, keratinization, permeability, attachment mechanisms, and defensive functions. The section also addresses the development of the gingival sulcus during tooth eruption, epithelial renewal, tooth cuticles, gingival fluid, and the composition and organization of gingival connective tissue and fibers.

nodes.title: Gingival Connective Tissue
Gingival Fibers
key_items: Renewal of Gingival Epithelium; Cuticular Structures on the Tooth; Gingival Fluid (Sulcular Fluid)
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on: renewal of gingival epithelium (mitotic rhythms, site/age/inflammation effects, junctional epithelial cell division, antimicrobial shedding, turnover times); cuticular structures on teeth (acquired vs developmental coatings, reduced enamel epithelium, coronal cementum, dental cuticle); gingival fluid (composition, transudate/exudate behavior, inflammation response, diffusion route, functions, biomarker potential); gingival connective tissue (composition, lamina propria layers, ground substance, fiber types, connective tissue attachment); gingival fibers (functions, groups including gingivodental/circular/transseptal/semicircular/transgingival fibers, tension generation); cellular elements (fibroblasts, mast cells, macrophages, inflammatory cells); and repair/regenerative capacity of gingival connective tissue.

nodes.title: Cellular Elements
nodes.summary: The text describes the structure and cellular composition of gingival connective tissue, including the arrangement and function of gingival fibers (gingivodental, circular, transseptal, semicircular, and transgingival), the role of fibroblasts in generating tension and maintaining connective tissue, the presence of various cells such as mast cells, macrophages, inflammatory cells, and the tissue's strong healing and regenerative capacity due to high turnover.

nodes.title: Repair of Gingival Connective Tissue
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy and structure of gingival connective tissue, including the arrangement of gingival fiber groups and their functions. It details the cellular components, especially fibroblasts, and the presence of immune cells in clinically normal gingiva. It also addresses the repair capacity of gingival connective tissue and provides an overview of the blood supply, microcirculation, lymphatic drainage, and associated changes during inflammation.

nodes.title: Blood Supply, Lymphatics, and Nerves
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on the gingiva. It describes the healing capacity of gingival connective tissue, the blood supply from supraperiosteal arterioles, periodontal ligament vessels, and interdental septal arterioles, as well as capillary patterns and vascular changes in inflammation. It also discusses lymphatic drainage, innervation, methods for visualizing blood vessels, and the correlation of clinical and microscopic features, including gingival color, the difference between attached gingiva and alveolar mucosa, and melanin pigmentation and repigmentation.

The section describes gingival connective tissue and associated periodontal topics. It covers the tissue's composition (lamina propria layers, ground substance, fiber types, connective tissue attachment), gingival fiber groups and functions, cellular elements (fibroblasts, mast cells, macrophages, inflammatory cells), and its repair/regenerative capacity. It also details blood supply, capillary and vascular changes in inflammation, lymphatics, innervation, and blood-vessel visualization. Clinical correlations include gingival color, attached gingiva vs alveolar mucosa, and melanin pigmentation/repigmentation. Additional content includes gingival epithelial renewal, tooth cuticular structures, and gingival fluid composition and function.

The section covers the microscopic features of the gingival epithelium and gingival connective tissue. It describes epithelial compartments, keratinocyte biology, keratinization, cell junctions, nonkeratinocyte cells, basal lamina, basement membrane ultrastructure, and the structural and metabolic features of oral, sulcular, and junctional epithelia, including their permeability, attachment, and defensive roles. It also addresses sulcus development, epithelial renewal, tooth cuticles, and gingival fluid. The connective tissue portion covers lamina propria layers, ground substance, fiber types, connective tissue attachment, gingival fiber groups, cellular elements, repair capacity, blood supply, vascular changes in inflammation, lymphatics, innervation, and blood-vessel visualization. Clinical correlations include gingival color, attached gingiva versus alveolar mucosa, and melanin pigmentation/repigmentation.

It explains gingival color, physiologic melanin pigmentation and repigmentation, size, contour, shape of interdental papillae, consistency, surface texture with stippling, and position. It also discusses the concept of continuous tooth eruption, including active and passive eruption, the clinical/anatomic crown and root, four stages of passive eruption, and physiologic versus pathologic recession. Finally, it introduces the periodontal ligament as a complex connective tissue surrounding the root and connecting it to alveolar bone.

The section provides an abstract and key words for the chapter on the periodontium: the normal periodontium comprises gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone; these distinct components function as a single unit, with extracellular matrix interactions linking adjacent compartments and pathologic changes affecting maintenance, repair, or regeneration. The subsections cover gingival anatomy and function, including attached gingiva, interdental gingiva, gingival sulcus/probing depth, clinical landmarks, measurement considerations, and variations in papillae. Microscopic features are described in detail for both gingival epithelium and connective tissue, including keratinization, cell junctions, basement membrane, epithelial roles in permeability and host defense, sulcus development, epithelial renewal, tooth cuticles, gingival fluid, connective tissue fibers, cell types, repair, blood supply, lymphatics, and innervation. Clinical and microscopic findings are correlated for color, melanin pigmentation, size, contour, papilla shape, consistency, stippling, and position; continuous tooth eruption is discussed with active and passive eruption, crown/root relationships, four stages of passive eruption, and physiologic versus pathologic recession. The section also introduces the periodontal ligament as the connective tissue connecting the root to alveolar bone.

Position

nodes.title: Periodontal Fibers

nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontal ligament, describing its fibers, cellular elements, and ground substance. It details fiber types and remodeling, the major cell populations including fibroblasts and epithelial rests of Malassez, immune/defense cells, and the composition and biologic roles of the ground substance. A figure illustrating epithelial rests is also included.

nodes.title: Ground Substance
nodes.summary: The text describes the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontal ligament, covering its fiber systems, cellular elements, ground substance, and calcified structures such as cementicles. It details fibroblasts, epithelial rests of Malassez, and defense cells, as well as the composition and biologic roles of the ground substance. The functions of the periodontal ligament are categorized as physical, formative/remodeling, nutritional, and sensory. Physical functions include tooth support and shock absorption, explained by tensional and viscoelastic theories, and the transmission of occlusal forces through principal fibers and tooth rotation. The formative/remodeling role involves cellular responses to mechanical forces during physiologic and orthodontic tooth movement.
