It describes the PDL space, principal and Sharpey fibers, collagen composition and types, the six principal fiber groups, additional fiber systems, and fiber remodeling. Cellular elements include fibroblasts, epithelial rests of Malassez, immune/defense cells, and neurovascular-associated cells. The ground substance composition and biologic roles are covered, along with calcified structures such as cementicles. Periodontal ligament functions are categorized as physical, formative/remodeling, nutritional, and sensory, including shock absorption theories, occlusal force transmission, tooth rotation, and PDL-width regulation. Cementum is also described, including its structure, acellular/cellular types, collagen, Sharpey fibers, incremental lines, and Schroeder's classification.

nodes.title: Cementum
key_items: Permeability of Cementum; Cementoenamel Junction; Cementodentinal Junction; Thickness of Cementum
Permeability of Cementum; Cementoenamel Junction; Cementodentinal Junction
Exposure of Cementum to the Oral Environment
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal ligament sensory innervation and neural ending types, PDL width homeostasis, and the structure, composition, types, classification, thickness, permeability, and clinical relationships of cementum (including cementoenamel and cementodentinal junctions). It also addresses hypercementosis and its causes/diagnosis, cementum resorption and repair mechanisms, molecular factors and growth factors involved in cementum regeneration, ankylosis, effects of cementum exposure to the oral environment, and the anatomy and components of the alveolar process.

nodes.title: Alveolar Process
Ankylosis
nodes.summary: The text covers cementum pathology and repair, ankylosis, cementum exposure to the oral environment, and the anatomy of the alveolar process. It describes cementum resorption by osteoclasts, cementum repair and regeneration, the uncertain origin of cementoblasts, the potential role of epithelial rests of Malassez, and growth factors used in regeneration. It defines ankylosis as fusion of cementum and alveolar bone with periodontal ligament obliteration, discusses its causes and occurrence, and notes that exposed cementum can be penetrated by substances and bacteria, leading to cementum caries. It then details the alveolar process: its tooth-dependent nature, components (cortical plate, alveolar bone proper/lamina dura/cribriform plate, cancellous supporting bone, interdental septum), the distinction of basal bone, and the distribution of compact and cancellous bone in supporting teeth.

nodes.title: Exposure of Cementum to the Oral Environment
nodes.summary: The text covers several aspects of periodontal anatomy and biology: cementum repair and regeneration, including the role of rests of Malassez and growth factors; ankylosis, its causes, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, and relation to implants; exposure of cementum to the oral environment and bacterial invasion; the structure and function of the alveolar process and its components; bone composition and the organic/inorganic matrix; bone remodeling and the cellular mechanisms of osteoblastic formation and osteoclastic resorption; and the detailed histology of bone cells, socket wall, bundle bone, and Sharpey fibers.

nodes.title: Cells and Intercellular Matrix
nodes.summary: The text describes the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on alveolar bone. It explains bone remodeling as a coordinated process of resorption by osteoclasts and formation by osteoblasts, including osteoclast origin, activity, hormonal regulation, acid-mediated demineralization, and the detailed sequence of resorption. It also covers osteoblast differentiation, bone formation, osteocytes and canaliculi, blood supply, bone growth, Haversian systems, the structure of the socket wall, bundle bone and Sharpey fibers, and cancellous bone with trabeculae and endosteal cells.

nodes.title: Socket Wall
nodes.summary: The text describes the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on alveolar bone. It covers bone remodeling and the coupled activities of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, including mechanisms of bone resorption, hormonal regulation, and the cellular sequence of resorption. It details alveolar bone formation, osteocytes and canaliculi, blood supply, Haversian systems, socket wall composition, bundle bone and Sharpey fibers, cancellous bone, bone marrow, periosteum and endosteum, interdental septum anatomy, and osseous topography. It also notes clinical implications related to tooth position, bone height, and radiographic findings.

nodes.title: Alveolar Bone: Marrow, Periosteum, Endosteum, Septum, Topography
nodes.summary: The page covers alveolar bone biology, including cancellous bone structure and bundle bone changes during tooth migration, bone marrow types and jaw locations, the structure and function of periosteum and endosteum, the composition and variations of the interdental septum, and osseous topography influenced by tooth position and angulation.

nodes.title: Osseous Topography
nodes.summary: The text discusses alveolar bone structure and biology in the periodontium. It covers bundle bone changes during mesial tooth migration; cancellous bone pattern and bone marrow distribution, including red-to-yellow marrow conversion and occasional red marrow foci in jaws; periosteum and endosteum layers and their role in bone-size regulation; interdental septum composition, variability, crest-to-CEJ measurements, and determinants; osseous topography variations with tooth version and root angulation; fenestration and dehiscence definitions, prevalence, risk factors, and surgical importance; and alveolar bone remodeling, including local and systemic influences such as parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and vitamin D3, with manifestations adjacent to the periodontal ligament and periosteum.

nodes.title: Fenestration and Dehiscence
nodes.summary: The text covers structural and anatomical features of the periodontium, including interdental septa and radiographic findings, normal bone contour, fenestrations and dehiscences of alveolar bone, and the remodeling process of alveolar bone with its local and systemic influences and effects on bone height, contour, and density.

nodes.title: Remodeling of Alveolar Bone
nodes.summary: The text covers anatomical and developmental features of the periodontium, including radiographic appearance of interdental septa and lamina dura, normal bone contour variations, fenestration and dehiscence defects, alveolar bone remodeling, and the development of the attachment apparatus, cementum, and periodontal ligament.

The section covers the alveolar process and its associated periodontal structures, including cementum pathology and repair, ankylosis, and exposure of cementum to the oral environment. It details alveolar process anatomy and components, bone composition and cells, socket wall histology, bundle bone and Sharpey fibers, cancellous bone, bone marrow, periosteum and endosteum, interdental septum anatomy and radiographic appearance, and osseous topography. It also discusses fenestration and dehiscence, alveolar bone remodeling with hormonal and local influences, clinical and radiographic implications, and the development of the attachment apparatus, cementum, and periodontal ligament.

nodes.title: Development of the Attachment Apparatus
key_items: Alveolar Bone; Physiologic Migration of the Teeth
nodes.summary: This text covers periodontal anatomy and development, including variations in the buccal alveolar plate and dehiscence/fenestration; the formation of the attachment apparatus via Hertwig epithelial root sheath and epithelial diaphragm; cementum development from cementoblasts and cementoid matrix; periodontal ligament fiber organization, Sharpey fibers, and stem cells; alveolar bone formation from matrix vesicles to lamellar bone and its origin from dental follicle/neural crest; physiologic mesial migration and associated bone remodeling; and the periodontium's response to external forces, including increased function, trauma from occlusion, and disuse atrophy, with a table comparing periodontal space widths under different functional states.

nodes.title: External Forces and the Periodontium
nodes.summary: The text covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, focusing on alveolar bone development and mineralization, physiologic mesial migration of teeth, the effects of external/occlusal forces on the periodontium, and the vascularization of supporting structures. It describes how osteoblasts initiate mineralization via matrix vesicles and hydroxyapatite crystal formation, leading to woven and then lamellar bone; how alveolar bone develops from dental follicles and merges with basal bone; and how teeth migrate mesially with accompanying bone remodeling. It explains that alveolar bone and the PDL adapt to occlusal forces, with increased function causing hypertrophy-like changes and reduced function causing disuse atrophy, and that excessive force can produce trauma from occlusion. It also details the three blood supply sources to the PDL, the arrangement of PDL vessels, regional differences in blood supply, and the vascular supply to alveolar bone.

nodes.title: Vascularization of the Supporting Structures
nodes.summary: The text covers the effects of decreased occlusal function and orthodontic forces on periodontal tissues, emphasizing microvascular changes and bone remodeling. It then details the vascularization of the supporting structures, including the sources and distribution of the periodontal ligament blood supply, bone vasculature, venous drainage, and lymphatic drainage pathways. Figure captions illustrate atrophic periodontal changes and vascular supply in animal models, and references are noted as being on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text is from Chapter 3 on the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium. It details the periodontal ligament's vascular supply, venous drainage, arteriovenous anastomoses, and lymphatic drainage pathways to regional lymph nodes. It also includes the chapter's reference list, with a note that full references are available on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text consists of a long reference list for Chapter 3 on the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium, followed by the opening of Chapter 4 on aging and the periodontium. Chapter 4 discusses the importance of understanding aging effects due to increased tooth retention and aging populations, notes limitations in the evidence base, and narrows its scope to biologic and microbiologic changes. It reviews aging effects on the gingival epithelium, including structural changes, junctional epithelium migration, and gingival recession, and comments on research trends and related aging topics such as cognitive impairment and chronic inflammation.

Chapter 3 covers the anatomy, structure, and function of the normal periodontium, emphasizing its four components—gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone—as a single integrated unit whose extracellular-matrix interactions mean pathology in one component can affect maintenance/repair/regeneration of others. It describes the oral mucosa zones, clinical and microscopic gingival anatomy (attached/interdental and marginal gingiva, papillae, landmarks, gingival sulcus/probing depth; keratinization, junctions, basement membrane, permeability, host defense, sulcus development, epithelial renewal, tooth cuticles, gingival fluid, connective-tissue fibers, cells, repair, blood supply, lymphatics, innervation) and clinical-microscopic correlations (color, melanin pigmentation, size, contour, consistency, stippling, position). Tooth eruption, including active/passive eruption, crown/root relationships, four passive-eruption stages, and recession, is addressed. The periodontal ligament is detailed in terms of fibers (principal, Sharpey, six groups, remodeling), collagen, cellular elements, ground substance, cementicles, functions, shock absorption, force transmission, and width regulation. Cementum content includes types, structure, classification, junctions, thickness, permeability, hypercementosis, resorption/repair, regenerative factors, ankylosis, and oral exposure. The alveolar process section covers anatomy, bone cells/histology, socket wall, bundle bone, cancellous bone, marrow, periosteum/endosteum, interdental septum, osseous topography, fenestration/dehiscence, and remodeling. Development of the attachment apparatus (including Hertwig root sheath, cementum and PDL formation, and alveolar bone mineralization), physiologic mesial migration, effects of external/occlusal forces (increased function, trauma from occlusion, disuse atrophy), vascularization/venous and lymphatic drainage, and the chapter's references are also included.

nodes.title: 4 Aging and the Periodontium
CHAPTER 4
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses aging and the periodontium, emphasizing the growing need for periodontal care as tooth retention increases. It reviews evidence on biologic and microbiologic aging effects, highlighting limitations such as inconsistent definitions and confounding systemic diseases. Specific findings include gingival epithelial thinning and decreased keratinization, altered epithelial structure, and conflicting evidence on junctional epithelial migration. The consensus is that gingival recession results from cumulative inflammation/trauma rather than aging alone. The chapter also notes limited direct research, potential of molecular techniques, and related areas like cognitive impairment, systemic health, and osteoporosis.

nodes.title: Effects of Aging on the Periodontium Gingival Epithelium
nodes.summary: The chapter discusses aging and the periodontium, emphasizing increasing tooth retention and life expectancy and the need for periodontal care in older adults. It reviews limitations of the evidence, the restricted biologic/microbiologic scope, and associations with cognitive impairment. It describes age-related changes in gingival epithelium, connective tissue, periodontal ligament, cementum, alveolar bone, and immunosenescence, while concluding that aging alone does not clearly affect periodontal healing, disease risk, or treatment outcomes. Broader factors such as cognitive/motor decline and systemic diseases are important, and age alone should not be a barrier to good periodontal health.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses the relationship between aging and the periodontium. It highlights the growing importance of this topic due to increased tooth retention and life expectancy, and notes that older periodontitis patients often have multiple comorbidities. Age-related changes are described in periodontal tissues and the host response via immunosenescence, but evidence does not show that aging alone worsens periodontal healing or disease risk. Aging also appears to have minimal effect on treatment outcomes. Therefore, age alone should not limit periodontal health, though cognitive decline, motor decline, and systemic diseases should be considered.

nodes.title: Key Words
Age-Related Changes in Periodontal Tissues and Bacterial Plaque
nodes.summary: This page covers age-related changes in the periodontium. It begins with a nonhuman primate finding needing further research and a key fact that gingival recession is due to trauma or periodontitis, not aging. Gingival connective tissue becomes coarser and denser with more stabilized collagen. The periodontal ligament undergoes cellular and structural changes, width varies with tooth function, and homeostatic mediators such as RANKL, OPG, and interleukins are important; older cells show increased proinflammatory gene expression with possible compensatory OPG increases and reduced proliferation. Cementum thickens, especially apically and lingually, and becomes more irregular. Alveolar bone changes resemble general bone aging, but extraction socket healing and implant success are not age-related, although grafts from older donors have less osteogenic potential. Bacterial plaque changes with age may involve increased accumulation and altered subgingival flora, with pathogen shifts partly reflecting ecological factors.

nodes.title: Bacterial Plaque
nodes.summary: The text reviews aging effects on the periodontium, covering structural and cellular changes in gingival connective tissue, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone; age-related alterations in bacterial plaque and immune-inflammatory responses; and evidence on aging and periodontal disease progression. It concludes that age alone is not a true risk factor for periodontitis, with cumulative exposures, smoking, plaque, and susceptibility playing stronger roles, while some age-related changes in tissues and host responses exist.

nodes.title: Immune and Inflammatory Responses
nodes.summary: The text covers microbial findings related to probing depth and chlorhexidine use, immune and inflammatory responses in aging, and the effects of aging on periodontal disease progression. It discusses immunosenescence, cellular immune differences, CRP as an inflammatory marker, nutrition and serum folate, experimental gingivitis responses, cumulative tissue damage, risk factor analyses, and longitudinal progression. The overall conclusion is that age is not a true risk factor for periodontitis but rather a background factor; the passage ends with an incomplete sentence about age-associated decreased risk.

The section covers aging and the periodontium, including the relevance of aging to periodontal health and disease; age-related structural and cellular changes in gingival connective tissue, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone; bacterial plaque changes; immune and inflammatory responses; and evidence on aging and periodontal disease progression. Figures demonstrate gingival margin changes with continued eruption, tooth wear, recession, and overeruption. The overall conclusion is that age alone is not a true risk factor for periodontitis and should not limit periodontal health, whereas cumulative exposures, smoking, plaque, and susceptibility are stronger determinants.

nodes.title: Effects of Aging on the Progression of Periodontal Diseases
nodes.summary: This text covers aging and the periodontium, including microbial colonization and chlorhexidine effects, immunosenescence and inflammatory/immune changes, CRP as an inflammatory marker, nutrition and folate as potential periodontal risk factors, experimental gingivitis responses in older adults, the distinction between age-related attachment loss and cumulative exposures, evidence that age is not a true risk factor for periodontitis, longitudinal studies of disease progression, and the finding that aging has minimal impact on periodontal treatment response. It also notes that cognitive/motor skills and medical history matter more, and mentions a key fact, case scenario, and references on the companion website.

nodes.title: Aging and the Response to Treatment of the Periodontium
nodes.summary: The text discusses aging in relation to periodontal treatment. It notes that successful treatment depends on patient plaque control and professional debridement, and studies show no age-related differences in treatment response despite histologic changes. Poor plaque control and lack of therapy can worsen disease, especially with age. Aging affects periodontal tissues and immune responses but has negligible impact on treatment responsiveness. However, aging may increase risks such as root caries, while older patients may show better treatment compliance. The key fact emphasizes that biologic aging minimally affects treatment response, whereas cognitive/motor skills and medical history matter more. A case scenario and references are provided on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
key_items: Aging and the Response to Treatment of the Periodontium
nodes.summary: The text discusses the effects of aging on periodontal disease and treatment. It states that aging is not a true risk factor for periodontitis and does not significantly affect the transition from health or gingivitis to periodontitis. Treatment response is similar across age groups, though inadequate plaque control leads to continued attachment loss and faster progression without therapy. Aging has minimal biologic impact on treatment responsiveness, but factors such as root caries risk and patient compliance are relevant. It includes a key fact, a case scenario with questions and answers, and a comprehensive reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text provides a reference list for Chapter 4 on aging and the periodontium, then begins Chapter 5 on the classification of periodontal diseases. It outlines the chapter topics, explains classification principles based on extent, severity, progression, and localization, and highlights the dynamic nature of periodontal diagnoses with examples such as healthy reduced periodontium and gingivitis on a reduced periodontium. It also references the 1999 classification, the upcoming 2018 AAP/EFP update, and introduces plaque-induced gingival diseases.

This section covers aging and the periodontium, emphasizing the growing need for periodontal care as tooth retention and life expectancy increase and older patients often have comorbidities. It reviews limitations of the evidence and age-related structural, cellular, and immunosenescent changes in gingival epithelium, connective tissue, periodontal ligament, cementum, alveolar bone, and host response. Gingival recession is attributed to cumulative inflammation/trauma rather than aging. The section also covers plaque/microbial changes, inflammatory markers, nutrition, experimental gingivitis, and evidence that aging alone does not increase periodontitis risk or affect healing and treatment response; cumulative exposures, smoking, plaque, and susceptibility are more important. Treatment response is similar across age groups, but plaque control, cognitive/motor skills, medical history, root caries risk, and patient compliance are relevant. Figures illustrate tooth eruption, wear, recession, and overeruption. The section ends with key facts, a case scenario, references, and a transition to Chapter 5.

This section covers the normal periodontium in two main parts. The first describes the anatomy, structure, and function of the periodontium as an integrated unit of gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. It details oral mucosa zones, gingival anatomy and histology, clinical correlations, tooth eruption and passive eruption stages, periodontal ligament fibers and function, cementum types and pathology, alveolar process anatomy and remodeling, development of the attachment apparatus, mesial migration, effects of occlusal forces, and vascular and lymphatic drainage. The second part addresses aging and the periodontium, reviewing age-related structural, cellular, and immunosenescent changes, limitations of the evidence, effects on host response, plaque and inflammatory changes, nutrition, experimental gingivitis, and the conclusion that aging alone does not increase periodontitis risk or impair healing or treatment response. It emphasizes cumulative exposures, smoking, plaque, and susceptibility, and highlights clinical considerations for older patients such as comorbidities, plaque control, compliance, motor and cognitive skills, medical history, and root caries risk. The section includes figures, key facts, a case scenario, references, and a transition to the next chapter.

nodes.title: II Classification and Epidemiology of Periodontal Diseases
5 Classification of Diseases and Conditions Affecting the Periodontium
CHAPTER 5
nodes.summary: The text introduces Chapter 5 on the classification and epidemiology of periodontal diseases, explaining that classification relies on clinical manifestations, extent, severity, progression, and localization. It emphasizes that periodontal diagnoses are dynamic, as patients may shift between periodontitis, healthy but reduced periodontium, and gingivitis on a reduced periodontium. The chapter presents the 1999 International Workshop classification and the upcoming AAP/EFP 2018 update, which aims to improve diagnostic accuracy. It also covers gingival diseases, focusing on plaque-induced gingivitis, its commonality, and its distinction from periodontitis, including its occurrence on a stable, reduced periodontium.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Dental Plaque–Induced Gingival Diseases
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification and epidemiology of periodontal diseases, emphasizing that classification relies on clinical manifestations and considers extent, severity, progression, and localization. It highlights the dynamic nature of periodontal diagnoses, including transitions among periodontitis, healthy but reduced periodontium, and gingivitis on a reduced periodontium. It references the 1999 International Workshop classification, the updated AAP/EFP 2018 classification system, and the companion website. It also describes plaque-induced gingivitis as the most common gingival disease and clarifies its distinction from periodontitis, noting that it can occur with or without attachment loss, including on treated periodontitis-affected teeth.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text discusses the classification of periodontal diseases and conditions, emphasizing that it is based on clinical manifestations due to changing scientific knowledge. The classification considers extent, severity, rate of progression, and localization, serving as a universal guide for therapy. It acknowledges that diagnoses can change over time and is grounded in the latest international consensus.

nodes.title: Keywords
Classification of Periodontal Diseases and Gingivitis on Reduced Periodontium
nodes.summary: The page presents a classification of periodontal diseases and conditions, covering gingival diseases, chronic and aggressive periodontitis, periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases, necrotizing periodontal diseases, periodontal abscesses, endodontic-periodontal lesions, and developmental or acquired deformities. It provides details on chronic periodontitis extent and severity and notes that plaque-induced gingival diseases may occur with stable attachment loss. The text and Key Fact explain that inflamed gingiva on a tooth with previously treated, stable periodontitis should be diagnosed as 'gingivitis on a reduced periodontium,' requiring clinical attachment levels and radiographs for diagnosis.

nodes.title: Periodontitis as a Manifestation of Systemic Diseases Necrotizing Periodontal Diseases
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification of periodontal diseases and conditions, including the major categories from Box 5.1 (gingival diseases, chronic and aggressive periodontitis, periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases, necrotizing diseases, abscesses, endodontic-periodontal lesions, and developmental/deformity conditions) and detailed subcategories from Box 5.2 for plaque-induced and non-plaque-induced gingival diseases. It explains the concept of gingivitis on a reduced periodontium for treated patients with stable attachment loss, the extent and severity criteria for chronic periodontitis, the etiology and histology of plaque-induced gingivitis, and two clinical/radiographic examples illustrating plaque-related gingivitis and gingivitis on a reduced periodontium.

nodes.title: Gingivitis Associated With Dental Plaque Only
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification of periodontal diseases, specifically gingival diseases, distinguishing between dental plaque-induced and non-plaque-induced conditions. It details plaque-induced categories, including gingivitis associated with plaque only, systemic factors, medications, and malnutrition, and lists non-plaque-induced lesions of bacterial, viral, fungal, genetic, systemic, allergic, traumatic, and foreign-body origins. It also explains the pathogenesis of plaque-induced gingivitis, emphasizing plaque as the primary etiologic factor, the histological changes, reversibility with plaque removal, and the diagnosis of gingivitis on a reduced periodontium. Systemic and medication-related modifying factors are described, including endocrine changes, pregnancy, diabetes, blood dyscrasias such as leukemia, and drug-induced gingival overgrowth.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Modified by Systemic Factors
nodes.summary: The text discusses the importance of oral hygiene for gingival health, then covers gingival diseases modified by systemic factors and medications. Systemic factors such as hormonal changes and diabetes can worsen plaque-induced gingivitis, with pregnancy specifically increasing gingival inflammation and severity through hormonal effects on oral bacteria, including Prevotella intermedia. Leukemia and other blood dyscrasias can cause swollen, bleeding gingiva. Medications, including phenytoin, cyclosporine, and calcium channel blockers, can also cause gingival overgrowth.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Modified by Medications
nodes.summary: The text covers categories of gingival diseases and conditions affecting the periodontium, emphasizing plaque as the primary cause of gingival inflammation and the importance of oral hygiene. It describes gingival diseases modified by systemic factors such as hormonal changes, pregnancy, diabetes, and blood dyscrasias; medication-induced gingival overgrowth; malnutrition-related gingival changes; non-plaque-induced autoimmune lesions such as benign mucous membrane pemphigoid; and gingival diseases of specific bacterial origin, including gonorrhea, syphilis, and streptococcal infection.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Modified by Malnutrition
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal disease classification, focusing on medication-induced gingival enlargement, malnutrition-related gingival diseases, non-plaque-induced gingival lesions of autoimmune/idiopathic origin, and gingival diseases caused by specific bacteria, including examples and clinical features.

nodes.title: Non–Plaque-Induced Gingival Lesions
Gingival Diseases of Specific Bacterial Origin
nodes.summary: The text covers classification of gingival diseases affecting the periodontium, focusing on medication-induced gingival overgrowth, malnutrition-related gingival changes, and non–plaque-induced lesions. It also describes gingival diseases of specific bacterial, viral, and fungal origins, including their clinical features, causative agents, and treatment considerations, along with relevant clinical images and a case scenario.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases of Viral Origin
nodes.summary: The text covers clinical cases and descriptions of gingival diseases. It presents a case of benign mucous membrane pemphigoid with histologic and immunofluorescent findings, and a case of primary herpetic infection treated with acyclovir. It describes viral gingival diseases, especially herpesvirus infections, their lesion characteristics, reactivation triggers, and antiviral treatment. A clinical correlation highlights the distinctive prodromal symptoms of varicella zoster virus. It also discusses fungal gingival diseases, noting their increased occurrence in immunocompromised patients and after broad-spectrum antibiotic use, with candidiasis being the most common oral fungal infection.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases of Fungal Origin
nodes.summary: The text discusses classifications of gingival diseases affecting the periodontium, covering viral, fungal, genetic, systemic, traumatic, and foreign-body-related origins, with clinical features, examples, diagnostic considerations, and treatment notes, along with relevant clinical correlations and figure illustrations.

nodes.title: Gingival and Periodontal Conditions Affecting the Periodontium
nodes.summary: The page covers periodontal and gingival disease classification, including fungal infection with candidiasis and its HIV-associated form; gingival diseases of genetic origin such as hereditary gingival fibromatosis; gingival manifestations of systemic conditions and allergic reactions; traumatic lesions from self-inflicted, toothbrush, iatrogenic, or accidental causes; and foreign-body reactions such as amalgam tattoos.

nodes.title: Foreign-Body Reactions
key_items: Gingival Diseases of Genetic Origin; Gingival Manifestations of Systemic Conditions
nodes.summary: The text covers various periodontal conditions: fungal infections like candidiasis with its clinical presentations and diagnosis; genetic gingival diseases such as hereditary gingival fibromatosis; gingival manifestations of systemic conditions including allergic reactions; traumatic lesions from self-inflicted, toothbrush, iatrogenic, or accidental causes; foreign-body reactions like amalgam tattoos; and an overview of periodontitis, defining it as an inflammatory disease with attachment loss distinguishing it from gingivitis.

The section covers non–plaque-induced gingival lesions and their classification, including medication-induced gingival overgrowth and malnutrition-related changes. It describes gingival diseases of specific bacterial, viral, and fungal origin—notably herpesvirus infections, varicella zoster prodromal symptoms, and candidiasis including HIV-associated forms—as well as genetic causes such as hereditary gingival fibromatosis, systemic and allergic manifestations, traumatic lesions, and foreign-body reactions like amalgam tattoos. Clinical cases (benign mucous membrane pemphigoid and primary herpetic infection) and an overview of periodontitis distinguishing attachment loss from gingivitis are also included.

The section opens with an abstract and keywords for a chapter on classification of diseases and conditions affecting the periodontium. It presents the classification framework based on clinical manifestations, extent, severity, rate of progression, and localization, and lists the major categories: gingival diseases, chronic and aggressive periodontitis, periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases, necrotizing periodontal diseases, periodontal abscesses, endodontic-periodontal lesions, and developmental or acquired deformities. It explains chronic periodontitis extent and severity, distinguishes periodontitis from gingivitis by attachment loss, and describes 'gingivitis on a reduced periodontium' in treated patients with stable attachment loss, diagnosed using clinical attachment levels and radiographs. The section details plaque-induced gingivitis, emphasizing plaque as the primary cause, its histology, reversibility with plaque removal, and oral hygiene. It covers modifying factors including systemic conditions (hormonal changes, pregnancy, diabetes, blood dyscrasias such as leukemia), medications (phenytoin, cyclosporine, calcium channel blockers), and malnutrition. It also covers non-plaque-induced gingival lesions of bacterial, viral, fungal, genetic, systemic/allergic, traumatic, and foreign-body origins, with examples such as herpesvirus infections, candidiasis, hereditary gingival fibromatosis, benign mucous membrane pemphigoid, and amalgam tattoos, along with illustrative clinical/radiographic cases.

nodes.title: Periodontitis
Localized Form
nodes.summary: The text describes the rationale and outcome of the 1999 AAP classification revision: previous categories such as adult, refractory, early-onset, and prepubertal periodontitis were not supported as distinct entities, and prepubertal forms were recognized as periodontitis due to systemic disease. It also notes local-factor destruction can occur before age 35 and aggressive disease may be familial/age-independent. The resulting classification comprises chronic periodontitis (features, modifiers, localized/generalized and mild/moderate/severe criteria), aggressive periodontitis (core features, associated findings, localized/generalized criteria), and periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, with detailed hematologic and genetic examples and a 'not otherwise specified' category. Refractory periodontitis is not considered a distinct clinical entity, and continued post-therapy attachment/bone loss is poorly defined and applies to multiple disease entities.

nodes.title: Generalized Form
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification of periodontal diseases, focusing on the 1999 AAP classification of periodontitis into chronic, aggressive, and periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease. It details the clinical features, extent and severity subclassifications, localized and generalized forms, and associated systemic and genetic conditions. It also discusses measurement of clinical attachment levels, the 2015 AAP update recommending probing-depth thresholds, the upcoming 2018 AAP/EFP grouping of chronic and aggressive periodontitis into one category, and related developmental, mucogingival, and occlusal conditions.

nodes.title: Chronic Periodontitis
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses the classification of periodontal diseases and conditions, primarily using the 1999 classification with updates from the AAP 2015 proposal. It covers chronic periodontitis in detail, including its prevalence, progression, local and systemic influencing factors, extent and severity classification, clinical attachment loss measurement, and probing depth considerations. It also includes Box 5.4 categories of tooth-related factors, mucogingival deformities, and occlusal trauma, notes the AAP/EFP 2018 classification change grouping chronic and aggressive periodontitis as simply 'periodontitis', and describes aggressive periodontitis as rapid progression in healthy individuals with minimal plaque and calculus.

nodes.title: Aggressive Periodontitis
key_items: 1. Tooth anatomic factors; 4. Cervical root resorption and cemental tears
4. Cervical root resorption and cemental tears
nodes.summary: The text discusses the classification of periodontal diseases, primarily using the 1999 AAP system with updates from 2015 and 2018. It details chronic periodontitis as the most common form, including its causes, progression, extent, and severity based on clinical attachment loss and probing depths, along with diagnostic challenges. It then covers aggressive periodontitis, highlighting its rapid progression, genetic/familial association, and localized/generalized forms. Finally, it addresses periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, explaining when that diagnosis applies versus chronic periodontitis modified by systemic conditions, and notes that the 2018 classification groups chronic and aggressive periodontitis together simply as 'periodontitis.'

nodes.title: Periodontitis as a Manifestation of Systemic Disease
nodes.summary: The text covers classification of periodontal diseases, focusing on aggressive periodontitis, periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome, sarcoidosis, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. It contrasts aggressive and chronic periodontitis definitions, describes the clinical features and systemic links of these conditions, explains PLS genetics, pathogenesis, microbiology, and management, summarizes oral findings and treatment of sarcoidosis, and defines MRONJ in the context of bisphosphonate therapy. Multiple clinical cases and radiographic images illustrate the conditions.

The section defines periodontitis and explains its distinction from gingivitis through clinical attachment loss, discussing the importance of measuring attachment levels rather than relying solely on probing depths. It covers clinical signs, cyclic/episodic disease activity, and the limitations of periodontal probing. The classification of periodontitis is traced from early consensus workshops (1989, 1993) through the 1999 AAP system, which established chronic periodontitis, aggressive periodontitis, and periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, with detailed features, extent/severity criteria, and systemic/genetic associations. It also addresses the 2015 AAP update, the 2018 AAP/EFP change grouping chronic and aggressive periodontitis into a single 'periodontitis' entity with staging and grading, and includes related conditions such as tooth-related factors, mucogingival deformities, occlusal trauma, Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome, sarcoidosis, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw.

nodes.title: Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw
nodes.summary: The text covers several periodontal conditions: Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome (PLS) including its pathogenesis, microbial associations, clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and multidisciplinary treatment; sarcoidosis with its systemic and oral manifestations, histologic findings, and steroid treatment; medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) discussing bisphosphonate use, definition, incidence, risk factors, clinical presentation, management, and updated terminology; and necrotizing periodontal diseases, specifically necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG) and necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis (NUP), including clinical characteristics, predisposing factors, and distinctions between the two forms.

nodes.title: Necrotizing Periodontal Diseases
nodes.summary: This section covers classification and features of periodontal conditions: MRONJ, necrotizing periodontal diseases (NUG and NUP), necrotizing stomatitis, periodontal abscesses, and endodontic-periodontal lesions. It describes MRONJ epidemiology, diagnosis, limited treatment options, conservative management, prevention, and AAOMS terminology. It then details clinical features, risk factors, and HIV/malnutrition associations of necrotizing diseases. Periodontal abscess classification and the mechanism by which endodontic infections can cause periodontal destruction are also explained, along with the potential need for reconstructive surgery. Figures illustrate the discussed conditions.

nodes.title: Abscesses of the Periodontium
nodes.summary: The text covers necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis and necrotizing stomatitis in immunocompromised patients, including their clinical features, associated risk factors, and classification. It also describes periodontal abscesses and endodontic-periodontal lesions, focusing on disease progression, clinical presentation, and the potential need for reconstructive surgery.

nodes.title: Periodontitis Associated With Endodontic Lesions
nodes.summary: This text describes necrotizing periodontal conditions in immunocompromised/HIV patients, including NUP and necrotizing stomatitis; classifies periodontal abscesses; explains endodontic-periodontal, periodontal-endodontic, and combined lesions with treatment considerations; and discusses tooth-related factors and dental restorations that predispose individuals to plaque accumulation, inflammation, attachment loss, and bone loss.

nodes.title: Developmental or Acquired Deformities and Conditions
Localized Tooth-Related Factors That Modify or Predispose Individuals to Plaque-Induced Gingival Diseases or Periodontitis
key_items: Cervical Root Resorption and Cemental Tears
nodes.summary: This text covers periodontal-endodontic lesions, including primary endodontic lesions, periodontal-endodontic lesions, and combined lesions, emphasizing the need to control endodontic infection before periodontal treatment. It also discusses localized tooth-related factors that predispose to periodontal disease, such as anatomic factors, dental restorations, root fractures, cervical root resorption, cemental tears, mucogingival deformities around teeth and edentulous ridges, and occlusal trauma. Treatment considerations include root canal therapy, scaling and root planing, periodontal surgery, grafting, implants, decoronation, and soft-tissue correction. The text also references the updated AAP/EFP 2018 classification system.

nodes.title: Periodontal Classification: Mucogingival Deformities and Occlusal Trauma

Mucogingival Deformities and Conditions of the Edentulous Ridges

nodes.title: Occlusal Trauma
nodes.summary: This text from Chapter 5 covers classification of periodontal diseases and conditions. It discusses management of ankylosed teeth, mucogingival deformities around teeth and edentulous ridges, surgical corrective options, occlusal trauma references, and includes multiple clinical figures demonstrating treatment outcomes. It also directs readers to the companion website for the 2018 AAP/EFP classification, case scenarios, and references.

The section describes developmental or acquired deformities and conditions related to periodontal disease. It covers localized tooth-related factors that modify or predispose individuals to plaque-induced gingival diseases or periodontitis, including anatomic factors, dental restorations, root fractures, cervical root resorption, cemental tears, mucogingival deformities, and occlusal trauma. It also covers periodontal-endodontic lesions and stresses controlling endodontic infection before periodontal treatment. Management includes root canal therapy, scaling and root planing, periodontal surgery, grafting, implants, decoronation, soft-tissue correction, and surgical correction of mucogingival or edentulous ridge defects. Ankylosed teeth are managed differently in growing versus adult patients. The section references the 2018 AAP/EFP classification and companion website materials.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text is from Chapter 5 on classification of periodontal diseases and conditions. It presents clinical images related to ridge grafting and implant restoration, followed by seven case-based scenarios covering conditions such as gingivitis on a reduced periodontium, oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis in AIDS, medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, drug-induced gingival overgrowth, and pyogenic granuloma. Each case includes patient background, clinical findings, a question, answer, and explanation. The chapter ends with an extensive reference list on periodontal disease classification and related systemic and genetic conditions.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text presents a reference list from an earlier periodontal section and the beginning of Chapter 6 on periodontal disease epidemiology. It covers the definition and purpose of epidemiology, the historical bacterial/infection paradigm in periodontology, the roles of different epidemiologic study designs, the hierarchy of evidence, and the distinction between systematic reviews and expert opinion.

The section covers the classification and epidemiology of periodontal diseases and conditions. It presents classification frameworks based on clinical manifestations, extent, severity, progression, and localization, including the dynamic nature of periodontal diagnoses and updates from 1999 to the 2018 AAP/EFP system. It details plaque-induced and non-plaque-induced gingival diseases, modifying factors, and the distinction between gingivitis and periodontitis. Periodontitis is thoroughly described, including diagnostic criteria, historical classifications, chronic/aggressive forms, systemic manifestations, staging/grading, and related conditions such as tooth-related factors, mucogingival deformities, occlusal trauma, Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome, sarcoidosis, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. The section also covers necrotizing periodontal diseases, periodontal abscesses, endodontic-periodontal lesions, and developmental or acquired deformities, with management considerations. It concludes with clinical case scenarios and references, and transitions into Chapter 6 on periodontal disease epidemiology, including study designs and evidence hierarchy.

nodes.title: 6 Fundamentals in the Methods of Periodontal Disease Epidemiology
Fundamentals of Periodontal Disease Epidemiology and Study Designs
nodes.summary: This page introduces fundamentals of periodontal disease epidemiology, including the WHO definition, the role of epidemiology in studying disease distribution and causes, and the debate over whether periodontal diseases are infectious. It describes major epidemiologic study designs—observational and interventional—with examples, essential study characteristics, and the importance of evidence levels. It also contrasts systematic reviews with expert opinion reviews, emphasizing the higher objectivity and evidence ranking of systematic reviews.

nodes.title: Systematic Review versus Expert Opinion
nodes.summary: This chapter by Hujoel and Kotsakis introduces fundamental epidemiologic methods for studying periodontal diseases. It defines epidemiology, explains the need for epidemiologic evidence in testing the infectious-disease paradigm, and describes observational and interventional study designs, including case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, randomized/nonrandomized trials, and their roles in identifying and confirming causes of chronic disease. It also covers key characteristics of epidemiologic studies, limitations of animal-model evidence, the Oxford levels of evidence, the distinction between systematic and expert-opinion reviews, and basic concepts such as incidence, prevalence, and measures of association.

nodes.summary: This text covers fundamental concepts and methods in periodontal disease epidemiology. It discusses the value and limitations of systematic reviews, the role of epidemiological studies in identifying disease causes and guiding research, and evidence linking smoking and other risk factors to periodontal disease. It defines and illustrates prevalence, risk, odds, and incidence rates, including differences between incidence and prevalence. It also describes clinically recorded periodontal measures, such as probing depth, bleeding on probing, recession, mobility, furcation involvement, and the Gingival Index, along with examples of specific examination protocols like NHANES III and NIDCR measures.

nodes.title: Periodontal Measures Typically Recorded Clinically
key_items: Bleeding on Probing versus Gingival Index
nodes.summary: The text covers core epidemiologic concepts applied to periodontal disease: incidence versus prevalence, incidence rates, and risk populations. It describes clinically recorded periodontal measures, distinguishes the Gingival Index from bleeding on probing, and explains sensitivity and specificity. It discusses the challenge of correlated periodontal sites within patients and the translation of site-level data into epidemiologic measures. It also contrasts true and surrogate periodontal endpoints, provides examples, and outlines challenges in periodontal epidemiology, including inconsistent surrogate measures, changing methodologies, and evidence of declining periodontitis prevalence in the United States.

nodes.title: Fundamentals of Periodontal Disease Epidemiology: Measures, Endpoints, Challenges
key_items: Translating Periodontal Measures Into Traditional Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence
True and Surrogate Measures of the Periodontal Condition
nodes.summary: This page covers fundamental issues in periodontal disease epidemiology. It defines attachment loss as the distance from the cementoenamel junction to the bottom of the gingival sulcus measured at selected sites by Ramfjord’s indirect method, and defines sensitivity and specificity. It explains that periodontal sites within a patient are correlated—smoking suppresses bleeding, for example—so traditional epidemiologic risk and prevalence measures were difficult to apply; patient-level summaries were common, and modern methods now permit site-specific analyses. True endpoints are tangible, patient-important outcomes such as tooth loss, quality of life, and self-reported bleeding, whereas surrogate endpoints are intangible proxies such as probing depth, bleeding, and microbiologic/immunologic measures; surrogates can mislead, as with systemic antibiotics improving attachment gain but potentially increasing tooth loss. Challenges include frequent changes and diversity in surrogate measures, poor evidence that surrogates predict patient-important outcomes, lack of diagnostic codes for tooth loss, era-dependent indices such as Russell’s Periodontal Index, and limited patient-centered outcome data. Evidence cited indicates that U.S. periodontitis prevalence is dropping.

nodes.title: Challenges of Obtaining Epidemiologic Measures of Periodontal Conditions and Diseases
key_items: Translating Periodontal Measures Into Traditional Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence

nodes.summary: This text covers fundamentals of periodontal disease epidemiology, including measurement of attachment loss, sensitivity versus specificity, and difficulties in translating site-specific periodontal measures into traditional epidemiologic measures due to correlated sites within patients. It distinguishes true endpoints that matter to patients from surrogate endpoints, which can be misleading, and highlights challenges such as changing measures, lack of tooth-loss diagnostic codes, survival bias, and the diversity of surrogate endpoints. It also presents evidence of declining periodontitis prevalence in the United States and describes epidemiologic study designs, particularly randomized controlled trials and the requirements for reliable causal inference.

The abstract summarizes the chapter's focus on epidemiologic methods for periodontal disease, including study designs and measures of association. The broader content covers fundamental epidemiologic concepts: measuring disease occurrence through prevalence, risk, odds, and incidence rates; incidence versus prevalence; systematic reviews; and evidence linking smoking and risk factors to periodontal disease. It also describes clinically recorded periodontal measures, including probing depth, bleeding on probing, recession, mobility, furcation involvement, Gingival Index, attachment loss via Ramfjord's indirect method, and examples such as NHANES III and NIDCR. The text explains sensitivity and specificity, the challenge of correlated periodontal sites within patients, and translation of site-level data into epidemiologic measures. It distinguishes true patient-important endpoints from surrogate endpoints and highlights how surrogates can mislead. Challenges addressed include changing and inconsistent surrogate measures, lack of tooth-loss diagnostic codes, survival bias, era-dependent indices, and limited patient-centered data. Evidence of declining US periodontitis prevalence and epidemiologic study designs, especially randomized controlled trials and causal inference requirements, are included.

nodes.title: Epidemiologic Study Designs
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal disease epidemiology in the US using national data tables for adults and seniors across time periods, discusses methodological challenges such as surrogate outcomes and survival bias, and describes the three main epidemiologic study designs—randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case–control studies—with examples and quality considerations. It also explains concepts of disease causation, including sufficient, component, and necessary causes, using destructive periodontal disease as an example.

The Cause of Periodontal Disease for the Patient Sitting in Your Chair

It reviews suspected modifiable risk factors including tobacco smoking, nutrition, and dental plaque, and addresses uncertainty in assigning disease causation to individual patients. It also discusses periodontal diagnosis, including the distinction between conditions and diseases, diagnostic tests, and three approaches to translating clinical findings into diagnoses: normative/arbitrary, risk-based, and treatment-based reference values. Finally, it notes the evolving nature of periodontal disease diagnoses and classification systems.

It distinguishes periodontal conditions from diseases using WHO definitions and discusses diagnostic challenges. It lists available diagnostic tests and describes three approaches to translating test results into diagnoses: normative/arbitrary cutoffs, risk-based reference values, and treatment-based definitions. It also critiques the instability of periodontal disease classifications, the influence of the infection paradigm, and the need for diagnostic systems that improve patient outcomes. References are provided on a companion website.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text critiques the infection-paradigm basis of periodontal diagnosis and classification. It highlights the historical instability of periodontal diagnoses, exemplified by the rise and fall of periodontal dystrophies/periodontosis, and argues that classifications should not be based on assumed causes because evidence for infection is lacking, smoking and diabetes act independently, and multifactorial chronic diseases cannot be reliably causally named. It also suggests consensus classification systems may be irrelevant without evidence of benefit to patients, while simple diagnostic systems can be clinically useful for severity and prognosis. It refers to Chapter 5 for further discussion and includes a reference list for Chapter 6.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text provides a reference list for Chapter 6 on periodontal disease epidemiology, then introduces Chapter 7 on periodontal disease pathogenesis by Philip M. Preshaw. It defines pathogenesis as the origination and development of disease, discusses the historical evolution of understanding—from Miller's focal infection theory and resulting unnecessary dental clearances, to its questioning in the 1930s and rejection by a 1952 JAMA editorial—and explains how treatment strategies have changed accordingly. The chapter outline covers histopathology, inflammatory and immune responses, clinical signs, resolution of inflammation, and host susceptibility. A clinician's corner highlights that periodontitis results from bacteria in the biofilm stimulating an immune-inflammatory response that damages tissue, and understanding these processes is key to improving management.

This section covers the fundamentals of methods in periodontal disease epidemiology. It defines epidemiology and periodontal disease concepts, discusses whether periodontal diseases are infectious, and describes major observational and interventional study designs, evidence levels, and the superiority of systematic reviews over expert opinion. It explains measures of disease occurrence and association, causal concepts, and suspected risk factors. It also addresses clinical periodontal measurements, diagnostic approaches and classification challenges, methodological issues such as surrogate endpoints, survival bias, and correlated sites, US prevalence trends, and introduces the next chapter on periodontal disease pathogenesis.

The section covers classification and epidemiology of periodontal diseases. It describes classification systems from 1999 to the 2018 AAP/EFP framework, including clinical manifestations, severity, progression, and localization. It distinguishes plaque-induced and non-plaque-induced gingival diseases, gingivitis versus periodontitis, and details periodontitis diagnostic criteria, historical forms, systemic manifestations, staging and grading. It also addresses related conditions such as mucogingival deformities, occlusal trauma, tooth-related factors, and specific diseases, as well as necrotizing periodontal diseases, abscesses, endodontic-periodontal lesions, and deformities. It includes case scenarios and references. The section then covers epidemiological fundamentals: definitions, infectious nature, study designs, evidence hierarchy, systematic reviews, measures of occurrence and association, causality, risk factors, clinical measurements, diagnostic/classification challenges, methodological issues, US prevalence trends, and introduces the next chapter on pathogenesis.

nodes.title: III Etiology of Periodontal Disease
7 Periodontal Disease Pathogenesis
CHAPTER 7
nodes.summary: The text discusses periodontal disease pathogenesis, defining it as the step-by-step disease development process. It traces the historical evolution of understanding, from the focal infection era and its later rejection to the 1970s view of plaque as the sole cause, emphasizing that treatment strategies change with improved knowledge. It explains that periodontitis results from the host's immune-inflammatory response to subgingival biofilm bacteria, which causes the tissue damage recognized clinically, and highlights the importance of studying pathogenesis for advancing treatment.

nodes.title: Why is studying periodontal pathogenesis important?
nodes.summary: This chapter, authored by Philip M. Preshaw, covers periodontal disease pathogenesis, defining the term and explaining how the disease develops through step-by-step processes. It traces historical concepts from the focal infection theory to modern understanding, highlighting how treatment strategies have evolved based on knowledge of disease mechanisms. The text emphasizes that periodontitis arises from a complex interaction between subgingival biofilm and the host immune–inflammatory response, with tissue damage resulting from excessive and dysregulated inflammation. It also introduces key inflammatory mediators and the concept of host susceptibility, and stresses the importance of understanding pathogenesis for improving management of periodontitis.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
89.e1
CHAPTER 7 Periodontal disease Pathogenesis
Abstract
The successful management of a complex disease such as periodontitis requires detailed understanding of the pathogenic processes that result in development and progression of the condition. Although the subgingival biofilm plays a fundamental role in initiating and per- petuating periodontitis, the tissue damage that characterizes the disease results predominantly from prolonged, excessive, and dysregulated immune–inflammatory responses to the bacterial challenge. In this chapter, the role of inflammation and immunity in the development and progression of periodontitis is reviewed, and the role of specific inflammatory mediators is considered. The concept of host susceptibil- ity is introduced, and its importance for understanding disease susceptibility is addressed.
Keywords gingivitis periodontitis chronic periodontitis innate immunity adaptive immunity inflammation cytokines prostaglandins matrix metalloproteinases chemokines RANKL osteoprotegerin

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text covers the pathogenesis of periodontal disease, emphasizing that while subgingival biofilm initiates periodontitis, the main tissue destruction results from excessive and dysregulated host immune-inflammatory responses. It discusses susceptibility using the Sri Lankan tea laborer study, the limitations of the plaque-centric model, the polymicrobial nature of the disease, and the unique anatomy of the periodontium. It also describes the histopathology of healthy and inflamed gingival tissues, the dentogingival junction, and the epithelial structures, particularly the junctional epithelium.

nodes.title: Histopathology of Periodontal Disease
Clinically Healthy Gingival Tissues
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal disease pathogenesis, including the distinction between gingivitis and periodontitis, limitations of the plaque-only causation model, and evidence from Löe's Sri Lankan study showing variable host susceptibility. It explains that biofilm bacteria initiate inflammation, but the host's immune-inflammatory response determines disease progression, and periodontitis is not a classic single-pathogen infection. The unique anatomy of the periodontium, histopathology of clinically healthy gingiva, detailed structure and function of the dentogingival junction (gingival, sulcular, and junctional epithelia), junctional epithelium features, connective tissue components, protective mechanisms involving GCF and leukocytes, development of gingivitis, host response variation, and reversibility with plaque control are all described.

nodes.title: Histopathology of Gingivitis and Periodontitis
Gingival Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text describes the epithelial and connective tissue components of the dentogingival unit, focusing on the characteristics of gingival, sulcular, and junctional epithelia. It details the structure, attachment, cell turnover, and leakiness of the junctional epithelium, as well as the role of the connective tissue in maintaining integrity. It then explains the continuous low-grade inflammatory state present even in clinically healthy gingiva, the function of gingival crevicular fluid and defense cells, and the structural and innate mechanisms that prevent overt gingivitis. The text also covers how increased plaque leads to gingivitis, variability in individual host responses, and the uncertain ability to predict progression to periodontitis. Finally, it summarizes the histopathology of gingivitis and periodontitis, including inflammatory cell infiltration, collagen depletion, vascular changes, and reversibility with improved oral hygiene.

nodes.title: Junctional Epithelium
nodes.summary: The text details the structure and function of the dentogingival unit, focusing on the epithelial components (gingival, sulcular, and junctional epithelium) and connective tissue, including the junctional epithelium's unique leaky nature and its role in immune cell migration and periodontal pathogenesis. It also explains the low-grade inflammation present even in clinically healthy gingiva, the defense mechanisms that prevent overt gingivitis, and the variability of host responses. The histopathology of gingivitis and periodontitis is described using Page and Schroeder's four stages—initial, early, established, and advanced—with their characteristic cellular infiltrates, tissue changes, collagen loss, epithelial proliferation, and bone resorption, emphasizing that these are histologic descriptions based mainly on animal studies rather than clinical diagnoses.

nodes.title: Histologic Stages of Gingivitis and Periodontitis
nodes.summary: The page covers the classic histologic stages of gingival inflammation and periodontitis—initial, early, established, and advanced—as described by Page and Schroeder. It details each stage's clinical correlation, timeline, vascular changes, inflammatory infiltrate, collagen destruction, epithelial changes, and progression to periodontitis with bone resorption. It also notes that these are histologic descriptions based largely on experimental animals, are not intended for clinical diagnosis, and are illustrated in Figs. 7.2 and 7.3.

nodes.title: The Established Lesion
key_items: Initial Lesion (Corresponds With Clinically Healthy Gingival Tissues)

Established Lesion (Corresponds With Established Chronic Gingivitis)
Advanced Lesion (Marks the Transition From Gingivitis to Periodontitis)
nodes.summary: The text presents Page and Schroeder's four histologic stages of gingivitis and periodontitis—initial, early, established, and advanced—with their clinical correlates (healthy gingiva, early gingivitis, chronic gingivitis, and transition to periodontitis with attachment and bone loss). It details the histologic features of each stage, including vascular changes, GCF flow, leukocyte migration, collagen destruction, epithelial proliferation, pocket formation, and bone resorption. It emphasizes that these are histologic descriptions based largely on animal studies, not clinical diagnoses, and elaborates on the mechanisms, progression factors, reversibility with plaque control, and limitations of the classification.

nodes.title: The Advanced Lesion
nodes.summary: The text describes the histologic features of gingivitis and periodontitis, the progression from established gingivitis to advanced periodontitis, and the pathogenic mechanisms involved. It emphasizes that although microbial factors initiate disease, most tissue destruction results from the host inflammatory response. It covers the roles of LPS, lipoteichoic acid, bacterial enzymes and noxious products, and microbial invasion, detailing how these factors drive inflammation, collagen and bone loss, and the perpetuation of periodontal pockets.

The section covers the histopathology of gingivitis and periodontitis, beginning with the dentogingival unit—gingival, sulcular, and junctional epithelia and connective tissue—emphasizing the junctional epithelium's leaky structure, attachment, turnover, and role in immune-cell migration. It explains that clinically healthy gingiva exhibits continuous low-grade inflammation countered by gingival crevicular fluid, defense cells, and structural/innate barriers, and that plaque accumulation leads to gingivitis with variable host responses and uncertain progression. It details Page and Schroeder's four histologic stages (initial, early, established, and advanced), including clinical correlates, vascular/inflammatory changes, GCF flow, leukocyte migration, collagen loss, epithelial proliferation, pocket formation, and bone resorption, while noting reversibility with plaque control and the animal-based, non-clinical nature of the classification. Finally, it describes pathogenic mechanisms: microbial products initiate disease, but the host inflammatory response is responsible for most tissue destruction and perpetuation of periodontal pockets.

The section covers the pathogenesis and histopathology of periodontal disease, distinguishing gingivitis from periodontitis and critiquing the plaque-only causation model using evidence such as Löe's Sri Lankan study. It explains that biofilm bacteria initiate inflammation but the host immune-inflammatory response determines progression, and that periodontitis is not a classic single-pathogen infection. The histology of clinically healthy gingiva is described, including the dentogingival junction, junctional epithelium features, connective tissue components, and protective mechanisms involving GCF and leukocytes. Plaque accumulation leads to gingivitis with variable host responses and reversibility through plaque control. The section also details Page and Schroeder's four histological stages of gingivitis and periodontitis, covering vascular and inflammatory changes, GCF flow, leukocyte migration, collagen loss, epithelial proliferation, pocket formation, and bone resorption, while noting the classification's animal-based nature. Finally, it emphasizes that although microbial products initiate disease, the host inflammatory response causes most tissue destruction and perpetuates periodontal pockets.

It describes microbial virulence factors including LPS, lipoteichoic acid, bacterial enzymes and noxious products, gingipains, microbial invasion, fimbriae, and bacterial/eDNA. It then details host-derived inflammatory mediators—cytokines, prostaglandins, and MMPs—and their roles in tissue breakdown. A clinical correlation notes that bacterial invasion of tissues is not well-defined clinically and should not alone justify antibiotic therapy.

nodes.title: Host-Derived Inflammatory Mediators

This section covers inflammatory responses in the periodontium, explaining that subgingival biofilm triggers a self-perpetuating inflammatory cycle, while host-derived mediators—not bacteria directly—cause most tissue destruction. It describes microbial virulence factors such as LPS, lipoteichoic acid, gingipains, fimbriae, and eDNA, along with eDNA functions in biofilm biology. The section then details host inflammatory mediators: cytokines, prostaglandins, and MMPs, including MMP classification/inhibitors and the IL-1 family (IL-1β, IL-1α, IL-1Ra, IL-18). It further addresses specific mediators in periodontal disease (IL-1 family, TNF-α, IL-6, PGE2, MMPs, chemokines, anti-inflammatory cytokines), COX/NSAID considerations, neutrophil roles, and how these processes produce clinical signs such as tooth mobility and tooth loss. It also notes a rheumatoid arthritis analogy and emphasizes that bacterial invasion alone does not justify antibiotic therapy.

It describes MMPs and their role in tissue breakdown and bone remodeling, chemokines directing leukocyte migration, anti-inflammatory cytokines balancing inflammation, and the progression from gingival inflammation to clinical pocket formation and alveolar bone loss. It also details the RANK/RANKL/OPG system in osteoclast activation and the active resolution of inflammation via lipoxins, resolvins, and protectins, including experimental evidence in periodontitis models.

nodes.title: Resolution of Inflammation
key_items: Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor-κB Ligand and Osteoprotegerin

It then describes the active resolution of inflammation through lipid mediators such as lipoxins, resolvins, and protectins, including experimental evidence that resolvin E1 can reverse periodontitis-associated bone loss in an animal model. Finally, it addresses the host immune response in periodontal pathogenesis, emphasizing the integrated roles of innate and adaptive immunity, periodontal anatomy, microbial biofilm interactions, and protective factors such as saliva and commensal microbiota.

nodes.title: Immune Responses in Periodontal Pathogenesis

It then covers immune responses in periodontal pathogenesis, emphasizing that dysregulated immunity drives chronic inflammation and that innate and adaptive immunity function as an integrated, dynamic network. It describes innate immune barriers including saliva and its antimicrobial constituents, and the role of epithelial tissues as sites of bacterial interaction and invasion. It details P. gingivalis invasion mechanisms, epithelial changes in periodontitis, antimicrobial peptides, and epithelial production of MMPs and cytokines, including P. gingivalis-mediated IL-8 inhibition and possible local immune suppression.

It begins with a table of P. gingivalis virulence factors and their immune effects, then describes gingival crevicular fluid as a host-defense transport medium. It explains pathogen recognition by PRRs and MAMPs, particularly bacterial LPS interactions with TLRs, and the resulting cytokine networks that regulate innate and adaptive immunity. Finally, it details neutrophil function and migration in periodontal health and inflammation.

Adaptive immune elements such as APCs, T-cell subsets, and B cells are also addressed, along with the balance between protective immunity and tissue destruction in periodontal disease.

nodes.title: Adaptive Immunity

nodes.summary: The text covers host immune and inflammatory responses in periodontal disease pathogenesis, including innate mechanisms such as neutrophil migration, proteases, ROS, and NETs; adaptive immunity involving APCs, T-cell subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, and others), B cells, and antibodies; cytokine networks and feedback loops; and the concept of individual host susceptibility, highlighting hyperinflammatory responders and risk factors such as smoking and diabetes. It also emphasizes that immune responses determine clinical disease presentation and tissue destruction.

The section covers innate and adaptive immune responses in periodontal pathogenesis. It discusses innate defenses such as saliva, epithelial tissues, and gingival crevicular fluid; P. gingivalis invasion and virulence; PRR/TLR recognition; cytokine networks; and the central role of neutrophils including NETs, proteases, and ROS. It also addresses adaptive immunity involving APCs, T-cell subsets, B cells, and antibodies, along with the balance between protective immunity and tissue destruction. The potential protective role of resolvin RvE1 and host susceptibility factors such as smoking, diabetes, and hyperinflammatory phenotypes are highlighted as determinants of clinical disease presentation.

nodes.title: Concept of Host Susceptibility
nodes.summary: The text covers antibody responses in periodontal disease and the concept of host susceptibility. Antibodies to periodontal pathogens are produced locally by plasma cells, mainly as IgG in GCF, with fewer IgM/IgA and salivary IgA; polyclonal responses can lead to autoantibodies. Antibody profiles vary by disease type and are regulated by cytokines and Th1/IFN-γ signaling, and treatment can alter titers, but whether antibodies are protective or pathogenic is unclear. Host susceptibility determines disease progression: individuals differ in inflammatory responsiveness, with hyperresponders experiencing greater inflammation for the same bacterial challenge and hyporesponders being more resistant. There is a threshold between stable and progressive disease that varies among individuals and can shift with environmental factors. Modern models emphasize that although bacteria initiate inflammation, most tissue destruction is caused by the host response, and dysregulation of inflammatory networks is central. A biologic systems model incorporates person-level, genetic/epigenetic, biologic phenotype, and clinical phenotype factors, and the goal is to identify hyperinflammatory at-risk individuals for prevention.

nodes.title: References

It also summarizes periodontitis pathogenesis as bacterial-induced inflammation that causes tissue damage, influenced by genetic and environmental risk factors. This section covers periodontal disease pathogenesis, defining it as the step-by-step process by which periodontitis develops. It traces historical understandings from the focal infection theory to the plaque-centric model and the current view that periodontitis results from a complex interaction between subgingival biofilm bacteria and the host's immune-inflammatory response. The tissue destruction characteristic of periodontitis is caused predominantly by excessive, dysregulated inflammation rather than by bacteria directly. The section describes the histopathology of healthy and diseased gingival tissues, including the junctional epithelium, gingivitis, and periodontitis stages. It details microbial virulence factors, host inflammatory mediators such as cytokines, prostaglandins, MMPs, chemokines, and anti-inflammatory cytokines, and the RANK/RANKL/OPG system in alveolar bone loss. It also covers active resolution of inflammation by lipid mediators, innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, and the role of neutrophils. The concept of host susceptibility is introduced, emphasizing individual differences in inflammatory responsiveness and risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, and hyperinflammatory phenotypes. A biologic systems model integrates person-level, genetic/epigenetic, biologic phenotype, and clinical phenotype factors to explain disease susceptibility and presentation. Clinical signs such as pocket formation, tooth mobility, and tooth loss are linked to underlying pathogenic mechanisms, and a case scenario illustrates diagnosis and initial therapy of chronic periodontitis.
