nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Bacteria play a pivotal role in the development of periodontal diseases. Within the oral cavity, literally hundreds of different species can be found, although just few of them are linked with disease. These bacteria have developed ingenious ways to maintain themselves within the oral cavity and to interact with each other and their host. The complexity of these interactions is reflected in different etiologic models that have been proposed over the years. Knowledge of these bacteria is important for understanding the etiology and treatment of periodontal diseases. Moreover, not only bacteria are relevant. Yeasts, viruses, and protozoa are also of importance for various oral diseases. This chapter opens the micobiologic world to the reader.

This section covers the structure, composition, and microbiology of mature dental plaque biofilms. It describes plaque as a resilient biofilm that cannot be removed by rinsing, distinct from materia alba and calculus, and composed predominantly of bacteria along with archaea, yeasts, protozoa, and viruses. The biofilm architecture is heterogeneous, with fluid-filled channels, microcolonies, and a matrix containing organic and inorganic materials; mineralization of plaque leads to calculus, with differences between supragingival and subgingival calculus. The section also contrasts supragingival and subgingival plaque, discusses anaerobic bacteria in periodontal pockets, and reviews methods such as FISH, immunofluorescence, and confocal microscopy that reveal biofilm organization and uncultured bacteria. The text also addresses factors influencing supragingival plaque formation, including exponential growth kinetics, microbial community shifts observed in experimental gingivitis, and the typical topographic pattern favoring protected areas such as gingival margins, interdental spaces, and enamel surface irregularities.

It describes subgingival plaque composition, predominant bacterial species, host-cell involvement, bacterial invasion of tissues and dentinal tubules, pocket-depth variation, and site-specific roles in gingivitis, calculus/root caries, and periodontitis, as well as biofilm formation on prostheses and implants. It then outlines plaque accumulation in phases: rapid formation of a two-layer acquired pellicle; initial bacterial adhesion via transport, reversible adhesion, and strong attachment involving adhesins, receptors, and primary colonizers; and plaque maturation through coadhesion/coaggregation, secondary colonizers, and a shift toward gram-negative anaerobes. nodes.title: Surface Microroughness
nodes.summary: The text explains that plaque formation begins in shear-protected areas and is strongly influenced by surface irregularities and roughness. Rough intraoral surfaces accumulate more plaque and more pathogenic bacteria, with a threshold around Ra 0.2 μm below which smoothing has little additional benefit. Surface roughness is more important than surface free energy. Individual differences in plaque formation also exist, with heavy versus light plaque formers influenced by salivary factors and flow; however, both types take days to show visible plaque, so heavy plaque formation is not an excuse for poor oral hygiene. A cited study found early differences in plaque complexity but no discernible differences from days 3 to 14.

nodes.title: Individual Variables That Influence Plaque Formation

It highlights that plaque starts in sheltered areas, surface roughness above a threshold (Ra ≈ 0.2 μm) promotes plaque, roughness matters more than surface free energy, and heavy formers cannot justify poor hygiene. It also describes variations within the dental arch, enhanced plaque formation near inflamed gingivae, reduced nighttime growth, and that age does not affect plaque amount but older patients experience more gingival inflammation.

The section introduces the biofilm mode of bacterial living, emphasizing that in nature bacteria form multispecies, surface-associated communities at nutrient-rich interfaces, and that the oral cavity is uniquely suited because teeth provide hard, nonshedding surfaces. Biofilms are microbial cells embedded in an extracellular polymeric matrix, are up to 1000 times more resistant to antimicrobials than planktonic cells, and support complex competitive/mutualistic interactions, cell–cell signaling, DNA exchange, and heterogeneous architecture with microcolonies, water channels, and fronds. Applied to dental plaque, the section covers mature plaque biofilm structure and composition, its distinction from materia alba and calculus, supragingival versus subgingival plaque, calculus formation, anaerobic pocket microbiology, imaging methods, coaggregation, and microbial spatial relationships. Do older people form more plaque?
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal biofilm microbiology: plaque formation is not age-dependent or spontaneously removed by eating; subgingival plaque regrows rapidly after debridement due to residual bacteria and surface irregularities. Implant studies show rapid colonization and surface-roughness effects. Biofilm bacteria depend on metabolic interactions with each other and the host, communicate through quorum sensing and signals such as AI-2, and exhibit both mutualistic and competitive interactions. Biofilm bacteria are highly resistant to antimicrobials due to multiple mechanisms, and periodontal pathogens can be transmitted between people, as demonstrated by genetic fingerprinting.

It first contrasts the nonspecific plaque hypothesis, which attributes disease to total plaque accumulation, with the specific plaque hypothesis, which emphasizes particular pathogenic bacteria. It then describes the ecologic plaque hypothesis, which integrates both views by explaining that host factors, inflammation, and environmental changes cause an ecological shift or dysbiosis in plaque microbiota, favoring gram-negative anaerobes and resulting in periodontitis.

nodes.title: Ecologic Plaque Hypothesis
nodes.summary: The text describes the evolution of concepts explaining the role of dental plaque in periodontal diseases. It covers the nonspecific plaque hypothesis, which emphasizes plaque quantity and still underlies current treatment, despite being superseded. It then discusses the specific plaque hypothesis, which focuses on qualitative microbial composition and specific pathogens, including advances in bacterial identification and evidence from association studies, along with their limitations. Next, the ecologic plaque hypothesis unifies these views by emphasizing microbial homeostasis and dysbiosis driven by host and environmental factors. The keystone pathogen hypothesis and the polymicrobial synergy and dysbiosis model explain how low-abundance pathogens can disrupt the microbiota. Finally, the text addresses complicating factors in pathogen identification, including microbial complexity and the episodic nature of periodontitis progression.

nodes.title: Peri-implantitis
nodes.summary: The text covers several periodontal conditions and their microbiology. Localized aggressive periodontitis causes severe bone destruction in adolescents and requires mechanical debridement plus systemic antibiotics due to A. actinomycetemcomitans tissue invasion. Aggressive periodontitis is a severe form in younger adults dominated by P. gingivalis, P. intermedia, T. forsythia, and Treponema spp. Necrotizing periodontal diseases involve necrosis of gingival tissues, often with stress or HIV infection, and contain high levels of spirochetes and F. nucleatum. Periodontal abscesses are acute destructive lesions with specific symptoms and polymicrobial pathogens. Peri-implantitis affects osseointegrated implants with bone loss and has a varied microbiota, including periodontal pathogens and opportunistic organisms; implant failures cluster within patients, implying systemic factors. Finally, the text discusses virulence factors of periodontopathogens, emphasizing adhesive proteins, tissue-destructive factors, and immune evasion, and argues that focusing on disease-causing molecules may be more useful than targeting specific bacteria.

This section covers the microbiologic specificity of periodontal diseases, beginning with the evolution of plaque hypotheses from nonspecific plaque quantity to specific pathogens and the ecologic plaque hypothesis, and extending to the keystone pathogen hypothesis and polymicrobial synergy/dysbiosis model. It discusses complicating factors in pathogen identification, criteria for defining periodontopathogens, and host susceptibility factors including genetics, smoking, viral infections, stress, and race. It details the microbiota associated with periodontal health, gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, localized and generalized aggressive periodontitis, necrotizing diseases, periodontal abscesses, and peri-implantitis, including key bacterial pathogens, newly identified taxa, beneficial bacteria, viral associations, and microbial shifts. It also addresses diagnostic and therapeutic implications, including antibiotic use, limitations of microbial testing, and the potential value of targeting virulence mechanisms rather than individual bacteria.

Finally, it mentions molecular diagnostic advances and the potential for probiotic or microbial replacement therapy.

nodes.title: 9 Practical Molecular Biology of Host–Microbe Interactions
CHAPTER 9
nodes.summary: The text introduces a chapter on the molecular biology of host–microbe interactions in periodontal disease. It explains that periodontal destruction is primarily mediated by the host immune response to bacterial biofilms, rather than direct bacterial action. Key concepts include the roles of tolerance and vigilance in maintaining periodontal health, the diversity of the oral microbiome, the nature of MAMPs, and how MAMP–PRR signaling drives innate immune responses through cytokines and type I interferons.

151.e1
CHAPTER 9 Practical Molecular Biology of Host–Microbe Interactions
Abstract
This chapter focuses on molecular aspects of host–microbe interactions in periodontal disease. To avoid redundancy with other chapters addressing the pathophysiology of periodontitis, we emphasize the direct recognition of microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) at pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs). PRRs that predominantly recognize bacteria, including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and nucleotide- binding oligomerization domain–like receptors (NLRs), are discussed in detail, along with their associated signal transduction pathways. Complement and antimicrobial peptides are covered briefly, highlight- ing their influence on PRR signaling. Finally, immunomodulatory therapeutic interventions targeting host-microbe molecular interactions in periodontitis are examined mechanistically.
Keywords
microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) complement system crosstalk tolerance vigilance

nodes.title: Keywords

It details TLR classification, structure, signaling mechanisms (MyD88-dependent and independent, NOD amplification, MAPK/NF-κB activation), and PRR expression across innate, adaptive, and mesenchymal cells, emphasizing the innate–adaptive immune continuum. Complement and antimicrobial peptides are briefly mentioned for their influence on PRR signaling, and immunomodulatory therapies targeting these interactions are examined mechanistically. Tables catalog PRR–MAMP binding and biologic mediator induction by periodontal bacteria.

nodes.title: 10 Resolution of Inflammation
CHAPTER 10
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces inflammation resolution as an active biochemical process regulated by endogenous and therapeutic lipid mediators, especially lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins. It covers the protective role of inflammation, the controlled nature of acute inflammation, and the potential to prevent and treat chronic diseases, with applications in periodontal tissue prevention, maintenance, and regeneration. The text also reviews the historical understanding and cardinal signs of inflammation, the cellular and molecular mechanisms of innate immunity, the role of neutrophils, macrophages, cytokines, Toll-like receptors, and lipid mediators, and the dynamic classification of inflammatory mediators. An online-only section addresses systemic links to diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and pregnancy outcomes.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Inflammation has protective functions that are regulated by multiple endogenous interactions with the host cells and microbiome. Acute inflammation is temporally and spatially controlled to maintain homeostasis. Four specialized lipid mediator families activate resolu- tion signals (lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins). Understand- ing the crosstalk of resolution signals in tissue response to injury has the potential to prevent and treat chronic diseases. The therapeutic applications of inflammation resolution include prevention, mainte- nance, and regeneration of periodontal tissues. This chapter presents fundamental concepts of resolution as an active biochemical mecha- nism regulated by endogenous/therapeutic lipid mediators. Novel concepts of resolution mediators in tissue regeneration and potential therapeutic applications are also discussed.
Keywords resolution inflammation chronic diseases lipids therapeutics

CHAPTER 10 Resolution of inflammation

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text covers the chapter's abstract and introductory sections on resolution of inflammation. It emphasizes that inflammation is protective but must be actively resolved by specialized lipid mediators; failure to resolve leads to chronic diseases, including periodontal diseases. It discusses the roles of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, NF-κB signaling, and the complex regulation of mediator activity. It also details key facts on pro-resolution versus anti-inflammation, the active nature of resolution, and the biosynthesis of lipid mediators from arachidonic acid via COX and LO pathways, including prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and HETEs. The chapter highlights therapeutic implications for tissue regeneration and periodontal health.

nodes.title: Acute Inflammation Is Self-Limited
nodes.summary: The text explains inflammation as a complex, context-dependent process involving pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators under NF-κB regulation. It emphasizes that resolution of inflammation is an active, enzymatically controlled process mediated by specialized lipid mediators, not passive decay. It details the biosynthesis and actions of arachidonic acid-derived eicosanoids, then describes the major pro-resolving SPM classes—lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins—including their synthesis pathways, receptors, and anti-inflammatory/pro-resolution functions. Finally, it applies these concepts to periodontal diseases, explaining that gingivitis is reversible but unresolved inflammation due to dysbiosis leads to chronic periodontitis and tissue destruction.

nodes.title: Unresolved Chronic Inflammation in Periodontal Diseases
key_items: Therapeutic Actions of Resolution Mediators; CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
nodes.summary: The text covers the biology of resolution of inflammation, focusing on pro-resolution lipid mediators—lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins—and their biosynthesis, receptors, and functions in resolving inflammation, promoting efferocytosis, and tissue regeneration. It discusses unresolved chronic inflammation in periodontal diseases, explaining how dysbiosis, host modifiers, and resolution failure contribute to periodontitis, and highlights therapeutic actions of resolution mediators in periodontal disease models and clinical trials. The text also addresses the systemic link between periodontal and systemic diseases, detailing mechanisms connecting periodontitis with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, and concludes that resolution mediators are promising for treating inflammatory and metabolic diseases.

nodes.title: Systemic Link
nodes.summary: The text discusses the biologic mechanisms linking periodontal disease with systemic inflammatory diseases, emphasizing innate and adaptive immune activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, acute-phase proteins, and chronic inflammation. It reviews periodontal-systemic associations in type 2 diabetes (shared risk, HbA1c reduction after periodontal therapy), cardiovascular disease (atherogenesis, bacteremia, inflammation, and management recommendations), cancer (associations with total and site-specific cancers, including genetic confounding), and adverse pregnancy outcomes (pathogen routes, inflammatory mediators, and complications). It also presents a table of pro-resolution lipid mediators and their protective actions in periodontitis, diabetes, colitis, retinopathy, and bone healing. Finally, it explains resolution of inflammation as an active mediator-driven process that restores homeostasis and promotes tissue regeneration; unresolved inflammation underlies chronic diseases and can become systemic.

It includes a clinical case scenario about a 30-year-old male with gingival inflammation, with findings and case-based questions explaining that plaque-induced inflammation is the primary etiology, bone loss is not a modulator of gingivitis, and prostaglandins are not resolution mediators. The chapter also provides references and companion website materials.

nodes.summary: The text includes the extensive reference list for Chapter 10 on resolution of inflammation in a periodontology section, then introduces Chapter 11 on precision dentistry and the genetics of periodontal disease risk and treatment. It explains that most diseases arise from gene-environment interactions, with periodontitis as a complex trait where inherited DNA variation and environment contribute roughly equally. Despite many association studies, specific genetic determinants and treatment-response genes are largely unknown. The chapter discusses the enormous scale of genomic hypothesis testing, the recent feasibility of whole-genome studies, and the need for dentists to interpret genomic information for future personalized periodontal care.

The section presents resolution of inflammation as an active, mediator-driven biochemical process that restores homeostasis and promotes tissue regeneration, contrasting with passive decay and anti-inflammation. It covers the protective, self-limited nature of acute inflammation, the historical understanding and cardinal signs, and innate immune mechanisms including neutrophils, macrophages, cytokines, Toll-like receptors, and NF-κB. It details eicosanoid biosynthesis from arachidonic acid and the major pro-resolving lipid mediator families—lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins—including their synthesis, receptors, and functions such as efferocytosis. These concepts are applied to periodontal diseases, explaining reversible gingivitis versus chronic periodontitis from dysbiosis/resolution failure, and therapeutic applications of resolution mediators in tissue regeneration and clinical trials. The section also discusses systemic links of periodontitis to type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and summarizes protective actions of pro-resolution mediators in several inflammatory conditions. It includes a clinical case, references, companion materials, an online-only systemic section, and a transition to precision dentistry and the genetics of periodontal disease.

nodes.title: 11 Precision Dentistry
Chapter Outline
nodes.summary: This chapter on precision dentistry and periodontal genetics covers the inherited basis of periodontitis, the role of gene-environment interactions, and the limited progress so far in identifying specific genes and treatment-response variants. It discusses research challenges such as sample size, statistical power, and genome-wide testing, and emphasizes the potential for personalized periodontal treatment. The text includes a comprehensive eTable 11.1 of gene association studies, reviews genomic advances and their limitations, and explains genetic epidemiology concepts such as population and pedigree patterns, natural selection, genetic drift, population differences in aggressive periodontitis, and twin studies.

nodes.title: Genomic Advances in the 21st Century
Patterns in Populations and Pedigrees
nodes.summary: The text discusses the promise and current limitations of genomic medicine in dentistry, particularly periodontology. It emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary collaboration, the impact of the genomics revolution, and the importance of population and pedigree studies in genetic epidemiology. It covers natural selection and genetic drift, population differences in periodontitis, twin studies and heritability, limitations of segregation analysis for complex diseases, modern DNA-based genetic markers and technologies, types of DNA variation, and the usefulness and limitations of linkage analysis. It also references a glossary of genetic terms and a table of study techniques.

nodes.title: Searching for Answers in the DNA
nodes.summary: The text discusses genetic approaches to studying periodontitis. It covers segregation analysis and its limitations for complex diseases; DNA marker technologies and types of genetic variation; linkage analysis and why it fails for complex diseases; and detailed genetic study designs including candidate gene, case–control, twin, familial aggregation, segregation, linkage, and GWAS. It highlights the success of GWAS in finding common small-effect risk variants, the problem of missing heritability, and the potential of next-generation sequencing. It also emphasizes the need for well-matched study populations and warns against overinterpreting segregation analyses for complex diseases like periodontitis, whose genetic architecture involves multiple genes, environmental factors, and many gene functions beyond traditional host defense terms.

The section covers genomic advances in the 21st century as applied to dentistry and periodontology. It discusses the promise and limitations of genomic medicine, the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, and population and pedigree studies in genetic epidemiology. It addresses natural selection, genetic drift, population differences in periodontitis, twin studies, heritability, DNA markers, types of genetic variation, and the usefulness and limitations of linkage and segregation analyses. It also reviews genetic study designs including candidate gene, case–control, twin, familial aggregation, segregation, linkage, and GWAS. The text highlights GWAS success in finding common small-effect risk variants, the issue of missing heritability, and the potential of next-generation sequencing, while emphasizing the need for well-matched populations and caution in interpreting studies of complex diseases like periodontitis, whose genetic architecture involves multiple genes, environmental factors, and diverse gene functions.

Periodontitis in Genetic Syndromes and Other Diseases

It describes leukocyte adhesion deficiency as an example, explains that periodontitis susceptibility involves broader biologic processes, and lists rare genetic syndromes associated with periodontitis, including specific gene mutations such as cathepsin C. It also presents a table of genetic disorders, their mutated genes, and functions, and highlights the clinical importance of recognizing these conditions, referring patients to genetic specialists, and using databases like OMIM. Finally, it introduces the topic of inherited genetic variation in nonsyndromic aggressive and chronic periodontitis.

nodes.title: Nonsyndromic Aggressive and Chronic Periodontitis
Periodontitis in Genetic Syndromes and Other Diseases

It covers rare syndromic forms, including their genetic and environmental causes, affected genes and functions, clinical manifestations such as severe periodontitis and early tooth loss, and the need for genetic counseling and use of OMIM. It then addresses nonsyndromic aggressive and chronic periodontitis, reviewing heritability evidence, limitations of earlier genetic approaches, and the role of candidate-gene association studies. The discussion highlights widespread problems with small sample sizes and inconsistent phenotyping, and illustrates with power calculations and literature search data why large, well-designed studies—even with negative results—are needed to identify genuine genetic risk variants.

nodes.title: Oral Manifestations of Chédiak–Higashi Syndrome
nodes.summary: The text discusses the genetic epidemiology and association-study limitations of periodontitis, emphasizing that most published candidate-gene findings are underpowered, inadequately adjusted for multiple testing, and inconsistent. It contrasts this with successful GWAS approaches requiring large sample sizes, presents power calculations and a literature review showing most studies use too few cases, and notes publication bias. It also covers nonsyndromic classification, heritability, and specific gene functions, along with clinical correlations for Chédiak–Higashi syndrome and Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, and summarizes the current gene list from curated tables, including the only GWAS-identified gene GLT6D1.

nodes.title: Ehlers–Danlos Syndromes
nodes.summary: The text reviews genetic association studies in periodontitis, highlighting that most studies are underpowered due to small sample sizes and likely affected by publication bias. It summarizes findings from 298 publications and Table 11.3, covering many candidate genes and their proposed functions, along with evidence for aggressive and chronic periodontitis. It notes inconsistent results and possible explanations, including heterogeneity, multiple testing, and phenotype definition. Clinical correlations describe Ehlers–Danlos syndrome and Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome in relation to periodontal disease. GWAS findings are discussed, including the GLT6D1 association in aggressive periodontitis, the lack of replication, and the absence of robust associations in chronic periodontitis GWAS and exome sequencing studies. Finally, the text emphasizes the need for better disease classification and larger, family-based studies to understand the genetic architecture of periodontitis.

The section covers genetic susceptibility to periodontitis, including rare syndromic forms and the focus on nonsyndromic aggressive and chronic periodontitis. It reviews heritability evidence, candidate-gene association studies, and their limitations, emphasizing small sample sizes, inconsistent phenotyping, multiple-testing issues, heterogeneity, and publication bias. Power calculations and literature data show why large, well-designed studies are needed. It discusses GWAS findings—particularly GLT6D1 in aggressive periodontitis and the lack of robust findings in chronic periodontitis—along with clinical correlations for Chédiak–Higashi syndrome, Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, and Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome. It also summarizes curated gene lists and concludes that better classification and larger, family-based studies are necessary.

nodes.title: Challenges and Opportunities for the Future
nodes.summary: The text reviews the genetics of periodontitis, emphasizing inconsistent candidate gene findings and potential explanations, describes Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome and implant treatment, and details GWAS results including GLT6D1 and the lack of replicated associations. It covers the complex polygenic architecture that likely underlies chronic periodontitis, challenges in disease classification, and the potential of quantitative traits and family studies. It also discusses missing heritability, future genomic and bioinformatics approaches, and precision dentistry, including genotype-guided treatment and the limited evidence for IL-1 genetic testing.

The section opens with genetic association studies for disease risk, using periodontitis as an example: case-control comparisons of genotype frequencies identify risk-associated and protective genotypes, and careful matching (race/ethnicity, smoking, age, gender) is needed to prevent population stratification. It also covers GWAS methodology and its successes in complex diseases, common small-effect risk variants and attributable risk, discovery of unsuspected genes and non-genic regions, missing heritability, the better predictive value of nongenetic risk factors, and next-generation sequencing for rare variants. The subsection on genetic syndromes describes periodontitis in inherited conditions such as leukocyte adhesion deficiency, rare syndromes with gene mutations (including cathepsin C), a table of genetic disorders/mutated genes/functions, clinical recognition/referral to genetic specialists and OMIM, and notes that 'host response' terminology captures only part of relevant gene functions. The nonsyndromic subsection reviews heritability, candidate-gene studies and their limitations (small samples, inconsistent phenotyping, multiple testing, heterogeneity, publication bias), the need for large well-designed studies, GWAS findings (GLT6D1 in aggressive periodontitis, no robust chronic periodontitis findings), clinical correlations for Chédiak–Higashi, Ehlers–Danlos, and Papillon–Lefèvre syndromes, curated gene lists, and the need for better classification and family-based studies. The final subsection discusses inconsistent candidate findings, complex polygenic architecture, classification challenges, quantitative traits/family studies, missing heritability, future genomic/bioinformatics approaches, precision dentistry/genotype-guided treatment, limited evidence for IL-1 genetic testing, and Papillon-Lefèvre implant treatment.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Management of risk factors for periodontitis is now recognized as a fundamentally important component of periodontal care. Smoking is a major risk factor, with research studies confirming increased prevalence and severity of periodontitis in people who smoke, as well as reduced treatment outcomes in those who continue to smoke. Dental professionals have a vital role to play in informing and educat- ing patients about the harmful effects of smoking on oral and general health, and smoking cessation support should be seen as an integral component of periodontal therapy. This chapter reviews the evidence that confirms the negative consequences of smoking on periodontal health and provides practical advice on the role that dental clinicians can play in helping patients to quit smoking.
Keywords smoking smoking cessation nicotine periodontitis brief intervention nicotine replacement therapy cigarettes e-cigarettes

nodes.title: Effects of Smoking Cessation on Periodontal Treatment Outcomes
nodes.summary: The text discusses how tobacco smoking adversely affects periodontal and implant treatment outcomes. Smokers show less attachment gain and pocket reduction after surgical, regenerative, grafting, flap, and plastic surgery procedures, and have approximately double the risk of implant failure, along with higher risks of periimplantitis and bone loss. These negative effects persist despite regular maintenance therapy, with smokers experiencing deeper pockets, less attachment gain, and significantly higher tooth loss. Smoking cessation studies demonstrate that former smokers and quitters have better periodontal status and treatment responses than continuing smokers, including improved clinical attachment, greater probing depth reductions, and beneficial shifts in subgingival microbes. The text concludes that smoking is a major risk factor for periodontitis and that smoking cessation should be an integral and priority component of periodontal therapy in smokers. It also notes that a case scenario and references are available on the companion website.

Iatrogenic Factors
key_items: Materia Alba, Food Debris, and Dental Stains
nodes.summary: The text discusses the role of dental calculus and other local predisposing factors in periodontal disease. Calculus itself does not directly cause inflammation but acts as a nidus for plaque retention; subgingival calculus forms as a result of pocket formation and mineralized plaque, and its presence predicts attachment loss. Removal of plaque and calculus is essential to therapy. Materia alba and food debris are distinguished from plaque and are less important in gingivitis, while dental stains are mainly aesthetic. Iatrogenic factors such as defective restorations, endodontic complications, and malpositioned implants can harm periodontal tissues. Restoration margins, especially overhanging or subgingival margins, significantly affect periodontal health by promoting plaque retention, microbial shifts, inflammation, and bone loss; even well-fitted subgingival margins are detrimental, and subgingival roughness and marginal gaps further exacerbate plaque accumulation.

The section also includes management recommendations, a case-based discussion, a comprehensive reference list, and a transition to Chapter 14 on systemic influences and endocrine disorders such as diabetes mellitus.

This section on the etiology of periodontal disease covers seven chapters. It explains the pathogenesis of periodontitis as a complex interaction between subgingival biofilm bacteria and the host immune-inflammatory response, emphasizing dysregulated inflammation as the main cause of tissue destruction. It describes biofilm and periodontal microbiology, including plaque formation, microbial virulence, and disease-associated microbiota. It details molecular host-microbe interactions, including TLR/NLR signaling and antimicrobial mediators. It presents resolution of inflammation as an active process involving specialized pro-resolving mediators and their relevance to periodontal disease and systemic health. It reviews precision dentistry and the genetics of periodontitis, including GWAS findings and the limited clinical utility of genetic testing. It establishes smoking as a major risk factor and discusses mechanisms and cessation strategies. Finally, it covers dental calculus and other local predisposing factors that retain plaque and contribute to periodontal disease, along with their clinical management.

nodes.title: IV Relationship between Periodontal Disease and Systemic Heath
14 Influence of Systemic Conditions
CHAPTER 14
nodes.summary: The text introduces the relationship between systemic conditions and periodontal disease, emphasizing that bacteria are necessary but not sufficient for periodontitis, and that host immune response and systemic diseases can influence disease severity and progression. Periodontal infections may also adversely affect systemic health. The chapter then begins discussing endocrine disorders and hormonal changes, focusing on diabetes mellitus: its pathophysiology, complications, US prevalence, and type 1 diabetes characteristics.

nodes.title: Endocrine Disorders and Hormonal Changes
nodes.summary: Chapter 14 reviews how systemic conditions influence periodontal disease, covering endocrine and hormonal changes, hematologic and immune disorders, genetic disorders, stress and psychosomatic conditions, nutritional influences, medications, other systemic conditions, and conclusions, with additional content online. It emphasizes that while periodontitis has a bacterial etiology, host immune response and systemic conditions are major determinants of disease severity; systemic conditions do not cause periodontitis but predispose, accelerate, or increase its progression, and periodontal infections can adversely affect systemic health. Diabetes mellitus is discussed in detail, including its metabolic effects, complications, prevalence, and type 1 versus type 2 forms. The abstract and keywords highlight host susceptibility and key terms such as diabetes mellitus, leukemia, immune compromise, hormonal changes, nutritional influences, medications, and psychosocial stress.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: This text summarizes the introduction to a chapter on how systemic conditions influence periodontitis. It states that while bacteria in biofilm cause periodontitis, host susceptibility varies, and systemic diseases or conditions—such as poorly controlled diabetes, immune compromise, and psychosocial stress—can worsen disease by impairing host defenses. The chapter reviews multiple systemic influences including endocrine, hematologic, immune, genetic, stress-related, nutritional, and medication-related factors. Importantly, these conditions do not directly cause periodontitis but predispose, accelerate, or increase its progression.

nodes.title: Keywords
Oral Manifestations
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification and features of type 1, type 2, and secondary diabetes mellitus, including gestational diabetes, and highlights diabetes as a major metabolic disease with systemic complications. It describes oral manifestations associated with diabetes, especially in poorly controlled cases, and extensively discusses the relationship between diabetes and periodontal disease, including prevalence, severity, risk factors, clinical features, and effects on healing. It also reviews bacterial pathogens in periodontal pockets of diabetic patients and notes that the exact microbial role remains unproven.

nodes.title: Bacterial Pathogens
nodes.summary: The text discusses how diabetes influences the periodontium, illustrated by clinical cases showing gingival inflammation, abscesses, bone loss, and occlusal problems. It presents epidemiological evidence from Pima Indians linking type 2 diabetes to destructive periodontitis, increased edentulousness, and a higher periodontitis risk. It also covers proposed mechanisms: altered subgingival bacteria due to elevated glucose levels, impaired PMN/monocyte/macrophage function, and altered collagen metabolism with AGE/RAGE-related damage, all contributing to increased susceptibility to periodontal destruction.

nodes.title: Polymorphonuclear Leukocyte Function
nodes.summary: The text describes a clinical case of a 60-year-old type 2 diabetes patient with periodontal findings, including missing teeth, supereruption, inflammation, abscess, and bone loss. It then explains systemic mechanisms linking diabetes to periodontal disease: impaired polymorphonuclear leukocyte function in poorly controlled diabetes weakens host defense; altered collagen metabolism due to chronic hyperglycemia leads to AGE accumulation, collagen cross-linking, and reduced tissue repair; and poor glycemic control increases susceptibility to infection and destructive periodontal disease.

nodes.title: Altered Collagen Metabolism
nodes.summary: The text covers how systemic conditions influence periodontal disease, focusing on diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and female sex hormones. For diabetes, it describes impaired PMN function, altered collagen metabolism, and AGE/RAGE accumulation as mechanisms increasing susceptibility to destructive periodontal disease, supported by clinical cases of type 2 and type 1 diabetes with abscesses and bone loss. It then defines metabolic syndrome and reviews evidence linking obesity, systemic inflammation, and periodontitis, while noting the need for more research. Finally, it summarizes gingival and oral changes associated with female hormonal fluctuations during puberty, pregnancy, and menopause.

nodes.title: Metabolic Syndrome
nodes.summary: The text covers a clinical case of periodontal abscess in a diabetic patient, the role of chronic hyperglycemia and AGEs/RAGEs in periodontal disease, the relationship between obesity/metabolic syndrome and periodontitis including proposed mechanisms and evidence, and the effects of female sex hormone changes on gingival and oral tissues during puberty, pregnancy, and menopause.

nodes.title: Female Sex Hormones
nodes.summary: The text covers systemic conditions influencing periodontal health. It begins with a clinical case of periodontal abscess in a diabetic patient and explains how chronic hyperglycemia and AGEs/RAGEs affect collagen and periodontal disease. It then discusses metabolic syndrome and obesity as risk indicators for periodontitis, including proposed inflammatory mechanisms. A major section addresses female sex hormone effects on the gingiva during puberty, menstruation, pregnancy, hormonal contraceptive use, and menopause, detailing clinical features and mechanisms. Finally, it describes hyperparathyroidism and its oral manifestations, including bone changes and loss of lamina dura.

nodes.title: Hyperparathyroidism
key_items: 212.e2 PART 2 BI ologIC BASIS of PERI oDonTology; Hormonal Contraceptives
212.e2 PART 2 BI ologIC BASIS of PERI oDonTology
nodes.summary: The text covers the effects of systemic conditions on the periodontium. It details pregnancy-related gingival changes, including inflammation, bleeding, edema, tumors, hormonal influences, and microbial shifts; hormonal contraceptive effects on gingival inflammation and periodontal destruction; menopausal gingivostomatitis with its oral signs and symptoms; hyperparathyroidism and its oral manifestations, including brown tumors and lamina dura loss; and hematologic and immune deficiencies, emphasizing bleeding signs, diagnostic workup, and the role of leukocyte disorders such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis in severe periodontal destruction.

The section introduces the concept that systemic diseases and conditions do not cause periodontitis but can predispose, accelerate, or worsen its progression. It reviews how endocrine disorders such as diabetes mellitus, hormonal changes, hematologic disorders, immune deficiencies, genetic disorders, stress, psychosomatic disorders, nutritional deficiencies, and certain medications influence the periodontium. Specific content includes diabetes and its oral manifestations, bacterial pathogens, impaired polymorphonuclear leukocyte function, altered collagen metabolism, AGE/RAGE mechanisms, metabolic syndrome and obesity, female sex hormone effects across puberty, pregnancy, contraception, and menopause, hyperparathyroidism with its oral bone changes, and hematologic/immune deficiencies such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis that contribute to severe periodontal destruction.

nodes.title: Hematologic Disorders and Immune Deficiencies
Leukocyte (Neutrophil) Disorders
nodes.summary: The text discusses how hematologic disorders and immune deficiencies affect the periodontium. It emphasizes the roles of blood cells, diagnostic considerations for bleeding disorders, oral signs such as petechiae and ecchymosis, and primary or secondary immunodeficiencies. It details leukocyte disorders, including neutropenia and agranulocytosis, their severity, causes, oral manifestations, and association with aggressive periodontitis. It also covers leukemia classification, pathophysiology, and periodontal manifestations, including leukemic infiltration, bleeding, ulcerations, and infections.

nodes.title: Leukemia
nodes.summary: The text covers systemic conditions influencing periodontal health, focusing on blood dyscrasias and related disorders. It describes agranulocytosis and cyclic neutropenia, including their oral manifestations and diagnosis. It extensively discusses leukemia: its pathogenesis, classification, and periodontal/oral manifestations such as leukemic infiltration and gingival enlargement, bleeding, ulceration, and infections. It also addresses genetic disorders that predispose to periodontitis through neutrophil defects, the role of psychosocial stress and coping in periodontal disease, and the oral/periodontal effects of anemia and thrombocytopenia.

nodes.title: Anemia
nodes.summary: The text describes anemia and thrombocytopenia. It defines anemia, lists its causes and morphological classifications, and details the oral and systemic manifestations of pernicious anemia, iron deficiency anemia, sickle cell anemia, and aplastic anemia. It then defines thrombocytopenia and purpura, explains possible causes of thrombocytopenic purpura, and outlines its clinical features, oral manifestations, and the improvement of gingival disease after removal of local irritants.

nodes.title: Thrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: The text discusses systemic conditions affecting the oral cavity, focusing on anemias (pernicious, iron deficiency, sickle cell, aplastic) and their oral manifestations, thrombocytopenia and thrombocytopenic purpura with gingival/oral bleeding changes, antibody deficiency disorders (agammaglobulinemia/CVID) with predisposition to aggressive periodontitis, and rare immunodeficiencies—Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, lazy leukocyte syndrome, leukocyte adhesion deficiency—that cause severe periodontal disease, along with Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome's skin and periodontal features and tooth loss.

nodes.title: Periodontal Manifestations of Immunodeficiency and Genetic Syndromes
nodes.summary: The text describes several immune and genetic disorders associated with periodontal disease. It covers antibody deficiency disorders, including congenital X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia and acquired common variable immunodeficiency, both marked by recurrent bacterial infections and aggressive periodontitis. It also covers Chédiak–Higashi syndrome, a rare organelle disorder causing abnormal lysosomes, albinism, bleeding, and recurrent infections; lazy leukocyte syndrome, characterized by neutropenia, defective chemotaxis, and severe periodontal destruction; leukocyte adhesion deficiency, caused by CD18 integrin failure leading to impaired leukocyte migration and severe early-onset periodontal disease; and Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome, an autosomal-recessive condition with hyperkeratotic skin lesions, severe periodontitis, early tooth loss, and characteristic microscopic and microbial findings.

nodes.title: Papillon–Lefèvre Syndrome
key_items: Antibody Deficiency Disorders; Chédiak–Higashi Syndrome; Lazy Leukocyte Syndrome
nodes.summary: The text describes systemic and immunodeficiency conditions that predispose patients to severe periodontal disease. It covers antibody deficiency disorders (congenital X-linked agammaglobulinemia and acquired common variable immunodeficiency), Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, lazy leukocyte syndrome, leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome, and Down syndrome. For each condition, it details the underlying immune defect, genetic/clinical features, systemic manifestations, oral and periodontal findings, and mechanisms such as B-cell deficiency, neutrophil dysfunction, defective leukocyte adhesion, or impaired chemotaxis, emphasizing aggressive periodontitis and early tooth loss.

nodes.title: Down Syndrome
nodes.summary: The text covers clinical images and descriptions of Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome and Down syndrome periodontitis, including neutrophil-related pathogenesis for Papillon-Lefèvre and immune defects in Down syndrome. It discusses stress-induced immunosuppression and its mechanisms (cortisol and neurotransmitters) affecting periodontal destruction, the impact of stress and depression on periodontal therapy outcomes and wound healing, self-inflicted/psychosomatic oral injuries, and nutritional influences, concluding that nutritional deficiencies alone do not cause gingivitis or periodontitis.

nodes.title: Stress, psychiatry, and nutrition in periodontal health
key_items: Influence of Stress on Periodontal Therapy Outcomes
nodes.summary: The page covers how stress influences periodontal health through behavioral and immune pathways, including cortisol and neurotransmitter effects, and notes that periodontal pathogens are still required for disease. It discusses evidence that depression and stress impair periodontal therapy outcomes and wound healing, and that personality and coping style affect treatment response. It also addresses psychiatric/self-inflicted oral injuries and concludes that nutritional deficiencies alone do not cause gingivitis or periodontitis.

This section covers hematologic and immunodeficiency disorders that affect periodontal health, including leukocyte disorders (neutropenia, agranulocytosis, cyclic neutropenia), leukemia, anemias (pernicious, iron deficiency, sickle cell, aplastic), and thrombocytopenia/thrombocytopenic purpura, detailing their systemic and oral manifestations. It then describes immunodeficiencies and genetic syndromes predisposing to severe periodontitis: antibody deficiencies (Bruton agammaglobulinemia, CVID), Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, lazy leukocyte syndrome, leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome, and Down syndrome, emphasizing underlying immune defects and aggressive periodontal disease. Finally, it addresses the roles of stress, depression, coping style, and nutrition in periodontal disease, noting that stress can impair immunity and treatment outcomes, while nutritional deficiencies alone do not cause gingivitis or periodontitis.

nodes.title: Nutritional Influences
Stress, Psychiatric, and Nutritional Influences on Periodontal Health
key_items: Influence of Stress on Periodontal Therapy Outcomes
nodes.summary: The page covers how stress, psychiatric factors, self-inflicted injury, and nutrition relate to periodontal health. It explains behavioral and immune mechanisms of stress-induced immunosuppression, including cortisol and neurotransmitter effects, while emphasizing that periodontal pathogens are essential for disease. It also discusses evidence that depression and stress worsen periodontal therapy outcomes and wound healing, personality and coping factors in treatment response, self-injurious oral habits, and the limited role of nutritional deficiencies in causing gingivitis or periodontitis.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Influence of Self-Inflicted Injury
nodes.summary: The text covers how stress influences periodontal health through behavioral changes and immunosuppression involving cortisol and neurotransmitters, with periodontal pathogens remaining essential. It reviews evidence that stress, depression, personality, and coping skills affect periodontal therapy outcomes and wound healing. It also describes psychiatric/self-inflicted oral injuries, nutritional influences on periodontal disease and inflammation, and medication effects on periodontal tissues, focusing on bisphosphonates, including their structure, mechanisms, clinical uses, history, and association with osteonecrosis of the jaw.

nodes.title: Medications
nodes.summary: The text discusses how nutrition and certain medications influence periodontal health. Nutritional deficiencies can impair host defense and modulate inflammation; antioxidant-rich diets are beneficial, while refined carbohydrates are detrimental. Medications such as bisphosphonates and corticosteroids may adversely affect periodontal tissues, with bisphosphonates detailed in terms of their use, chemical structure, mechanisms of osteoclast inhibition, and link to osteonecrosis of the jaw. Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies are covered: vitamin A deficiency causes epithelial and gingival changes, vitamin D deficiency affects alveolar bone and mineralization, and vitamin E deficiency has limited oral effects. Water-soluble vitamin deficiencies, particularly B-complex deficiencies, are described with their oral manifestations: thiamin causes beriberi, riboflavin causes ariboflavinosis, niacin causes pellagra, and folic acid deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and periodontal necrosis without inflammation.

nodes.title: Fat-Soluble Vitamin Deficiency
key_items: Vitamin A Deficiency; Vitamin D Deficiency; Vitamin E Deficiency
nodes.summary: The text covers deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and E and water-soluble B-complex vitamins. Vitamin A deficiency causes epithelial degeneration and skin/mucosal/ocular effects, with no proven human periodontal link but animal evidence of gingival changes and impaired healing. Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets/osteomalacia and alveolar bone abnormalities in animals, with radiographic changes resembling hyperparathyroidism. Vitamin E deficiency is antioxidant-related with no known oral disease association, though it may help gingival wound healing in rats. B-complex deficiency, usually multiple, produces oral signs such as gingivitis, glossitis, glossodynia, angular cheilitis, and mucosal inflammation. Specific deficiencies include thiamin (beriberi), riboflavin (ariboflavinosis), niacin (pellagra), and folic acid, each with distinct systemic and oral manifestations.

nodes.title: Water-Soluble Vitamin Deficiency
key_items: Vitamin A Deficiency; Vitamin D Deficiency; Vitamin E Deficiency
Possible Etiologic Factors; Epidemiologic Studies; Gingivitis
220.e2 PART 2 BI ologIC BASIS of PERI oDonTology
nodes.summary: The text covers deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and E and water-soluble vitamins B and C, plus protein deficiency, focusing on their oral and periodontal effects. Vitamin A deficiency affects epithelial integrity and has animal-based periodontal changes but no proven human link. Vitamin D deficiency affects calcium-phosphorus balance causing rickets/osteomalacia and alveolar bone changes in animals. Vitamin E deficiency has antioxidant effects but no established oral disease relationship. B-complex deficiencies cause oral mucosal changes, glossitis, angular cheilitis, and gingivitis modified by plaque; individual B vitamins (thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, folic acid) have specific manifestations. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gingival bleeding and impaired healing, but does not cause gingivitis or periodontitis without plaque; epidemiologic studies show no causal relationship, though deficiency can aggravate plaque-induced disease. Protein deficiency causes systemic and periodontal tissue degeneration, osteoporosis from reduced bone formation, and increased vulnerability to bacterial plaque.

nodes.title: Protein Deficiency
nodes.summary: The text covers vitamin C deficiency, protein deficiency, bisphosphonates and BRONJ, and corticosteroids in relation to periodontal disease. Vitamin C deficiency shows weak associations with periodontal disease in smokers and mainly worsens preexisting disease; without plaque it causes minimal gingival changes. Protein deficiency causes hypoproteinemia, systemic changes, periodontal tissue degeneration, and alveolar bone loss by impaired bone formation, increasing vulnerability to plaque and trauma. The bisphosphonate section includes a medication table, mevalonate pathway mechanism, effects on keratinocytes and bone, pharmacology, BRONJ definition/staging/clinical features/incidence/risk factors, and clinical trials on bisphosphonates for periodontal bone loss. Corticosteroids generally do not increase gingival inflammation, and immunosuppressed renal transplant patients may have less inflammation than controls. Figures illustrate the mevalonate pathway and clinical BRONJ cases.

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: The text covers bisphosphonate-induced osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ), including clinical photographs of maxillary and mandibular bone exposure, risk factors, precipitating events, and findings from a retrospective study on IV bisphosphonate patients. It also explains the mevalonate-pathway mechanism of bisphosphonates and reviews evidence on bisphosphonates for periodontal bone loss, including animal studies and clinical trials with etidronate and alendronate. The text discusses corticosteroids: their systemic effects on periodontal disease, findings in renal transplant immunosuppressed patients, animal evidence of adverse bone/periodontal effects, and stress-related cortisol responses. It then covers osteoporosis: definition, prevalence, BMD/T-score criteria, fracture consequences, and the complex, conflicting research on osteoporosis and periodontitis, including tooth-loss studies, cross-sectional studies, and a longitudinal study linking estrogen deficiency and osteopenia to alveolar bone loss. The conclusion emphasizes that systemic conditions do not cause periodontitis but can predispose or accelerate it, and notes online materials, a case scenario, and references on the companion website.

This section covers nutritional, stress-related, psychiatric, and medication influences on periodontal health. It explains how stress and psychiatric factors cause immunosuppression and affect periodontal therapy outcomes and wound healing, while emphasizing that periodontal pathogens remain essential. It reviews self-inflicted oral injuries, dietary effects on inflammation and host defense, and the limited role of nutritional deficiencies in causing periodontal disease. Detailed attention is given to fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and E; water-soluble vitamins B and C; and protein deficiency and their oral and periodontal manifestations. Medication effects are discussed, especially bisphosphonates and their association with osteonecrosis of the jaw, as well as corticosteroids. Osteoporosis and its complex relationship with periodontitis are also addressed. The section concludes that systemic conditions can predispose to or accelerate periodontitis but do not cause it.

nodes.title: Other Systemic Conditions
Osteoporosis
nodes.summary: The text covers systemic conditions relevant to dentistry: osteoporosis and its diagnosis via BMD/T-scores, epidemiology, fracture risks, and the controversial relationship with periodontitis including supporting and conflicting studies; congenital heart disease, its cyanotic features, oral manifestations, and endocarditis risk; tetralogy of Fallot and Eisenmenger syndrome with their specific cardiac defects and oral/periodontal findings; and hypophosphatasia, a rare skeletal disease causing premature primary tooth loss.

nodes.title: Congenital Heart Disease
nodes.summary: The text discusses systemic conditions relevant to periodontology. It first covers estrogen deficiency and postmenopausal osteoporosis as potential contributors to periodontitis progression, with hormone replacement therapy associated with improved oral health and a need for more longitudinal studies. It then describes congenital heart disease, including prevalence, cyanosis, chronic hypoxia, polycythemia, endocarditis risk, and oral/dental abnormalities. Tetralogy of Fallot is detailed as a four-defect cyanotic condition with specific clinical and oral manifestations that may improve after corrective surgery. Eisenmenger syndrome is explained as a complication of large ventricular septal defects leading to pulmonary vascular changes, shunt reversal, cyanosis, and reported periodontitis. Finally, hypophosphatasia is summarized as a rare skeletal disease with premature primary tooth loss. The text also includes figure captions showing clubbing in tetralogy of Fallot and oral inflammation/periodontal destruction in the same patient.

nodes.title: Hypophosphatasia
key_items: 224.e2 PART 2 BI ologIC BASIS of PERI oDonTology
nodes.summary: The text covers systemic conditions affecting the periodontium and oral cavity. It discusses the potential role of estrogen deficiency in periodontitis progression in osteopenic/osteoporotic women and the possible benefits of hormone replacement therapy. It then describes congenital heart disease, including its general features and oral manifestations, with specific sections on tetralogy of Fallot and Eisenmenger syndrome, emphasizing cyanosis, periodontal changes, and the likely role of poor oral hygiene in dental disease. Hypophosphatasia is covered as a rare skeletal disease causing premature primary tooth loss and reduced cementum, resembling aggressive periodontitis in adolescents. Finally, metal intoxications are reviewed: bismuth, lead, mercury, and other chemicals, detailing their systemic effects and oral signs such as gingival pigmentation, ulceration, salivation, and alveolar bone destruction.

nodes.title: Metal Intoxication
key_items: Bismuth Intoxication; Lead Intoxication; Mercury Intoxication
Bismuth Intoxication; Lead Intoxication; Mercury Intoxication
nodes.summary: The text describes oral manifestations of hypophosphatasia, including tooth loss and reduced cementum formation; covers metal intoxication from bismuth, lead, mercury, and other chemicals, detailing their systemic symptoms and oral signs such as gingival pigmentation, ulceration, salivation, and bone destruction; presents a clinical case of Dilantin-induced gingival overgrowth with a case-based question and answer; and concludes with an extensive numbered reference list spanning 49 citations on various systemic-periodontal topics.

The section reviews systemic conditions relevant to dentistry and periodontology. It covers osteoporosis, including BMD/T-scores, epidemiology, fracture risk, and its controversial relationship with periodontitis, as well as estrogen deficiency and possible benefits of hormone replacement therapy. It describes congenital heart disease, emphasizing cyanosis, chronic hypoxia, polycythemia, endocarditis risk, and oral/dental abnormalities, with detailed discussions of tetralogy of Fallot and Eisenmenger syndrome and their periodontal and oral findings. Hypophosphatasia is covered as a rare skeletal disease causing premature primary tooth loss and reduced cementum. The section also reviews metal intoxications from bismuth, lead, mercury, and other chemicals and their oral manifestations, includes a clinical case of Dilantin-induced gingival overgrowth, and concludes with a 49-citation reference list.

nodes.title: References
224.e5
nodes.summary: This text is a bibliography of 160 references for a chapter on the influence of systemic conditions on periodontal health. It covers literature on diabetes, bisphosphonate-associated osteonecrosis, hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, osteoporosis, hematologic and neutrophil disorders, Down syndrome, Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome, psychosocial stress, obesity/metabolic syndrome, immunosuppression, congenital heart disease, and other systemic diseases affecting the periodontium, along with related epidemiological and animal studies.

nodes.title: 224.e7
nodes.summary: The text is a bibliography/reference list for a chapter on the influence of systemic conditions on the periodontium. It consists of numbered citations to journal articles, case reports, reviews, and textbooks from 1916 to 2017. Entries cover diabetes, obesity/metabolic syndrome, sex hormone effects, osteoporosis and bone density, bisphosphonates and jaw osteonecrosis, nutritional deficiencies, hematologic and immunologic diseases, hyperparathyroidism, toxic and occupational exposures, psychosocial factors, and potential systemic impacts of periodontal disease. No narrative text or conclusions are included; the content is solely references.

nodes.title: 224.e9
nodes.summary: The text contains the tail end of a Chapter 14 reference list on systemic influences on periodontal and oral health, followed by the opening of Chapter 15 on how periodontal infection affects systemic health. The references cover conditions such as diabetes, bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis, nutrition, genetic/immune disorders, hormones, and bone density. Chapter 15 introduces the concept of periodontal medicine and outlines topics including cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, pregnancy outcomes, respiratory diseases, and asthma. Its opening discussion emphasizes that periodontitis is an inflammatory infectious disease involving subgingival bacteria, but host susceptibility and the immunoinflammatory response are essential—bacteria alone are not sufficient to cause disease.

The References section consists mainly of bibliographies for a chapter on how systemic conditions influence periodontal health, citing literature on diabetes, bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis, hormones, nutrition, osteoporosis, hematologic and immune disorders, genetic syndromes, psychosocial stress, obesity, and other systemic diseases. It also includes the end of the reference list for Chapter 14 and the beginning of Chapter 15, which introduces periodontal medicine and discusses how periodontal infection may affect systemic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, pregnancy outcomes, and respiratory diseases, highlighting the role of host susceptibility and the immunoinflammatory response.

This section reviews how systemic conditions influence periodontal disease. It emphasizes that periodontitis is caused by bacteria but that host susceptibility and systemic diseases are key modifiers; these conditions do not cause periodontitis but predispose, accelerate, or worsen it. Covered influences include endocrine and hormonal changes (particularly diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome/obesity, female sex hormone changes, hyperparathyroidism), hematologic disorders and immune deficiencies (leukocyte disorders, leukemia, anemias, thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiencies, and genetic syndromes), stress and psychiatric factors, nutritional influences (vitamins and protein deficiency), medications (bisphosphonates, corticosteroids, and phenytoin), osteoporosis, congenital heart disease, hypophosphatasia, and metal intoxications. The section also notes that periodontal infections can adversely affect systemic health, includes clinical examples, and provides references, transitioning into Chapter 15 on periodontal medicine.

nodes.title: 15 Impact of Periodontal Infection on Systemic Health
Chapter Outline
nodes.summary: This chapter text introduces the impact of periodontal infection on systemic health, outlining a range of related topics such as cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, pregnancy outcomes, respiratory diseases, and asthma. It explains that periodontal disease is an inflammatory, bacteria-initiated condition influenced by host and environmental factors, and that systemic disorders can modify its course. The field of periodontal medicine asks whether periodontal infection can have effects beyond the oral cavity and act as a risk factor for systemic disease. The pathobiology section emphasizes that periodontitis is caused by specific gram-negative bacteria in a subgingival biofilm, but bacteria alone are insufficient; host susceptibility is essential. This host susceptibility accounts for variable disease onset, progression, and treatment response, analogous to how respiratory pathogens affect susceptible individuals more severely. Overall, the text highlights the bidirectional relationship between oral and systemic health and the central role of host response.

nodes.title: Pathobiology of Periodontitis
nodes.summary: This chapter text introduces the impact of periodontal infection on systemic health. It explains that periodontitis is an inflammatory, bacteria-initiated disease involving a susceptible host and subgingival biofilm, and that host susceptibility influences disease severity and treatment response. The text revisits the focal infection theory, describing its historical rise and fall, and emphasizes the need for evidence-based clinical practice. It outlines systemic conditions associated with periodontal infection, including cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, diabetes, adverse pregnancy outcomes, respiratory diseases, kidney disease, autoimmune conditions, cognitive disorders, and certain cancers. It also notes that selected topics such as pregnancy outcomes, COPD, and acute respiratory infections are available online-only.

nodes.title: Focal Infection Theory Revisited
nodes.summary: The text discusses the relationship between periodontal infection and systemic health. It explains that variations in host immune responses can either impair defense against subgingival microorganisms or cause excessive inflammation, both leading to periodontal destruction. Periodontal infection may influence many systemic conditions, with strong evidence for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, diabetes, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and respiratory diseases, and weaker evidence for kidney disease, certain cancers, rheumatoid arthritis, and cognitive disorders. The chapter revisits the focal infection theory, describing William Hunter's 1900 claim that oral sepsis caused systemic illness and that tooth extraction was curative; this theory collapsed in the mid-20th century due to failed extractions and lack of evidence. The text concludes that current interest in oral-systemic links must be supported by rigorous evidence so the hypothesis does not again fall into disrepute.

nodes.title: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
nodes.summary: The text covers the impact of periodontal infection on systemic health, beginning with the bidirectional relationship between periodontal disease and systemic conditions, the varying strength of evidence for different associated diseases, and a boxed list of affected organ systems. It revisits the focal infection theory, its historical acceptance, and its later discreditation, then explains the modern evidence-based approach, including levels of evidence and the cholesterol/MI example. It describes the subgingival environment as a bacterial reservoir capable of causing bacteremias and systemic effects, reviews studies linking periodontal disease to increased mortality, and introduces the association between periodontitis and coronary heart disease/atherosclerosis.

nodes.title: Periodontal Infection, Systemic Health, Mortality, and Cardiovascular Disease
key_items: Subgingival Environment as a Reservoir for Bacteria
nodes.summary: The page discusses the historical focal infection theory, noting its lack of evidence and harmful consequences, and then reviews current knowledge on periodontal infection and systemic health. It describes the subgingival environment as a reservoir of gram-negative bacteria whose products enter the circulation via ulcerated epithelium, causing persistent host challenges and bacteremias. It summarizes studies linking periodontal disease to increased mortality, including the Veterans Affairs Dental Longitudinal Study, a Northern Ireland cohort, and a type 2 diabetes study, while emphasizing that these associations do not prove causation due to shared risk factors. It also introduces the connection between periodontal disease, coronary heart disease, and atherosclerosis, referencing the 2013 AAP/EFP workshop.

nodes.title: Periodontal Disease, Coronary Heart Disease, and Atherosclerosis
Subgingival Environment as a Reservoir for Bacteria
nodes.summary: The text covers the historical focal infection theory and its lack of evidence, the subgingival environment as a bacterial reservoir with systemic access, and evidence linking periodontal disease to mortality and cardiovascular disease. It reviews specific studies, including the Normative Aging/VA Dental Longitudinal Study and Northern Ireland cohort, showing periodontitis predicts higher mortality and cardiovascular events, while emphasizing association versus causation and the role of shared risk factors. It also introduces the 2013 AAP/EFP Workshop on periodontitis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

nodes.title: Periodontal Disease and Mortality
nodes.summary: The text reviews the historical focal infection theory and the need for evidence-based evaluation of oral-systemic links. It describes the subgingival environment as a bacterial reservoir that can cause bacteremias and systemic immunoinflammatory responses. It covers studies linking periodontal disease to increased mortality, coronary heart disease, and atherosclerosis, highlighting both supportive and conflicting findings, the confounding role of smoking, and the conclusion that while periodontitis is epidemiologically associated with increased cardiovascular risk, causality remains unproven. It also introduces mechanisms such as endothelial damage, atherogenesis, and thrombogenesis in ischemic heart disease.

nodes.title: Effects of Periodontal Infection
nodes.summary: The text covers the impact of periodontal infection on systemic health, particularly cardiovascular disease. It presents evidence from cross-sectional, longitudinal, and meta-analytic studies linking periodontitis to coronary heart disease and myocardial infarction, especially in younger individuals, while noting that causality is unproven and smoking is a major confounder. It also describes possible biological mechanisms, including increased blood viscosity and coagulability, bacteremia and endotoxemia from daily activities, platelet aggregation induced by oral bacteria, and promotion of atherosclerosis through endothelial injury, inflammatory cells, oxidized LDL, cytokines, and plaque rupture. It further notes that periodontal pathogens can be found in atherosclerotic plaques and that individual variation in host inflammatory responses influences susceptibility to periodontal disease.

nodes.title: Role of Periodontal Disease in Atherosclerotic Myocardial or Cerebral Ischemia
nodes.summary: The text discusses how periodontal infection impacts systemic health, focusing on atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events, stroke, erectile dysfunction, and diabetes. It describes mechanisms by which periodontal pathogens and their products—especially PAAP-positive S. sanguinis and P. gingivalis—cause platelet aggregation, thromboembolism, endothelial damage, atheroma formation, and vessel narrowing. It highlights the hyperinflammatory monocyte/macrophage phenotype (MØ+) as a shared risk factor for periodontitis and cardiovascular disease, and the role of systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and fibrinogen. Evidence shows periodontal treatment can reduce systemic inflammation and improve endothelial function. Periodontitis is associated with increased risk of ischemic stroke and erectile dysfunction. Lastly, diabetes is a risk factor for periodontitis, and periodontal disease is considered the sixth complication of diabetes, with clinical recommendations for dental referral.

nodes.title: Role of Periodontal Disease in Erectile Dysfunction
nodes.summary: The text covers the systemic impact of periodontal infection, focusing on three main areas: vascular health, erectile dysfunction, and stroke, along with the diabetes-periodontal disease relationship. It explains that reducing periodontal inflammation through scaling and root planing improves endothelial function, though long-term effects on cardiovascular events remain uncertain. It describes evidence linking periodontitis to erectile dysfunction and ischemic stroke, including epidemiological findings and possible mechanisms such as atherosclerosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and platelet aggregation. Finally, it discusses how diabetes increases periodontal disease risk and severity, leading to periodontal disease being called the sixth complication of diabetes, and notes clinical recommendations for dental referrals.

The section covers the systemic impact of periodontal disease, particularly its links to coronary heart disease and atherosclerosis. It discusses the historical focal infection theory and the subgingival environment as a bacterial reservoir capable of causing bacteremias and systemic inflammation. Evidence from epidemiological and meta-analytic studies associates periodontitis with increased mortality, cardiovascular events, myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke, especially in younger individuals, but causality remains unproven and smoking is a major confounder. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial injury, atheroma formation, platelet aggregation, increased blood viscosity, inflammatory markers, and pathogens in atherosclerotic plaques. The section also highlights a hyperinflammatory monocyte/macrophage phenotype as a shared risk factor, beneficial effects of periodontal treatment on endothelial function, associations with erectile dysfunction, and the bidirectional relationship between diabetes and periodontal disease, with periodontal disease described as the sixth complication of diabetes and dental referral recommended.

nodes.title: Periodontal Disease and Stroke
nodes.summary: The text discusses the systemic impact of periodontal infection, focusing on vascular health, erectile dysfunction, stroke, and diabetes. Periodontal treatment improves endothelial and vascular markers, but effects on acute cardiovascular events remain unproven. Periodontitis is associated with erectile dysfunction, with supportive epidemiological studies, a systematic review, and a small intervention trial showing improvement after periodontal therapy. Periodontal disease is linked to ischemic stroke, with severe periodontitis increasing stroke risk by roughly threefold; mechanisms include atherosclerosis, systemic inflammation, elevated fibrinogen/CRP, and bacteremia-induced platelet aggregation. Finally, diabetes and periodontal disease are bidirectional, with periodontal disease recognized as the sixth complication of diabetes, and clinical guidelines advise dental referral for diabetic patients.

nodes.title: Periodontal Disease and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
nodes.summary: Periodontal infection is linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes: preterm/low-birth-weight infants are exposed to maternal oral organisms, women with LBW infants have worse periodontitis and higher GCF IL-1/PGE2, and periodontal disease raises preeclampsia risk. Periodontal treatment during pregnancy has mixed evidence for improving pregnancy outcomes but is safe in the second/third trimester, local anesthetics are acceptable, and child development is unaffected. Periodontal disease also shares inflammatory mechanisms with COPD, is associated with COPD especially in smokers, and periodontal therapy may reduce COPD exacerbations. Community-acquired pneumonia is not clearly associated with oral hygiene/periodontal disease, but hospital-acquired pneumonia is linked to oropharyngeal and dental-plaque colonization by respiratory pathogens and periodontitis. Oral hygiene interventions, including selective oropharyngeal decontamination, reduce nosocomial pneumonia and respiratory infections in high-risk and nursing home populations.

Abstract
Gingival enlargement has many causes and can manifest with different clinical characteristics. Most common forms of gingival enlargement are linked to the systemic use of various medications. Because many forms of gingival enlargement are associated with systemic factors and conditions, understanding the exact pathogenesis of lesions is essential for targeting treatment. This chapter focuses on the clinical, etiologic, and pathologic aspects of gingival enlargement that are used for designing better approaches to therapy.
