It explains the classification of biofilm-induced inflammatory periodontal diseases based on inflammation and attachment loss, including gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, and healthy with a reduced periodontium, and discusses the current three-tier severity system based on clinical attachment loss, its limitations, and the role of radiographs in assessing severity.

nodes.title: Functional Occlusal Relationships
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal examination and diagnosis, including complications of crossbite, the importance of assessing functional occlusal relationships, radiographic examination requirements (intraoral, bitewing, and panoramic radiographs), and laboratory tests when systemic factors are suspected. It then explains periodontal diagnosis as synthesizing history and examinations to determine disease, severity, and extent. Biofilm-induced inflammatory periodontal diseases are classified by the presence of inflammation and attachment loss into healthy, biofilm-induced gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, and healthy with a reduced periodontium. Chronic periodontitis severity is based on clinical attachment loss, with noted limitations and the use of radiographic bone loss for correlation.

The section covers the full scope of periodontal examination and diagnosis. It describes periodontal charting and electronic records, bleeding indices, pocket detection by probing, limitations of radiographs, disease activity assessment via clinical attachment level measurements and the Florida Probe, and evaluation of alveolar bone loss through probing, bone sounding, and identification of interdental craters. Furcation invasion detection and the Glickman classification are included, along with detailed characterization of periodontal abscesses and their differential diagnosis from gingival and periapical abscesses. The section also addresses tooth wear mechanisms and occlusal facets, dental stains, root hypersensitivity, proximal contacts, and tooth mobility physiology, grading, and causes, including inflammation, attachment loss, and occlusal trauma. Trauma from occlusion is diagnosed by periodontal tissue injury, with signs such as mobility, widened PDL, angular bone defects, and pathologic migration. Additional examination findings include percussion sensitivity and closed-jaw/functional occlusal relationships, with attention to malalignment, faulty contacts, food impaction, and malocclusion features. Radiographic requirements and laboratory tests for systemic evaluation are reviewed. Finally, the section explains synthesizing findings into a periodontal diagnosis and classifying biofilm-induced inflammatory periodontal diseases, with severity based on clinical attachment loss and radiographic bone loss correlation.

nodes.title: Periodontal Examination and Diagnosis: Occlusion, Radiography, Lab Tests, Classification
nodes.summary: The page covers crossbite-related occlusal issues, functional occlusal examination, radiographic examination requirements and the role of panoramic imaging, and laboratory aids for detecting systemic contributions to periodontal disease. It then describes periodontal diagnosis as integrating history, clinical, radiographic, and laboratory findings to determine disease type, severity, and extent. Biofilm-induced inflammatory periodontal diseases are diagnosed by the presence of inflammation and attachment loss: healthy, biofilm-induced gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, or healthy with a reduced periodontium. Severity of chronic periodontitis is based on clinical attachment loss, but this system is considered inadequate because inflammation should also be considered, particularly as the link to systemic disease. Table 32.3 correlates severity with clinical attachment loss and distance from the alveolar crest to the cementoenamel junction on radiographs.

nodes.title: Periodontal Diagnosis

nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal examination and diagnosis, including crossbite effects, functional occlusal relationship examination, radiographic requirements (intraoral, bitewing, panoramic), laboratory aids for systemic disease, and the diagnostic process for biofilm-induced inflammatory periodontal diseases. It details classification of severity and extent based on inflammation, attachment loss, clinical attachment loss, and radiographic findings, including the 30% threshold for localized versus generalized disease. It also discusses patient education and biofilm control assessment, emphasizing the need for patients to demonstrate and improve oral hygiene before treatment. CHAPTER 33 Radiographic Aids in the diagnosis of Periodontal disease
Abstract
Radiographs are a valuable tool in the assessment of the periodontal osseous structures. Various two- and three- dimensional imaging modalities offer choices for imaging pathologic processes that affect the periodontium. Understanding the technical aspects of each modality and how disease is depicted allows the proper selection of radiographic modalities for the estimation of severity, determination of prognosis, and evaluation of treatment outcomes. In this chapter, we discuss the appearance of periodontal disease in standard intraoral projections and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging, as well as the advantages and limitations of these imaging approaches in the management of the patient with periodontal disease.
Keywords radiographs periapical CBCT periodontal status

nodes.title: Bone Destruction in Periodontal Disease
nodes.summary: The text covers radiographic aids in diagnosing periodontal disease. It describes normal interdental bone anatomy, the superiority of bitewing radiography for accurately showing posterior alveolar bone levels, and the use of vertical bitewings for severe bone loss. It explains that radiographs underestimate early and actual bone loss, show remaining rather than lost bone, and are affected by x-ray angulation and technique. It details the amount, distribution, and patterns of bone loss—horizontal versus angular/vertical—and the limitations of radiographs in revealing craters, facial/lingual involvement, and troughlike lesions. It notes that nutrient canals are normal variants that can mimic disease, and that radiographs cannot distinguish active from treated/inactive periodontal disease, requiring clinical assessment. It also outlines the radiographic signs of periodontitis: early lamina dura fuzziness, wedge-shaped radiolucencies, crestal erosion, progressive septal bone loss, and horizontal root lines, concluding that periodontal bone level assessment should combine clinical and radiographic findings.

This section covers the radiographic appearance and diagnostic aids for periodontal disease. It describes periodontitis changes including lamina dura fuzziness, crestal cortication disruption, wedge-shaped radiolucencies, progressive interdental bone loss, reduced septal height, and horizontal radiopaque lines, while emphasizing that radiographs underestimate bone loss and must be combined with clinical assessment. It also covers interdental craters as irregular, poorly demarcated radiolucencies on alveolar bone crests; furcation involvement with diagnostic criteria requiring multiple radiographs and clinical probing; and periodontal abscess as a discrete lateral radiolucency that is often inconclusive, making clinical examination essential. Clinical probing with radiopaque indicators such as probes and gutta-percha points is described for revealing true osseous extent. Localized aggressive periodontitis shows bilateral vertical bone loss in incisor/first molar areas that may generalize but spares premolars. Trauma from occlusion causes lamina dura loss, PDL widening, and alveolar/cancellous changes, best detected faciolingually and correlated clinically. Finally, digital intraoral radiography using CCD/CMOS and PSP technologies offers enhancement, artifacts, electronic records, and telediagnosis, while CBCT adds three-dimensional assessment of defects not well seen on conventional radiographs.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text discusses the diagnostic limitations of periapical radiographs in assessing periodontal bone loss and the added value of CBCT. It provides examples where CBCT detected deep vertical, three-wall defects and palatal-extending defects that were invisible or underestimated on periapical radiographs. CBCT is superior for visualizing buccal/lingual morphology, early furcation defects, three-wall defects, fenestrations, and dehiscence, but not for advanced furcation or one/two-wall/troughlike defects. However, CBCT has higher radiation dose and cost and should be reserved for selected cases when two-dimensional imaging is insufficient. The conclusion emphasizes that periapical radiographs are essential in periodontal evaluation but often underestimate bone loss; they should be updated every 2 years and interpreted with clinical parameters. Longitudinal periapical comparisons are only reliable for dramatic changes. CBCT offers more accurate three-dimensional assessment and will likely be used more widely in the future.

nodes.summary: The text discusses factors that determine periodontal prognosis. Subgingival restoration margins and discrepancies are harmful compared with well-contoured supragingival margins. Anatomic factors such as short tapered roots, enamel projections/pearls, bifurcation ridges, root concavities, developmental grooves, root proximity, and furcation access can predispose to disease and complicate treatment, worsening prognosis. Tooth mobility may be correctable if caused by inflammation or occlusal trauma, but not if due to bone loss; splinting can help. Caries, restorability, endodontic status, and root resorption must be considered; treated nonvital teeth have similar prognosis to vital teeth. Prosthetic factors include preserving enough teeth for function/aesthetics/abutments and the increased risks for abutment teeth, especially post-endodontic distal abutments. Prognosis also relies on general diagnostic criteria including age, severity, genetic susceptibility, and systemic disease. Immediate goals focus on eliminating infection and inflammation to achieve oral health; intermediate goals aim to reconstruct a functional, aesthetic, and durable dentition; long-term goals involve maintaining health through prevention, daily hygiene, and professional recall. The treatment plan is presented as a comprehensive case-management blueprint covering emergency care, extractions, periodontal, endodontic, restorative, orthodontic, prosthetic, and aesthetic considerations, as well as treatment sequencing. It also highlights that prognosis is based on diagnosis, treatment decisions are made based on prognosis and to improve it, and diagnosis/prognosis evolve during therapy. Except for emergencies, treatment should not begin until a plan is established.

The text also stresses the importance of patient commitment and education, and states that the ultimate goal is long-term oral health through a flexible treatment plan based on examination, diagnosis, prognosis, and patient needs. It then covers electronic dental records (EDRs), including their functionalities, growing adoption and usage statistics, advantages in data analysis and periodontal charting, and the chapter's scope regarding decision support systems and future developments in dentistry.

CHAPTER 37 Electronic Dental Records and Decision Support Systems
Abstract
The increased use of electronic dental records (EDRs) for patient care is generating vast amounts of data that could provide significant benefits to clinicians and researchers. Until now, clinicians have been able to track only individual patient outcomes through paper- based records. At the same time, researchers typically spend consider- able time transcribing data from paper into electronic form to analyze data. Analyzing electronic data can generate new knowledge in real time. This chapter discusses the use EDRs in dental practices in the United States, Europe, and other countries; the decision support systems available to assess periodontal disease; and the future of EDRs.
Keywords electronic dental records decision support systems dental informatics risk assessment

It then addresses the need for standards in dental record content, noting that no standard content model exists but recommendations include personal, demographic, medical/dental history, examination, diagnosis, treatment plan, and informed consent data. Finally, it introduces clinical decision support systems (CDSSs), explaining their purpose, how they generate recommendations, and their delivery through electronic health records, email, text, or printouts, while noting that decision support system types have been extensively studied in medicine, including human diagnostic research.

Pediatric sedation requires special caution, including avoiding preoperative sedatives except in extraordinary cases. It then focuses on cardiovascular diseases, especially hypertension, describing its prevalence, the JNC-7 blood pressure classification system including prehypertension and two stages of hypertension, diagnostic criteria, age-related risk from the Framingham study, and the distinction between primary and secondary hypertension. Clinical recommendations include physician consultation, short appointments, and stress reduction for cardiovascular patients.

The chapter also mentions e-only content on renal, liver, pulmonary, pregnancy, and infectious diseases, plus additional online resources for thyroid/parathyroid disorders, adrenal insufficiency, purpuras, and blood dyscrasias. Overall, it provides safety parameters, treatment guidelines, and clinical scenarios to help clinicians manage medically compromised patients safely.

nodes.title: Cardiac Considerations in Periodontal Treatment of Medically Compromised Patients

It describes emergency treatment for angina using nitroglycerin, deferring dental therapy for at least 6 months after myocardial infarction, and consulting the physician after cardiac surgery. It discusses congestive heart failure causes, risks of uncontrolled CHF, medication side effects, and patient positioning/stress-reduction modifications. It covers pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, including consultation, older unipolar pacemaker electromagnetic interference, and defibrillator activation risks. It also covers infective endocarditis, its organisms, acute and subacute forms, and the 2008 AHA change recommending prophylaxis only for highest-risk cardiac conditions.

nodes.title: Cerebrovascular Accident
nodes.summary: This text covers periodontal treatment considerations for medically compromised patients, specifically those susceptible to infective endocarditis, those who have had a cerebrovascular accident (stroke), and patients with diabetes. For infective endocarditis risk, it emphasizes eliminating periodontal infection, using antibiotic prophylaxis for all procedures, chlorhexidine rinses, minimizing visits, spacing appointments appropriately, and maintaining recall care. For post-stroke patients, it advises waiting 6 months before elective periodontal therapy, minimizing stress, using cautious anesthesia and sedation, managing anticoagulants with physician consultation, monitoring blood pressure, and addressing oral hygiene difficulties. For diabetes, it highlights recognizing undiagnosed or poorly controlled disease, consulting physicians, interpreting glucose tests, managing infections, and limiting advanced periodontal therapy until glycemic control is established.

nodes.title: Thyroid and Parathyroid Disorders
nodes.summary: This chapter section discusses periodontal treatment for medically compromised patients, specifically thyroid/parathyroid disorders and adrenal insufficiency. For thyroid disease, controlled patients need minimal treatment changes, uncontrolled or thyrotoxic patients should be deferred until stabilized, hyperthyroid patients need stress/infection control and cautious use of vasopressors, and hypothyroid patients need careful sedative/narcotic administration. Parathyroid patients can receive routine therapy after medical management, but untreated disease may involve renal disease, uremia, hypertension, and arrhythmia risk. Adrenal insufficiency requires awareness of crisis manifestations and causes, especially exogenous corticosteroid-induced HPA suppression. Most dental/periodontal procedures do not require corticosteroid supplementation, but high-risk situations such as major surgery, significant blood loss, or very low adrenal function require physician consultation and supplementation. Stress-reduction protocols and profound local anesthesia help minimize risk. Testing for adrenal reserve, equivalent corticosteroid doses, and coverage regimens are also covered.

nodes.title: Adrenal Insufficiency
450.e1
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal treatment considerations in medically compromised patients, focusing on thyroid/parathyroid disorders and adrenal insufficiency. It emphasizes that well-managed thyroid disease requires only minimal treatment changes, while inadequately managed hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis should not receive periodontal therapy until stabilized; caution is needed with vasopressors in hyperthyroidism and with sedatives/narcotics in hypothyroidism. Parathyroid disease is treatable after medical management, but untreated patients may have renal and calcium-related complications. The adrenal insufficiency section discusses risks of acute adrenal crisis in primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, the effects of corticosteroid use, HPA axis suppression, and the rarity of adrenal crisis in dental procedures. It notes that most patients do not require supplemental steroids, but physician consultation and corticosteroid coverage are indicated for high-risk procedures or patients with very low adrenal function. Diagnostic tests and corticosteroid equivalent dosing are described, along with eBox 39.1 for adrenal crisis signs and eTable 39.1 for equivalent corticosteroid doses.

nodes.title: Periodontal treatment of patients with purpuras, blood dyscrasias, renal disease
nodes.summary: This page covers periodontal treatment of medically compromised patients, specifically thrombocytopenic purpuras, nonthrombocytopenic purpuras, blood dyscrasias, and renal disease. Purpuras are hemorrhagic diseases causing petechiae or ecchymoses. In thrombocytopenia, care aims to reduce inflammation, with physician referral, scaling/root planing safe above 60,000 platelets, surgery only above 80,000, and possible platelet transfusion. Nonthrombocytopenic purpuras result from vascular fragility or thrombasthenia; treatment is direct pressure for at least 15 minutes and avoiding surgery until platelet defects resolve. Blood dyscrasias can alter healing, bleeding, tissue appearance, and infection susceptibility, requiring clinical awareness and referral. Renal disease requires physician consultation and modified periodontal care: blood pressure monitoring, laboratory evaluation, infection elimination, avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs, and safe drug choices. Dialysis modes include IPD, CAPD, and hemodialysis; hemodialysis patients need hepatitis screening, antibiotic prophylaxis for shunts/fistulas, treatment after heparin effects subside, shunt protection, and referral for uremic complications. Renal transplant patients need pretransplant dental evaluation to remove nonmaintainable teeth because of infection and bleeding risks.

The section covers periodontal treatment modifications for medically compromised patients, focusing on endocrine disorders and expanding to bleeding, hematologic, and renal conditions. Endocrine topics include diabetes management with glycemic control and hypoglycemia precautions; thyroid disease with deferral of uncontrolled or thyrotoxic patients and cautious drug use; parathyroid disease with monitoring for renal and cardiovascular complications; and adrenal insufficiency with recognition of crisis, corticosteroid supplementation for high-risk procedures, and emergency hydrocortisone. Additional coverage includes infective endocarditis prophylaxis, stroke and hemorrhagic disorder considerations, coagulation evaluation and management, liver disease and vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy with INR thresholds, leukemia, purpuras, blood dyscrasias, and bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis. Specific purpura guidance is provided for thrombocytopenic and nonthrombocytopenic conditions. Renal disease management includes dialysis considerations, infection prevention, drug precautions, shunt protection, and renal transplant pretransplant dental evaluation. Throughout, the emphasis is on individualized care, physician consultation, laboratory monitoring, conservative treatment, infection prevention, and stress reduction.

For pulmonary disease, it outlines obstructive and restrictive types, warning signs requiring medical referral, and specific periodontal therapy guidelines to avoid respiratory distress, manage asthma patients, and avoid treating active respiratory infections except in emergencies.

nodes.title: Anticoagulant or Antiplatelet Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers dental management of patients on bisphosphonates, anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, and corticosteroids. For bisphosphonate patients, it emphasizes assessing BRONJ risk through medical history, radiographs, and possibly CTX testing, though CTX remains controversial; invasive procedures should generally be avoided in IV bisphosphonate patients. For anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, evidence supports continuing these medications during dental procedures because bleeding risk is low and stopping therapy increases risks of serious thromboembolic events. For corticosteroid users, routine dental treatment usually does not require supplemental steroids, but blood pressure should be monitored, ulcerogenic drugs avoided, and postoperative pain controlled to limit cortisol needs.

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: The text covers management of medically compromised dental patients, focusing on four areas: BRONJ risk assessment in bisphosphonate users, including CTX testing and risk factors; anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, where continuing these medications during minor oral procedures is supported over discontinuing; corticosteroid use, with guidance that routine dental care rarely requires steroid supplementation while major surgery may; and immunosuppression/chemotherapy, emphasizing infection prevention, pre-chemotherapy dental evaluation, and timing treatment around blood counts. It also details radiation therapy effects and management, including preirradiation dental care, extraction timing, ORN risk, fluoride use, and palliative measures for mucositis.

nodes.title: Immunosuppression and Chemotherapy
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal management of medically compromised patients, focusing on three areas: corticosteroid supplementation, immunosuppression and chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. It explains when steroid supplementation is or is not needed, including risks for adrenal crisis. For immunosuppressed and chemotherapy patients, it emphasizes impaired host defenses, increased infection risk, conservative/palliative treatment, coordination with oncologists, and timing of dental care based on blood counts. For radiation therapy, it details preirradiation evaluation and treatment, radiation side effects such as xerostomia, radiation caries, and osteoradionecrosis, the importance of extracting high-risk teeth before radiation, fluoride and prophylaxis during radiation, and palliative postirradiation care.

nodes.title: Radiation Therapy

nodes.title: Prosthetic Joint Replacement

Finally, it addresses periodontal management during pregnancy, emphasizing minimizing the inflammatory response, limiting treatment to safe nonemergency procedures, avoiding supine hypotensive syndrome, and cautiously using medications and radiographs.

It also addresses periodontal management during pregnancy, emphasizing minimizing inflammation, safe timing, positioning to avoid supine hypotensive syndrome, cautious medication use, and radiograph safeguards. Finally, it discusses infectious disease precautions, focusing on hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, E, G, and TTV), their transmission, chronic infection risks, vaccine availability, high-risk groups, and the need for universal precautions in periodontal practice.

nodes.summary:
465.e1
CHAPTER 41 Periodontal Therapy in the Female Patient
Abstract
Throughout the female lifespan, there are hormonal changes that may cause physiologic changes that alter clinical periodontal or implant therapy. Estrogen and progesterone may impact oral osseous and soft tissues, as well as the patient’s response to therapy. Puberty, pregnancy, and menopause are stages that require clinical alteration and may impact the outcomes of treatment. This chapter provides guidance for clinicians during the female continuum.
Keywords periodontal disease female pregnancy puberty preterm low birthweight menopause

nodes.summary:
475.e1
CHAPTER 42 Periodontal Treatment for older Adults
Abstract
The adult population older than 65 years of age is growing at the rate of 10,000 per day in the United States. Most older adults have natural teeth for their lifetime due to the success since World War II of the dental profession in educating the public, treating the oral cavity, and preventing future disease. Chapter 42 explores aspects of periodontal care for older adults, including demographics, the role of the primary care team in ensuring safety, periodontal disease in older adults, treatment planning, disease prevention, and mainte- nance of periodontal health throughout the aging process.

Generalized forms are less likely to remit spontaneously than localized forms. Treatment emphasizes early detection, radiographic assessment of disease progression, a regimented approach, and patient education.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
479.e1
CHAPTER 43 Treatment of Aggressive and Atypical Forms of Periodontitis
Abstract
Aggressive periodontitis and other atypical forms of periodontal disease may not respond as expected or as favorable to conventional periodontal therapy as chronic periodontitis. Fortunately, a relatively small percentage of patients with periodontal disease are diagnosed with aggressive periodontitis. Other atypical forms of periodontal disease such as necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis are also less prevalent. Patients who are diagnosed with periodontal disease that is refractory to treatment are very limited, as well. Aggressive periodontitis and atypical diseases are challenging for dentists and dental hygienists. This chapter presents current treatment approaches to these usually destructive forms of periodontal disease.
Keywords aggressive periodontitis refractory necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis

nodes.title: Keywords
Conventional Periodontal Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers management of aggressive periodontitis, emphasizing early diagnosis, the patient's role, family screening, and frequent maintenance care. Conventional therapy may be less predictable, and advanced teeth often have poor prognosis. Surgical resective therapy has limitations, while regenerative therapy shows potential in localized cases but is limited in severe horizontal bone loss. Antimicrobial therapy is introduced as necessary because periodontal pathogens like Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans persist and can reinfect after conventional treatment.

nodes.summary: The text discusses treatment of aggressive periodontitis, emphasizing early diagnosis, family screening, and the patient's role. Conventional therapy includes education, scaling and root planing, and maintenance, with variable outcomes. Surgical resective and regenerative therapies are considered, including a successful regenerative case report. Antimicrobial therapy is central, particularly systemic antibiotics such as tetracycline and amoxicillin-metronidazole, as adjuncts to mechanical debridement. Microbial testing, local antibiotic delivery, full-mouth disinfection, and host modulation are also covered. Restorative and implant considerations stress early extraction of hopeless teeth, preserving bone for implants, and planning for future tooth loss while using dental implants with caution but generally favorable outcomes.

nodes.title: Managing Aggressive Periodontitis: Antimicrobial Therapy, Host Modulation, and Implant Planning
nodes.summary: This page covers management strategies for aggressive periodontitis, including antimicrobial approaches such as microbial testing, empiric systemic antibiotics, and local delivery; full-mouth disinfection with chlorhexidine and its evidence; host modulation therapy; and treatment planning considerations emphasizing early extraction of compromised teeth, preserving bone, use of removable prostheses, limited role of tooth transplantation, and use of dental implants with or without bone augmentation.

nodes.title: Treatment Planning and Restorative Considerations
key_items: Local Delivery; Full-Mouth Disinfection; Host Modulation
nodes.summary: The text covers antimicrobial and therapeutic approaches for aggressive and atypical periodontitis, including microbial testing, local antibiotic delivery, full-mouth disinfection, and host modulation. It discusses treatment planning and restorative considerations, emphasizing early extraction of compromised teeth, preservation of bone for implants, and implant use with attention to occlusal overload. Periodontal maintenance is detailed, including visit components, recall intervals, risk factors, and the importance of frequent monitoring. Necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis is described as an immune-compromised-associated condition requiring medical workup, debridement, antimicrobial therapy, and physician collaboration. The chapter concludes that these periodontitis forms are challenging due to their rarity, severity, and unpredictable response to conventional therapy.

nodes.title: Periodontal Maintenance
nodes.summary: Chapter 43 addresses aggressive and atypical periodontitis. It warns about occlusal overload risk for implants in periodontally compromised dentitions, especially with few implants in a mobile remaining dentition without stable vertical stops. For aggressive-periodontitis maintenance, patients must be stable and free of clinical signs/pathogens; each maintenance visit includes medical history, risk assessment, comprehensive periodontal/oral exam, root debridement, prophylaxis, and oral hygiene review, with plaque visualization before debridement if hygiene is poor. Frequent maintenance is critical: studies of 25 and 13 patients showed effective maintenance, with disease progression arrested in 95% of initially affected lesions in the latter; risk factors included high bacterial counts (P. gingivalis, T. denticola), acute episodes, tooth loss, smoking, and stress. Recall intervals are initially no longer than 3 months, every 3-4 weeks if disease is active, and adjusted over time; younger patients need closer monitoring, and persistent disease may require microbial testing. Collaboration among periodontist, dentist, hygienist, and physician is needed; monitor for weight loss, depression, and malaise; reinforce patient education. NUP is rare, often in immunocompromised patients (0-6% in HIV/AIDS); it requires medical workup, consultation, and rule-out of hematologic disease. NUP treatment includes debridement with scaling/root planing, local anesthesia, ultrasonic irrigation, oral hygiene support, chlorhexidine, systemic analgesics/antibiotics, and antifungal/antiviral agents as needed; successful treatment depends on resolving the underlying systemic condition. Refractory periodontitis is not a separate entity; before labeling it, rule out inadequately treated periodontitis, poor plaque control, and endodontic infection. Management includes intensive maintenance, scaling/root planing, surgery, and systemic antibiotics; if initial antibiotics fail, microbial testing and susceptibility testing are indicated. Antibiotic resistance is a concern, especially tetracycline. Regimens discussed include amoxicillin-clavulanate, metronidazole, clindamycin (with caution for Clostridium difficile colitis), azithromycin, and combinations such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or metronidazole-amoxicillin for A. actinomycetemcomitans, metronidazole-doxycycline for recurrence prevention, and metronidazole-ciprofloxacin for enteric-rod-associated recurrence. The chapter concludes that these forms are challenging but uncommon; case scenario and references are on the companion website.

This section of Chapter 43 covers treatment of aggressive and atypical periodontitis. It opens with the chapter abstract and keywords: aggressive periodontitis, refractory, and necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis. The subsections describe conventional periodontal therapy, antimicrobial therapy, treatment planning and restorative considerations, periodontal maintenance, necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis, and refractory periodontitis. Key themes are that these diseases are uncommon but destructive and respond unpredictably; early diagnosis, patient/family involvement, frequent maintenance, antimicrobial therapy (systemic/local antibiotics, full-mouth disinfection, host modulation), early extraction and implant planning, and careful follow-up are needed. NUP requires medical workup and collaborative management, and refractory cases require excluding other causes, using susceptibility testing, and considering antibiotic resistance. The chapter concludes with challenges and companion website resources.

nodes.title: Periodontitis Refractory to Treatment

nodes.title: References

The first visit includes thorough medical history and physical/oral examination, with periodontal probing deferred. Initial NUG therapy focuses on reducing microbial load and removing necrotic tissue using topical anesthesia, gentle swabbing, irrigation, and superficial calculus removal with ultrasonic scalers.

This section covers treatment of aggressive, refractory, and necrotizing ulcerative forms of periodontitis. It emphasizes that these uncommon destructive diseases respond unpredictably to conventional therapy, require early diagnosis, radiographic monitoring, antimicrobial and mechanical therapy, maintenance, and often extraction/implant planning. Necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis needs medical collaboration, and refractory cases require excluding other causes, microbial testing, and addressing antibiotic resistance or host factors. The section also contains the chapter abstract, keywords, a clinical case scenario, and references, followed by the beginning of Chapter 44 on acute gingival disease and NUG management.

CHAPTER 44

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
488.e1
CHAPTER 44 Treatment of Acute Gingival Disease
Abstract
Patients with acute gingival disease typically present with pain. Treatment of acute gingival disease is aimed at alleviating symptoms and determining the etiology of disease. A thorough history and examination is critical to making a proper diagnosis and determining the etiology. Risk and etiologic factors that are identified need to be eliminated when possible to effectively treat the acute gingival disease. This chapter presents current treatment for acute gingival disease conditions, including necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, and pericoronitis.
Keywords aggressive periodontitis refractory necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis

nodes.title: Keywords
Instructions to the Patient
nodes.summary: The text covers management of acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG), emphasizing immediate treatment with gentle lavage, avoidance of subgingival scaling/curettage during the acute phase, and postponement of surgical procedures until the patient is symptom-free for 4 weeks. Antibiotics are recommended only for moderate or severe cases with systemic symptoms, using amoxicillin or alternatives. Detailed patient instructions include hygiene, diet, rest, pain control, and follow-up. Both topical and systemic drugs are adjuncts only; complete local treatment is necessary to prevent recurrence. Follow-up visits at 1-2 days and about 5 days later assess improvement, allow scaling as tolerated, and establish a comprehensive periodontal treatment plan, including biofilm control, counseling, and continued chlorhexidine use. The text stresses that patients must complete comprehensive periodontal care even after acute symptoms resolve, and includes a figure of a NUG patient before and after initial treatment.

nodes.title: Second Visit
nodes.summary: The text covers the treatment and follow-up of acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG). It describes initial management with painless irrigation and lavage, contraindications to subgingival scaling and surgery, and antibiotic regimens for systemic cases. Detailed patient instructions address rinses, rest, gentle oral hygiene, analgesics, and follow-up. Second and third visits involve evaluation, scaling, biofilm control education, comprehensive periodontal treatment planning, and counseling. The stages of gingival healing are described. Additional considerations include surgical contouring for residual deformities and the importance of avoiding escharotic drugs; all drug therapy is only adjunctive to complete local treatment.

nodes.title: Gingival Changes With Healing

It emphasizes that escharotic drugs should be avoided because they are necrotizing and impair healing.

Most periodontal abscesses arise from incomplete subgingival calculus removal in existing pockets, but other triggers include surgery, maintenance, antibiotics, recurrent disease, tooth fracture/perforation, foreign bodies, and poorly controlled diabetes. nodes.title: Periodontal Versus Pulpal Abscess

It describes three types—gingival, periodontal, and pericoronal abscesses—and explains that periodontal abscesses usually arise in existing pockets, often due to incomplete calculus removal, and may be triggered by procedures, antibiotics, recurrent disease, tooth perforation, fracture, or foreign bodies, with diabetes as a predisposing factor. It contrasts acute and chronic abscesses, outlines the need for differential diagnosis between periodontal and pulpal abscesses, and notes that treatment typically involves drainage, possibly with antibiotics or surgery.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
The periodontal abscess is a localized periodontal inflammation complicated by the accumulation of exudate entrapped in a periodontal pocket. This results in a localized swelling and usually requires incisional release of the exudate. At times, it will require antibiotic therapy along with the surgical drainage of the exudate. This chapter will classify and discuss the etiology and treatment of this periodontal problem.
Keywords acute exacerbation pericoronal abscess chronic abscess preexisting pocket drainage suppuration lymphadenopathy

nodes.title: 46 Endodontic-Periodontic Lesions
CHAPTER 46

It notes that pulpal infection more often causes secondary periodontal breakdown (retrograde periodontitis), while periodontal infection affecting pulp is less frequent; treatment typically begins with endodontic therapy followed by reevaluation. nodes.title: Abstract

It explains that pulpal and periodontal infections usually occur independently but can spread between tissues, with pulpal-to-periodontal migration being more common and causing bone loss, suppuration, pocketing, and fistulas. Treatment typically starts with endodontic therapy followed by reevaluation, often leading to periodontal healing. The chapter also highlights implications for implant therapy, especially retrograde peri-implantitis caused by recurrent endodontic bacteria, and discusses classification, initiating factors, biologic effects, differential diagnosis, and treatment considerations.

nodes.title: Keywords

Communication occurs via accessory canals, dentinal tubules, and iatrogenic defects. nodes.title: Classification of Pulpal and Apical Diseases

It describes how caries and microbial challenges trigger pulpal inflammation via immune mediators, leading to increased intrapulpal pressure, necrosis, apical periodontitis, abscess formation, and sinus tracts. It emphasizes that persistent periapical inflammation can jeopardize implant success, outlines prevention and treatment options based on implant stability, describes extraradicular causes such as actinomycosis, calculus, and biofilms that often require surgical management, and reviews clinical and radiographic findings needed to distinguish pulpal from periodontal abscesses, including patient symptoms and study data on periodontal abscess characteristics.

It describes characteristic features of apical versus periodontal abscesses, drainage patterns, relevant studies, and factors predisposing to periodontal abscesses. Finally, it discusses treatment considerations: root canal therapy alone resolves pulpal-origin lesions and secondary periodontal defects, whereas true combined endo-perio lesions require both endodontic and periodontal treatment.

It discusses risk factors and drainage patterns of acute periodontal and apical abscesses, the use of coronal integrity, radiographic features, and pulp vitality testing to differentiate pulpal from periodontal origin, and treatment considerations. Primary pulpal lesions with secondary periodontal defects often resolve with root canal therapy alone, while combined endo-perio lesions require both endodontic and periodontal therapy, with endodontic treatment performed first. Management of acute periodontal and apical abscesses is detailed, including drainage, debridement, antibiotics when indicated, and analgesics. A case scenario illustrates diagnosis of a vertical root crack and its distinction from periodontal disease, along with frequently affected teeth and conservative endodontic access. Treatment principles emphasize endodontic therapy first followed by reevaluation, with true combined lesions requiring both endodontic and periodontal therapy. The section also includes clinical cases, online-only content, and a reference list.

Periodontal abscess treatment is explored in depth, emphasizing drainage, debridement, antibiotics when indicated, surgical options, extraction, and a two-phase strategy for acute and underlying chronic conditions. nodes.title: Treatment Sessions
nodes.summary: The text covers Phase I periodontal therapy, also called initial, nonsurgical, or cause-related therapy. It explains its rationale, goals, required components, and treatment session planning. Phase I therapy aims to eliminate microbial causes and contributing local factors, halt disease progression, and restore oral health. It is essential for all periodontal patients and may be sufficient alone or serve as preparation for surgery. The success of subsequent surgical treatment depends on the plaque control achieved during Phase I. Components include patient education, oral hygiene instruction, calculus removal, restoration correction, treatment of caries, orthodontic movement, management of food impaction and occlusal trauma, extractions, and antimicrobial therapy. Planning must consider multiple patient and dental factors, and several sessions are often needed. The abstract emphasizes that this phase determines patient compliance and guides decisions on whether surgical therapy is needed.

nodes.title: Decision to Refer for Specialist Treatment
nodes.summary: The text discusses phase I periodontal therapy, including the effects of overhanging restorations on gingival inflammation and the need to inform patients about possible post-therapy changes such as root sensitivity and longer-looking teeth. It covers decisions to refer patients for specialist treatment, citing evidence that surgery is beneficial in deep pockets >6 mm while scaling and root planing is better in shallower pockets. A critical probing depth of 5.4 mm and a practical 5-mm referral standard are explained, along with the relationship between clinical attachment loss and tooth support. Additional referral considerations include disease extent, root length, tooth mobility, instrumentation difficulty, restorability, patient age, and persistent inflammation. The conclusion emphasizes that phase I therapy controls inflammatory factors through patient education, scaling and root planing, and adjunctive treatments; reevaluation is essential; many patients are managed without surgery; and surgery is reserved for deep pockets or significant attachment loss, especially for patients who maintain good plaque control.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text discusses criteria for referring patients to a periodontal specialist, emphasizing that the 5-mm probing depth alone is insufficient. It lists factors such as disease extent, bone loss, root length, tooth mobility, instrumentation difficulty, restorability, patient age, and persistent inflammation after phase I therapy. It then summarizes phase I periodontal therapy, which aims to control inflammation through patient education, scaling and root planing, caries control, restorative replacement, occlusal therapy, orthodontics, and habit cessation. Reevaluation is essential, and many patients respond to phase I therapy alone. Surgery is considered for deep pockets or attachment loss of 5 mm or more after phase I therapy, and patients who cannot maintain daily plaque control are poor surgical candidates and require close recall monitoring.

It also notes that many patients respond to nonsurgical therapy alone, while others with deep pockets or significant attachment loss may need surgical intervention by specialists, and that poor daily plaque control makes surgery inadvisable, requiring close recall maintenance. Phase I periodontal therapy is the initial nonsurgical/cause-related phase aimed at controlling inflammation by eliminating microbial and local factors. It includes patient education, plaque/biofilm control instruction, scaling and root planing with hand and ultrasonic instruments, correction of defective restorations and caries, management of occlusal trauma and food impaction, extractions, and antimicrobial therapy. Treatment requires multiple sessions and is followed by reevaluation after about 4 weeks; adjunctive lasers, photodynamic therapy, curettage, and full-mouth disinfection have limited evidence. Healing typically includes reduced inflammation, long junctional epithelium, recession, and transient root sensitivity. Referral to a specialist is considered for deep pockets (>6 mm benefit from surgery; critical probing depth 5.4 mm, practical 5-mm threshold), significant attachment loss, and factors such as disease extent, root length, mobility, instrumentation difficulty, restorability, age, and persistent inflammation. Many patients respond to nonsurgical therapy alone; surgery is reserved for deep pockets or attachment loss ≥5 mm, especially in patients with good plaque control. The chapter also provides references and introduces Chapter 48 on plaque biofilm control.

It explains the importance of daily plaque biofilm removal for preventing and treating gingivitis and periodontal disease, citing Löe's classic 1965 study and ADA recommendations. It emphasizes that brushing alone is inadequate because plaque begins interdentally, and patients often leave most biofilm on posterior and interproximal surfaces. The chapter also discusses the role of chemical agents and fluoride, the need for professional maintenance, and special challenges for periodontal patients, with a clinical correlation noting that stopping plaque control for 7–21 days causes reversible gingivitis and bacterial shifts.

This chapter discusses the etiology, the examination methods, and the possible treatments for patients with bad breath.
