It notes the unreliability of self-assessment and offers clinical advice. Treatment strategies include mechanical tongue cleaning, periodontal therapy, mouthrinses, and chewing gum. Additional diagnostic methods covered are saliva incubation testing, electronic nose technology, and chair-side tests such as BANA, beta-galactosidase, ninhydrin, and amine colorimetric assays.

nodes.title: Saliva Incubation, Electronic Nose, and Chair-Side Tests for Halitosis
nodes.summary: The page covers diagnostic approaches for halitosis, including the saliva incubation test, electronic nose, and chair-side tests. It details compounds detected in incubated saliva headspace, organoleptic evaluation, electronic nose technology, and commercial chair-side tests such as BANA, beta-galactosidase, ninhydrin, and newer amine colorimetric assays, including their correlation with organoleptic ratings and VSC levels.

nodes.title: Chair-Side Test
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnostic methods for halitosis, including saliva incubation headspace analysis, electronic nose technology, and chair-side tests such as BANA, β-galactosidase, ninhydrin, and colorimetric amine assays. It then reviews treatment and management options, including chlorhexidine, essential oils, chlorine dioxide, two-phase oil-water rinses, triclosan, amine/stannous fluoride, hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing lozenges, baking soda, and metal salt solutions, with emphasis on zinc-based products and VSC conversion. Mechanisms, efficacy, comparative outcomes, and limitations are described for each approach.

nodes.title: Oral Rinses and Agents for Managing Breath Malodor
nodes.summary: The page covers various agents and formulations used to manage breath malodor. Chlorhexidine is highlighted as the most effective antiplaque and antigingivitis rinse, with VSC reduction but side effects. Essential oils, chlorine dioxide, two-phase oil-water rinses with CPC, triclosan, amine/stannous fluoride, hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing lozenges, and baking soda are each described for their mechanisms and clinical effects on oral malodor. The final section discusses conversion of volatile sulfur compounds by metal salt solutions, emphasizing zinc's effectiveness, safety, and synergy with other active ingredients in reducing VSCs and organoleptic scores.

nodes.title: Conversion of Volatile Sulfur Compounds
key_items: Chlorhexidine; Essential Oils; Chlorine Dioxide; Two-Phase Oil-Water Rinse; Triclosan; Amine Fluoride or Stannous Fluoride; Hydrogen Peroxide; Oxidizing Lozenges; Baking Soda
nodes.summary: The text reviews agents and methods for managing breath malodor, including chlorhexidine, essential oils, chlorine dioxide, two-phase oil-water rinses, triclosan, amine/stannous fluoride, hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing lozenges, baking soda, metal salt solutions (especially zinc), chewing gum, and masking strategies. It covers mechanisms, efficacy, side effects, and clinical study findings for each, and concludes with the importance of proper diagnosis and etiologic treatment of halitosis.

nodes.title: Masking the Malodor
nodes.summary: The text discusses approaches to managing breath malodor, including chewing gums with antibacterial, tea extract, or zinc acetate agents that reduce volatile sulfur compounds, and masking methods with rinses or lozenges that only provide short-term relief. Increasing saliva flow via chewing gum or liquid intake helps solubilize malodorous compounds. The conclusion emphasizes the socioeconomic and diagnostic importance of breath malodor, the need for proper etiologic diagnosis and treatment, and the importance of not overlooking serious diseases, using multidisciplinary consultation or trial intraoral therapies when needed. Further resources are referenced.

The section covers fundamentals of malodor detection, including the factors influencing odor perception—olfactory response, threshold concentration, odor power, volatility, and substantivity—with data on key malodorous compounds and their decay over time. It explains the need for log transformation of instrumental measurements to correlate with organoleptic scores and describes anosmia testing for odor judges. The rest of the section addresses breath malodor diagnostic methods: organoleptic assessment, Halimeter volatile sulfur monitoring, gas chromatography/OralChroma, microscopic and oropharyngeal examination, tongue-coating scoring, unreliability of self-assessment, saliva incubation testing, electronic nose technology, and chair-side tests. Management strategies include mechanical tongue cleaning, periodontal therapy, mouthrinses, chewing gum, and various agents (chlorhexidine, essential oils, chlorine dioxide, CPC, triclosan, amine/stannous fluoride, hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing lozenges, baking soda, and zinc/metal salt solutions), as well as masking and salivary flow enhancement. The section concludes by emphasizing proper etiologic diagnosis and treatment, the importance of not overlooking serious diseases, and the potential need for multidisciplinary consultation or trial therapies.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text covers treatments and management of breath malodor. It discusses chewing gum formulated with antibacterial agents, tea extracts, and zinc acetate to reduce volatile sulfur compounds, as well as masking methods and saliva stimulation. It concludes that proper diagnosis and etiologic treatment are crucial because malodor can signal serious diseases, and it recommends multidisciplinary consultation or trial therapy when needed. Additional materials, including a case scenario and references, are available on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
Masking the Malodor
nodes.summary: The text covers approaches to reducing and masking breath malodor, including antibacterial, tea-extract, and zinc acetate chewing gums; the limited benefit of pleasant-smelling masking agents; and the role of saliva flow. It concludes by emphasizing proper diagnosis and etiologic treatment, noting that tongue coating and periodontitis are common causes but other diseases must be considered. It then presents a case scenario of a 63-year-old woman with bleeding gums and bad breath, where the cause is tongue coating and periodontitis, and the recommended management includes explanation, oral hygiene instruction, and periodontal treatment.

nodes.title: 530.e1
nodes.summary: The text presents three case scenarios on breath malodor. The first case involves a 63-year-old woman with periodontitis and tongue coating causing halitosis, managed with explanation, oral hygiene instruction, and periodontal treatment. The second case describes a healthy young woman with perceived bad breath but normal objective measurements, diagnosed as pseudo-halitosis and treated with explanation, education, and reassurance. The third case involves a woman with halitosis caused by tonsil stones, referred to an ENT specialist. The chapter also illustrates use of organoleptic scoring and Halimeter volatile sulfur compound measurements in evaluating halitosis.

nodes.title: 530.e3
nodes.summary: The text is a chapter on breath malodor presenting Case Scenario 49.3, a 30-year-old woman with intermittent halitosis and throat stones. Clinical findings show good oral hygiene and healthy teeth/periodontium but inflamed tonsils with visible tonsil stones. Diagnostic scores indicate low nasal and tongue coating odor but higher oral cavity odor and elevated volatile sulfur compounds. The case-based questions identify tonsil stones as the most plausible cause and recommend referral to an ENT specialist. The chapter also includes a bibliography of 49 references on halitosis and related topics.

This section covers the diagnosis and management of breath malodor, including methods to reduce or mask it such as antibacterial, tea-extract, and zinc acetate chewing gums, the limited benefit of pleasant-smelling masking agents, and the role of saliva flow. It emphasizes the importance of proper diagnosis and etiologic treatment, with tongue coating and periodontitis as common causes. Several case scenarios illustrate halitosis caused by tongue coating and periodontitis, pseudo-halitosis, and tonsil stones, including appropriate management and ENT referral. The use of organoleptic scoring and Halimeter measurements is also described. The section ends with a bibliography of 49 references on halitosis and related topics.

nodes.title: References
530.e5
nodes.summary: The text is a reference list for a chapter on breath malodor (halitosis), covering its microbiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, clinical measurement, associated oral and systemic conditions, and treatment approaches. It includes studies on volatile sulfur compounds, tongue and periodontal bacteria, oral hygiene interventions such as mouthrinses, dentifrices, tongue scrapers, and chewing gums, as well as links to periodontal disease, Helicobacter pylori, gastroesophageal reflux, diabetes, liver and kidney diseases, and other systemic disorders. Epidemiological and psychological aspects, including halitosis prevalence, pseudohalitosis, and olfactory assessment, are also represented.

nodes.title: 530.e7
nodes.summary: The text begins with a bibliography of references on breath malodor research, including studies on volatile sulfur compounds, mouthrinses, and related clinical investigations. It then introduces Chapter 50 on scaling and root planing, covering the classification of periodontal instruments by purpose, instrument materials and design, and detailed information on periodontal probes, including their use, types, and features. The chapter also notes that some content is available only online.

The section consists largely of a numbered bibliography (references 1–49) for a chapter on halitosis/breath malodor. The cited works cover microbiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, clinical measurement, and treatment of halitosis, including volatile sulfur compounds, tongue and periodontal bacteria, oral hygiene products, and links to periodontal and systemic diseases, as well as epidemiological and psychological aspects. The section also transitions to Chapter 50 on scaling and root planing, describing the classification of periodontal instruments by purpose, instrument materials/design, and periodontal probes, with a note that some content is online only.

This section covers breath malodor (halitosis), defining it as socially unacceptable bad breath affecting about one in four people and causing significant psychosocial and economic impact. It classifies halitosis into genuine (physiologic or pathologic), pseudo-halitosis, and halitophobia, and identifies intraoral causes—especially tongue coating and periodontal disease—as responsible for about 90% of cases, with volatile sulfur compounds produced by oral bacteria; extraoral causes are also noted. Epidemiology shows variable prevalence (20%–35%), with self-reports overestimating the problem and no consistent sex or age differences except more frequent treatment-seeking by women. The section details diagnostic methods, including organoleptic testing, Halimeter measurements, gas chromatography/OralChroma, oropharyngeal and tongue examinations, saliva incubation, electronic nose, and chair-side tests, along with principles of odor perception. Management includes mechanical tongue cleaning, periodontal therapy, mouthrinses, chewing gums, various chemical agents, masking, and saliva stimulation. It emphasizes proper etiologic diagnosis because malodor can indicate serious disease, and mentions case scenarios and multidisciplinary referral. The section also includes online-only content, a reference bibliography, and a transition to Chapter 50.

nodes.title: 50 Scaling and Root Planing*
Chapter Outline
nodes.summary: The chapter covers scaling and root planing and classification of periodontal instruments by purpose: probes for pocket measurement, explorers for detecting deposits/caries, scaling/root-planing/curettage instruments with their subclasses, endoscopes for subgingival visualization, and cleansing/polishing instruments. It also discusses instrument materials and manufacturing, instrument parts (working end, shank, handle), selection of small instruments to avoid soft-tissue injury, and specific periodontal probe designs including the WHO and Nabers probes. Online-only content addresses general instrumentation principles, scaling and root planing principles, and instrument sharpening.

nodes.title: Classification of Periodontal Instruments
Periodontal Probes
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses scaling and root planing, emphasizing the classification, design, and use of periodontal instruments. It describes periodontal probes for measuring pockets, explorers for detecting deposits and caries, and various scaling/curettage instruments including sickle scalers, curettes, hoe/chisel/file scalers, implant instruments, and ultrasonic/sonic devices. It also covers periodontal endoscopes, polishing instruments, instrument materials and sharpening considerations, the parts of instruments, specific probe designs, probing technique, and explorer limitations. The chapter notes that additional online content covers general instrumentation principles, scaling and root planing techniques, and instrument sharpening.

nodes.title: Explorers
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instruments, focusing on their parts, types, and uses. It describes periodontal probes, including several specific calibrated designs and a furcation probe, and explorers used to detect subgingival deposits, caries, and root smoothness. It also explains pocket probing technique, introduces scaling and curettage instruments, and details the design and function of sickle scalers.

nodes.title: Scaling and Curettage Instruments
Sickle Scalers
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instrumentation and scaling/root planing instruments. It describes the basic parts of periodontal instruments and probes, lists various types of periodontal probes and explorers with their uses and limitations, and explains probing technique. It then details the five basic scaling instruments, focusing on sickle scalers and curettes. Sickle scaler design, uses, types, shank adaptations, and technique are described, and curettes are identified as the preferred instruments for deep subgingival scaling, root planing, and soft tissue curettage.

nodes.title: Curettes
Universal Curettes
nodes.summary: The text discusses periodontal instruments, focusing on curettes and their role in subgingival scaling and root planing. It describes the curette's design—spoon-shaped blade, rounded toe, cutting edges on both sides, and semicircular cross section—and explains why it is safer and more effective than sickle scalers for deep pockets. The text classifies curettes into universal and area-specific types. Universal curettes have blades at a 90-degree angle to the shank and can be adapted to most areas by changing finger rest, fulcrum, and hand position; examples include Barnhart, Columbia, Younger-Good, McCall's, and Indiana University curettes. Gracey curettes are described as area-specific instruments designed with angled blades for particular regions of the dentition.

nodes.title: Area-Specific Curettes
Gracey Curettes.
nodes.summary: The text describes periodontal curettes used in scaling and root planing, including their design features, advantages over sickle scalers, and classification into universal and area-specific types. Universal curettes work in most areas, have a 90-degree blade face, and use both cutting edges; Gracey area-specific curettes have offset blades, one working cutting edge, and specific indications for different tooth surfaces. It also covers Gracey pairings, differences between Gracey and universal curettes, rigid versus finishing shanks, newer Gracey #15-16 and #17-18 modifications, and extended-shank After Five curettes for deep pockets.

nodes.title: Extended-Shank Curettes.
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal scaling and root planing instruments, focusing on Gracey area-specific curettes, universal curettes, and their comparison. It describes modified Gracey designs (#15-16 for posterior mesial surfaces, #17-18 for posterior distal surfaces), extended-shank After Five curettes for deep pockets, and mini-bladed Mini Five curettes for difficult-access areas, including rigid and finishing variants and their clinical indications.

nodes.title: Mini-Bladed Curettes.
nodes.summary: The text describes various Gracey curette modifications and related instruments used in periodontal scaling and root planing, including After Five extended-shank curettes, Mini Five and Micro Mini Five mini-bladed curettes, Gracey Curvettes, periodontal maintenance curettes, and Langer/Mini-Langer curettes. It covers their design features, clinical indications, availability in rigid or finishing versions, and advantages for accessing difficult areas with reduced tissue trauma. It also mentions Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken instrument fragments.

nodes.title: Periodontal Curette Types and Instrument Variations
nodes.summary: The page covers periodontal instrument designs, especially mini-bladed and curette variations. It compares three mini-bladed anterior instruments, describes the development and features of periodontal maintenance Gracey curettes introduced in 2015, explains their modifications in blade size, angle, shank length, and rigidity, and notes their clinical indications and limitations. It also describes Langer and Mini-Langer curettes, which combine Gracey shanks with universal blades, and mentions Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken instrument fragments.

This section covers area-specific curettes used in periodontal scaling and root planing, focusing on Gracey curettes and their variations. It describes universal versus area-specific designs, Gracey features, pairings, and differences from universal curettes. It also details modified instruments including Gracey #15-16 and #17-18, extended-shank After Five curettes, mini-bladed Mini Five and Micro Mini Five curettes, Gracey Curvettes, periodontal maintenance curettes introduced in 2015, and Langer/Mini-Langer curettes. Rigid and finishing shank options, clinical indications, advantages for difficult-access areas, and Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken fragments are also covered.

The section opens by describing the five basic scaling instruments and then focuses on sickle scalers, including their design, supragingival use, subgingival limitations, stroke, and various blade sizes and shank types for different areas. It then introduces curettes as the preferred instruments for deep subgingival scaling and root planing, detailing their spoon-shaped blade, rounded toe, dual cutting edges, and semicircular cross section. Curettes are classified into universal and area-specific types: universal curettes have blades at a 90-degree angle to the shank and are adaptable to most areas, while area-specific Gracey curettes have angled blades for specific regions. The section also covers modified curette designs such as After Five, Mini Five, Micro Mini Five, Curvettes, periodontal maintenance curettes, and Langer/Mini-Langer curettes, along with rigid and finishing shank options and Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken fragments.

nodes.title: Schwartz Periotrievers
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instrumentation, including mini-bladed instruments, periodontal maintenance Gracey curettes and their design features and clinical indications, Langer and Mini-Langer curettes, Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken tips, plastic and titanium instruments for implant maintenance, and hoe scalers for calculus ledges.

nodes.title: Plastic and Titanium Instruments for Implants
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instruments, including Langer curettes, a magnetic Periotriever for retrieving broken instrument tips, plastic and titanium instruments for implant maintenance, and hoe scalers for calculus ledges. It emphasizes using plastic or titanium instruments on implants to prevent damage, describes mini-bladed titanium curettes for gentle biofilm and light calculus removal, notes their limitations with heavy deposits and peri-implantitis, and details the design and use of hoe scalers.

nodes.title: Hoe Scalers
key_items: Plastic and Titanium Instruments for Implants
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instrumentation, including Langer curettes, retrieval of broken instrument tips with the Schwartz Periotriever, plastic and titanium instruments for implant maintenance, and detailed descriptions of hoe scalers, files, and chisel scalers. It emphasizes proper use, design features, indications, and precautions to avoid damaging tooth roots or implants.

nodes.title: Files
nodes.summary: The text describes dental scaling and root planing instruments, including implant curettes, hoe scalers, files, and chisel scalers. It covers their designs, specific uses, and precautions: hoe scalers use two-point contact and a pull stroke for stability; McCall's set provides access to all tooth surfaces; files break up heavy calculus but risk root damage and are not for fine scaling, with mini-bladed curettes preferred; chisel scalers are for tight proximal surfaces in anterior teeth. A learning box reinforces the primary function of files.

nodes.title: Chisel Scalers
nodes.summary: This text from a chapter on scaling and root planing describes periodontal instrumentation. It covers hoe scalers (two-point contact, pull stroke, McCall's set), files (crushing calculus but risk of gouging), chisel scalers for tight proximal surfaces, Quétin furcation curettes for furcation deposits, diamond-coated files for final root finishing, a brief reference to ultrasonic/sonic instruments, and the dental endoscope for subgingival viewing. It also illustrates titanium implant curettes and other instruments in figures.

nodes.title: Periodontal Instruments: Curettes, Diamond Files, Ultrasonic, Endoscope
nodes.summary: This page covers periodontal instrumentation. It first describes a chisel used from the facial surface with a push motion to remove calculus without nicking the tooth. It then discusses Quétin furcation curettes, which are hoe-like instruments with shallow half-moon tips for furcation areas, available in small and larger widths to remove burnished calculus and minimize root damage. Diamond-coated files are described as fine-grit abrasive instruments used for final root surface finishing, especially with a dental endoscope, to remove residual deposits and create a smooth polished surface while avoiding overinstrumentation. Ultrasonic and sonic instruments are noted for biofilm removal, scaling, curetting, and stain removal. Finally, the dental endoscope is described as a subgingival fiberoptic system with disposable sheath, irrigation, and video imaging for diagnosis and treatment.

nodes.title: Dental Endoscope
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instruments and techniques: a curved chisel for proximal calculus removal; Quétin furcation curettes for accessing recessed furcation deposits; diamond-coated files for final root surface finishing and polishing; ultrasonic/sonic instruments for biofilm and calculus removal; the Perioscopy dental endoscope for subgingival visualization, debridement guidance, and evaluation of caries, restorations, fractures, and resorption; and rubber cups and bristle brushes for coronal cleansing and polishing. It also emphasizes precautions to avoid root, cementum, and gingival damage.

This section covers scaling and curettage instruments, beginning with basic periodontal instrument parts, probes, explorers, and probing technique. It details sickle scalers and curettes—including universal and area-specific Gracey designs and modified curettes—as key scaling tools. It also covers Schwartz Periotrievers for retrieving broken tips, plastic and titanium instruments for implant maintenance, hoe scalers, files, chisel scalers, Quétin furcation curettes, diamond-coated files, ultrasonic/sonic instruments, the dental endoscope, and polishing aids such as rubber cups and bristle brushes, with emphasis on proper technique and precautions to avoid damaging teeth, roots, gingiva, or implants.

nodes.title: Cleansing and Polishing Instruments
nodes.summary: The text discusses the Perioscopy dental endoscope system for subgingival visualization and instrumentation, which detects deposits, enables thorough root debridement, and evaluates subgingival conditions. It then covers cleansing and polishing instruments: rubber cups, bristle brushes, dental tape, and air-powder polishing devices, including their uses, precautions, and limitations. It highlights the effectiveness of glycine or erythritol powder air polishing for biofilm removal, especially subgingivally and on implants, and lists contraindications and safety measures for air-powder polishing. Finally, it summarizes that periodontal instruments serve examination, calculus/biofilm removal, and root planing, with additional details online.

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.summary: The text covers subgingival air polishing with a specialized disposable tip using glycine or erythritol powder, noting its effectiveness for biofilm removal without soft tissue abrasion compared to manual or ultrasonic instruments. It lists contraindications and precautions, including medical conditions, powder selection, aerosol risks, chlorhexidine rinse, and high-speed evacuation. It then summarizes the chapter's scope on periodontal instruments and root planing, followed by general principles of instrumentation covering positioning, visibility, retraction, instrument design, and fundamental handling concepts. Finally, it details patient and operator positioning for accessibility and methods for achieving visibility, illumination, and retraction during periodontal procedures.

The section classifies and describes periodontal instruments, covering their parts, materials, sharpening, and general handling principles. It details examination instruments such as periodontal probes and explorers, scaling and curettage instruments including sickle scalers, curettes, specialized and implant instruments, and ultrasonic/sonic devices. It also covers advanced aids like periodontal endoscopy and polishing instruments, with emphasis on air-powder polishing for biofilm removal, including indications, contraindications, and safety precautions. The section further addresses instrumentation principles such as patient and operator positioning, visibility, illumination, and retraction.

nodes.title: General Principles of Instrumentation
Accessibility: Positioning of Patient and Operator
nodes.summary: The text covers general principles of periodontal instrumentation, emphasizing proper positioning of the patient and operator, illumination, retraction, sharp instruments, awareness of tooth morphology and tissue condition, and knowledge of instrument design. It details operator and patient positioning for maxillary and mandibular arches, the use of direct and indirect vision/illumination with a mouth mirror, and retraction techniques using the mirror and fingers to ensure visibility and accessibility during scaling and root planing.

nodes.title: Visibility, Illumination, and Retraction
key_items: General Principles of Instrumentation; LEARNING BOX e50.1
nodes.summary: The text covers the general principles of periodontal instrumentation, including patient and operator positioning for accessibility, illumination and visibility via direct or indirect methods, retraction techniques and precautions, instrument sharpness and maintenance, and maintaining a clean operative field. It emphasizes that effective instrumentation requires proper posture, visibility, sharp instruments, knowledge of tooth morphology and instrument design, grasp and stroke concepts, and management of saliva, blood, and debris during procedures.

nodes.title: Condition and Sharpness of Instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers clinical periodontal procedures, including retraction techniques using mirrors and fingers, precautions to protect lips and avoid herpetic lesions, the importance of sharp, sterile instruments for effective and atraumatic scaling, and methods to maintain a clear operative field using suction, gauze, water, and air while noting that gingival bleeding may be due to inflammation rather than technique.

nodes.title: Maintaining a Clean Field
nodes.summary: The text covers methods for achieving visibility and access during periodontal instrumentation, including retraction techniques, precautions for lip protection, and the preference for direct vision and illumination. It emphasizes the need for clean, sterile, sharp instruments and a clear operative field managed by suction, gauze, water, and air. It also discusses instrumentation stability, focusing on the modified pen grasp as the optimal grasp for periodontal instruments, the limitations of the palm and thumb grasp, and the importance of a finger rest as a stable fulcrum.

nodes.title: Instrument Stabilization
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal instrumentation, including gingival retraction techniques, the importance of instrument stabilization, the modified pen grasp as the preferred instrument grasp, finger rests and fulcrums (intraoral and extraoral) and their variations, and instrument activation through adaptation. It emphasizes the need for stability, control, and precise adaptation to avoid injury and achieve effective instrumentation.

nodes.title: Instrument Activation
Adaptation
nodes.summary: The text discusses extraoral fulcrums and instrument activation in scaling and root planing. It describes palm-up and palm-down extraoral fulcrums for maxillary posterior instrumentation, and reinforcement of fulcrums using the index finger or thumb. It then explains two key aspects of instrument activation: adaptation, which is placing the working end against the tooth contour correctly, and angulation, which is the angle between the blade face and tooth surface. Correct adaptation and angulation are essential to avoid tissue trauma, ensure effective calculus removal, and properly scale, root plane, and insert instruments.

nodes.title: Angulation
nodes.summary: The text covers instrumentation principles in scaling and root planing, including the three segments of a Gracey curette blade, proper blade adaptation using the lower third with handle rolling, correct angulation (0 degrees for insertion, 45–90 degrees for scaling/root planing, greater than 90 degrees for gingival curettage, and the burnishing effects of incorrect angulation), lateral pressure control (firm/moderate/light, avoiding burnishing or root gouging), and the three basic stroke types (exploratory, scaling, root-planing) with vertical, oblique, and horizontal directions. It also discusses factors determining stroke use, the characteristics of exploratory and scaling strokes, the wrist/forearm versus finger motion debate, and the push stroke technique.

nodes.title: Lateral Pressure
nodes.summary: The text covers instrumentation principles in scaling and root planing, including angulation for curettage, lateral pressure control to avoid burnishing or root damage, the three stroke types (exploratory, scaling, and root-planing), stroke directions, factors determining stroke use, and the debated roles of wrist/forearm versus finger motion, including push stroke technique.

nodes.title: Strokes
key_items: Lateral Pressure; LEARNING BOX e50.12; LEARNING BOX e50.14
nodes.summary: The text covers instrumentation techniques for scaling and root planing, including gingival curettage angulation, lateral pressure control and its effects, the three stroke types (exploratory, scaling, root-planing) and their directions and determinants, stroke activation methods with wrist/forearm versus finger motion, and the contraindication of push strokes. It also describes the design, use, adaptation, advantages, and limitations of universal curettes, followed by the unique features and area-specific pairings of Gracey curettes.

The section covers instrument activation in scaling and root planing, including extraoral fulcrums for maxillary posterior areas, proper adaptation of the working end to the tooth, correct angulation for insertion, scaling/root planing, and curettage, lateral pressure control, the three basic stroke types and their directions, activation using wrist/forearm versus finger motion and push stroke considerations, and the design, use, and features of universal and Gracey curettes.

It describes the root-planing stroke, universal curette design and adaptation, and the limitations of universal curettes. It then details Gracey curettes, including their area specificity, unique design features, correct cutting edge selection, offset blade angulation, and principles of use. Extended-shank and mini-bladed Gracey curettes are discussed in terms of indications, technique, and effectiveness. Finally, the text defines scaling and root planing, states their primary objective of restoring gingival health, and notes the microbiological shift toward health-associated bacteria after instrumentation.

This section covers the general principles of periodontal instrumentation. It addresses patient and operator positioning for accessibility in both arches, illumination and visibility through direct and indirect methods with a mouth mirror, and retraction techniques using the mirror and fingers, with precautions to protect the lips and avoid herpetic lesions. It emphasizes the importance of sharp, sterile instruments and maintaining a clean operative field using suction, gauze, water, and air. Instrument stabilization is discussed through the modified pen grasp, finger rests, and intraoral/extraoral fulcrums. Instrument activation includes adaptation of the working end, correct angulation for insertion, scaling/root planing, and curettage, lateral pressure control, three basic stroke types and directions, and activation using wrist/forearm versus finger motion. The section also details scaling and root planing instruments, specifically universal curettes and their limitations, Gracey curettes with their area specificity and design features, and extended-shank and mini-bladed Gracey curettes. Finally, it defines scaling and root planing, states that the primary objective is restoring gingival health, and notes the microbiological shift toward health-associated bacteria after instrumentation.

nodes.title: Principles of Scaling and Root Planing
Definitions and Rationale
key_items: Mini-Bladed Gracey Curettes; LEARNING BOX e50.23; LEARNING BOX e50.24; LEARNING BOX e50.26
Principles of Scaling and Root Planing Definitions and Rationale
nodes.summary: The text covers the characteristics, uses, and clinical guidelines for mini-bladed Gracey curettes, emphasizing their role in supplementing conventional instruments for difficult-to-access areas, specific handle and stroke recommendations, and evidence of their effectiveness. It then explains the definitions and rationale of scaling and root planing, including their objective to restore gingival health by removing biofilm, calculus, and endotoxin, the differences and relationship between the two procedures, the need to avoid excessive root substance removal, and the importance of treatment planning and mastery of these skills. Finally, it describes visual and tactile detection skills necessary for assessing deposits and root irregularities before and during instrumentation.

nodes.title: Detection Skills
key_items: LEARNING BOX e50.29; LEARNING BOX e50.31
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal scaling and root planing. It contrasts enamel and root-surface deposits, noting that root calculus requires removal of a portion of the root surface but that excessive dentin/cementum removal should be avoided. It emphasizes that scaling and root planing are part of the initial treatment phase, with appointment planning based on multiple clinical factors, and that mastery of these skills is essential. It also covers detection skills, including visual and tactile examination of deposits and irregularities. It describes supragingival scaling techniques and instruments, then explains the greater difficulty of subgingival scaling and root planing, including instrument choices and limitations, and concludes with the use of universal or area-specific (Gracey) curettes.

nodes.title: Supragingival Scaling Technique
nodes.summary: The text covers instrumentation for scaling and root planing, emphasizing that detection skills are as important as technique. It describes supragingival scaling, including the instruments used, proper technique, and precautions with sickles. It then discusses the greater complexity of subgingival scaling and root planing, the challenges posed by harder, tenacious calculus and soft tissue, the reliance on tactile sensitivity, the advantages of curettes, the use of other instruments such as sickles, hoes, files, and ultrasonic tips, and the need for careful assessment and follow-up instrumentation.

nodes.title: Subgingival Scaling and Root-Planing Technique
Periodontal Scaling Techniques: Supragingival and Subgingival Instrumentation
key_items: 545.e14 PART 3 CliniCAl PERiodonTiCs; LEARNING BOX e50.34; LEARNING BOX e50.35; LEARNING BOX e50.36; LEARNING BOX e50.37
nodes.summary: This page from Part 3 Clinical Periodontics covers supragingival and subgingival scaling techniques. It emphasizes that detection skills are as important as scaling and root-planing mastery. Supragingival scaling is easier due to direct visibility and freedom of movement; sickles, curettes, and ultrasonic/sonic instruments are used, with specific adaptation, angulation, and stroke technique. Subgingival scaling and root planing are more difficult because calculus is harder and more tenacious, tissue and bleeding obscure vision, and pocket walls restrict strokes. The curette is preferred, but other instruments such as sickles, hoes, files, and ultrasonic devices are also discussed, including their limitations and hazards. The page also notes that thin ultrasonic tips on low power may burnish heavy calculus, so ultrasonic scaling must be followed by explorer assessment and further curette instrumentation when needed.

nodes.title: Area-Specific (Gracey) Curettes

nodes.summary: The text describes procedures for sharpening dental curettes. For universal curettes, the operator uses a palm grasp, braces the arm, applies the stone to the lateral surface at 100–110 degrees to the blade face, and uses short strokes from shank to toe while preserving the rounded toe and minimizing wire edges. Sharpening the face of the blade is discouraged because it causes improper beveling, weakens the blade, and creates wire edges. For Gracey curettes, the same lateral-surface technique is used, but the blade is offset, and only the lower outer cutting edge is sharpened; the curved contour must be preserved. Extended-shank, mini-bladed, and periodontal maintenance Gracey curettes are sharpened in the same manner despite having different blade lengths.

546.e1
CHAPTER 51 Sonic and Ultrasonic Instrumentation and Irrigation
Abstract
Power scalers such as sonic scalers, magnetostrictive, and piezo scalers are mainstays of clinical practice. They are efficient tools for both deplaquing and calculus removal. For home use, the pulsating oral irrigator, also called a water flosser, can help remove plaque and prevent and reduce gingivitis.

nodes.title: Home and Self-Applied Irrigation
nodes.summary: The text discusses oral irrigation as a self-care periodontal measure. It notes the limitation of ultrasonic deplaquing due to limited lateral subgingival lavage dispersion. The oral irrigator, introduced in 1962 and now commonly called a water flosser, is supported by evidence as safe and effective for improving periodontal health, removing biofilm, and being comparable to dental floss when added to brushing. Its mechanism relies on pulsation and pressure: decompression allows subgingival penetration, compression expels bacteria and debris, and shear hydraulic forces remove biofilm. Effective home units deliver 1200–1400 pulses per minute at at least 60 psi, and higher pressures are safe. The text cautions that research from one irrigator brand should not be applied to other brands because settings differ. It also includes figures illustrating pulsation zones and examples of dental water jet devices.

nodes.title: Mechanism of Action of Irrigation

The text describes recommended device specifications, various tip types for supragingival and subgingival use, and addresses safety concerns, emphasizing that clinical evidence refutes myths about tissue trauma, bacterial penetration, increased pocket depth, and elevated bacteremia risk. It summarizes clinical outcomes showing improvements in gingivitis, bleeding, probing depth, biofilm removal, and periodontal pathogens, often exceeding string floss when added to brushing. It also highlights benefits for special populations such as orthodontic, implant, crown/bridge, and diabetic patients, and notes that antimicrobial agents can enhance irrigation effects.

nodes.title: Clinical Outcomes of Irrigation

Evidence shows irrigation reduces biofilm, bacteria, pathogens, gingivitis, bleeding on probing, inflammation, and probing depth, while improving oral health in patients with gingivitis, implants, orthodontics, crown/bridge work, diabetes, and periodontal maintenance. Historical and emerging studies show irrigation can outperform flossing, especially when added to toothbrushing, and antimicrobial agents enhance results. Special tips benefit orthodontic and implant patients. The provided text ends mid-sentence.

Irrigation is effective for various patient groups, including those with orthodontics, implants, diabetes, and periodontal maintenance, and may outperform flossing in some measures. Antimicrobial agents enhance irrigation effects, and the irrigator removes biofilm effectively. Special tips benefit implant and orthodontic patients, and irrigator use after scaling is comparable to minocycline therapy. The conclusion highlights that power scalers can be used for all scaling purposes with outcomes similar to hand instrumentation, and home irrigation is safe and effective for a broad range of patients.

It also discusses pharmacologic implications, guidelines for antibiotic use as adjuncts to scaling and root planing, plaque sampling, evidence-based benefits and limitations, biofilm considerations, decision-making factors, and a conclusion noting that adjunctive antibiotics like metronidazole and tetracycline provide small additional attachment gains, with decisions based on clinical findings, patient history, and preferences.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text covers the role of systemic antibiotics as adjuncts to scaling and root planing in treating periodontal diseases. It summarizes evidence that antibiotics improve attachment levels, particularly tetracycline and metronidazole, but are not effective alone. It emphasizes the need for physical biofilm disruption, the limitations in current knowledge about antibiotic selection, dosage, timing, long-term outcomes, and risks, and the importance of individualized clinical decision-making. It concludes that scaling and root planing alone are effective, adjunctive antibiotics provide modest additional benefits without significant adverse effects, and treatment decisions should integrate clinical findings, patient history, preferences, and discussions of risks and benefits. Chapter highlights and companion website resources are also noted.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text covers systemic anti-infective therapy for periodontal diseases, emphasizing evidence that systemic antibiotics, particularly tetracycline and metronidazole, as adjuncts to scaling and root planing improve attachment levels, especially in aggressive periodontitis, while stand-alone antibiotics are not beneficial. It highlights the importance of biofilm disruption, limitations in evidence about antibiotic regimens and risks, and the need for individualized clinical decision-making based on patient history and findings. The conclusion states that scaling and root planing alone are effective and adjunctive antibiotics provide modest additional gains without significant adverse effects. It also includes chapter highlights, a case scenario of localized aggressive periodontitis in a penicillin-allergic patient, and a reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text contains the Chapter 52 reference list on systemic anti-infective periodontal therapy and the beginning of Chapter 53 on locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials. It explains the rationale for local controlled-release antimicrobials in treating chronic periodontitis, their use as monotherapy or adjuncts to scaling and root planing, and the evidence-based approach to their clinical application. It describes the U.S. products available, including chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, and minocycline microspheres, and notes the prototype tetracycline fiber. Detailed information is provided on the chlorhexidine chip and doxycycline gel, including composition, storage, placement, indications, mechanism of action, and clinical considerations.

This section is Chapter 52 on systemic anti-infective therapy for periodontal diseases, authored by Ciancio and Mariotti. It explains that subgingival bacterial biofilms invade tissues and resist host defenses and antibiotics, making mechanical debridement essential and systemic antibiotics adjunctive. It defines anti-infective agents, antibiotics, antiseptics, disinfectants, bacteriostatic/bactericidal actions, and the dual mechanisms of tetracyclines. It reviews major antibiotic classes—tetracyclines, metronidazole, penicillins (amoxicillin and amoxicillin-clavulanate), cephalosporins, clindamycin, ciprofloxacin, and macrolides/azithromycin—including pharmacology, dosing, efficacy, adverse effects, precautions, and azithromycin cardiovascular risks. It covers sensitivity testing, combination/serial regimens such as metronidazole–amoxicillin and metronidazole–ciprofloxacin for aggressive/refractory periodontitis, antibiotic resistance, patient compliance and counseling, risk factors, host immune modulation/possible NSAIDs, and the lack of standardized evidence. The conclusion is that scaling and root planing alone are effective, adjunctive antibiotics, particularly tetracycline and metronidazole, give modest attachment gains without significant adverse effects, and decisions should be individualized based on clinical findings, patient history, and preferences. The section also includes a panoramic image, a case scenario of localized aggressive periodontitis in a penicillin-allergic patient, chapter highlights, companion website resources, and references, and transitions into Chapter 53 on locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials, describing the chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, minocycline microspheres, and prototype tetracycline fiber.

nodes.title: 53 Locally Delivered, Controlled-Release Antimicrobials
Chapter 53: Locally Delivered, Controlled-Release Antimicrobials
nodes.summary: The page covers Chapter 53 on locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials for treating chronic periodontitis. It explains that these agents are placed directly into periodontal pockets to maintain effective drug levels, unlike systemic or rinse-based chemical therapies, and are used as monotherapy or adjuncts to scaling and root planing. It lists the U.S. products—chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, and minocycline microspheres—and mentions the tetracycline fiber as the prototype no longer available. The chlorhexidine chip is described in detail: its size, drug content, biodegradable gelatin matrix, storage, placement, clinical indication, 7–10 day drug release, antimicrobial mechanism, lack of microbial flora alteration, and need to avoid flossing for 10 days. The doxycycline gel section describes its two-syringe composition, storage, and final 10% doxycycline hyclate formulation.

nodes.title: Doxycycline Gel
nodes.summary: The text reviews locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials for chronic periodontitis. It explains that chronic periodontitis is a bacterial infection and that while SRP is effective, conventional chemical approaches have limited benefit. Local controlled-release agents provide direct, sustained antimicrobial delivery into periodontal pockets and are safe and effective, often used adjunctively with SRP. It describes the U.S. products: chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, and minocycline microspheres, along with the discontinued but historically relevant tetracycline fiber. Specific details are given for the chlorhexidine chip and doxycycline gel. The abstract emphasizes that randomized clinical trials show these agents either match SRP alone or enhance SRP outcomes, especially by increasing the proportion of patients with ≥2 mm pocket depth reduction. Preliminary evidence supports use in maintenance, but more research is needed, and clinicians should consider routinely offering adjunctive local antimicrobial therapy with SRP.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text discusses locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. It highlights SRP as the effective foundation of treatment, reducing microbial flora and PPD, and describes three available antimicrobials: minocycline, doxycycline, and chlorhexidine. Evidence shows they are equivalent to SRP alone or more effective as adjuncts, with clinician consensus favoring adjunctive use. Multiple RCTs confirm adjunctive therapy improves PPD reduction, including a higher percentage of patients achieving ≥2 mm reduction. Preliminary data support their use in long-term maintenance, though more trials are needed. The text notes these agents may be underutilized and advocates for routine adjunctive use with SRP according to package inserts.

It then explains the rationale for local controlled release: periodontitis is a multifactorial bacterial infection, mechanical therapy alone is insufficient, GCF flow and biofilm resistance require high local drug concentrations that only controlled-release formulations can achieve, and systemic delivery is not equivalent.

nodes.title: Drug Development and Registration
Locally Delivered, Controlled-Release Antimicrobials: Magnitude of the Effect
key_items: Pharmacokinetics; Chlorhexidine Chip; Doxycycline Gel; Minocycline Microspheres
Locally Delivered, Controlled-Release Antimicrobials: Magnitude of the Effect
nodes.summary: This text covers the pharmacokinetics and clinical effectiveness of locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials for chronic periodontitis. It explains the rationale for local delivery, gives detailed pharmacokinetic profiles for the chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, and minocycline microspheres, and describes drug development and regulatory considerations. It reports a systematic literature search and summarizes clinical trial results organized by trial size: larger phase III–style trials show that SRP plus a locally delivered antimicrobial significantly improves probing depth reduction over SRP alone, while smaller trials yield mixed hypothesis-generating results. The text then addresses statistical versus clinical significance, concluding that the approximately 0.2–0.7 mm additional probing depth reduction is clinically meaningful, parallels the benefit seen with periodontal surgery compared with SRP, and is supported by multiple consensus statements and adequate well-controlled trials.

nodes.title: Statistical Versus Clinical Significance
nodes.summary: This text reviews clinical evidence and regulatory considerations for locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials as adjuncts to scaling and root planing (SRP). Trials are categorized by sample size and robustness: larger phase III-like trials consistently show significantly greater probing depth reductions with adjunctive therapy versus SRP alone (mean differences about 0.2–0.7 mm), while smaller trials are mixed and hypothesis-generating; monotherapy with local delivery is at least equivalent to SRP. It explains statistical versus clinical significance, noting that small absolute differences can still be clinically meaningful, especially with percentage improvements of 22%–68%, greater proportions achieving ≥2 mm probing depth reduction, and comparisons to periodontal surgery; an osteoporosis trial (zoledronic acid vs placebo) illustrates this principle. The text also covers drug development phases (I–IV), FDA registration requirements, the need for adequate and well-controlled phase III trials, and trial design considerations including type I/type II error control and alpha ≤ .05. Overall, adjunctive therapy is considered statistically and clinically significant, though more trials are needed.

nodes.title: Phases of Drug Development
nodes.summary: The text discusses locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials in periodontal therapy, noting that surgical and nonsurgical outcomes are generally similar and that adjunctive local antimicrobial therapy is statistically and clinically significant, illustrated by an osteoporosis trial showing large relative risk reduction despite low absolute rates. It also covers drug development phases before FDA approval, specialized pharmacology studies, regulatory clearance requirements, and trial design considerations, emphasizing type I error control and alpha levels.

nodes.title: Surgical Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers adjunctive therapies to nonsurgical periodontal treatment, focusing on locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials. It discusses evidence for local antimicrobials and systemic low-dose doxycycline as adjuncts to SRP, the uncertain benefit of combining them, and results from a factorial trial involving SRP, systemic antimicrobials, and surgery. It also examines locally delivered antimicrobials as adjuncts to surgical and regenerative periodontal procedures, noting promising pilot results but the need for controlled trials and lack of regulatory approval. Finally, it addresses peri-implantitis, presenting studies in which minocycline microspheres or doxycycline gel improved clinical outcomes around implants compared with control treatments.

nodes.title: Peri-implantitis
nodes.summary: This text from a clinical periodontics chapter discusses locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials as adjunctive periodontal therapy. It covers combination adjunctive therapy with host-modulating agents, use after surgical and regenerative periodontal procedures, off-label treatment of peri-implantitis, effects in smokers, adverse effects and cautions, and cost-effectiveness considerations. Evidence suggests adjunctive local antimicrobials can enhance SRP outcomes and possibly surgical results, though comparative and long-term data are limited. No definitive conclusions can be made regarding the most efficacious adjunctive regimen, and additional well-controlled trials are needed for several applications.

nodes.title: Locally Delivered Controlled-Release Antimicrobials: Peri-Implantitis, Smoking, Safety, Costs
key_items: Adverse Effects and Cautions for Use
nodes.summary: The page covers the use of locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials in peri-implantitis and periodontitis, including a clinical study showing potential benefit but lacking a control group; evidence that adjunctive therapy may help smokers but remains inconclusive; FDA-labeled cautions and adverse effects; and cost-effectiveness considerations, including a chlorhexidine chip trial and a comparative economic analysis.

nodes.title: Costs and Outcomes
key_items: Adverse Effects and Cautions for Use
nodes.summary: The text discusses locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. It covers a peri-implantitis study where adjunctive minocycline microspheres or photodynamic therapy after mechanical debridement reduced probing depth and microbial/inflammatory markers but lacked a control group and showed no between-group differences; these agents are not labeled for peri-implantitis but warrant Phase III trials. Smoking is reviewed as a risk factor, with evidence that adjunctive antimicrobials enhance SRP in smokers similarly to nonsmokers, though a systematic review found insufficient specific evidence. Adverse effects and cautions include hypersensitivity, microbial overgrowth, pregnancy, tooth discoloration (tetracyclines), avoiding abscessed sites, and postponing mechanical hygiene; common reactions include headache, infection, pain, toothache, and oral symptoms, with toothache significantly higher for chlorhexidine chips. Costs and outcomes are addressed: adjunctive therapy adds costs but may reduce surgical needs and tooth loss; a cost-effectiveness ranking (tetracycline fibers > chlorhexidine chips > minocycline microspheres) was criticized for its method. Meta-analyses show clinical attachment and probing depth benefits, and some evidence suggests reduced alveolar bone loss and bone resorption markers. Non-U.S. agents have less robust data, but a meta-analysis supports additional probing depth reduction. Future research needs include long-term maintenance trials, registries, new indications, and cost-effectiveness studies.

nodes.title: Clinical Studies of Non-U.S. Agents
nodes.summary: The text covers adjunctive locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials in periodontal therapy: microbiologic effects of minocycline microspheres on red complex bacteria, radiographic bone changes with chlorhexidine chips, effects on bone-resorption and inflammatory GCF markers, cost-effectiveness concepts, trials of non-U.S. agents, a meta-analysis supporting additional probing depth reduction, and future research directions including long-term maintenance studies and new indications.

nodes.title: Considerations for Future Research
nodes.summary: The text covers the clinical evidence, microbiologic effects, radiographic and biomarker outcomes, cost-effectiveness, non-U.S. product trials, future research directions, case examples, and conclusions regarding locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials as adjuncts to scaling and root planing in periodontal therapy. It highlights reductions in red complex bacteria with minocycline microspheres, potential effects on bone loss and inflammatory markers, the need for robust trials and cost-effectiveness evaluation, ongoing research into growth factors and anti-inflammatory/other agents, and the overall conclusion that these adjunctive therapies are effective, safe, and should be incorporated based on evidence rather than personal experience.

The section covers the clinical use of locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials as adjuncts to scaling and root planing. It addresses evidence for efficacy in reducing probing depth and enhancing SRP outcomes; FDA approval, informed consent, and legal implications; off-label use in combination adjunctive therapy, surgical/regenerative procedures, and peri-implantitis; effects in smokers; adverse effects and cautions; costs and cost-effectiveness; microbiologic, radiographic, and biomarker outcomes; and non-U.S. agents. Future research directions include long-term maintenance trials, registries, new indications, cost-effectiveness studies, and growth factor/anti-inflammatory agents. Overall, adjunctive local antimicrobials appear effective and safe, but comparative, long-term, and cost-effectiveness data are limited, no definitive most efficacious regimen can be concluded, and further well-controlled trials are needed.

nodes.title: Case Reports

It reviews current and investigational agents and clinical trials, such as chlorhexidine chips, PDGF-BB with beta-TCP, FGF2, trafermin, sargramostim, and flurbiprofen, as well as preclinical and experimental therapies. Case report indications include adjunctive or monotherapy use. The conclusion emphasizes that adjunctive locally delivered antimicrobials significantly improve SRP outcomes and that clinical decisions should be evidence-based.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: The text covers locally delivered controlled-release antimicrobials in nonsurgical periodontal therapy, including clinical cases showing that localized SRP plus minocycline microspheres reduces probing depths and bleeding. It reviews research on chlorhexidine chips, growth factors, NSAIDs, and many other experimental agents. Evidence supports adjunctive use as significantly more effective than SRP alone with a known safety profile, and SRP plus adjunctive therapy may become the new standard. A case scenario and case-based questions address patient selection, minocycline's mechanism of action, and U.S. product availability, followed by an extensive reference list.

The text then introduces Chapter 54 on host modulation, covering its definition, historical introduction by Williams and Golub, the paradigm shift in understanding periodontitis pathogenesis, the role of host response in disease susceptibility, systemic disease associations highlighted in the Surgeon General's report, and the chapter's outline including systemic/local agents, sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline, and emerging therapies.

Section 53 covers locally delivered, controlled-release antimicrobials for chronic periodontitis. It explains the rationale for placing antimicrobials directly into periodontal pockets to achieve sustained therapeutic levels, describes U.S. products (chlorhexidine chip, doxycycline gel, minocycline microspheres) and the discontinued tetracycline fiber prototype, and provides specific details on the chlorhexidine chip and doxycycline gel. It reviews pharmacokinetics showing high crevicular fluid levels with low systemic exposure, clinical trial evidence supporting equivalence or adjunctive superiority to SRP alone—particularly for ≥2 mm pocket depth reductions—and preliminary support in maintenance. It also addresses drug development/regulatory issues, off-label uses, clinical considerations such as smokers, adverse effects, cost-effectiveness, and outcomes; case reports; experimental agents; and conclusions favoring adjunctive use with SRP. The section includes case-based questions and references, and transitions to Chapter 54 on host modulation.

nodes.title: 54 Host Modulation
CHAPTER 54
nodes.summary: The text covers the concept of host modulation in periodontal therapy, including its definition, historical development, and the evolving understanding of periodontitis as a disease influenced by host response rather than plaque alone. It discusses the connection between periodontal and systemic diseases, the role of host modulation therapy as an adjunct to mechanical treatment, and the clinical use of sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD) as the only approved systemically administered host-modulating agent. It also addresses comprehensive periodontal management, potential applications to other chronic inflammatory diseases, and future directions for host modulatory therapies.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text discusses periodontitis as a disease driven by both bacterial pathogens and destructive host responses, and emphasizes the need for integrated treatment addressing both components. Host modulation therapy, particularly sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD) as an adjunct to scaling and root planing, is highlighted as an effective approach supported by clinical trials. SDD should be used within a comprehensive periodontal treatment strategy including antibacterial measures and risk factor management. The text also notes potential applications of HMT to other chronic systemic diseases, the future development of additional HMTs, and the broader health impact of managing periodontal inflammation.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: This text covers the role of host modulation therapy (HMT) in managing periodontitis. It explains that periodontitis results from both bacterial pathogens and destructive host immune-inflammatory responses, and that HMT aims to reduce excessive tissue destruction while preserving normal defenses. The only approved systemic HMT is sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD), used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing within a comprehensive treatment plan. The text also discusses the host response as the main driver of tissue breakdown, the mechanisms of HMT, potential benefits for other chronic inflammatory diseases, and systemically administered agents such as NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, and tetracyclines. It specifically details NSAIDs' mechanism, study findings, and side effects, and the passage ends mid-sentence regarding long-term NSAID periodontal benefits.

nodes.title: Systemically Administered Agents
nodes.summary: The text covers host modulation therapy (HMT) for periodontitis, emphasizing that the host immune-inflammatory response to plaque bacteria causes most periodontal tissue destruction. It explains the pathogenesis, the balance between destructive and protective mediators, risk factors, and HMT targets. It reviews systemically administered agents, including NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, and sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (Periostat), which is the only FDA-approved HMT as an adjunct to scaling and root planing. It also mentions locally administered NSAIDs and other emerging HMT classes, while noting the limitations, side effects, and lack of approval for most agents.

nodes.title: Locally Administered Agents
key_items: Enamel Matrix Proteins, Growth Factors, and Bone Morphogenetic Proteins
nodes.summary: The text covers host modulatory therapy (HMT) in periodontitis. Systemic NSAIDs and selective COX-2 inhibitors are not recommended because of side effects and lack of indication. Bisphosphonates have some evidence of benefit but carry significant risks, including jaw osteonecrosis. SDD (Periostat) is the only FDA/ADA-approved systemic HMT for chronic periodontitis as an adjunct to SRP, with clinical evidence showing added benefit; a modified-release form is also used. Local HMTs include topical NSAIDs, which are not approved, and surgical regenerative products such as Emdogain, GEM 21S, and Infuse, with noted adverse effects of BMPs. Effective comprehensive periodontal management requires integrating bacterial control, host response modulation, risk factor modification, particularly smoking cessation, patient education and compliance, and long-term maintenance care.

nodes.title: Host Modulation and Comprehensive Periodontal Management
key_items: Enamel Matrix Proteins, Growth Factors, and Bone Morphogenetic Proteins

nodes.title: Sub-antimicrobial–Dose Doxycycline
Mechanisms of Action
nodes.summary: The text covers risk factors and management strategies for periodontitis, emphasizing smoking cessation, diabetic control, collaboration with medical colleagues, and modification of modifiable risks. It lists complementary treatments including patient education, SRP, antibacterial therapy, host modulation with HMT, risk reduction, and surgery, and cites a study showing that combining SDD with locally delivered doxycycline and SRP gave optimal clinical improvements. It then focuses on sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD/Periostat), the only FDA-approved systemic HMT adjunct to SRP, and discusses tetracyclines' broad therapeutic uses. The mechanisms involve down-regulation of MMPs, especially MMP-8 and MMP-9, reduced cytokine levels, and stimulation of osteoblastic activity and new bone formation. Clinical research demonstrated doxycycline's effectiveness as an MMP inhibitor, the safety of SDD 20 mg regarding antimicrobial resistance and microflora, and its ability to reduce collagenase levels during therapy with rebound after cessation.

nodes.title: Clinical Research Data on Distinct Patient Populations
key_items: General Patient Populations; High-Risk Patients: Smokers
nodes.summary: The text covers host modulation in periodontal therapy, focusing on sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD) as an adjunct to scaling and root planing. It emphasizes risk factor management, including smoking cessation and diabetes control, and outlines periodontal treatment strategies such as patient education, SRP, antimicrobials, host modulation, risk reduction, and surgery. SDD is described as the only FDA-approved systemic host modulation agent for periodontitis, acting by down-regulating matrix metalloproteinases and other inflammatory mediators to reduce connective tissue breakdown and bone resorption. Clinical trial data demonstrate improved probing depths, clinical attachment gains, and reduced collagenase/bone breakdown markers in general, smoker, and genetically susceptible patient populations. The text also discusses the pleiotropic mechanisms of doxycycline, the safety of SDD on microbial flora, prolonged therapy requirements, and candidate selection with contraindications such as tetracycline allergy, pregnancy, lactation, and young children.

nodes.title: Suggested Uses and Other Considerations
Candidate Patients
nodes.summary: The text discusses host modulation therapy with sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD) in periodontitis. It presents evidence that SDD reduces gingival crevicular fluid MMP-8, MMP-13, and ICTP, a bone collagen breakdown marker, versus placebo. It reviews IL-1 genotype/PAG-related susceptibility, noting conflicting findings and that genotype-positive patients may respond to SDD when SRP alone does not lower biochemical markers. It also describes clinical studies showing SDD as an adjunct improves probing depth reductions in susceptible and smoker patients without rebound, plus ongoing research in diabetic, osteoporotic, geriatric, and smoker populations. Practical considerations include patient selection and contraindications; indications for chronic and aggressive periodontitis; side effects; dosing and sequencing with SRP; combining SDD with surgery or local antimicrobials; and monitoring treatment outcomes. The overall conclusion is that periodontitis involves both bacterial and host-response components, and integrated therapy addressing both is needed for successful long-term management.

The section also addresses candidate selection, contraindications, dosing, sequencing, combinations with surgery or local antimicrobials, maintenance, special populations, emerging therapies, and potential systemic effects, concluding that successful periodontitis management requires addressing both bacterial and host-response components.

nodes.title: Emerging Host Modulatory Therapies
nodes.summary: The text covers emerging host modulatory therapies for periodontitis, including CMTs, anticytokine drugs, resolution mediators, nutritional supplements (n-3 PUFAs), curcumin-based PEZBINs/CMCs, SAGE, and stem cell approaches. It also discusses host modulation in systemic disorders, emphasizing bacteremia, inflammatory mediators, links to cardiovascular disease and diabetes, and potential systemic benefits of periodontal host modulators.

nodes.title: Host Modulation Factors in Systemic Disorders
nodes.summary: The text discusses emerging host modulatory therapies (HMTs) for periodontitis, including chemically modified tetracyclines (CMTs), anticytokine drugs, resolution mediators like resolvin E1, nutritional supplements such as fish oil and low-dose aspirin, curcumin-based MMP inhibitors (PEZBINs/CMCs), SAGE, and potential stem cell therapies. It also covers the role of host modulation in systemic disorders, explaining how periodontitis-related bacteremia and inflammation can exacerbate cardiovascular disease and diabetes, and how host modulators may benefit these conditions. The text includes a list of references.

nodes.title: References

It then introduces Chapter 55 on occlusal evaluation and therapy, outlining its topics and discussing the role of occlusion in periodontitis, emphasizing that occlusal trauma is tooth-specific and can amplify inflammatory attachment loss rather than cause it, and that evidence-based conclusions are limited by ethical constraints on prospective human trials.

This section on host modulation covers the role of the host immune-inflammatory response in periodontitis and the use of host modulation therapy as an adjunct to mechanical treatment. It reviews systemically administered agents, emphasizing that sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (SDD/Periostat) is the only approved systemic HMT, while NSAIDs are not recommended and bisphosphonates carry significant risks. Locally administered options and surgical regenerative products are also discussed. Comprehensive periodontal management requires combining antibacterial therapy, host modulation, risk factor modification, patient compliance, and maintenance. The text details SDD mechanisms, clinical benefits, safety, and treatment considerations, then covers emerging therapies such as CMTs, anticytokine drugs, resolvins, n-3 PUFAs, curcumin-based agents, SAGE, and stem cells. It also addresses links between periodontal inflammation and systemic diseases such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes, concludes with the chapter's references, and introduces Chapter 55 on occlusal evaluation and therapy.

nodes.title: 55 Occlusal Evaluation and Therapy
CHAPTER 55
nodes.summary: This chapter text addresses the role of occlusion in periodontitis, emphasizing that occlusal trauma is a tooth-specific factor that can amplify, but not cause, inflammatory attachment loss. It covers pathogenesis, the need for precise site-specific periodontal diagnosis, limitations of historical research, and evidence that eliminating occlusal interferences improves periodontal therapy outcomes. It also discusses evidence-based decision-making challenges and support from animal studies, concluding that occlusion must be evaluated and managed according to each patient's unique susceptibility.

nodes.title: Evidence-Based Decision Making
nodes.summary: The chapter addresses occlusal evaluation and therapy in relation to periodontitis, emphasizing that occlusal trauma can amplify, but not independently cause, attachment loss in susceptible patients. It covers pathogenesis, evidence-based decision making, clinical examination, parafunction, and therapy. Key points include the tooth-specific nature of occlusal trauma effects, the importance of precise periodontal and occlusal diagnosis, the use of mounted diagnostic casts in centric relation, the need to recognize often-unnoticed parafunction, and the necessity of controlling inflammation before definitive treatment planning.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text discusses the relationship between occlusal trauma and periodontitis in susceptible patients, emphasizing that excessive occlusal forces can amplify attachment loss. Accurate evaluation requires understanding occlusal function, using mounted diagnostic casts, and recognizing parafunction. Patient awareness and education improve acceptance of treatment, while control of inflammation is a prerequisite for diagnosis and planning. Recent human studies provide evidence that occlusal trauma amplifies rather than independently causes attachment loss, enabling evidence-based treatment decisions.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: This text from Chapter 55 on occlusal evaluation and therapy covers the relationship between occlusal forces and periodontitis. It explains that excessive occlusal forces can amplify attachment loss in patients susceptible to periodontitis but do not independently cause it. Accurate evaluation requires knowledge of harmonious occlusion, mounted diagnostic casts in centric relation, assessment of occlusal contacts and trauma, and patient education about often-unrecognized parafunction and mobile teeth to improve acceptance of treatment. Clinical inflammation must be eliminated before diagnosis and treatment planning. Recent human statistical studies provide site-specific evidence supporting the amplifying role of occlusal trauma. Research findings include increased alveolar bone loss, osteoclasts/RANKL expression, immune complexes, and inflammatory mediators from diseased periodontal ligament fibroblasts under compression. The text also discusses the spectrum of occlusal force: inadequate force causes atrophy and instability, physiologic force maintains health and stability, and excessive force causes injury and resorption; healthy patients can adapt and repair, while periodontitis patients may experience amplified damage. Terminology defines centric relation and disclusion, and Figure 55.1 illustrates the occlusal force spectrum from none to excessive.

nodes.title: Terminology
nodes.summary: The text covers how occlusal forces affect the periodontium, including experimental evidence linking inflammation plus trauma to greater bone loss, osteoclast activity, RANKL expression, immune complexes, and adverse fibroblast responses. It discusses the spectrum of occlusal force from disuse atrophy to physiologic stability to excessive force injury, emphasizing that periodontitis combined with excessive force amplifies periodontal destruction. It defines key occlusal terminology, explains normal occlusal function and dysfunction involving centric relation, maximal intercuspation, excursions, working/nonworking contacts, and interferences, and highlights the importance of distinguishing inflammatory intolerance from occlusal forces on reduced periodontal support. It also addresses parafunction, particularly awake clenching and sleep bruxism, and their associations with TMJ dysfunction, orofacial pain, and periodontal attachment loss.

nodes.title: Occlusal Function and Dysfunction
nodes.summary: The text provides a glossary of occlusal terminology and discusses occlusal function, dysfunction, and parafunction. It explains trauma from occlusion, centric relation, the centric relation closure arc, maximal intercuspation, condylar displacement, posterior tooth stability, ideal occlusal relationships, working/nonworking contacts, and occlusal interferences. It highlights how inflammation and reduced periodontal support affect tolerance to occlusal forces and emphasizes the need to distinguish various types of occlusal force problems. It also covers bruxism and awake clenching, their potential effects on periodontal tissue, TMJ dysfunction, orofacial pain, and diagnostic challenges.

nodes.title: Parafunction
nodes.summary: This text covers occlusal evaluation and therapy in periodontology. It defines key occlusal terms, explains normal and dysfunctional occlusal relationships, and describes how occlusal forces interact with periodontal health, inflammation, and tooth mobility. It discusses parafunction, including awake clenching and sleep bruxism, alongside associated factors such as TMJ dysfunction, orofacial pain, SSRI use, and sleep-disordered breathing. The clinical examination section covers patient interview, temporomandibular disorder screening, tooth mobility and fremitus testing, and centric relation assessment techniques for diagnosing occlusal problems and planning therapy.

nodes.title: Conclusions

It concludes that occlusal therapy should be based on thorough evaluation, starting with antiinflammatory treatment and reversible appliance therapy before irreversible options, particularly for periodontitis patients. A case scenario and references are available online.
