It concludes that occlusal therapy should follow a careful sequence starting with antiinflammatory treatment and reversible appliance therapy before irreversible options. A case scenario illustrates a periodontitis patient with persistent tooth mobility despite successful antiinflammatory therapy, with case-based questions explaining that root form and size indicate expected stability and that occlusal trauma likely explains residual mobility. This section covers occlusal evaluation and therapy in periodontal patients. It explains that occlusal trauma does not cause periodontitis but can amplify attachment loss in susceptible patients, with underlying inflammatory and mechanical pathways. It reviews terminology, normal and dysfunctional occlusion, the spectrum of occlusal force, parafunction, and clinical examination techniques such as mounted casts, centric relation assessment, mobility/fremitus testing, and TMD screening. Diagnosis must distinguish inflammatory intolerance from occlusal forces on reduced periodontal support. Therapy is stepwise: anti-inflammatory treatment, reversible appliance therapy, then occlusal adjustment if needed, with occlusal stability before restorative and implant care. The section concludes with evidence-based decision-making, a case scenario, and references.

nodes.title: 56 Orthodontics

CHAPTER 56

nodes.title: Benefits of Orthodontic Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers the adjunctive role of orthodontic therapy in interdisciplinary periodontal and implant treatment. It emphasizes that orthodontic tooth movement benefits adult periodontal-restorative patients by improving oral hygiene access, smile aesthetics, and periodontal conditions. It lists seven specific benefits: better cleaning access from aligned teeth, improvement of osseous defects through vertical repositioning, correction of gingival margin aesthetics, forced eruption for fractured teeth, closure of open gingival embrasures, improved adjacent tooth positioning before implants, and correction of mesially tipped molars. nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Orthodontic tooth movement may be of substantial benefit to the adult periorestorative patient. Many adults who seek routine restorative dentistry have problems with tooth malposition, which compromises their ability to clean and maintain their dentition. If these individuals also are susceptible to periodontal disease, tooth malposition may be an exacerbating factor that could cause premature loss of specific teeth.

nodes.title: Preorthodontic Osseous Surgery
nodes.summary: The text discusses the relationship between periodontal osseous defects and orthodontic treatment. It emphasizes that the need for preorthodontic osseous surgery depends on defect type. Osseous craters are two-wall interproximal defects that do not improve with orthodontics and may require surgical reshaping if not maintainable nonsurgically. Three-wall intrabony defects can be treated with regenerative therapy, and orthodontics can follow once stable. Hemiseptal defects, often around tipped or supererupted teeth, are usually correctable with orthodontics alone, so preorthodontic surgery is inadvisable. Periodontal inflammation must be controlled before orthodontics, and post-treatment stabilization and reassessment are needed.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Treatment of Osseous Defects
Hemiseptal Defects
nodes.summary: The text covers the relationship between orthodontics and periodontal osseous defects. It describes how different defect types—craters, three-wall intrabony defects, and hemiseptal defects—are managed before or during orthodontic treatment, with illustrative case examples. Key principles include controlling biofilm and inflammation, determining when preorthodontic osseous surgery is needed, using regenerative therapy for three-wall defects, correcting hemiseptal defects orthodontically, and avoiding orthodontic creation of defects by considering marginal ridge and bone level relationships when placing brackets. It also emphasizes postoperative stabilization, monitoring during extrusion, and the importance of bracket/band positioning in advanced horizontal bone loss.

nodes.title: Advanced Horizontal Bone Loss
nodes.summary: The text covers orthodontic considerations in periodontally involved patients, emphasizing biofilm control, bracket placement relative to bone rather than crown anatomy when periodontal disease or marginal ridge discrepancies exist, the risk of hemiseptal defects, the role of equilibration and possible endodontic therapy, management of advanced horizontal bone loss, and special management of furcation defects including recall schedules and hemisection timing depending on whether roots will be moved apart.

nodes.title: Furcation Defects
nodes.summary: This text covers orthodontic-periodontal considerations. It describes how bracket placement should be adjusted according to bone level in periodontally compromised patients to improve crown-to-root ratio and bony architecture, often with equilibration. It addresses management of furcation defects, including recall schedules, hemisection before or after orthodontics, orthodontic root separation, and extraction with implants when teeth are not salvageable. It also discusses orthodontic separation of roots that are too close to improve periodontal health, and the management of fractured anterior teeth, detailing forced eruption versus extraction based on root length and root form, including eruption amount needed and risks of thin roots or wide root canals.

nodes.title: Root Proximity
nodes.summary: The text covers implant placement as orthodontic anchors, including timing and restorative considerations; management of root proximity by orthodontic root separation; and evaluation of fractured anterior teeth using forced eruption versus extraction, focusing on the first two of six criteria: root length and root form. It emphasizes biologic width, crown-to-root ratio, ferrule, radiographic planning, root morphology, and the importance of maintaining periodontal health and occlusion.

nodes.title: Fractured Teeth and Forced Eruption
nodes.summary: The text covers orthodontic-periodontal interactions, including using implants as orthodontic anchors with proper timing and placement; separating roots of posterior teeth to improve periodontal health; managing fractured teeth via forced eruption versus extraction based on specific criteria; techniques and stabilization required for forced eruption; surgical management of gingival margins and embrasures after eruption; and retaining hopeless teeth as orthodontic anchorage when inflammation is controlled, as illustrated by a case using a hopeless first molar, with alternative treatment options and a 6-month post-orthodontic stabilization period before reevaluation.

nodes.title: Hopeless Teeth Maintained for Orthodontic Anchorage
nodes.summary: The text covers orthodontic-periodontal interactions, including using hopeless teeth as orthodontic anchorage, gingival changes after extrusion and their surgical/restorative management, and correction of uneven gingival margins. It presents cases involving a hopeless first molar used to upright an impacted third molar before bridge placement, and orthodontic intrusion of an abraded/overerupted central incisor to correct a gingival margin discrepancy. It also details ideal gingival form criteria for maxillary anterior teeth, diagnostic criteria for choosing orthodontic versus surgical correction, and the importance of periodontal diagnosis, inflammation control, patient-specific factors, and post-orthodontic reevaluation.

The section covers orthodontic-periodontal management of osseous defects and related conditions. It emphasizes controlling biofilm and inflammation, assessing defect types such as hemiseptal, three-wall, and crater defects, and timing preorthodontic osseous surgery or regenerative therapy. Bracket and band placement should be guided by bone levels rather than crown anatomy in periodontally compromised patients, often with equilibration and possible endodontic therapy. Furcation defects require careful recall, hemisection timing, orthodontic root separation, or extraction with implants. Root proximity can be managed by orthodontic separation, and implants may serve as orthodontic anchors. Fractured teeth are managed by forced eruption or extraction based on root length and form, with attention to biologic width and crown-to-root ratio. Hopeless teeth can be maintained as orthodontic anchorage when inflammation is controlled, and gingival margin discrepancies can be corrected orthodontically, with post-orthodontic stabilization and reevaluation emphasized throughout.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Treatment of Gingival Discrepancies
nodes.summary: The text discusses orthodontic-periodontal interrelationships, focusing on management of hopeless teeth, gingival margin discrepancies, severe incisal abrasion/overeruption, and open gingival embrasures. It describes criteria for deciding between surgical and orthodontic treatments, the use of hopeless teeth as temporary anchors, orthodontic intrusion techniques and timing, causes and solutions for open embrasures, the difficulty of surgically creating missing papillae, and a case scenario with treatment alternatives. It concludes with a reference list.

It contrasts typical orthodontic patients with more complex periodontal patients, notes the use of implants as anchorage for tooth movement, and highlights the need for accurate tooth positioning and periodontal health during treatment. The section outlines therapeutic interactions, including using tooth movement physiology to achieve periodontal changes, and stresses the importance of interdisciplinary planning and execution. Key topics include anchorage, TADs, miniscrews, forced eruption, direct and indirect anchorage, and orthodontic acceleration techniques.

nodes.title: Keywords

nodes.title: Implant Interactions in Orthodontics
Planning Phase
Implant Anchorage in Orthodontics
key_items: Implant Interactions in Orthodontics Planning Phase
nodes.summary: The text discusses implant-orthodontic interactions during treatment planning. Implants may serve either as orthodontic anchorage devices (often TADs placed early and later explanted) or as eventual tooth replacements placed after orthodontic site development; occasionally they serve both roles. Implants and miniscrews provide absolute anchorage because they are immovably fixed to bone, unlike teeth, so they improve predictability, simplify mechanics, eliminate compliance issues, and allow en masse tooth movement. The implant's long-term role determines placement: restorable implants require restorative considerations, while TADs are positioned based on orthodontic and anatomic factors and can be used for direct or indirect anchorage. Orthodontic site preparation is also essential for successful implant placement and restoration. Figure examples demonstrate direct and indirect anchorage configurations.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Site Preparation
CHAPTER 56 Orthodontics 583.e17
nodes.summary: The text covers orthodontic strategies for implant site development, emphasizing the importance of precise tooth position. It contrasts congenitally missing teeth, where neighboring roots converge and require root torquing/control, with teeth lost later, where drifting teeth are corrected by simpler uprighting. Orthodontic eruption can be used to augment soft and hard tissues: sulcular eversion leads to keratinized gingiva via Atherton tissue, and tension on periodontal fibers stimulates bone deposition through Wolff's law. The text also notes that hopeless teeth can be erupted and extracted to enhance the site, and it describes treatment phases including direct and indirect anchorage, space management with fixed appliances, and root parallelism. Case efigures illustrate space restoration, drifting correction, and tissue changes, while the learning box stresses orthodontic movement as essential for proper site and adjacent-tooth preparation before implant placement.

This section covers orthodontic site preparation for implant placement, emphasizing the role of orthodontic movement in achieving successful implant outcomes. It discusses temporary anchorage devices with direct and indirect strategies and various placement sites, as well as implant-supported direct anchorage for tooth replacement. It highlights the need for precise root positioning, using orthodontic eruption to augment soft and hard tissues, and the possibility of erupting hopeless teeth before extraction. It also outlines treatment phases such as anchorage management, space management with fixed appliances, and root parallelism, concluding that orthodontic preparation is essential before implant placement.

The Planning Phase section covers the role of implants and temporary anchorage devices in orthodontics, emphasizing their use as absolute anchorage and the importance of orthodontic site preparation. It explains how implants may serve as anchorage, tooth replacements, or both; how direct and indirect anchorage configurations are used; and how orthodontic movement—such as precise root positioning, eruption for tissue augmentation, and managing hopeless teeth—is necessary to prepare the site for successful implant placement and restoration.

nodes.title: Orthodontic Acceleration

The section also discusses orthodontic acceleration, contrasting traditional appliance-based approaches with modern biological methods, detailing surgical techniques (PAOO, piezocision, micro-osteoperforation) and non-surgical stimulatory devices (AcceleDent, VPro5). nodes.title: Surgical Pocket Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers phase II periodontal therapy, the surgical phase of periodontal treatment. It describes the purposes of surgery, including controlling periodontal disease, correcting anatomic conditions, and facilitating implants. It outlines surgical objectives: improving tooth prognosis and aesthetics, accessing root surfaces, reducing pocket depth, and reshaping tissues. It also categorizes surgical procedures into pocket reduction surgery (resective and regenerative), periodontal plastic surgery (aesthetic and gingival augmentation), and pre-prosthetic surgery (crown lengthening, ridge augmentation, implants). Surgical pocket therapy is discussed as a means to access deep roots and remove subgingival deposits, with challenges posed by deep pockets and root irregularities. The text emphasizes reevaluation after phase I therapy and notes that surgery is indicated when pockets persist or access is needed.

nodes.title: Abstract:
nodes.summary:
Abstract:
After completion of phase I therapy, which consists of patient educa- tion, biofilm control, and thorough root therapy, the involved peri- odontal areas are reevaluated. Many cases may not require phase II therapy when gingival tissue shrinkage eliminates or reduces the periodontal pockets. Phase II therapy becomes necessary when access for root therapy is required or correction of anatomic or morphologic defects is necessary. Placement of dental implants can be part of this therapy.

nodes.title: Periodontal Pocket Therapy: Elimination, Maintenance, Reevaluation, and Critical Zones
nodes.summary: This page covers periodontal pocket therapy, including the concepts of pocket elimination versus maintenance, the importance of reevaluation after phase I therapy, and the critical zones used to select pocket surgery techniques. It explains that treatment uncovers recession caused by disease and aims to restore a normal sulcus with attachment gain. It compares pocket elimination and maintenance, emphasizing that attachment level is the most important predictor of progression, while residual pockets can be maintained with regular scaling, root planing, and monitoring. It reviews research on attachment changes after root planing versus modified Widman flap surgery, and notes that some pocket depth recurs regardless of technique, so maintaining stability is the goal. It stresses reevaluation 1 to 9 months after phase I therapy before making surgical decisions. Finally, it describes the four critical zones for selecting surgical treatment: soft tissue pocket wall, tooth surface, underlying bone, and attached gingiva.

Phase II periodontal therapy is the surgical phase considered after Phase I reevaluation. It is indicated when residual pockets require root access, correction of anatomic/morphologic defects, or implant placement; many cases do not require surgery if tissue shrinkage eliminates pockets. Its objectives are controlling disease, improving tooth prognosis and aesthetics, accessing root surfaces, reducing pocket depth, correcting anatomic problems, and reshaping tissues. Surgical procedures are classified as pocket reduction (resective/regenerative), plastic/aesthetic, pre-prosthetic, and implant-related. Pocket therapy emphasizes access to subgingival deposits, with discussion of pocket elimination versus maintenance, attachment level as the strongest predictor, outcomes of root planing and modified Widman surgery, and the need for 1–9 month reevaluation. Four critical zones guide technique selection: soft tissue wall, tooth surface, bone, and attached gingiva. Indications, selection criteria, and methods for gingival pockets, incipient periodontitis, and moderate-to-severe periodontitis are covered, noting anterior teeth are often managed nonsurgically or with papilla-preserving/modified Widman/apically displaced flaps, while posterior areas often require surgery for access, bone defects, and furcations. Phase II may encompass resective, regenerative, plastic, aesthetic, pre-prosthetic, and implant procedures; the chapter also includes references and introduces Chapter 58 on periodontal and peri-implant surgical anatomy.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Periodontal surgery is an adjunct to nonsurgical periodontal therapy and an essential treatment modality in the management of periodontal disease. This chapter describes the rationale for periodontal surgery to treat periodontal disease and the fundamentals of periodontal surgery, which include incision design, papilla management, flap management, and flap stabilization. Surgical techniques of both gingival and flap surgeries are presented in details.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text discusses the treatment of gingival enlargement, emphasizing that the choice of therapy depends on the underlying cause. Chronic inflammatory enlargement is managed with scaling and root planing, sometimes followed by periodontal surgery. For medication-induced enlargement, drug substitution is first considered but not always feasible; surgery is often needed, with gingivectomy for limited areas and flap surgery for moderate/severe or extensive cases. Gingivectomy is quick and simple but has risks such as bleeding, pain, and loss of keratinized tissue, while flap surgery is more demanding but avoids these limitations. Abstract
The main rationale for osseous surgery is based on the assumption that discrepancies in the level and shapes of the bone and gingiva predisposes a person to the recurrence of the periodontal pocket depth postsurgically. This concept is not universally accepted, but the resective recontouring of the bone in many cases may be the only logical treatment choice. This chapter presents the examination, treatment planning, terminology, and surgical techniques utilized for osseous resective surgery.

nodes.title: Osseous Resection Technique
Instrumentation
nodes.summary: This section covers resective osseous surgery, focusing on instrumentation and the sequential osseous reshaping technique. Instrumentation can include hand instruments, rongeurs, rotary burs, and piezoelectric devices, with rotary instruments used for osteoplasty and hand instruments for precise ostectomy; care is needed to avoid irreversible bone or root damage. The recommended sequence is vertical grooving, radicular blending, flattening interproximal bone, and gradualizing marginal bone, though not all steps are always required and the order minimizes unnecessary bone removal. Vertical grooving thins the alveolar housing, radicular blending smooths the radicular surface, and both are osteoplastic procedures useful for shallow craters, ledges, and early furcation defects. Flattening interproximal bone addresses hemiseptal and one-walled defects but is limited in advanced lesions due to excessive bone loss.

nodes.title: Resective Osseous Surgery: Steps, Indications, and Limitations
nodes.summary: The page discusses resective osseous surgery in periodontal treatment. It presents the recommended sequential steps: vertical grooving, radicular blending, flattening interproximal bone, and gradualizing marginal bone, emphasizing that although not all steps are always needed, the sequence should be followed to minimize unnecessary bone removal. Vertical grooving thins the alveolar housing and highlights radicular contours using rotary instruments, but is contraindicated with thin bone or close roots. Radicular blending smooths the radicular surface as an extension of grooving. Both steps are osteoplastic and do not remove supporting bone, and together they manage shallow craters, thick ledges, and early furcations. Flattening interproximal bone removes small amounts of supporting bone for horizontally uneven interproximal defects, but is limited in advanced lesions because large hemiseptal defects would require excessive bone removal. The text also references figures showing instruments, osseous reshaping steps, and flap surgery examples.

CHAPTER 63 Periodontal Regeneration and Reconstructive Surgery
Abstract
Intrabony and furcation defects are sequelae of periodontal disease. Ideally, these defects are managed in a timely fashion through periodontal regeneration. At one time, results were inconsistent. Now, various surgical approaches including bone replacement grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), and the use of biologic agents are capable of regenerating these defects in a predictable fashion. This chapter reviews the current strategies and clinical decision making for optimizing regenerative success.
Keywords periodontal regeneration periodontal diseases bone grafting tissue engineering

nodes.title: Keywords
Histologic Methods
nodes.summary: The text discusses methods for evaluating periodontal reconstruction, covering histologic and clinical approaches. Histologic analysis in animal models uses reference notches to define regeneration and identify healing patterns such as repair, regeneration, root resorption, and ankylosis, while human histologic evidence is limited to ethically justified extractions. Clinical evaluation relies on probing measurements of pocket depth, attachment level, and bone level, with attachment level considered more reliable, though probe penetration varies with inflammation and error is greater in furcations. It also explains that healing outcomes depend on whether epithelial, connective tissue, bone, or periodontal ligament cells predominate.

nodes.title: Clinical Methods
nodes.summary: The text describes methods for evaluating periodontal regeneration and reconstructive surgery outcomes. Histologic analysis is the definitive method, typically using animal models with notches to define true regeneration, while human histologic evidence is rare. Clinical methods rely on probing to measure pocket depth, attachment, and bone level, with limitations due to inflammation and probing error; stents and bone probing under anesthesia improve accuracy. Radiographic methods require standardization and have limitations, though subtraction radiography and CADIA enhance accuracy. Surgical reentry provides direct bone crest visualization and measurement but requires a second procedure and cannot distinguish the type of attachment formed.

nodes.title: Radiographic Methods
nodes.summary: The text discusses methods for evaluating periodontal regeneration and probing limitations. It explains that probing penetration is influenced by tissue inflammation and has inherent measurement error, which bone probing under anesthesia can reduce. Radiographic methods require standardization, have limitations, and are less reliable than probing, though subtraction radiography and combined analysis improve accuracy. Surgical reentry provides direct bone assessment but requires a second procedure and cannot distinguish the type of attachment formed.

nodes.title: Surgical Reentry

It emphasizes that probing depth can be affected by inflammation and does not necessarily reflect attachment level changes, while radiographs often underestimate bone changes and require standardization. Surgical reentry gives direct bone visualization but needs a second operation and cannot distinguish new attachment from long junctional epithelium. A detailed table compares regenerative materials and approaches, including various bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration, enamel matrix derivatives, and growth factors, with clinical attachment gain, defect fill, and histologic outcomes. nodes.title: Scaffold or Supporting Matrices
Periodontal Regeneration: Growth Factors, Stem Cells, and Scaffolds
key_items: Bone Morphogenetic Proteins for Periodontal and Implant Site Regeneration
Use of Recombinant Human Fibroblast Growth Factor 2 for Periodontal Regeneration
nodes.summary: The page covers periodontal regeneration and reconstructive surgery, focusing on three therapeutic approaches. Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are differentiation factors that induce stem cells toward bone-forming cells; BMP levels in bone grafts are too low for activity, and recombinant BMPs are being studied despite ankylosis concerns. Recombinant human FGF-2 promoted periodontal regeneration in animal studies and a Phase II clinical trial showed significant alveolar bone gain at 0.3% without adverse effects. Cell therapy using cellular bone allografts supplies concentrated multipotential stromal cells with an osteoinductive molecular signature, offering an alternative to autografts and showing success in implant site and periodontal defect cases. Finally, scaffolding matrices are discussed for their roles in providing physical support, serving as barriers in GTR/GBR, and enabling cellular migration and proliferation.

nodes.title: Calcium Sulfate
nodes.summary: The text, from a chapter on periodontal regeneration and reconstructive surgery, reviews scaffold materials for oral tissue engineering. An eTable lists allografts (DFDBA, FDBA), xenografts (anorganic bovine bone, hydroxyapatite), alloplasts (tricalcium phosphate, hydroxyapatite, bioactive glass, hard tissue replacement polymer, coralline calcium carbonate), and polymers/collagens with commercial names. Scaffolds can support cell attachment/proliferation and can time-release signaling molecules. FDBA/DFDBA are common bone graft choices with variable osteogenic potential; FDA-unregulated growth-factor combinations are used off-label. β-TCP plus rhPDGF-BB is biocompatible, osteoconductive, and resorbs, with ~45% PDGF-BB release over 10 days; newer β-TCP coatings with rhGDF-5 show superior regeneration. Collagen carriers support cell activities and bone formation when purified as atelocollagen. Calcium sulfate is resorbable, usable in infected sites, has barrier and angiogenic properties, releases FGF with dissolution, and carries rhPDGF-BB for about 16 days. PLGA/PGA polymers are promising but cause inflammation, foreign body reactions, and local acid accumulation. Further elucidation of absorption/release kinetics is needed for optimal regenerative outcomes.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
The morphology of the multirooted tooth presents unique challenges to periodontal therapy. If access and removal of biofilm and subgin- gival calculus is one of the main objective of periodontal therapy, the furcation invasion, which results in the periodontal bone loss between the roots of the molar dentition, presents a most difficult and in many instances almost impossible situation to instrument the root surface. Many teeth with moderate to advanced furcation involvement will result in a guarded to poor periodontal prognosis when a single rooted tooth/teeth with equivalent attachment loss will present a fair to good prognosis. This chapter will present the diagnosis, prognosis, and the numerous treatment approaches to this complex periodontal problem.

Surgical options include osseous resection and regeneration, but regenerative results are variable. Extraction is considered for advanced through-and-through defects in noncompliant or high-risk patients, while dental implants provide an alternative. nodes.summary: The text describes platelet concentrates, focusing on two generations: platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF). nodes.title: The Second Generation of Platelet Concentrates: Platelet-Rich Fibrin
nodes.summary: The text describes two generations of platelet concentrates. First, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a complex autologous preparation requiring anticoagulants, centrifugation, and thrombin; it is used in orthopedics and oral surgery but has inconsistent evidence and practical drawbacks. Second, leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF), introduced in 2001, is a simpler, low-cost fibrin biomaterial rich in platelets, growth factors, fibronectin, vitronectin, thrombospondin, and leukocytes. The chapter details L-PRF preparation: rapid blood collection, centrifugation at 400g for 12 minutes using the Intraspin centrifuge, no anticoagulants, and formation of a fibrin clot between red blood cells and platelet-poor plasma. The clot can be compressed into strong membranes or plugs that release growth factors for 7–14 days and promote healing and regeneration. Step-by-step chair-side protocols for preparing L-PRF clots, membranes, and plugs are included.

nodes.title: Preparation of L-PRF
nodes.summary: The text describes L-PRF (leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin) as a cost-effective and streamlined platelet concentrate, classified by leukocyte content and containing most platelets and leukocytes. It details the preparation method: blood collection in special tubes, rapid centrifugation within 60 seconds using the IntraSpin centrifuge at 400g RCF for 12 minutes, and formation of three layers—RBCs, PPP, and the fibrin clot. Step-by-step protocols are provided for making L-PRF clots, membranes, and plugs, including compression techniques, membrane thickness, stability, and usage timelines. The text also covers the biologic properties of L-PRF: platelets concentrated in the clot's lower face release growth factors and antimicrobial substances, contribute to hemostasis and immune functions, and leukocytes are concentrated in the fibrin matrix. Membranes are strong, release growth factors for 7–14 days, and have applications in regeneration.

It details L-PRF preparation protocols for clots, membranes, and plugs, its biologic properties including sustained growth-factor release over 7–14 days and immune/healing modulation, and its applications in natural tissue regeneration, natural bone regeneration, and extra-oral nonhealing ulcers. nodes.title: Extraoral Applications of L-PRF
nodes.summary: The text covers extraoral and periodontal applications of leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF). Extraorally, L-PRF is used for difficult chronic ulcers such as diabetic foot ulcers, pressure ulcers, surgical wounds, and venous leg ulcers, where standard and advanced treatments often fail or are costly; clinical cases show L-PRF can achieve complete closure. Its effects are attributed to high platelet/leukocyte content and sustained release of growth factors and cytokines, with possible immune-regulatory and anti-infection benefits. In periodontal bony defects, L-PRF acts like guided tissue regeneration: membranes seal the defect, exclude epithelium/connective tissue, allow periodontal/periosteal cells to regenerate, and promote neo-angiogenesis and osteoblast activity. Clinical evidence shows L-PRF provides additional pocket reduction, attachment gain, and bone fill, works with bone substitutes, and performs similarly to enamel matrix derivative. Figure captions also illustrate ulcer healing and growth-factor release, as well as the fibrin-clot formation mechanism used in L-PRF block preparation.

nodes.title: L-PRF and Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jawbone

nodes.title: 67 Periodontal Microsurgery
CHAPTER 67
nodes.summary: This chapter covers periodontal microsurgery, defined as surgery performed under ×10 or greater magnification using a surgical microscope. It emphasizes improved visual acuity and manual dexterity, allowing precise, minimally invasive incisions with small instruments and sharp blades. This approach reduces tissue injury and morbidity and promotes rapid primary intention healing. The text discusses magnification systems, microsurgical sutures, and e-only content on aesthetic periodontal microsurgery and microsurgical knots. It also highlights the broader trend toward minimally invasive techniques, the ability to adjust working magnification, and the goal of atraumatic tissue handling for optimal wound closure and healing.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text introduces periodontal microsurgery as a surgical refinement using microscopic magnification to enhance visual acuity, dexterity, and motor coordination. It is applied not only in surgery but also in diagnostic and non-surgical procedures. The ability to adjust magnification enables less invasive periodontal surgery with smaller sites and fewer vertical incisions. This approach is part of a broader trend toward minimally invasive medicine, aiming for atraumatic tissue handling and primary wound closure to improve healing, overcoming the limits of normal vision through visual advantage.

nodes.title: Microsurgical Knots

It describes two basic knots: the square/reef knot, which is stable, lies flat, and self-locks during edema, and the English surgeon’s knot, which uses double loops for better control and has a hollow center allowing tissue expansion without ligation. It also mentions the granny knot as one that unties easily, notes that both knots are tied with instruments, and includes references on microsurgical techniques and periodontal microsurgery.

nodes.title: 68 Lasers in Periodontal and Peri-implant Therapy
CHAPTER 68
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses lasers in periodontal and peri-implant therapy, covering laser physics and biologic interactions, clinical applications, and the management of periodontitis and peri-implantitis. It traces the history of lasers from Maiman's first working laser in 1960 to the revival of dental laser use in the 1990s. Applications include surgical and nonsurgical periodontal therapy, cutting tissue, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy for biofilm disruption, and low-level laser therapy for wound healing. The chapter emphasizes that current evidence is limited by small, heterogeneous studies and a lack of well-designed RCTs, so lasers can only be considered equivalent, not superior, to conventional therapies. It also explains laser principles, including wavelength-dependent interactions such as absorption, reflection, scattering, transmission, and ablation.

The text emphasizes that current evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and lacking robust RCTs, so lasers should be considered at best equivalent to conventional therapies, with adoption possibly justified by non-clinical factors. It also explains laser mechanisms—absorption, reflection, scattering, transmission, and ablation—and cautions that outcomes depend on wavelength, power, and exposure time. The chapter includes e-only sections on specific laser types and management of periodontitis and peri-implantitis, and highlights the need for well-designed controlled studies to validate perceived advantages.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
696.e1
CHAPTER 69 Preparation of the Periodontium for Restorative Dentistry
Abstract
Periodontal health is the sine qua non, a prerequisite, of successful comprehensive dentistry. To achieve the long-term therapeutic targets of comfort, good function, treatment predictability, longevity, and ease of restorative and maintenance care, active periodontal infection must be treated and controlled before the initiation of restorative, aesthetic, and implant dentistry. In addition, the residual effects of periodontal disease or anatomic aberrations inconsistent with realizing and maintaining long-term stability must be addressed. This phase of treatment includes techniques performed in anticipation of aesthetic or implant dentistry, such as clinical crown lengthening, covering denuded roots, alveolar ridge retention or augmentation, and implant site development.

nodes.summary: The chapter describes preparation of the periodontium for restorative dentistry. Periodontal health and control of active disease are essential before restorative, aesthetic, or implant treatment. The process involves emergency treatment, extraction of hopeless teeth, oral hygiene instructions, scaling and root planing, reevaluation, periodontal surgery, and adjunctive orthodontic therapy, followed by preprosthetic surgery such as crown lengthening, soft tissue grafting, ridge preservation, and ridge reconstruction. Treatment must be individualized and adaptable, addressing inflammation, plaque-retentive factors, deep pockets, and anatomic or residual disease problems to ensure long-term stability and successful restorative care.

These procedures are indicated before prosthetic restoration, with orthodontic tooth movement, or for comfort and aesthetics, with at least 2 months of healing recommended after grafting. It also discusses preservation of ridge morphology after tooth extraction to minimize alveolar ridge resorption, which is useful for future implants, fixed bridge pontics, and avoiding unaesthetic deformities. Crown-lengthening procedures are described as being performed to provide retention form for proper tooth preparation and impression making.

nodes.summary: This text from Chapter 69 covers periodontal preparation for restorative dentistry, focusing on surgical crown lengthening. It describes how crown lengthening improves access and retention for restoring mandibular molars, and emphasizes preserving biologic width—about 2 mm, composed of 0.97 mm junctional epithelium and 1.07 mm connective tissue attachment—by placing restorative margins 0.5 mm into the 0.69 mm gingival sulcus. It differentiates when gingivectomy is sufficient (>3 mm soft tissue with adequate attached gingiva) versus when a flap procedure with osseous recontouring is required (<3 mm soft tissue or inadequate attached gingiva). It also notes that at least 1 mm of sound tooth structure must be present above the gingival margin for restorations in caries or fracture cases. Finally, it lists indications and contraindications for surgical crown lengthening.

nodes.title: Contraindications
nodes.summary: This text covers periodontal preparation for restorative dentistry, emphasizing biologic width maintenance, indications and contraindications for surgical crown lengthening, criteria for choosing gingivectomy versus flap with osseous recontouring, and the need for at least 1 mm of sound tooth structure above the gingival margin. It also describes techniques for managing alveolar ridge defects using soft tissue grafting with an ovate pontic and bone grafting with a barrier membrane for implant placement. Two case scenarios illustrate the rationale for surgical crown lengthening and soft-tissue grafting, with correct answers including retention, biologic width, aesthetics, recession prevention, root protection, sensitivity reduction, and aesthetic tooth length.

nodes.title: 698.e7
nodes.summary: The text presents two case scenarios on periodontium preparation for restorative dentistry. The first case involves surgical crown lengthening for a fractured tooth, justified by retention, biologic width preservation, and aesthetic gingival levels, with alternatives like orthodontic extrusion if aesthetics are compromised. The second case involves soft-tissue grafting for gingival recession, addressing prevention of further recession, root protection, sensitivity reduction, and aesthetics, with recession attributed to bone dehiscence and inflammation.

nodes.title: CASE SCENARIO 69.2 Patient: 44-year-old female
nodes.summary: The text presents four case scenarios on preparing the periodontium for restorative dentistry. It covers surgical crown lengthening for fractured or carious teeth to ensure retention, preserve biologic width, and maintain aesthetics; soft-tissue grafting for gingival recession to protect roots and improve appearance; management of drug-induced gingival overgrowth before orthodontic/restorative treatment through medication adjustment and periodontal therapy; and crown lengthening to retain a structurally damaged tooth. Each case emphasizes completing periodontal treatment and considering aesthetic and biologic principles.

nodes.title: Answer: F
nodes.summary: The text is from Chapter 69 on preparing the periodontium for restorative dentistry. It presents two case scenarios. Case 69.3 involves a 64-year-old man with amlodipine-induced gingival enlargement, and the correct management is all of the listed steps: medical consultation for possible medication change, scaling and root planing, oral hygiene education, reevaluation, possible surgical reduction, and prevention. Case 69.4 involves a 55-year-old man with a fractured tooth, where surgical crown lengthening followed by crown restoration is the correct option to retain the tooth while respecting biologic width. The chapter also includes a substantial list of references on periodontal and restorative topics.

The section covers alveolar ridge reconstruction after tooth loss using soft tissue augmentation for small defects and hard tissue grafting with barrier membranes for larger defects or implant sites, as well as socket grafting with bovine bone and calcium sulfate to preserve gingival and papillary architecture. It also discusses surgical crown lengthening as periodontal preparation for restorative dentistry: preserving biologic width (~2 mm), placing restorative margins 0.5 mm into the sulcus, maintaining at least 3 mm from gingival margin to bone crest, choosing gingivectomy versus flap with osseous recontouring based on soft tissue and attached gingiva, and ensuring adequate sound tooth structure above margins in caries or fracture cases. Indications and contraindications for crown lengthening are considered, with implant replacement as an alternative. Case scenarios illustrate crown lengthening, soft-tissue grafting for recession, management of drug-induced gingival overgrowth, and retention of damaged teeth, emphasizing biologic width, aesthetics, periodontal health, and appropriate restorative planning.

This section covers periodontal preparation for restorative dentistry, including preprosthetic plastic surgery for gingival augmentation and root coverage, ridge preservation after extraction, crown-lengthening procedures with attention to biologic width and restorative margins, and alveolar ridge reconstruction using soft or hard tissue techniques for pontic or implant sites. It also addresses socket grafting to preserve gingival and papillary architecture, surgical crown-lengthening considerations such as gingivectomy versus flap with osseous recontouring, indications/contraindications, and case scenarios emphasizing biologic width, aesthetics, periodontal health, and appropriate restorative planning.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text comprises the reference list for Chapter 69 on preparing the periodontium for restorative dentistry, followed by the beginning of Chapter 70 on restorative interrelationships. Chapter 70 discusses the inseparable relationship between periodontal health and restorations, emphasizing that restorations must be compatible with the periodontium for long-term success. Key topics include margin placement options (supragingival, equigingival, subgingival), biologic width and its clinical significance, the periodontal risks of subgingival margins, and restorative indications for subgingival placement. The chapter also references online supplementary content, aesthetic tissue management, occlusal considerations, and a patient education animation.

Chapter 69 covers preparing the periodontium before restorative dentistry, emphasizing that periodontal health and control of active disease are essential for successful restorative, aesthetic, and implant treatment. It describes the rationale for periodontal therapy, including stable gingival margins, preparation access, anticipation of tissue changes, prevention of mobility and attachment loss, structural defense, and support for aesthetic and implant procedures. A logical, evidence-based, individualized treatment sequence is outlined: first controlling active disease through emergency treatment, extraction of hopeless teeth, oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, reevaluation, periodontal surgery, and adjunctive orthodontic therapy; then performing preprosthetic surgery such as crown lengthening, soft tissue grafting/root coverage, ridge preservation/reconstruction, socket grafting, and implant-site development, with attention to biologic width and restorative margins. The chapter also stresses addressing residual or anatomic problems, accurate diagnosis, comprehensive treatment planning, and interdisciplinary care. Supplementary online content and a patient education animation are noted, along with the reference list and a preview of Chapter 70 on periodontal-restorative relationships, margin placement, biologic width, and subgingival margin risks.

nodes.title: 70 Restorative Interrelationships
CHAPTER 70
nodes.summary: Chapter 70 discusses the interrelationship between restorative dentistry and periodontal health, emphasizing that restorations must be compatible with surrounding tissues to ensure long-term success and aesthetics. It covers biologic considerations of margin placement, including supragingival, equigingival, and subgingival options, and explains biologic width and its clinical significance. The chapter also outlines reasons for subgingival margins, references supporting research, and notes additional resources such as the companion website and a patient education animation.

nodes.title: Biologic Considerations Margin Placement and Biologic Width
nodes.summary: The chapter discusses the intimate relationship between restorative dentistry and periodontal health, focusing on margin placement, biologic width, aesthetics, and restoration design. It also notes online-only and supplementary educational content, and summarizes that restorations must respect biologic width, contours, and pontics to support periodontal health and aesthetics.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Periodontal health is intimately tied to most aspects of restorative dentistry. The location and integrity of the restorative margins must be designed to respect the integrity of the periodontal biologic width. The contours of the restorations and any pontics can and will affect the health and aesthetics of the periodontal tissues. Successful restorative therapy is a key component of creating and maintaining a healthy oral environment.

key_items: Margin Placement Guidelines; Provisional Restorations; Marginal Fit; Crown Contour
nodes.summary: The text covers restorative margin placement in relation to periodontal tissues, focusing on biologic width. It explains that equigingival margins are possible with modern ceramics, while excessive subgingival margins risk violating biologic width, leading to recession or inflammation. It defines average and variable biologic width, describes diagnostic methods such as probing to bone, and provides margin placement guidelines based on sulcus depth. It also discusses provisional restoration requirements, effects of overcontouring, subgingival debris, surgical and orthodontic correction of biologic width violations, and a clinical e-figure example. Finally, it introduces clinical margin placement rules and gives the first rule for shallow sulci.

nodes.title: Correcting Biologic Width Violations
nodes.summary: The text explains how to correct biologic width violations: surgically removing bone or orthodontically extruding the tooth, with surgery being faster and preferred when crown lengthening improves aesthetics, and extrusion indicated for interproximal or facial violations with correct gingival levels. It details surgical bone removal with a safety zone and risks, two extrusion techniques, and postoperative stabilization. It then covers clinical margin placement, emphasizing gingival health and a rule for placing margins no more than 0.5 mm below the crest when sulcus depth is 1.5 mm or less, while noting that modern all-ceramic restorations reduce the need for subgingival margins. Clinical eFigs illustrate a case of biologic width violation treated by orthodontic extrusion and surgical repositioning.

nodes.title: Clinical Procedures in Margin Placement
nodes.summary: The text covers correction of biologic width violations through surgical bone removal or orthodontic extrusion, and details clinical procedures for margin placement, including three rules based on sulcus depth, the use of gingivectomy to reduce deep sulci, and tissue retraction techniques using cords to position subgingival margins and take impressions.

nodes.title: Tissue Retraction
701.e3
nodes.summary: The text describes restorative margin placement and tissue retraction techniques for subgingival preparations. It covers two approaches: a single-deflection-cord technique for shallow sulci (rule 1) and a two-deflection-cord plus impression-cord technique for deep sulci (rule 2). It emphasizes protecting gingival tissue, selecting appropriately sized retraction cords, exposing margins for impressions, and using electrosurgery as an alternative to remove overhanging tissue while preserving tissue height. It also includes eFig captions illustrating stable tissue levels and margin positioning references.

nodes.title: 701.e5
nodes.summary: The text covers technical steps for placing subgingival margins in patients with altered eruption or deep sulcus using multiple deflection cords and an impression cord, plus correct electrosurgery tip positioning. It also discusses hypersensitivity to dental materials, emphasizing nickel allergy and the greater importance of surface roughness over composition, and addresses aesthetic management of interproximal embrasures, papilla height relative to bone and contact points, clinical studies by Van der Velden and Tarnow, ideal contact placement, tissue health assessment, and the use of provisional restorations to guide margin and soft-tissue positioning.

The section covers tissue retraction techniques for subgingival preparations, including cord-based methods for shallow and deep sulci, margin exposure, and electrosurgery as an alternative. It also addresses dental material hypersensitivity, particularly nickel allergy and surface roughness, along with aesthetic considerations for interproximal embrasures, papilla height, ideal contact placement, tissue health assessment, and the role of provisional restorations in guiding margin and soft-tissue positioning.

nodes.title: Hypersensitivity to Dental Materials
nodes.summary: The text covers hypersensitivity to dental materials, emphasizing that reactions are mainly linked to nonprecious alloys like nickel and that surface roughness matters more than composition for plaque accumulation and inflammation, so smooth subgingival surfaces are critical. It then discusses aesthetic management of interproximal embrasures, including the relationship between papilla height, bone level, biologic width, and restorative contours. It presents clinical guidelines: maintaining contact-to-bone distance of 5 mm prevents open embrasures, while longer distances reduce papilla fill probability; ideal contact is 2–3 mm coronal to attachment; healthy mature tissues and provisional restorations are necessary for accurate assessment. It also notes the risk of recession if the papillary sulcus exceeds 3 mm and that the common problem is a short papilla with a normal or shallow sulcus, managed by understanding papilla volume relative to bone.

It discusses evaluation of biologic width, rules for placing margins relative to sulcus depth, and correction of violations through surgical bone removal or orthodontic extrusion. Clinical procedures include tissue retraction with cords and electrosurgery. It also addresses hypersensitivity to dental materials, emphasizing nickel allergy and surface smoothness, and aesthetic management of interproximal embrasures based on papilla height, bone level, contact position, and provisional restorations.

nodes.title: Aesthetic Tissue Management
Managing Interproximal Embrasures
nodes.summary: The text discusses restorative-periodontal interrelationships, covering hypersensitivity to dental materials, interproximal embrasure and papilla management, pontic design, and restorative correction of open gingival embrasures and recession-related embrasure issues. It emphasizes that smooth material surfaces are more important than composition, that papilla height and embrasure form are governed by bone levels and biologic width, that provisional restorations are useful for diagnosis and treatment planning, and that restorative designs must balance aesthetics with hygiene access.

nodes.title: Correcting Open Gingival Embrasures Restoratively
nodes.summary: The text describes restorative management of open gingival embrasures. It identifies causes such as deficient papilla height, high contacts due to divergent roots, or excessively tapered tooth shape. Correction requires placing restoration margins 1 to 1.5 mm subgingivally and designing the emergence profile to move the contact apically toward the papilla while blending into the tooth. Direct bonded restorations are advantageous, while indirect restorations require provisional adaptation for 4 to 6 weeks. For gingival recession, anterior areas need apically placed contacts or tissue-colored ceramic papillae, whereas posterior areas must balance reducing food traps and maintaining interdental brush access. Figure captions emphasize that supragingival closure creates cleaning problems, subgingival placement is biologically safe, and a clinical example demonstrates successful treatment with bonded restorations.

nodes.title: Managing Gingival Embrasure Form for Patients With Gingival Recession
nodes.summary: The text covers restorative and surgical management of gingival embrasures and pontic design. It explains diagnosis and correction of open gingival embrasures, management of embrasure form in gingival recession for anterior versus posterior regions, ridge modification requirements for ideal ovate pontic contours, use of ovate pontics to preserve interdental papillae after extraction, limitations of ridge-lap pontic designs, and relevant clinical case illustrations.

nodes.title: Ridge Modification Procedures for Ideal Pontic Contours
nodes.summary: The text covers surgical ridge modification and pontic design, especially ovate pontics, including tissue thickness assessment, ridge requirements, augmentation, receptor site creation, soft-tissue impressions, and maintenance of interdental papillae after extraction. Full ridge-lap pontics are rejected, while modified ridge-lap pontics may be used when needed. A clinical case illustrates these principles. The text then discusses occlusal considerations in restorative therapy, emphasizing mutually protective occlusion, even contacts in MIP, anterior guidance, stable vertical dimension, and repeatable centric relation, with attention to force management for implants and nonmetallic restorations. Case scenarios and references are available online.

This section covers aesthetic tissue management in restorative dentistry, focusing on interproximal embrasures, papilla management, restorative correction of open gingival embrasures, embrasure form in gingival recession, pontic design with ridge modification, and occlusal considerations. It emphasizes that papilla height and embrasure form depend on bone levels and biologic width, smooth surfaces matter more than material composition, provisional restorations are valuable for planning, and designs must balance aesthetics and hygiene. It details subgingival margin placement and emergence profiles for closing open embrasures, anterior versus posterior recession strategies, ovate pontic and ridge modification techniques, and occlusal principles including mutually protective occlusion and force management for implants and nonmetallic restorations.

nodes.title: Occlusal Considerations in Restorative Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers ovate pontic design, occlusal principles in restorative therapy, restoration of root-resected teeth, and splinting. It describes ovate pontic dimensions and site preparation for aesthetics and hygiene, including a flattened option in less aesthetic areas. Occlusal management emphasizes a mutually protective occlusion with simultaneous MIP contacts, anterior/canine guidance on movement, harmony with the envelope of function, a stable vertical dimension, and repeatable centric relation. Root-resected tooth restoration focuses on conservative preparation, cast post-and-core foundations, hygiene-oriented contours, and possible aesthetic reconstruction. Splinting is discussed as a means of improving stability and comfort after addressing occlusal and inflammatory causes. Case scenarios and references are listed on the companion website.

nodes.title: Special Restorative Considerations
Root-Resected Teeth

It also discusses splinting therapy, including indications, the need to treat occlusion and periodontal inflammation first, and how splints distribute forces to improve stability and comfort.

nodes.title: Splinting
nodes.summary: The text covers restorative considerations for root-resected teeth, splinting of unstable teeth, and anterior aesthetic surgery. Root-resected teeth require conservative preparation, special post-and-core solutions, hygiene-oriented contours, and occasional aesthetic shaping; splinting is indicated for mobility, migration, or prosthetic support and requires treating occlusion and inflammation first with attention to connector and papilla space; anterior aesthetic surgery involves methods to alter gingival levels, with computer imaging or a fabricated surgical guide used to plan and execute predictable tissue positions and restorations.

It describes how the guide is used for incisions, bone recontouring, and suturing to establish proper biologic width and sulcus depth, with a detailed case example showing fabrication, approval, surgical use, and favorable long-term outcomes.

nodes.title: 704.e3
nodes.summary: The text describes the use of a surgical guide in periodontal-restorative surgery to establish the desired free gingival margin, guide osseous recontouring based on biologic width and sulcus depth, and aid suturing to reduce healing time. It includes postoperative outcomes and then presents two case scenarios with multiple-choice questions and explanations: one about closing open gingival embrasures, papilla height dependence on crestal bone height, and risks of subgingival margins; the other about stained veneer margins, appropriate margin placement in the aesthetic zone, cord placement on the junctional epithelium, and soft-tissue recession risk in thin biotypes.

nodes.title: 704.e5
nodes.summary: The text is a case-based educational section on restorative-periodontal interrelationships. It describes a patient with stained margins under old veneers, attributed to ferric-sulfate hemostatic agents, and reviews three multiple-choice questions covering margin depth in the aesthetic zone, cord placement resting on the junctional epithelium, and the higher recession risk associated with a thin biotype. It concludes with a long reference list on related periodontal and restorative dentistry topics.

The section covers anterior periodontal-restorative aesthetic surgery, focusing on the fabrication and use of a surgical guide to establish proper gingival margins, biologic width, osseous recontouring, and suturing. It also addresses clinical considerations such as papillary impingement, gingival-level changes, patient communication, and imaging limitations. The content includes a detailed case example with favorable outcomes, multiple-choice case-based questions on embrasure closure, papilla height, subgingival margins, veneer margin placement, cord placement, and thin-biotype recession risk, and concludes with a reference list.

This section covers special restorative considerations, including root-resected teeth, splinting, and anterior aesthetic surgery. For root-resected teeth, it emphasizes conservative tooth structure preservation, one-piece cast posts and cores, hygiene-oriented contours, management of root concavities, and aesthetic shaping in maxillary molars. Splinting is discussed for unstable teeth, with indications such as mobility, migration, or prosthetic support, and requires prior treatment of occlusion and periodontal inflammation to improve stability and comfort. Anterior aesthetic surgery focuses on using surgical guides to achieve predictable gingival margins, biologic width, osseous recontouring, and suturing, along with clinical considerations like papillary impingement, gingival-level changes, patient communication, and imaging limitations. The section also includes a favorable case example, case-based multiple-choice questions, and a reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text contains the Chapter 70 reference list and the opening of Chapter 71, which contrasts interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approaches to periodontal and implant care. It emphasizes the provider's responsibility to understand disease, risk factors, and treatment options before deciding whether to treat or refer. It reviews implant dentistry's history: general-practitioner innovators, Brånemark's early protocols, expansion of indications, regenerative techniques, limitations of early implants, and the shift from specialty-dominated care toward newer simplified and digital approaches. A clinical figure demonstrates a complex interdisciplinary implant case.

The section covers the intimate relationship between restorative dentistry and periodontal health, emphasizing margin placement (supra/equi/subgingival), biologic width dimensions/evaluation/correction, tissue retraction, and material/hypersensitivity considerations. It addresses aesthetic management of interproximal embrasures and papillae, provisional restorations, ovate pontics and ridge modification, and occlusal principles such as mutually protective occlusion and force management for implants/nonmetallic restorations. Restoration of root-resected teeth, splinting, and anterior aesthetic surgery with surgical guides are also discussed. Resources include abstract/keywords, companion website materials, case scenarios/case-based MCQs, the Chapter 70 reference list, and a transition to Chapter 71 on interdisciplinary vs multidisciplinary care and the history/evolution of implant dentistry.

nodes.title: 71 Multidisciplinary Versus Interdisciplinary Approaches to Dental and Periodontal Problems
CHAPTER 71
nodes.summary: The text contrasts the traditional interdisciplinary model of periodontal and dental implant care, where a team of dentists and specialists provides coordinated care, with the emerging multidisciplinary model, where a single provider manages multiple aspects of treatment. It emphasizes the need for strong diagnostic and treatment-planning knowledge, traces the evolution of implant dentistry from Brånemark’s early protocols and specialist-only training to broader indications and regenerative techniques, and notes early implant limitations and later technological advances. It also discusses the implications of this shift for general practitioners and periodontists, and the chapter outline addresses educational trends and future directions.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text contrasts interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approaches to dental and periodontal problems. Traditionally, care was delivered by a team of general dentists and specialists, while the multidisciplinary model involves a single provider delivering care across disciplines. The interdisciplinary team approach remains useful for complex cases, particularly when soft or hard tissues are deficient. The multidisciplinary model demands broad and deep knowledge from practitioners, especially general dentists, and also changes the role of periodontists, who must expand their skills beyond traditional specialty boundaries.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text contrasts interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approaches to dental and periodontal care. It explains that traditional care is interdisciplinary, with coordinated specialists, while an emerging multidisciplinary model involves a single provider delivering care across disciplines. Complex cases with soft or hard tissue deficiencies still often require an interdisciplinary team. Implant dentistry is a major driver of this shift, and the text emphasizes that periodontists should understand restorative aspects, be able to manage simple implant cases outside the aesthetic zone, and continue advanced soft and hard tissue procedures. It also discusses changing educational trends toward broader multidisciplinary training for general dentists, periodontists, and prosthodontists. Looking ahead, simple implant cases may be handled by one provider, interdisciplinary care will remain for advanced cases, and future periodontists will combine classic specialty expertise with broader restorative knowledge to support colleagues and improve patient care.

nodes.title: Educational Trends Toward Multidisciplinary Specialist Education in Implant Treatment
nodes.summary: The text discusses the shift from interdisciplinary to multidisciplinary approaches in dental implant care. It emphasizes the periodontist's need for spatial awareness and restorative knowledge to communicate effectively. Educational trends show expanded training opportunities and curriculum changes, enabling general dentists, prosthodontists, and surgical specialists to cross traditional boundaries. In the future, simple implant cases may be managed by a single well-trained provider, while interdisciplinary care remains for complex cases with tissue deficiencies. Periodontists will increasingly assist restorative colleagues, such as by taking implant impressions at surgery, while continuing their traditional specialty services.

nodes.title: The Future

It highlights the need for broader training, collaboration among dental specialists, and future trends toward simpler cases being managed by individual providers while interdisciplinary care continues for complex cases. It also emphasizes that long-term periodontal stability requires structured maintenance care after active treatment, explains why disease can recur despite successful therapy due to residual biofilm, intragingival bacteria, reinfection, and incomplete subgingival debridement, and notes the significant risks of tooth loss and attachment loss in noncompliant recall patients.

The section contrasts the traditional interdisciplinary model of dental and periodontal care, involving coordinated teams of general dentists and specialists, with the emerging multidisciplinary model, where a single provider manages multiple aspects of treatment. Implant dentistry is highlighted as a major driver of this shift, tracing its evolution from early specialist-only protocols to broader indications and technological advances. Educational trends are moving toward broader multidisciplinary training, allowing practitioners to cross traditional specialty boundaries. While simple implant cases may increasingly be managed by one provider, complex cases with soft or hard tissue deficiencies still require interdisciplinary teams. The role of periodontists is expanding to include restorative knowledge and collaborative responsibilities. The section also emphasizes the importance of supportive periodontal treatment, explaining why disease can recur after successful therapy and the risks associated with noncompliance in recall maintenance.

This section covers the essential relationship between periodontal health and restorative dentistry. It begins by explaining why periodontal therapy must precede restorative, aesthetic, and implant treatment, outlining the rationale and a staged sequence from disease control to preprosthetic surgery. It then details restorative interrelationships including margin placement, biologic width, tissue retraction, materials, aesthetics, occlusion, root-resected teeth, splinting, and surgical guides. Finally, it contrasts interdisciplinary versus multidisciplinary care, highlights implant dentistry's role in shifting toward single-provider treatment, notes when specialized teams are still needed, and emphasizes the importance of supportive periodontal maintenance and recall compliance.

nodes.title: VII Supportive Care and Results of Periodontal Treatment
72 Supportive Periodontal Treatment
Supportive Periodontal Treatment: Maintenance and Rationale
nodes.summary: This page introduces supportive periodontal treatment (SPT), emphasizing that maintaining periodontal health after therapy requires an ongoing maintenance program with regular recall visits. It highlights the importance of patient education and compliance, noting that noncompliant patients have markedly higher risks of tooth loss and attachment loss. The rationale for SPT explains that incomplete subgingival biofilm removal, persistent intragingival bacteria, bacterial transmission, and microscopic aspects of healing can allow disease recurrence even after successful initial therapy.

nodes.title: LEARNING BOX 72.2
nodes.summary: The text describes supportive periodontal treatment (SPT) as a critical maintenance phase following active periodontal therapy, emphasizing that regular recall visits and quality maintenance are essential for long-term tooth preservation. It highlights poor patient compliance, the increased risk of tooth loss and attachment loss in noncompliant patients, and the importance of patient education. The rationale for SPT includes incomplete subgingival biofilm removal, regrowth of biofilm, persistence of intragingival bacteria, possible reinfection, and limitations of scaling and root planing in deep pockets. The text also covers classification of posttreatment patients, risk assessment, referral to periodontists, and tests for disease activity.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
The rationale for supportive periodontal treatment (SPT) and specific methods of a maintenance program are presented. Classification of post-treatment patients, when to refer to periodontal specialists, and risk assessment are also discussed. Techniques and scheduling sup- portive periodontal treatments are presented. The long-term preserva- tion of the dentition is closely associated with the frequency and quality of recall maintenance. Patients who do not return for SPT lose more teeth than compliant patients. The therapist should use risk assessment to determine the frequency of SPT.
