nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text covers supportive periodontal treatment (SPT), including its rationale, maintenance program methods, patient classification, referral to periodontists, risk assessment, and scheduling. It emphasizes that long-term tooth preservation depends on the frequency and quality of recall maintenance, with noncompliant patients losing more teeth. It also presents correct and incorrect phase sequences, compliance statistics, biological healing with long junctional epithelium, effects of subgingival scaling on microflora, limitations of scaling at deep probing depths, the role of patient motivation, and the structure of maintenance visits—examination/evaluation, treatment and oral hygiene reinforcement, and scheduling—with each visit typically lasting about one hour.

nodes.title: Maintenance Program
LEARNING BOX 72.3
nodes.summary: The text covers the rationale and procedures for supportive periodontal treatment (maintenance). It emphasizes correct sequencing of treatment phases, the importance of maintenance after phase I, and patient compliance data. It explains biological reasons for maintenance—long junctional epithelium healing and microbial shifts after scaling—and notes that scaling/root planing is ineffective at deep probing depths. The maintenance program is described as periodic recall visits with three components: examination, treatment, and report/cleanup/scheduling. Detailed recall procedures include evaluating medical, oral, gingival, periodontal, occlusal, restorative, and implant status; individualized radiographic intervals; oral hygiene reinforcement; scaling, polishing, and antimicrobial placement; and scheduling. The text also stresses assessing plaque control by having patients perform hygiene before the visit and providing instruction until proficiency is achieved.

nodes.title: Examination and Evaluation
nodes.summary: The text describes the three-part supportive periodontal treatment (SPT) maintenance recall procedure: examination, treatment, and report/cleanup/scheduling, with approximate times and specific components for each. It explains that the recall examination focuses on detecting changes in oral and periodontal status, includes individualized radiographic examination with intervals based on patient condition, and stresses evaluating and reinforcing patient plaque/biofilm control. A table provides radiographic recall recommendations for various patient situations, with the caveat that clinical judgment governs radiograph use.

nodes.title: Checking of Plaque/Biofilm Control
nodes.summary: The text covers supportive periodontal treatment (SPT) maintenance visits, including the three-part recall appointment: examination, treatment, and report/cleanup/scheduling. The recall examination focuses on changes since the last visit, including medical history, oral pathology, hygiene, gingival and pocket changes, mobility, occlusion, caries, restorations, prostheses, and implants. Radiographic examination is individualized, with intervals based on caries risk, periodontal control, implants, and transfer patients. Plaque/biofilm control is assessed and reinforced through instruction and motivational interviewing. Treatment includes selective scaling and root planing, polishing, and antimicrobial irrigation for remaining pockets, while avoiding instrumentation of healthy shallow sites. The text also discusses causes and signs of periodontal disease recurrence, the importance of patient compliance and clinician responsibility, and the recommendation to delay retreatment decisions for 1–2 weeks. Clinical figures illustrate maintenance outcomes, compliance versus noncompliance, and recurrence, while tables summarize radiographic intervals and recurrence symptoms/causes.

nodes.title: Treatment
nodes.summary: The text covers supportive periodontal treatment, including patient education and plaque control, scaling and root planing for maintenance, avoidance of instrumenting healthy sites, and use of antimicrobial irrigation or devices. It also discusses causes and signs of periodontal disease recurrence, the dentist's role in patient motivation, the need for patient compliance before surgery, and the recommendation to delay retreatment decisions for 1–2 weeks. A figure illustrates consequences of noncompliance with periodontal maintenance.

nodes.title: Recurrence of Periodontal Disease
nodes.summary: The text covers supportive periodontal treatment: the importance of patient compliance and plaque control, the procedures involved in maintenance care, causes and signs of periodontal disease recurrence, classification of maintenance patients with recommended recall intervals, and the use of risk assessment tools such as PRA and PRC to guide follow-up and prognosis.

The Maintenance Program section describes supportive periodontal treatment (maintenance) as a programmed follow-up after active therapy. It covers the biological rationale and importance of maintenance, patient compliance, and the standard three-part recall appointment: examination, treatment, and report/cleanup/scheduling. The examination updates medical, oral, periodontal, occlusal, restorative, and implant status, uses individualized radiographic intervals, and evaluates plaque/biofilm control with instruction and motivational interviewing. Treatment includes education, selective scaling and root planing, polishing, and antimicrobial irrigation for remaining pockets while avoiding healthy sites. The section also discusses causes and signs of disease recurrence, the need for compliance and clinician responsibility, delaying retreatment decisions, patient classification/recall intervals, and risk assessment tools such as PRA and PRC, supported by figures and tables.

nodes.title: Classification of Posttreatment Patients and Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: The text covers supportive periodontal treatment after therapy, focusing on classification and risk assessment of recall patients, including the Merin classification and suggested recall intervals. It emphasizes that first-year patients need short recall intervals and that recall intervals depend on patient risk factors. Risk assessment tools such as the Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) and Periodontal Risk Calculator (PRC) are described, along with their limitations, and the importance of maintenance care is highlighted. The text also discusses referral of periodontal patients to specialists, the growing need for general dentists to understand periodontal disease, and guidelines from the American Academy of Periodontology for when co-management with a periodontist is appropriate.

nodes.title: Referral of Patients to the Periodontist
key_items: Referral of Patients to the Periodontist
nodes.summary: This section on supportive periodontal treatment covers periodontal risk assessment, referral to periodontists, and maintenance care. Risk assessment tools help determine SPT frequency, but no perfect prediction method exists. General dentists can manage many patients, but complex or advanced cases should be referred to specialists, and maintenance may be divided according to disease class. Disease activity cannot be accurately predicted, so clinicians use sequential probing and multiple risk factors; refractory cases may require bacterial culturing and antibiotics. Long-term tooth preservation depends on regular maintenance, and supportive periodontal therapy is a lifelong effort. A case scenario and references are available on the companion website.

nodes.title: Supportive Periodontal Treatment: Referral, Maintenance, and Disease Activity
nodes.summary: The page covers decisions about periodontal referral and maintenance: severe or localized disease, pockets of 5 mm or more, and furcation invasions usually warrant specialist treatment, and complex cases require a team approach. Maintenance is assigned based on initial disease classification, with Class A patients managed by the general dentist, Class C by the specialist, and Class B alternating. It then addresses tests for disease activity, noting that periodontal patients remain at risk for recurrence, sequential probing is most accurate for attachment loss, no test can reliably predict disease activity, and any adopted test must be validated for sensitivity, specificity, incidence, and predictive value; refractory cases may need culturing and antibiotics. The conclusion emphasizes that preserving teeth depends on the frequency and quality of recall maintenance, risk assessment, patient education, and compliance, since noncompliant patients lose more teeth. The page also mentions a case scenario and references on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text discusses referral and maintenance decisions in supportive periodontal treatment, emphasizing collaboration between general dentists and periodontists, disease severity-based recall classification, risk of recurrence, disease-activity testing, and the lifelong need for maintenance; it also includes two case-based Q&As and a comprehensive reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text provides a list of references for Chapter 72 on supportive periodontal treatment, then presents Chapter 73 'Results of Periodontal Treatment' by Robert L. Merin. This chapter outlines the prevention and treatment of gingivitis and loss of attachment, tooth mortality, and conclusion. It highlights evidence-based therapy showing periodontal treatment is effective. Gingivitis is reversible, with studies demonstrating that stopping oral hygiene leads to biofilm accumulation and gingivitis, which resolves after resuming hygiene and professional cleaning. Long-term and controlled studies (e.g., in California workers) confirm that gingival health can be maintained by oral hygiene and prophylaxis. For loss of attachment, longitudinal studies in Oslo and Sri Lanka are described to investigate natural periodontal disease progression. The chapter also includes a chapter outline and learning boxes.

This section covers supportive periodontal treatment (SPT) as the lifelong maintenance phase after active periodontal therapy, emphasizing that regular recall visits and quality maintenance are essential for long-term tooth preservation. It explains the biological rationale for SPT, the importance of patient education and compliance, and the structured recall visit consisting of examination, treatment, and scheduling. It also covers classification of posttreatment patients, risk assessment tools and their limitations, referral to periodontists and co-management guidelines, and tests for disease activity. The central message is that tooth preservation depends on the frequency and quality of maintenance, risk-based recall intervals, and patient compliance, since noncompliant patients lose more teeth. References, case scenarios, and a preview of Chapter 73 are also included.

nodes.title: 73 Results of Periodontal Treatment
Results of Periodontal Treatment: Gingivitis and Attachment Loss Prevention
key_items: Prevention and Treatment of Loss of Attachment
nodes.summary: This page from Chapter 73, 'Results of Periodontal Treatment,' discusses the effectiveness of periodontal therapy based on evidence. It covers prevention and treatment of gingivitis, emphasizing that gingivitis is reversible and controlled by oral hygiene and professional prophylaxis, supported by Löe's experiments and a 3-year study of telephone workers. It then introduces prevention of loss of attachment, describing long-term studies begun in the mid-1970s, including Löe's longitudinal investigations in Oslo and Sri Lanka.

nodes.title: Prevention of Loss of Attachment
nodes.summary: This chapter addresses the effectiveness of periodontal treatment in preventing and controlling periodontal disease and tooth loss. It reviews evidence that gingivitis is reversible and can be controlled by oral hygiene and professional prophylaxis, citing experimental and long-term studies. It also covers prevention of attachment loss and tooth mortality, showing that treated patients lose far fewer teeth than untreated patients, compliant maintenance reduces tooth loss, and smoking increases tooth loss. The chapter concludes that periodontal therapy is effective and that failing to diagnose or treat periodontal disease leads to unnecessary dental and systemic health problems.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The abstract evaluates the effectiveness of periodontal treatment in preventing disease progression and tooth loss. It states that good oral hygiene and prophylaxis control gingivitis and attachment loss, while treatment of moderate to advanced periodontitis significantly reduces tooth loss. Compared to treated patients, untreated patients lose 5–16 times more teeth, noncompliant patients lose 3 times more, and smokers lose about twice as many. Treatment is effective in preventing periodontal disease, stopping bone destruction, and reducing tooth mortality, while failure to treat causes unnecessary dental and systemic health risks. The chapter reviews studies on the natural history of periodontal disease, experimental gingivitis, gingivitis reduction, and tooth loss with and without therapy.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text discusses the effectiveness of periodontal treatment in preventing and controlling periodontal disease and tooth loss. It covers evidence that good oral hygiene and dental prophylaxis reduce gingivitis and attachment loss, and that treatment of moderate-to-advanced periodontitis significantly reduces tooth mortality. Comparisons of untreated vs treated populations, including Sri Lankan and Norwegian groups, show untreated disease progresses more rapidly and severely. Clinical studies demonstrate that treated and well-maintained patients lose far fewer teeth and have far less attachment loss than untreated or noncompliant patients, including data from university and private practice studies. The chapter also emphasizes that failing to treat periodontal disease leads to unnecessary dental problems and systemic health risks, and concludes that periodontal therapy, especially with biofilm control and maintenance, is effective in reducing disease progression and tooth loss.

nodes.title: Tooth Mortality
nodes.summary: This text reviews the results of periodontal treatment, focusing on attachment loss and tooth mortality. Treated and compliant patients show minimal attachment loss and greatly reduced disease progression, whereas untreated patients have substantially higher rates of attachment loss and tooth loss. Multiple long-term studies, including hospital- and private-practice-based trials, demonstrate that periodontal therapy, especially when combined with effective biofilm control and regular supportive maintenance, preserves teeth even in advanced disease. A small percentage of patients account for most tooth loss, and factors such as furcation involvement, smoking, and poor compliance increase risk. The text concludes that periodontal treatment is effective and necessary, and that periodontal disease may contribute to systemic health problems including pregnancy complications, heart disease, stroke, and diabetes.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: This text reviews long-term outcomes of periodontal treatment, showing that treated patients lose relatively few teeth—even those with furcation involvement or guarded prognosis—especially when compliant with supportive maintenance therapy. It contrasts these results with untreated periodontitis, where tooth mortality is substantially higher, and concludes that periodontal therapy effectively reduces tooth loss and may also lessen systemic health risks.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text presents data on tooth mortality in treated and untreated periodontitis patients, showing that periodontal treatment reduces tooth loss compared with no treatment. It stresses the importance of diagnosing and treating periodontal disease to prevent tooth loss and systemic health risks. It also includes a clinical case scenario of a stable patient after periodontal therapy, with the correct diagnosis of reduced but healthy periodontium, and provides a reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: This text begins with a bibliography of 42 references on periodontal disease and therapy, then moves to Part 4 of the book on oral implantology. Chapter 74 covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, including implant macrogeometry, hard and soft tissue interfaces, and clinical comparisons with teeth. It recounts the history of modern implant dentistry: Brånemark's discovery of osseointegration with titanium in the 1950s, the first patient in 1965, and long-term success with CP titanium implants. Older implant designs (blade, cylindrical press-fit, subperiosteal, transmandibular) are described as largely unsuccessful, while current endosseous implants are typically threaded cylinders or tapered screws. The text emphasizes that predictable bone apposition requires atraumatic preparation and prevention of micromovement during healing, and notes contributions by André Schroeder. Additional online-only content is mentioned for implant types and surface characteristics.

This section reviews evidence that periodontal treatment effectively prevents and controls periodontal disease and tooth loss. Good oral hygiene and professional prophylaxis control gingivitis, and periodontal therapy—especially with biofilm control and supportive maintenance—preserves attachment and reduces tooth mortality. Comparisons show untreated, noncompliant, and smoking patients lose far more teeth than treated compliant patients, while only a small percentage of patients account for most tooth loss. The section concludes that periodontal therapy is effective and necessary, avoiding unnecessary dental and systemic health risks, and includes a clinical case of a reduced but healthy periodontium. It closes with a 42-item reference list and transitions to Part 4 on oral implantology, outlining Chapter 74, the history of modern implants from Brånemark's discovery of osseointegration to current threaded/tapered endosseous designs, and associated healing requirements.

Section VII covers supportive periodontal care and treatment outcomes. It describes supportive periodontal treatment as the lifelong maintenance phase after active therapy, emphasizing that regular, high-quality, risk-based recall visits and patient compliance are essential to preserve teeth; it also details patient education, recall visit structure, posttreatment classification, risk assessment, referral/co-management, and disease-activity tests. It then presents evidence that periodontal treatment—especially with biofilm control and supportive maintenance—effectively prevents and controls periodontal disease, preserves attachment, and reduces tooth loss, while untreated, noncompliant, and smoking patients lose more teeth and a minority of patients account for most losses. The section concludes that periodontal therapy is effective and necessary, includes a clinical case of a reduced but healthy periodontium, references, and transitions to Part 4 on oral implantology, introducing Chapter 74 on implant history from Brånemark's osseointegration to modern threaded/tapered designs and healing requirements.

structure.summary: This section on clinical periodontics covers the full spectrum from diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning through nonsurgical and surgical therapy, periodontal-restorative interrelationships, and long-term supportive care. It includes frameworks for clinical significance, comprehensive examination, radiographic interpretation, risk assessment, prognosis, treatment sequencing, and electronic dental records/clinical decision support. It then addresses special-needs patient management and periodontal emergencies, followed by Phase I nonsurgical treatment and Phase II surgical procedures, including regenerative, plastic, and adjunctive technologies. It also emphasizes the interplay between periodontal health and restorative/implant dentistry, and concludes with supportive periodontal care, evidence of treatment outcomes, and a transition to oral implantology.

structure.title: 4 Oral Implantology

nodes.title: I Biology, Diagnosis, Biomechanics, and Treatment Plan
74 Peri-implant Anatomy, Biology, and Function
CHAPTER 74
nodes.summary: This chapter from Part 4 on Oral Implantology covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, including implant geometry (macrodesign), implant surface characteristics (microdesign), hard and soft tissue interfaces, and clinical comparisons between teeth and implants. It reviews the history of implant dentistry, beginning with Brånemark's discovery of osseointegration with titanium in the 1950s and the first successful patient treatment in 1965. It also discusses the evolution of implant designs, noting the failure of earlier types such as blade, press-fit cylindrical, subperiosteal, and transmandibular implants, and the contributions of researchers like André Schroeder. The text emphasizes that predictable osseointegration requires atraumatic bone preparation and prevention of micromovement during healing, and that current implants are predominantly cylindrical or tapered, screw-shaped/threaded designs.

nodes.title: Implant Geometry (Macrodesign)
nodes.summary: This chapter from an oral implantology textbook reviews peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function. It covers the history of modern implant dentistry, including Brånemark's discovery of osseointegration and the first patient treatment in 1965, as well as the contributions of André Schroeder. The text discusses implant geometry (macrodesign), including past failed designs and current threaded cylindrical/tapered forms, implant surface characteristics (microdesign), the hard and soft tissue interfaces around implants, and a clinical comparison of teeth and implants. It emphasizes the importance of understanding biologic principles for predictable long-term implant success and notes online-only content for additional implant types and surface details.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
732.e1
CHAPTER 74 Peri-implant Anatomy, Biology, and Function
Abstract
Osseointegrated dental implants can provide patients with predictable tooth replacement options, including but not limited to an implant- retained removable prosthesis and an implant-supported fixed prosthesis. Although implants are predictable and long lasting, there are biologic and functional problems. It is essential for clinicians to understand and appreciate the biologic aspects of dental implant therapy, including bone biology, the phenomenon of osseointegration, and the relationship of peri-implant soft tissues with dental implants. This chapter reviews implant design, implants surface characteristics, the biology of osseointegration, and the interface between implants and soft tissues. The functional aspects of osseointegrated dental implants is also considered.
Key Words implant geometry macrodesign implant surface characteristics microdesign hard tissue interface soft tissue interface implants

nodes.title: Key Words
Hard Tissue Interface
nodes.summary: The text covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, including implant designs, the histologic and clinical definitions of osseointegration, and the hard tissue interface as essential to implant success. It describes initial bone healing as similar to fracture healing, detailing the cellular and molecular events from inflammation through bone formation. It emphasizes conditions required for osseointegration, such as immobility and controlled inflammation, and warns that micromovements above 150 μm cause fibrous tissue formation, so occlusal loading must be avoided during early healing.

nodes.title: Initial Bone Healing
nodes.summary: The text covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, focusing on osseointegration definitions and the hard tissue interface as essential for implant success. It lists implant macrodesign categories and describes initial bone healing as fracture-like, requiring immobility and avoidance of excessive micromovement. The text then reviews several historical implant designs: blade implants (poor success, fibrous encapsulation, difficult removal), pins (cemented triads, easier removal), disk implants (lateral insertion, anecdotal success), and root-form/cylindrical implants, especially hollow-cylinder systems such as ITI and Core-Vent, which had unfavorable survival rates and were withdrawn; the passage ends mid-sentence regarding possible causes.

nodes.title: Historical Implant Designs and Their Clinical Outcomes
nodes.summary: The page covers historical dental implant designs—blade implants, pins, disk implants, and root form cylindrical implants—and their biological problems. Blade implants caused fibrous encapsulation, bone loss, peri-implantitis, poor success, and difficult removal. Pins offered easier removal but had similar infection and encapsulation issues. Disk implants provided strong vertical retention but also developed fibrous scar tissue and lacked reliable success data. Root form cylindrical implants, notably the ITI hollow-cylinder and Core-Vent systems, were designed to improve bone contact but the ITI system was withdrawn due to inferior survival. Two eFig captions illustrate a failing blade implant with radiolucency and an ITI hollow cylinder implant.

nodes.title: Root Form (Cylindrical) Implants
nodes.summary: The text reviews historical and current dental implant designs, their biological outcomes, and implant surface characteristics. It covers blade implants, pins, disk implants, root form (cylindrical) implants (hollow and solid, including ITI and IMZ systems), transmandibular implants, and subperiosteal implants, detailing insertion methods, complications such as fibrous encapsulation and peri-implantitis, survival rates, and reasons for abandonment or reduced use. It then describes modern threaded/tapered screw-shaped implants and explains how surface microtopography, energy, chemistry, and roughness enhance osseointegration by improving protein adsorption, cellular activity, and fibrin clot retention.

nodes.title: Dental Implant Designs and Surface Characteristics
nodes.summary: The page covers dental implant designs and surface characteristics. It first discusses IMZ cylindrical implants, including their shock absorber, short-term promise, poor long-term survival, and biomechanical shear issues. It then describes transmandibular implants for severely atrophic mandibles, covering the Small staple-bone and Bosker designs, survival rates, complications, and current rare use. Subperiosteal implants are described as custom frameworks for atrophic mandibles, with posts for prostheses, but poor survival and frequent infections also made them rare. The text then outlines modern threaded/cylindrical implant geometry, parallel versus tapered shapes, and implant surface microdesign modifications that improve healing and osteogenesis.

The section opens with an abstract and keywords for Chapter 74 on peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function. It covers the hard tissue interface and osseointegration, describing initial bone healing as fracture-like and requiring immobility and controlled inflammation; excess micromovement leads to fibrous tissue. It reviews historical implant designs—blade, pin, disk, root-form/cylindrical, transmandibular, and subperiosteal—and their biological complications, poor survival rates, or limited current use. It then describes modern threaded/tapered implant geometry and surface characteristics that promote osseointegration through improved protein adsorption, cellular activity, and clot retention.

nodes.title: Implant Surface Characteristics (Microdesign)
Transmandibular Implants
nodes.summary: The text discusses historical and modern dental implant designs and outcomes. It covers IMZ cylindrical implants with internal shock absorbers and their poor long-term survival, the mechanical disadvantages of cylindrical versus threaded implants, transmandibular implants for severely resorbed mandibles including the staple-bone and Bosker designs and their complication rates, and subperiosteal implants with their high failure and complication rates. It then describes current screw-shaped/threaded implants, parallel versus tapered geometries, and the importance of implant surface characteristics—such as topography, energy, and chemistry—in promoting bone healing and osseointegration.

nodes.title: Subperiosteal Implants
nodes.summary: The text discusses historical and current dental implant designs. It covers IMZ cylindrical implants and their poor long-term survival, transmandibular implants for severely resorbed mandibles, and subperiosteal implants, all of which are now rarely used due to complications or low success rates. It then describes modern threaded screw-shaped implants, including parallel and tapered geometries, and emphasizes implant surface characteristics and additive processes that modify microtopography and chemistry to enhance bone healing and integration.

nodes.title: Additive Processes
nodes.summary: The text covers peri-implant implant design and surface modifications. It contrasts parallel and tapered threaded implants, noting tapered designs reduce apical fenestration and aid immediate placement. It then describes additive surface treatments (coatings, plasma spraying, growth factors, hydroxyapatite, oxide layers) that roughen implants and enhance bone cell responses, and subtractive treatments (machining, acid etching, blasting) that improve osseointegration. Finally, it reviews implant material chemistry: carbon and hydroxyapatite implants fractured, noble metals/alloys corroded, and most current oral implants are made of an unspecified material in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Subtractive Processes
nodes.summary: The text discusses implant surface modifications, including illustrations of titanium plasma-sprayed rough surfaces and methods like plasma spraying, acid etching, and oxidizing. It explains subtractive processes that alter surface microstructure and chemistry to improve osseointegration, and notes the benefits of microscopic modifications such as acid etching. It also reviews implant surface chemical composition, mentioning failures of carbon, hydroxyapatite, and noble metals/alloys, and begins to state the material used for most modern oral implants.

nodes.title: Implant Surface Chemical Composition
nodes.summary: The text covers implant surface characteristics in oral implantology, including additive techniques like titanium plasma spraying and TiUnite oxidizing, as well as subtractive processes like machining, acid etching, and blasting that modify surface roughness to enhance osseointegration. SEM images illustrate different surface types. It discusses implant surface chemical composition, explaining why CP titanium is preferred over carbon, hydroxyapatite, or noble metals, and describes titanium's oxide layer, biomolecule adsorption, and the unproven benefit of calcium phosphate coatings. It also addresses surface free energy/wettability and microscopic roughness measurement, noting that roughened surfaces accelerate bone apposition but may have drawbacks, while surface topography influences protein adsorption, cellular responses, and cell orientation.

nodes.title: Implant Surface Free Energy and Microscopic Roughness
nodes.summary: The text covers implant surface properties, including wettability, microscopic roughness, and the biologic effects of surface topography on cell adhesion and bone apposition. It also discusses limitations of finite element analysis, the histologic progression of bone apposition, the cellular and thermal requirements for successful osteotomy healing, the importance of immobility and micromotion thresholds, the sequence from woven to lamellar bone, and long-term bone-to-implant stability, including primary and secondary implant stability.

nodes.title: Bone Remodeling and Function
nodes.summary: The text describes peri-implant biology and function, covering the osseous healing and remodeling process around dental implants, including osteoclast and osteoblast activity, vascular and oxygen requirements, temperature thresholds, aseptic technique, and the critical role of immobility and micromotion limits. It explains the sequence of woven bone formation and its replacement by lamellar bone, primary and secondary implant stability, factors affecting stability in different jaw sites, and considerations for early loading. It also details the soft tissue interface, including the peri-implant biologic width, epithelial attachment with hemidesmosomes, connective tissue morphology and fiber orientation, the absence of a periodontal ligament, and the potential of microgrooved implant surfaces to improve soft tissue sealing.

The section covers the evolution of dental implant designs from failed historical devices (IMZ cylindrical, transmandibular, subperiosteal) to modern threaded screw-shaped implants with parallel and tapered geometries, emphasizing implant surface characteristics such as topography, energy, and chemistry. It describes additive surface modifications (plasma spraying, coatings, growth factors, hydroxyapatite, oxide layers) and subtractive methods (machining, acid etching, blasting) that modify surface roughness and chemistry to enhance osseointegration. It explains why CP titanium is preferred over carbon, hydroxyapatite, and noble metals/alloys, and discusses titanium's oxide layer, biomolecule adsorption, and the unproven benefit of calcium phosphate coatings. The section also addresses surface free energy/wettability and microscopic roughness and their effects on protein adsorption, cellular responses, cell orientation, and bone apposition. Additionally, it covers peri-implant bone healing and remodeling, including osteoclast/osteoblast activity, vascular/oxygen requirements, temperature thresholds, aseptic technique, immobility and micromotion limits, woven-to-lamellar bone sequence, primary and secondary stability, early loading considerations, and the soft tissue interface with biologic width, epithelial attachment, connective tissue morphology, absence of periodontal ligament, and microgrooved surfaces for soft tissue sealing.

nodes.title: Soft Tissue Interface
nodes.summary: This chapter covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, focusing on implant stability and healing, the structure of peri-implant soft tissues, epithelial and connective tissue interfaces, the role of keratinized mucosa, vascular supply and inflammation, and clinical differences between teeth and implants. It emphasizes that implants lack a periodontal ligament and inserting Sharpey's fibers, have a biologic width of roughly 3–4.5 mm, respond to plaque similarly to teeth, but have reduced mobility, proprioception, and vascular supply, with important implications for occlusal loading and clinical management.

nodes.title: Clinical Comparison of Teeth and Implants
nodes.summary: The text covers peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, emphasizing similarities and differences between implants and natural teeth. Peri-implant soft tissues resemble those around teeth and show similar inflammatory responses to plaque, but implants lack a periodontal ligament, which affects movement, proprioception, and clinical management. This absence contraindicates implants in growing individuals and can cause problems with adjacent mobile teeth or occlusal overload. The conclusion stresses that understanding bone and soft tissue biology is essential for successful osseointegration and long-term implant maintenance.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text discusses implant contraindications in growing individuals due to lack of periodontal ligament and implant immobility, potential issues with implants near mobile teeth, and risks of overload leading to bone damage. It concludes that clinicians need a thorough understanding of bone biology, osseointegration, and both bone- and soft tissue-implant interfaces to ensure long-term implant success, and notes that a case scenario and references are available online.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text covers implant contraindications in growing patients due to lack of periodontal ligament and movement, problems with adjacent mobile teeth, and overload-induced bone loss. It concludes that understanding bone biology, the bone-implant interface, and soft tissue-implant interface is crucial for successful osseointegration and long-term implant maintenance. A case scenario describes a healthy 47-year-old male with maxillary central incisor implants requiring routine maintenance. Case-based questions with explanations address peri-implant tissue structure and attachment. A comprehensive reference list is included, with additional resources on the companion website.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text is from an oral implantology textbook section. It first presents a comprehensive reference list for Chapter 74 on peri-implant anatomy, biology, and function, including studies on implant-tissue interactions, osseointegration, implant surfaces, and clinical outcomes. It then introduces Chapter 75 on clinical evaluation of the implant patient, outlining its topics: case types and indications, risk factors and contraindications, posttreatment evaluation, and conclusion. The chapter discusses the evolution of dental implants from edentulous to partially edentulous applications, high success rates in suitable patients, and the importance of comprehensive patient and site evaluation. It details treatment options for edentulous patients, including implant-supported fixed hybrid prostheses and ceramo-metal fixed bridges, along with their indications and limitations regarding lip support, phonetics, and bone volume.

74 Peri-implant Anatomy, Biology, and Function reviews the biological basis of dental implant therapy. It covers the history and evolution of implant designs, from failed early forms to modern threaded cylindrical/tapered implants, and emphasizes the importance of implant geometry and surface characteristics (topography, chemistry, energy; additive and subtractive modifications) in promoting osseointegration. The section explains hard tissue biology, including fracture-like peri-implant bone healing requiring immobility, controlled inflammation, vascularity, and limited micromotion, as well as primary/secondary stability and loading implications. It describes the soft tissue interface: biologic width, epithelial and connective tissue attachment, absence of periodontal ligament, keratinized mucosa, and vascular considerations. It also clinically compares teeth and implants, noting implants' reduced mobility, proprioception, and blood supply, their similar plaque response, contraindications in growing patients, and risks of overload. The section concludes that understanding bone biology and the bone–implant and soft tissue–implant interfaces is essential for predictable long-term implant success, and it includes prosthodontic applications, case-based questions, references, and online resources.

nodes.title: 75 Clinical Evaluation of the Implant Patient
CHAPTER 75
nodes.summary: This chapter excerpt discusses the clinical evaluation of dental implant patients, covering the evolution and success of implant therapy, patient assessment, case types, and indications. It emphasizes that implants are now highly successful for edentulous and partially edentulous patients, with success rates of 90% to 95% in suitable candidates. Evaluation must include local bone assessment, prosthetic restorability, patient health, risk factors, and expectations. For edentulous patients, various implant-supported prostheses are described, including hybrid fixed bridges and ceramic-metal fixed bridges, along with their limitations such as inadequate lip support and potential phonetic issues.

nodes.title: Case Types and Indications Edentulous Patients
nodes.summary: The chapter covers the clinical evaluation of dental implant patients. It reviews the evolution of implant therapy, success rates, and the importance of comprehensive patient and site assessment. It describes indications for edentulous patients, including implant-supported fixed prosthetic designs, their advantages and limitations, and emphasizes the roles of imaging, implant size/spacing requirements, risk factors, contraindications, and posttreatment evaluation.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text is a chapter abstract on clinical evaluation of dental implant patients. It highlights the growing popularity and demand for dental implants, the necessity of thorough patient history and clinical examination, and the importance of assessing bone dimensions at implant sites. It emphasizes that radiographs, particularly CBCT, are essential for detecting ridge deficiencies and planning. The chapter covers implant size and spacing requirements, as well as risk factors and contraindications.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text is from Chapter 75 on clinical evaluation of implant patients. It emphasizes the importance of thorough patient history, clinical examination, and radiographic evaluation, especially CBCT, to assess bone quality and volume for implant placement. It discusses implant selection, dimensional requirements, spacing, risk factors, and contraindications. The chapter covers treatment considerations for fully edentulous patients, including implant-retained overdentures and fixed prostheses; partially edentulous patients with multiple missing teeth, including challenges and the need for adequate implant support; single-tooth implants, including success rates, mechanical challenges, and solutions; aesthetic considerations for anterior implants; and the comprehensive pretreatment evaluation process.

nodes.title: Pretreatment Evaluation
Single Tooth
nodes.summary: The text covers implant treatment considerations for long-span posterior bridges, the Kennedy Classification for edentulous spaces, single-tooth implant indications and outcomes, challenges with screw loosening and fracture and their solutions, aesthetic complexities of anterior single-tooth implants, and the importance of comprehensive pretreatment patient evaluation and examination.

nodes.title: Aesthetic Considerations
nodes.summary: The text covers implant treatment considerations: challenges with posterior multiunit fixed bridges and the need for adequate implant support; the Kennedy Classification of edentulous spaces; benefits and technical solutions for single-tooth implants; aesthetic challenges of anterior implants; the importance of comprehensive pretreatment evaluation, chief complaint assessment, realistic patient expectations, and thorough medical history review to determine candidacy and plan appropriate implant therapy.

nodes.title: Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: The text discusses clinical evaluation of dental implant patients, emphasizing the importance of a systematic history and examination to determine whether implant therapy is appropriate and to develop a comprehensive treatment plan with multiple options. It highlights the chief complaint process, focusing on understanding patient expectations, personal criteria for success, and satisfaction related to comfort, function, appearance, and quality of life. It also stresses the need for a thorough medical history to identify risk factors that may affect healing or surgery, with possible physical exams and laboratory tests. Additional points include the need for realistic expectations, involving family members in consultations, and recognizing additional surgical needs such as ridge or sinus augmentation.

nodes.title: Medical History
nodes.summary: This text covers the clinical evaluation of dental implant patients, emphasizing a systematic history and examination to determine candidacy and create a comprehensive treatment plan with multiple options. It details the chief complaint, medical history, dental history, intraoral examination, diagnostic study models, space requirements for implants, and hard tissue evaluation, including bone assessment and three-dimensional implant positioning considerations.

nodes.title: Dental History
nodes.summary: The text covers comprehensive pre-implant patient evaluation, including medical and dental history, intraoral examination, diagnostic study models, and hard tissue evaluation. It details minimal space requirements for implant placement: alveolar bone width/height, interdental mesial-distal distances for one or multiple implants, and interocclusal space for the restorative stack. It emphasizes treating existing pathology, assessing patient motivation and past experiences, measuring available bone and dental space, and considering anatomical limitations such as root orientation and jaw anatomy before implant therapy.

nodes.title: Intraoral Examination
nodes.summary: This text covers the clinical evaluation of dental implant patients, including medical assessment and clearance, dental history, intraoral examination, implant site and space requirements, diagnostic study models, hard and soft tissue evaluation, radiographic examination, and risk factors/contraindications. It details specific measurements for alveolar bone, interdental space, and interocclusal space; the importance of prosthetically driven planning with wax-ups and radiopaque guides; the debate over keratinized mucosa around implants; and medical/systemic factors, especially diabetes mellitus, that affect implant success and healing.

Pretreatment evaluation for dental implants is a comprehensive, systematic process that includes the chief complaint, realistic patient expectations, and family involvement when appropriate; thorough medical and dental history review; intraoral examination; hard and soft tissue assessment; diagnostic study models; radiographic evaluation; and measurement of alveolar bone, interdental, and interocclusal spaces. It also addresses prosthetically driven planning, anatomical limitations, implant support for long-span posterior bridges, Kennedy Classification of edentulous spaces, single-tooth implant indications and complications, anterior aesthetic challenges, additional surgical needs such as ridge or sinus augmentation, and risk factors including diabetes mellitus and keratinized mucosa considerations.

nodes.title: Conclusion

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
753.e1
CHAPTER 76 Diagnostic Imaging for the Implant Patient
Abstract
Radiographic imaging is a valuable tool in the assessment of patients receiving dental implants. Two- and three- dimensional imaging approaches are utilized to provide an accurate assessment of the anatomy of the osseous structures of the craniofacial complex. In this chapter, we discuss the advantages and disadvantages of standard intraoral and extraoral projections and complex imaging modalities such as multi-slice computed tomography (MSCT) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). We also provide a disciplined and methodical approach toward assessment of the available radiographs to maximize their usefulness towards improved outcomes.
Key Words radiographs periapical panoramic CBCT MSCT surgical guides

nodes.title: Key Words
nodes.summary: The chapter covers the role of radiographic imaging in dental implant patients. It describes the advantages and disadvantages of 2D modalities, including periapical, occlusal, and panoramic radiographs, and 3D cross-sectional modalities, mainly CBCT and MSCT, with an emphasis on radiation doses and FOV considerations. It highlights that intraoral and panoramic images are useful for initial assessment but limited by magnification, distortion, and 2D anatomy, while CBCT offers precise 3D evaluation of implant sites with lower radiation than MSCT. The content also includes table data on radiation doses, figure descriptions, and keywords such as surgical guides.

nodes.title: Cross-Sectional Imaging
nodes.summary: The text describes diagnostic imaging for implant patients. It first explains the limitations of panoramic radiography, including distortion, variable magnification (average 25%, range 10-30%), and inability to provide precise measurements, while noting its usefulness for overall initial assessment. It then covers cross-sectional imaging: CBCT and MSCT, with conventional tomography largely obsolete. CBCT provides 3D and multiplanar imaging, varying field-of-view sizes affecting radiation and resolution, and multiple advantages over 2D imaging, including accurate cross-sections, no magnification, digital tools, and lower radiation than CT. MSCT remains an alternative if CBCT is unavailable, offering good cross-sectional and 3D views but with higher radiation, cost, and metal artifacts. Interactive software can simulate implant placement and restorations from CT/CBCT data and generate surgical guides. Finally, patient evaluation should be systematic, use appropriate imaging, and aim to exclude pathology, identify anatomy, and measure bone quantity, quality, and location.

nodes.title: Interactive “Simulation” Software Programs

It also describes interactive software programs that simulate implant placement and generate surgical guides, and outlines the objectives of patient evaluation: excluding pathology, identifying anatomy, and assessing available bone.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
769.e1
CHAPTER 77 Prosthetic Considerations for Implant Treatment
Abstract
Succesful implant treatment requires a knowledgeable and skilled team of clinicians and technicians. At every step in the process, careful consideration must be given to the approach with the best prognosis for the given patient and their proposed treatment. This chapter focuses on the restorative/prosthodontic aspects of implant treatment. It will provide useful information to the entire treatment team based on the best available evidence.
Keywords implant prosthetics implant restorations abutments partially edentulous fully edentulous

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: The text covers prosthodontic planning and restoration of dental implants, including implant sizing and space requirements, determining the number of implants, fixed dental prostheses and cantilevers, implant-abutment connection designs (external, internal, and solid body), the role of microgap leakage and platform switching, and single-unit retention choices (cemented versus screw-retained). It emphasizes evidence-based decision-making, major versus minor complications, and clinical recommendations for improving implant prosthetic outcomes.

nodes.title: Abutment/Prosthesis Considerations for Single Units
Retention Method for Partially Edentulous Treatment: Cemented Prostheses, Screw-Retained Porcelain-Fused-to-Metal Options, Screw-Retained Full Contour Zirconia, and Hybrid Designs
nodes.summary: The text covers implant prosthetic considerations: challenges of solid body/tissue-level implants regarding cementation and abutment fracture; comparison of screw-retained versus cement-retained single-unit implant crowns, including indications, complications, porcelain fracture rates, screw loosening, retrievability, and cementation risks; emerging options like full-contour zirconia screw-retained crowns, hybrid screwmentable crowns, and lingual set screws; and abutment material selection with evidence on titanium, zirconia, gold alloy, and the importance of fit in preserving peri-implant tissues.

nodes.title: Abutment Material Selection
nodes.summary: This chapter covers prosthetic considerations for implant treatment, including hybrid crown designs (titanium base with ceramic) and lingual set screws for angled implants. It details abutment material selection, comparing titanium, zirconia, gold, and coated options in terms of biologic response, strength, and soft tissue aesthetics, emphasizing the critical accuracy of the abutment-implant interface. It also discusses abutment design and emergence profiles, noting that undercontouring and platform-switch designs preserve tissue, and that margin placement for cement-retained restorations must not exceed 1 mm subgingival to avoid cement-induced peri-implantitis, favoring custom abutments to accommodate gingival scalloping.

nodes.title: Abutment Design and Emergence Profile
nodes.summary: The text covers prosthetic considerations for implant treatment, including abutment materials and coatings, the importance of accurate abutment-implant fit, abutment margin placement no deeper than 1 mm subgingival to avoid cement-induced peri-implantitis, emergence profile design to preserve peri-implant tissue, custom abutment fabrication and margin communication, splinting of adjacent implants, and proper sealing of screw access channels. It emphasizes using titanium-base zirconia abutments, gold/pink coated titanium for aesthetics, undercontoured emergence profiles, and avoiding cotton in screw access in favor of gutta-percha, PTFE tape, or polyvinyl siloxane.

nodes.title: Covering the Screw Access
nodes.summary: The text covers prosthetic considerations for implant treatment, specifically screw access sealing, splinting of adjacent implants, and aesthetic-zone implant management. For screw access, it emphasizes proper sealing materials—cotton is discouraged due to bacterial proliferation and peri-implantitis risk, while gutta-percha, PTFE tape, and PVS are alternatives, with chlorhexidine cleaning before placement. For splinting, it reviews evidence showing that force-sharing does not significantly reduce bone loss or implant failure, so splinting is not routinely justified, though it may be useful in specific situations; cost and repair implications are important. For aesthetic-zone treatment, it highlights individual soft-tissue evaluation, tissue biotype, abutment color management, and the limitations of papilla regeneration around implants, including average papilla height measurements.

This section covers prosthetic considerations for single implant units. It reviews retention options—cemented prostheses, screw-retained PFM, screw-retained full-contour zirconia, hybrid screwmentable designs, and lingual set screws—including tissue-level implant challenges, screw vs cement comparisons, porcelain fracture/screw loosening, retrievability, and cementation risks. It discusses abutment material selection (titanium, zirconia, gold, coated) regarding biologic response, strength, soft-tissue aesthetics, and the critical fit of the abutment-implant interface. Abutment design and emergence profile principles emphasize undercontouring, platform-switch, subgingival margins no deeper than 1 mm for cement-retained restorations, custom abutments for scalloped gingiva, and margin communication. Screw-access sealing should avoid cotton and use gutta-percha, PTFE tape, or PVS after chlorhexidine. Splinting adjacent implants is not routinely justified due to lack of significant bone-loss/failure benefit, though it may be useful in specific cases and has cost/repair implications. Aesthetic-zone management includes individual soft-tissue evaluation, tissue biotype, abutment color, and the limitations of papilla regeneration, with average papilla height measurements.

nodes.title: Management of Partially Edentulous Implant Treatment in the Aesthetic Zone
Diagnosis and Treatment Planning
nodes.summary: This chapter covers prosthetic considerations for implant treatment, focusing on splinting decisions, aesthetic-zone management, and implant provisional restorations. Evidence shows splinting adjacent implants does not significantly reduce bone loss, so 'sharing forces' is not a valid indication, although splinting may still be appropriate in certain compromised situations; its main downside is costly long-term replacement, especially after PFM porcelain failure. In the aesthetic zone, treatment is individualized by lip dynamics, with peri-implant soft tissue and papilla management being major challenges; thin biotypes and gray color shifts require careful planning, abutment choices, and tissue shaping. Implant-retained provisional restorations are essential tools: they should be screw-retained, polished, and titanium at the apical emergence, and they support immediate loading, papilla preservation, and evaluation of aesthetics, phonetics, function, and hygiene before the definitive prosthesis is made.

Immediate provisionalization/loading is described, with criteria and benefits such as papilla preservation and reduced bone loss. Guidelines for provisional design—narrow smooth emergence, no tissue blanching, open embrasures—and management of angled implants are included. nodes.summary: The text covers fabrication of indirect and direct custom impression copings, emphasizing that customized copings preserve tissue contours for accurate definitive abutment and crown fabrication. Customized impression copings are described for preserving tissue contours. nodes.title: Fully Edentulous: Prosthetic Considerations
Edentulous Maxilla
nodes.summary: This text covers prosthetic considerations for implant treatment, beginning with custom impression copings: indirect lab-made copings for three or more units and direct intraoral copings for one or two units; customized copings preserve tissue contours so accurate abutments and crowns can be made. For the edentulous maxilla, options include conventional dentures, implant-assisted overdentures, and implant-supported fixed prostheses, with indications such as poor ridge form, combination syndrome, palatal intolerance, and preference for fixed restoration. Maxillary sinus anatomy limits posterior bone, so A-P spread is critical in treatment design; most edentulous maxillary patients benefit from a four-implant palateless overlay denture, especially for lip support, while fixed prostheses require six or more implants and at least 2 cm A-P spread. Immediate loading is possible with careful selection but carries higher maxillary failure risk; identified risk factors include opposing natural dentition, male gender, poor bone density, distal implant sites, and parafunction. CAD/CAM workflows are increasing but their accuracy depends on segmentation and processing. For the edentulous mandible, implant-assisted overdentures with two anterior implants and a bar or individual attachments improve retention and stability while directing loads to denture-bearing areas; fixed prostheses require four to six implants with at least 1 cm A-P spread and may reduce posterior mandibular resorption.

nodes.title: Edentulous Mandible

nodes.title: II Surgical Procedures

nodes.summary: This chapter, authored by Perry R. Klokkevold, describes basic implant surgical procedures, including general principles, one-stage and two-stage placement approaches, and a conclusion. It traces the foundation to Brånemark's original work and emphasizes atraumatic, precise surgical techniques, proper patient preparation, aseptic site preparation, and avoidance of bone overheating. Success depends on good primary stability, intimate bone-to-implant contact, and appropriate bone quality. The chapter notes normal bone remodeling and long-term stability of implants. nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
Surgical procedures for the placement of endosseous dental implants follow the same basic implant surgical procedures that were developed by P.I. Branemark and co-workers in Sweden in the 1960s and 1970s. It is essential to understand and follow these basic guidelines to predictably achieve osseointegration. Fundamental protocols must be followed for implant placement, regardless of whether implants are placed using a one-stage approach or a two-stage approach with a subsequent implant exposure surgery. These fundamentals apply to all implant systems. This chapter reviews the basic principles of implant surgery. Case presentations are used to demonstrate these important concepts.

nodes.title: Keywords
nodes.summary: This chapter covers localized bone augmentation and implant site development, focusing on reconstructing deficient alveolar ridges for prosthetically driven implant placement. It discusses simultaneous versus staged augmentation, extraction socket management, and materials and techniques used. The major underlying concept is guided bone regeneration (GBR), derived from guided tissue regeneration, which uses barrier membranes to exclude soft tissues and allow bone to regenerate. The text describes the biologic healing sequence, requirements such as blood supply, stabilization, osteogenic cells, space maintenance, and wound coverage, and details nonresorbable barrier membranes, including their advantages, disadvantages, and space-maintaining options such as grafts, tenting screws, and titanium-reinforced membranes.

Nonresorbable and resorbable membranes are compared, and bone graft mechanisms (osteoconduction, osteoinduction, osteogenesis), graft classifications, DFDBA controversy, particle size, and autogenous bone’s superiority are discussed.

nodes.title: Bone Graft Materials
nodes.summary: The text discusses localized bone augmentation and implant site development, focusing on resorbable barrier membranes and bone graft materials. Resorbable membranes offer advantages such as avoiding removal surgery and fewer exposure problems, but have drawbacks including degradation, mild inflammation, and collapse unless supported. Bone graft materials provide scaffolding and space for bone regeneration through osteoconduction, osteoinduction, and osteogenesis; various graft types differ in these properties. DFDBA osteoinduction is debated and affected by donor factors, particle size influences vascularization and bone ingrowth, and autogenous bone is regarded as the best graft material.

nodes.title: Autogenous Bone
nodes.summary: The text covers localized bone augmentation and implant site development, including resorbable barrier membranes, bone graft materials, autogenous bone harvesting, flap management, and horizontal ridge augmentation approaches. Resorbable membranes avoid a second surgery and have lower exposure risk, but may degrade, inflame, or collapse, so they require support and sufficient duration to promote bone formation. Bone grafts work through osteoconduction, osteoinduction, and osteogenesis; different graft classes vary in these properties, and particle size affects vascularization. Autogenous bone is considered the best graft source, with intraoral donor sites and specific surgical risks, especially in the mandibular symphysis. Flap management principles emphasize tension-free closure, remote incisions, and limited postoperative prosthesis use. For horizontal deficiencies, small defects can be grafted during implant placement, while larger defects may require staged reconstruction; particulate grafts and monocortical block grafts are both described, with indications, advantages, and limitations.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
817.e1
CHAPTER 81 Aesthetic management of Difficult Cases (minimally Invasive Approach)
Abstract
The demand for implant therapy to replace missing or failing teeth in the anterior aesthetic zone is challenging. This is especially true when there is extensive loss of bone support. Clinicians need to make decisions about how to approach the placement of implants in the aesthetic zone as well as how to manage hard and soft tissues. Although conventional treatment approaches (two-stage protocol) can be successful, there are limitations to aesthetic outcomes when multiple surgical interventions are required. Some cases are better managed with fewer surgical interventions. Immediate placement and immediate provisionalization (one-stage protocol) can offer more predictable aesthetic outcomes. This chapter uses case presentations to introduce the concept of minimally invasive surgical techniques and strategies to enhance aesthetic predictability of challenging cases.
Keywords aesthetics immediate implant placement minimally invasive approach

It emphasizes the challenges of extensive bone loss, the limitations of conventional two-stage protocols, and the benefits of immediate implant placement with immediate provisionalization in a one-stage approach for predictable aesthetic outcomes. It describes examples of compromised implant sites, defines minimally invasive surgery as minimizing invasiveness and the number of procedures, and outlines surgical strategies such as setting aesthetic goals, visualizing outcomes, preserving tissues, and overbuilding bone and soft tissue. It also highlights immediate one-stage placement for preserving peri-implant soft tissue, the importance of thorough preoperative evaluation including CT/CBCT when needed, and the risk of labial gingival recession, which can be managed by grafting particulate bone into the socket and augmenting labial soft tissue.

A clinical correlation reinforces the importance of accurate diagnosis.
