key_items: Surgical Management of Difficult Cases (Minimally Invasive Approach)
Patient Dental History and Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: The text discusses aesthetic management in difficult implant cases using minimally invasive approaches. It emphasizes that aesthetic failures often stem from incomplete examination and incorrect diagnosis/treatment planning, and lists key components of an aesthetic examination. It then presents a detailed case of a 70-year-old woman with severe periodontal disease in her maxillary incisors who desires immediate implant replacement without a removable prosthesis. The case covers her dental history, clinical and radiographic findings, treatment objectives to minimize surgical morbidity, and several treatment options with their risks and aesthetic implications. The final strategy is a minimally invasive approach aimed at achieving acceptable, predictable aesthetics while preserving interproximal tissues and supporting long-term function.

nodes.title: Surgical Strategy for Predictable Aesthetics
nodes.summary: The text covers the aesthetic management of difficult cases with a minimally invasive implant approach, using a detailed case of four periodontally compromised maxillary incisors. It presents treatment options, discusses the rationale for immediate placement of four implants with provisionalization, describes the surgical procedure including atraumatic extraction, palatal implant positioning, bone and free gingival grafting, and provisional crown fabrication, and reports 1-year outcomes showing good papilla and bone preservation with improved aesthetics.

nodes.title: Immediate Implant Placement and Provisionalization for Maxillary Incisors
nodes.summary: The page presents the treatment plan, rationale, sequencing, and surgical procedure for replacing four maxillary incisors with immediately placed implants and provisional restorations. It emphasizes coordinated planning, atraumatic extraction, palatal positioning of implants, primary stability, bone and soft tissue grafting, and splinted provisional crowns. One-year results show preserved papilla height, improved labial biotype, coronal gingival margins, and minimal bone saucerization.

nodes.title: Results
nodes.summary: The text covers aesthetic implant management using minimally invasive approaches. It first details a maxillary anterior case: a 70-year-old patient with compromised incisors treated by extraction, immediate placement of four tapered platform-switched implants, bone and soft tissue grafting, and immediate provisionalization, with excellent one-year aesthetic and bone preservation results. Surgical steps, treatment sequencing, and rationale are explained. The chapter concludes that successful aesthetic implant dentistry requires broad knowledge across surgical and restorative disciplines and mastery of minimally invasive techniques. The text then introduces a second case involving a 41-year-old woman with severe mandibular anterior infection, pain, and halitosis, who wants implant replacement with a fixed provisional. After describing her examination and treatment objectives, three treatment options are presented: extraction with removable provisional; extraction with socket/ridge grafting; and extraction with immediate placement of four implants plus grafting and a fixed implant-supported provisional. The third option is favored for preserving ridge height, reducing surgical morbidity, and enabling immediate fixed provisionalization when implant positioning is favorable.

Section Case Presentation 1 covers minimally invasive aesthetic implant management, beginning with the principle that inadequate examination causes incorrect diagnosis, treatment planning, and aesthetic failure, and listing components of a complete aesthetic examination. The chapter cases are outlined: first two address complex anterior bone loss; the final addresses posterior short, wide implants. Case 1 describes a 70-year-old woman with compromised maxillary incisors due to severe periodontitis, mobility, excessive overbite, parafunction, thin biotype, high gingival margins, and advanced bone loss, who refused a removable prosthesis and feared surgery. Treatment aimed to minimize surgical morbidity while achieving predictable aesthetics; options included a six-unit bridge, two immediate implants with a four-unit provisional, or four immediate implants with a four-unit prosthesis, each with risks. The chosen minimally invasive one-stage flapless strategy involved atraumatic extraction, palatal positioning of four immediate tapered platform-switched implants, simultaneous bone and free gingival grafting, and splinted provisional crowns; coordinated planning and primary stability were emphasized. One-year results showed preserved papilla height, improved labial biotype, coronal gingival margins, minimal bone saucerization, and good aesthetics. The section concludes that successful aesthetic implant dentistry requires broad surgical and restorative knowledge and mastery of minimally invasive techniques, then introduces a second case: a 41-year-old woman with severe mandibular anterior infection, pain, and halitosis desiring a fixed provisional; options included extraction with removable provisional, extraction with socket/ridge grafting, or extraction with four immediate implants plus grafting and a fixed provisional, the latter favored for ridge preservation, reduced morbidity, and immediate provisionalization when implant position is favorable.

nodes.title: Case Presentation 2
Case Presentation 2: Immediate Implants and Bone Augmentation for Mandibular Anterior Teeth
nodes.summary: This page presents Case 2 of a chapter on aesthetic management of difficult cases, focusing on a 41-year-old woman with severe periodontal and endodontic infections in her mandibular anterior teeth. It covers her dental history, chief complaints, examination findings, diagnosis, and treatment objectives, emphasizing elimination of infection and minimizing surgical procedures while achieving acceptable aesthetics and a fixed provisional. The text details three treatment options: removable provisional after extractions, bone grafting with delayed reconstruction, and immediate implant placement with bone grafting and a fixed provisional. The third option is presented as most favorable, especially in a one-stage approach, because implants support the graft, preserve ridge height, reduce morbidity, and allow an immediate fixed provisional.

nodes.title: Treatment Options
nodes.summary: The text describes a case of a 41-year-old woman with severe periodontal and endodontic infection of her mandibular anterior teeth, causing pain, halitosis, and bad taste. She has failing splinted PFM crowns and severe bone loss, with hopeless prognosis for the incisors. Treatment objectives are to eliminate infection promptly while minimizing surgical morbidity and providing acceptable aesthetics, preferably with a fixed provisional. Three treatment options are discussed: extraction with removable provisional leading to ridge collapse and poor aesthetics; extraction with grafting still requiring extensive surgery and unpredictable vertical ridge reconstruction; and immediate extraction with immediate implant placement, bone grafting, and a fixed provisional, which preserves ridge height and reduces surgical risk. The chosen surgical strategy involves one-stage implant placement when possible, using implants as tent poles to support graft and membranes, overbuilding the ridge, and aiming for predictable acceptable aesthetics with minimal intervention.

nodes.title: Surgical Strategy for Predictable Aesthetics
nodes.summary: The text describes a minimally invasive surgical approach for aesthetic implant restoration in a patient with infected mandibular incisors and severe bone loss. It includes a figure legend showing the clinical and radiographic progression from preoperative infection and bone destruction through implant planning, grafting, healing, and successful 4-year outcomes. The treatment goal is acceptable aesthetics rather than ideal. The chosen plan is extraction of the six mandibular incisors, immediate implant placement if the implant–bone relationship is favorable, particulate bone grafting with a barrier membrane, and immediate provisionalization. Initial therapy includes hygiene instructions, chlorhexidine rinses, and antibiotics. The surgical procedure uses full-thickness flaps, debridement, and either a one-stage or two-stage approach depending on bone architecture. Provisional restorations are used for 6 months before final restorations, and the text details the sequence and surgical steps.

nodes.title: Aesthetic Management of Difficult Cases: Treatment Planning and Surgical Sequence
nodes.summary: The page covers part of a chapter on minimally invasive aesthetic management of difficult cases. An eFig caption documents a case with periosteal flaps adapted around healing abutments, 3-month provisional healing with sufficient ridge height, 4-year esthetic implant restorations in a stable ridge with keratinized attached gingiva, and radiographs showing good bone regeneration and osseointegration. The treatment plan includes initial nonsurgical therapy, extraction of six mandibular incisors via full-thickness labial flap, and either immediate one-stage implant placement with simultaneous augmentation and provisionalization when bone is favorable, or a two-stage approach with grafting and flap closure when unfavorable. The sequence describes impressions for a surgical guide and Essex provisional, surgery, fixed provisional delivery at 1–2 weeks if one-stage, and final restoration after about 6 months. The surgical procedure details atraumatic extraction, flap designs, and debridement to prepare bone for implants and augmentation.

nodes.title: Surgical Procedure
nodes.summary: The text covers the minimally invasive aesthetic management of difficult implant cases, focusing on a detailed case of immediate implant placement, bone augmentation, and provisionalization in the anterior mandible despite extensive bone loss, with a favorable 4-year outcome. It then introduces a second case involving short, wide-diameter implants for a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge in a 65-year-old anxious patient, describing her dental history, chief complaint, and initial examination findings.

nodes.title: Results
nodes.summary: The text describes an immediate implant placement case in which extensive bone destruction initially suggested implantation might not be possible, but a surgical guide confirmed favorable implant–bone relationships. Four long implants were placed lingually within the bony envelope, with simultaneous autogenous and allograft bone augmentation and collagen membranes, followed by immediate provisionalization. Postoperative care and 4-year results showed stable osseointegration, good aesthetics, and bone maintenance. The approach was justified as minimally invasive despite its extent because it required only one surgery and 6 months of treatment, unlike multiple alternative procedures with greater morbidity and poorer aesthetic outcomes. The text then introduces Case Presentation 3: a 65-year-old woman with a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge who wants implants for chewing; examination shows extensive vertical resorption, narrow keratinized gingiva, low ridge height, and muscle pull, with radiographic measurement beginning but the text cutting off.

This section covers Case Presentation 2, an aesthetic implant case in a 41-year-old woman with severe infection and bone loss in the mandibular anterior teeth. It describes her presentation, treatment objectives, three treatment options, and the chosen minimally invasive surgical strategy involving immediate implants, bone grafting, and provisionalization. It details the surgical sequence, results at 4 years, and justification for the approach. The section ends by introducing Case Presentation 3, a 65-year-old woman with a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge requesting implants.

nodes.title: Case Presentation 3
Dental History and Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: The text discusses a dental implant case with extensive bone loss, explaining how immediate implant placement in a one-stage approach with simultaneous bone augmentation and provisionalization was performed despite initial concerns. It covers surgical principles, implant positioning, grafting with autogenous bone and allograft, membrane placement, flap management, provisional restorations, postoperative care, and 4-year successful results, concluding the approach is minimally invasive and patient-friendly. It then introduces Case Presentation 3, describing a 65-year-old woman with a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge who desires implants for better chewing, with examination findings of vertical ridge resorption, narrow keratinized gingiva, and muscle pulls; the description is cut off while measuring radiographic ridge height.

nodes.title: Examination and Diagnosis
nodes.summary: The text covers two dental implant cases. First, a 41-year-old patient with extensive post-debridement bone loss undergoes immediate one-stage implant placement with simultaneous bone augmentation and provisionalization. The strategy uses surgical guides, lingual intraosseous placement, long implants, autogenous/allograft bone with collagen membranes, and provisional restorations, achieving acceptable 4-year aesthetic and osseointegration outcomes with only one surgery and 6 months of treatment. Second, a 65-year-old woman with severe posterior mandibular resorption is treated with short, wide-diameter implants rather than complex vertical ridge augmentation. After reviewing options such as distraction osteogenesis, block/interpositional grafts, particulate grafts, BMPs, and nerve repositioning, the clinician places four short implants (three 5-mm wide and one 4-mm wide) with splinted platform-switched restorations; 13-month follow-up shows stable crestal bone despite long crown-to-implant ratios.

nodes.title: Implant Treatment for Severely Resorbed Posterior Ridge: Options and Plan
nodes.summary: This page presents a clinical implant treatment scenario for a severely resorbed posterior ridge with sufficient width but limited height. It covers the treatment objective of minimizing surgical morbidity, compares seven treatment options—including distraction osteogenesis, interpositional grafts, block and particulate vertical augmentation, BMPs, nerve repositioning, and short implants—and explains their drawbacks. The chosen plan uses short wide-diameter implants placed in a two-stage approach, with no special sequencing needed. The surgical procedure, including flap management, implant placement, and three-month restoration, is described, and the results show stable crestal bone at 13 months after loading despite a long crown-to-implant ratio.

nodes.title: Results
nodes.summary: The text covers a posterior implant case managed with short, wide-diameter implants to avoid extensive vertical ridge augmentation; it reviews alternative augmentation and nerve-repositioning options and their drawbacks, details the treatment plan, surgical procedure, and favorable long-term results, then presents an anterior aesthetic case (#8) with case-based questions and answers, followed by a reference list.

This section presents Case Presentation 3: a 65-year-old woman with a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge who desires implants for better chewing; examination shows vertical ridge resorption, narrow keratinized gingiva, and muscle pulls. It also reviews an earlier immediate implant case in a 41-year-old patient with extensive bone loss, detailing the one-stage immediate placement with simultaneous bone augmentation and provisionalization, including surgical guides, long implants, grafting with autogenous/allograft bone and collagen membranes, and favorable 4-year results. For the 65-year-old patient, the clinician evaluates alternative vertical ridge augmentation and nerve-repositioning options but chooses short, wide-diameter implants placed in a two-stage approach. The plan uses four short implants (three 5-mm wide and one 4-mm wide) with splinted platform-switched restorations; surgical flap management, implant placement, and three-month restoration are described. At 13 months after loading, crestal bone remains stable despite long crown-to-implant ratios. The Results subsection also includes an anterior aesthetic case (#8) with case-based questions and answers, followed by a reference list.

The section covers minimally invasive surgical management of difficult implant cases, beginning with the importance of a complete aesthetic examination of soft and hard tissues to avoid misdiagnosis and aesthetic failure. It presents three clinical cases: Case 1, a 70-year-old woman with periodontally compromised maxillary incisors, managed with a minimally invasive one-stage flapless approach using immediate platform-switched implants, simultaneous grafting, and provisional crowns, with good one-year aesthetic and bone stability outcomes; Case 2, a 41-year-old woman with severe mandibular anterior infection and bone loss, treated by immediate implant placement with grafting and fixed provisionalization, showing favorable 4-year results; and Case 3, a 65-year-old woman with a severely resorbed mandibular posterior ridge, for whom short, wide-diameter implants in a two-stage approach with splinted platform-switched restorations were chosen, with stable crestal bone at 13 months after loading. The section also includes an anterior aesthetic case with questions and answers and a reference list.

nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text is a chapter on dental implant microsurgery for immediate placement, preceded by a reference list of 40 implantology-related studies. It covers the advantages of implants over fixed bridges in the maxillary aesthetic zone, the role of microsurgery in improving implant drilling precision and soft tissue handling, minimally invasive microsurgical tooth extraction techniques that preserve tissue and reduce morbidity, and special considerations for drilling implant osteotomies in extraction sockets, including the use of palatal bone and visual feedback to guide drill direction.

The section covers minimally invasive aesthetic management of difficult implant cases, particularly in the anterior aesthetic zone with extensive bone loss. It contrasts conventional two-stage protocols with one-stage immediate implant placement and provisionalization, advocating for individualized planning and fewer surgical interventions. It presents surgical strategies, including flapless immediate placement, particulate bone grafting, and palatal soft tissue grafting, along with the importance of thorough preoperative evaluation and aesthetic risk management. Three clinical cases illustrate outcomes: two anterior cases treated with immediate one-stage approaches and one posterior case managed with short, wide implants in a two-stage approach. The section also discusses treatment options, complications, microsurgical principles, and includes references on implant microsurgery and related techniques.

nodes.title: 82 Dental Implant Microsurgery
Dental Implant Microsurgery: Immediate Placement, Extraction, Drilling
nodes.summary: The page covers dental implant microsurgery for immediate placement, emphasizing its benefits in the aesthetic maxillary anterior zone. It describes how microsurgical implant drilling improves precision and feedback, how microsurgical extraction is minimally invasive and tissue-preserving, and how implant drilling in extraction sockets is performed using visual feedback, with attention to palatal bone and drill tracking.

nodes.title: Implant Drilling in the Extraction Site
nodes.summary: The chapter covers dental implant microsurgery for immediate placement, focusing on replacing failing maxillary anterior teeth. It explains why implants are preferred over fixed bridges, how microscopic magnification improves implant drilling precision, angular orientation, and feedback during osteotomy, and how microsurgical techniques enable atraumatic extraction and socket drilling. It also discusses the importance of combining surgical and prosthetic skills, the benefits of immediate provisional restorations, reduced patient morbidity, and enhanced aesthetic outcomes.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses immediate dental implant placement using microsurgery, particularly in the esthetic anterior region. It highlights the clinical challenges of placing implants in extraction sockets and adding immediate provisionals, while emphasizing that microsurgical precision and magnification reduce errors and improve outcomes. Immediate implant-supported provisionals offer esthetic benefits and patient satisfaction but require careful surgical and prosthetic execution. Microsurgery improves healing, comfort, patient acceptance, motor coordination, and supports atraumatic techniques. The chapter also includes key words related to implant microsurgery and immediate restoration.

nodes.title: Key Words
Bone Grafting
nodes.summary: The text covers immediate dental implant microsurgery techniques, emphasizing microscope use for ideal implant positioning in the palatal socket wall and precise drilling speed/pressure control. It details bone grafting of the socket with xenograft and filtered bone, buccal connective tissue grafting to prevent gingival recession, and fabrication of an immediate provisional crown from a pre-extraction impression to preserve aesthetics and support gingival tissue.

nodes.title: Buccal Gingival Grafting
nodes.summary: The text covers three implant-prosthodontic procedures: socket grafting, buccal gingival grafting, and immediate provisional fabrication. Socket grafting uses xenograft topped with tetracycline-rinsed filtered bone and microfibrillar collagen to minimize buccal bone resorption. Buccal gingival grafting uses a palatal subepithelial connective tissue graft in a split-thickness envelope to augment or maintain gingival height and thickness and prevent recession. Immediate provisional fabrication creates a pre-extraction composite shell crown on a titanium abutment, refined under the microscope, to support gingival tissue, preserve aesthetics, obturate the socket, and contain grafts.

nodes.title: Immediate Provisional Fabrication
nodes.summary: The text covers techniques for immediate implant placement and provisionalization: socket bone grafting using xenograft and filtered bone; buccal gingival grafting with a subepithelial connective tissue graft to prevent recession; fabrication of an immediate provisional crown that mimics the extracted tooth and supports gingival tissue; management of immediate implant occlusion to minimize bone trauma; and creation of a custom impression transfer coping to preserve provisional gingival contours for the dental laboratory.

nodes.title: Immediate Implant Occlusion
nodes.summary: The text covers provisional restoration and occlusion protocols in immediate implant microsurgery. It describes finishing and curing of provisionals, the clinical benefits of immediate provisional restorations, techniques to minimize early loading trauma, and the fabrication of a custom impression transfer coping to preserve gingival contours for the dental laboratory.

nodes.title: Custom Impression Transfer Coping
nodes.summary: The text covers immediate dental implant provisionalization and restoration techniques, including fabrication of screw-retained provisional crowns with titanium abutments, finishing and light curing protocols, and clinical benefits of immediate provisionals. It discusses occlusion management to minimize implant loading, and details the creation and use of a custom impression transfer coping to preserve emergence profile and communicate gingival anatomy to the laboratory. Final restoration involves CAD/CAM zirconia abutments and copings for all-ceramic crowns, with accompanying clinical images showing outcomes over time.

nodes.title: Final Implant Restoration
nodes.summary: The text describes the fabrication and use of a custom impression transfer coping that replicates the provisional emergence profile using powder and monomer, with orientation marking and air-bubble minimization. It explains final implant restoration using custom transfer impressions and CAD/CAM zirconia abutments and copings for all-ceramic crowns, emphasizing zirconia's biocompatibility and translucency. The summary also highlights the importance of team communication among surgeon, restorative dentist, and technician to achieve aesthetic gingival support and matching tooth shape, and concludes with the advantages of microsurgery for tissue management, visualization, and seamless immediate tooth replacement.

The section covers immediate dental implant microsurgery in extraction sockets, emphasizing microscope use, magnification, and improved motor coordination for precise implant placement and atraumatic extraction. It details socket bone grafting with xenograft and filtered bone, buccal subepithelial connective tissue grafting to prevent recession, and immediate provisional crown fabrication from pre-extraction impressions. It also addresses occlusion management, custom impression transfer copings to preserve emergence profile, final CAD/CAM zirconia restorations, and the need for surgeon-restorative-technician communication. Overall, microsurgery enhances tissue management, esthetics, healing, and patient acceptance for immediate implant replacement of failing teeth.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text discusses dental implant microsurgery for immediate placement, highlighting zirconia's biocompatibility and translucency, a sequence ensuring accurate match of the final restoration to the provisional profile and original tooth shape, and collaborative teamwork. It concludes by emphasizing advantages such as better tissue management and visualization, representing a shift toward seamless immediate tooth replacement, with references available online.

It highlights zirconia's biocompatibility and translucency, the importance of matching the final restoration to the provisional emergence profile and original tooth shape, and the collaborative effort of the surgical, restorative, and laboratory team. This section covers dental implant microsurgery for immediate placement in the esthetic maxillary anterior region, particularly for failing teeth. It emphasizes the advantages of implants over fixed bridges and the use of microscopic magnification to improve drilling precision, angular orientation, feedback, and motor coordination. Microsurgical extraction is minimally invasive and tissue-preserving, and implant drilling in extraction sockets relies on visual feedback with attention to palatal bone and drill tracking. The section details socket bone grafting using xenograft and filtered bone, buccal subepithelial connective tissue grafting to prevent recession, immediate provisional crown fabrication from pre-extraction impressions, occlusion management, custom impression transfer copings to preserve emergence profile, and final CAD/CAM zirconia restorations matched to the provisional emergence profile and original tooth shape. Zirconia is noted for its biocompatibility and translucency. The importance of teamwork among the surgeon, restorative dentist, and laboratory technician is stressed. Overall benefits include improved healing, comfort, patient acceptance, esthetics, and tissue management with reduced morbidity. nodes.title: 83 Piezoelectric Bone Surgery
CHAPTER 83
nodes.summary: Chapter 83 covers piezoelectric bone surgery, an ultrasonic technique developed by Vercellotti and Mectron Medical Technology. It describes how the Piezosurgery device uses frequency-overmodulated ultrasonic vibrations (24–36 kHz with a superimposed 30–60 Hz sound wave) to selectively cut mineralized tissues while sparing soft tissues and minimizing heat. The chapter highlights the technique's advantages, including microprecision, selective cutting, intraoperative hemostasis and visibility, low surgical trauma, and improved healing compared with traditional burs and drills, which cause more tissue damage and inflammation. It reviews clinical applications such as periodontal surgery, crown lengthening, extractions based on periodontal tissue types, ultrasonic implant site preparation, and advanced implantology techniques including sinus lift, ridge expansion, and bone harvesting. It also notes the expansion of piezoelectric surgery into other medical fields, such as maxillofacial, otolaryngologic, neurosurgical, and orthopedic procedures.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary:
Abstract
The introduction of piezoelectric ultrasonic technology for bone surgery has changed many areas of dentistry, making it possible to obtain a greater degree of precision and intraoperative control in numerous techniques. This chapter reviews the clinical characteristics of ultrasonic cutting, namely microprecision, selective cutting, maximum visibility resulting from intraoperative hemostasis, and improved tissue healing. Additionally, the chapter introduces the reader to various clinical applications of Piezosurgery, including periodontal surgery, crown lengthening, extractions techniques based on periodontal tissue types, and ultrasonic implant site preparation. Advanced piezoelectric surgical techniques in implantology (sinus lift, ridge expansion, and bone harvesting) are also presented.

nodes.title: Key Words
nodes.summary: The text introduces piezoelectric bone surgery in dentistry, highlighting its benefits of precision, control, low surgical trauma, selective cutting, good visibility, and fast healing. It describes the clinical characteristics of ultrasonic cutting, including microprecision (light pressure of about 300 g, microvibrations around 80 μm) and selective cutting of mineralized tissues while sparing soft tissues. It also reviews clinical applications such as periodontal surgery, crown lengthening, extractions, implant site preparation, sinus lift, ridge expansion, and bone harvesting. Additionally, it details the Mectron Piezosurgery device, its dual-wave technology, and function settings for implant, cortical, cancellous, special, perio, and endo procedures.

nodes.title: Clinical Characteristics of Ultrasonic Cutting
key_items: Improved Hard Tissue Healing; Improved Soft Tissue Healing
nodes.summary: The text covers piezoelectric bone surgery using the Mectron Piezosurgery device, including its technology, function settings, inserts, and key clinical characteristics: microprecision, selective cutting, maximum visibility, and excellent healing. It explains how the device cuts mineralized tissue selectively while sparing soft tissues, the importance of light pressure, the cavitation effect for hemostasis and visibility, and improved hard and soft tissue healing with molecular evidence involving BMPs, TGF-β2, and cytokines. Clinical comparisons with rotary instrumentation show less trauma, less inflammation, faster healing, and reduced postoperative morbidity. The text also introduces clinical applications, especially periodontal surgery, and notes that Piezosurgery can perform nearly all techniques traditionally done with burs, drills, chisels, or saws.

nodes.title: Clinical Applications
Periodontal Surgery
key_items: Excellent Healing; Improved Hard Tissue Healing; Improved Soft Tissue Healing
nodes.summary: The text covers the mechanisms and clinical benefits of piezoelectric bone surgery, including cavitation, selective cutting of mineralized tissues, improved hard and soft tissue healing, and favorable biomolecular responses such as increased BMP-4 and TGF-β2. It also describes clinical applications, particularly in periodontal surgery, where Piezosurgery improves soft and hard tissue management, enables precise ostectomy and osteoplasty, supports grafting, and may expand regenerative treatment options. The section on crown lengthening begins with its classification as a common periodontal ostectomy procedure.

nodes.title: Crown Lengthening
nodes.summary: The text covers the use of Piezosurgery in periodontal surgery, including comparisons with manual instrumentation, surgical protocols, soft and hard tissue management, clinical applications, crown lengthening, and tooth extraction. Piezosurgery offers precise, less traumatic subperiosteal preparation, improved visibility, effective debridement, root-safe ostectomy, autogenous bone harvesting, and enhanced healing. It may expand regenerative indications for defects greater than 3.5 mm under magnification. Crown lengthening with Piezosurgery preserves root surfaces and improves healing compared with rotary instruments. Tooth extraction is classified into four anatomical types based on periodontal biotype and ligament status, guiding the choice of extraction technique and specific Piezosurgery inserts.

nodes.title: Tooth Extraction
nodes.summary: The text describes piezoelectric bone surgery applications in three areas. It covers clinical crown lengthening, including indications, surgical technique, Piezosurgery advantages, and histological evidence of improved healing. It then details tooth extraction with a four-type anatomic classification, associated surgical difficulty, risks, and recommended techniques/instruments for each type, emphasizing alveolar bone preservation. Finally, it covers ultrasonic implant site preparation, presenting study outcomes, clinical advantages, differential preparation, healing response, and the stepwise surgical protocol with specific Piezosurgery inserts.

nodes.title: Implant Site Preparation
nodes.summary: The text covers Piezosurgery applications in tooth extraction, implant site preparation, sinus lift, and ridge expansion. It describes three tooth extraction anatomies and recommended Piezosurgery techniques to preserve bone. It details UISP, including clinical success rates, advantages, surgical steps, and healing benefits. It also discusses sinus lift techniques with reduced membrane perforation risk and ridge expansion for narrow ridges using Piezosurgery, concluding that this technology enables minimally invasive, precise, and fast-healing bone surgery.

The section covers clinical applications of piezoelectric bone surgery, focusing on its mechanisms and benefits such as selective cutting, improved healing, and favorable biomolecular responses. It details its use in periodontal surgery, crown lengthening, tooth extraction, implant site preparation, sinus lift, and ridge expansion, highlighting precise tissue management, alveolar bone preservation, reduced complications, and enhanced regeneration. The overall conclusion is that Piezosurgery supports minimally invasive, precise, and fast-healing bone surgery across these clinical indications.

nodes.title: Advanced Clinical Applications
Sinus Lift
nodes.summary: The text discusses piezoelectric bone surgery applications in maxillary sinus lift and ridge expansion. It describes sinus lift techniques, comparing crestal osteotomy and lateral window approaches, and highlights the risk of Schneiderian membrane perforation with rotary instruments versus the reduced risk with Piezosurgery. Specific study findings are cited, including lower perforation rates with Piezosurgery and the benefit of lateral wall erosion before outlining the bony window. The step-by-step lateral window technique is outlined, including membrane elevation, grafting, and closure. A key fact explains that ultrasonic systems require less force and provide greater surgical control. The section on ridge expansion explains its use for increasing bone width and simultaneous implant placement, the importance of preoperative anatomy evaluation, the role of piezoelectric osteotomies and expanders, and its advantages and limitations. The passage ends mid-sentence regarding reducing the need to expand or displace the buccal cortical bone.

nodes.title: Ridge Expansion
nodes.summary: The text covers advanced piezoelectric bone surgery applications. It describes sinus lift techniques for maxillary sinus floor augmentation, including lateral window and crestal approaches, and highlights how Piezosurgery reduces Schneiderian membrane perforation compared with traditional rotary instruments. It details surgical steps, comparative study findings, and the advantages of piezoelectric erosion. It also covers ridge expansion for narrow ridges, including principles of bone elasticity, osteotomy techniques, implant site preparation, and the limitations of traditional drills. Finally, it mentions bone harvesting with Piezosurgery, including particulate bone chip harvesting using osteoplasty inserts.

The second case involves a 38-year-old woman with an ankylosed, impacted canine, where mesiodistal root sectioning is recommended for aesthetic outcomes because it minimizes pressure on the vestibular wall and reduces fracture risk.

Chapter 83 covers piezoelectric bone surgery (Piezosurgery), an ultrasonic technique developed by Vercellotti and Mectron Medical Technology. The Piezosurgery device uses frequency-overmodulated ultrasonic vibrations and dual-wave technology to selectively cut mineralized tissues while sparing soft tissue and minimizing heat. Its clinical characteristics include microprecision, selective cutting, excellent intraoperative visibility due to hemostasis, low surgical trauma, and improved healing, with molecular evidence involving BMPs, TGF-β2, and cytokines. Compared with rotary instruments, Piezosurgery produces less inflammation, faster healing, and reduced postoperative morbidity. The chapter reviews clinical applications including periodontal surgery, crown lengthening, tooth extraction, ultrasonic implant site preparation, sinus lift, ridge expansion, and bone harvesting, along with advanced techniques and added benefits such as extraction of ankylosed impacted canines and management of narrow or thick-walled sites. CHAPTER 85 Implant-Related Complications and Failures
Abstract
Implants have high rates of survival and success. However, implant- related complications and failures occur. Chapter 85 details the causes, treatment, and prevention of surgical, biologic, mechanical, aesthetic, and phonetic complications. Information is provided to enable dentists to identify and manage complications and the failures of implants and implant-supported restorations.

Aesthetic outcomes are assessed using indices such as the restorative index, pink aesthetic score, and combined pink/white aesthetic score. The prevalence data show technical complications are more common with overdentures than fixed restorations; common complications include veneer fracture, screw access hole loss, screw loosening and fracture, overdenture retention/relining issues, and rare implant fractures, which occur more often in partially edentulous posterior restorations supported by one or two implants.

Although dental implants are not vulnerable to caries, they are susceptible to mechanical and inflammatory-related biologic complica- tions. Long-term success of dental implants require sound treatment planning, precise surgical and restorative execution, and impeccable long-term maintenance. This chapter describes the evaluation and maintenance of dental implants.

Treatment of peri-implant mucositis is effective, whereas treatment of peri-implantitis is unpredictable. Prevention, early detection, and treatment of peri-implant inflammatorydiseases are essentialfor successfuloutcomes.
Referral of Patients to the Periodontist
The previously described guidelines allow many implants to be maintained quite well by primary dental care providers (i.e., general dentists). Referral to a periodontist should be considered if
peri-implantitis or peri-implant mucositis is diagnosed and cannot be resolved with improved oral hygiene and professional maintenance care. Early referral is advantageous to stop progression and limit the extent of bone loss.
A Case Scenario is found on the companion website www.expertconsult.com.

References for this chapter are found on the companion website www.expertconsult.com.

nodes.summary: The text covers supportive implant treatment, emphasizing prevention, early detection, and management of peri-implant diseases. It notes that peri-implant mucositis responds to treatment, while peri-implantitis is less predictable, and referral to a periodontist is advised for persistent cases. A detailed case scenario of a 73-year-old woman with peri-implantitis is presented, including clinical findings, diagnosis, and treatment approach, followed by three case-based questions with answers and explanations. nodes.title: References
nodes.summary: The text provides a reference list for Chapter 86 on supportive implant treatment and includes an excerpt from Chapter 87, 'Results of Implant Treatment.' It describes landmark Göteborg and Toronto studies that established the success and predictability of root-form implants, including specific survival rates for implants and prostheses in edentulous jaws. It then discusses how implant outcomes are defined, distinguishing implant survival from implant success, and explains the lack of a universally accepted success definition, variations in reporting criteria, and the challenges this creates for comparing study results. It also notes that while implant treatment is highly successful, failures and complications still occur.

The section describes supportive implant treatment, emphasizing that long-term success depends on professional maintenance and patient compliance. It covers the rationale for supportive care, including susceptibility to mechanical and biologic complications, peri-implant disease epidemiology, risk factors, and treatment limitations. It details the components of implant examination and assessment, including probing, microbial testing, stability testing, percussion, radiographs, biofilm control, and soft tissue evaluation. It also discusses restoration design for hygiene and favorable occlusion, cement removal, patient oral hygiene, titanium-safe professional instrumentation, and monitoring for prosthetic complications. Management of peri-implant diseases is addressed: mucositis responds well to nonsurgical treatment, whereas peri-implantitis is less predictable and may require surgical treatment with possible recurrence or implant removal. Early referral to a periodontist is advised for persistent disease. The section also includes a case scenario, references, and an excerpt on implant outcomes distinguishing survival from success, landmark Göteborg and Toronto studies, and variability in success criteria.

nodes.title: 87 Results of Implant Treatment
CHAPTER 87
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses results of implant treatment, beginning with landmark Göteborg and Toronto studies that established expectations for osseointegrated root-form implants and reported high implant and prosthesis survival rates in edentulous patients. It then explains that despite overall success, 100% success is impossible and implant failures occur in various forms. The chapter highlights the difficulty of defining and comparing implant outcomes due to inconsistent reporting methods and criteria, distinguishes implant survival from implant success, and notes classic success criteria such as those by Albrektsson and colleagues. It sets the stage for examining factors that influence implant outcomes, aesthetic results, and patient satisfaction.

nodes.title: Defining Implant Outcomes
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses the results and outcomes of implant treatment, drawing on landmark studies such as the Göteborg study and the University of Toronto replica study that established the predictability and survival rates of osseointegrated dental implants. It distinguishes between implant survival and implant success, notes the lack of a universally accepted definition of success, and explains how varying criteria complicate comparison of studies. The text also addresses factors influencing outcomes, including implant design, anatomic location, loading protocols, and bone augmentation, as well as aesthetic results and patient satisfaction.

nodes.title: Abstract
nodes.summary: The text is an abstract and introduction to a chapter on implant treatment outcomes. It highlights that dental implants are effective and predictable for replacing missing teeth, with generally good results, but notes challenges in comparing studies due to variations in design, protocols, and populations. It distinguishes between implant survival and success, noting that success lacks a clear definition and is less frequently reported. Risk factors, outcomes by anatomic location, implant design, loading protocols, bone augmentation, aesthetics, and patient satisfaction are covered.

nodes.title: Key Words
nodes.summary: This text covers implant treatment outcomes, emphasizing the distinction between implant survival and success. It notes that success criteria vary widely, which affects reported rates, and that survival often overestimates positive outcomes. Complications and peri-implant diseases are discussed, along with factors influencing outcomes, particularly anatomic location and bone quality, implant design, and other variables. The chapter also addresses esthetics and patient satisfaction, with illustrative clinical cases and key words listed.

nodes.title: Factors That Influence Implant Outcomes
key_items: Immediate Implant Placement; Immediate Occlusal Loading
nodes.summary: The text discusses challenges in defining and interpreting dental implant success versus survival, illustrated by a table showing how modified success criteria change reported rates and by examples of implants that survive but fail functionally or aesthetically. It then reviews factors influencing implant outcomes: anatomic location and bone quality, implant design features (surface, length, threads), placement and loading protocols (immediate placement, immediate occlusal loading, traditional loading), and bone augmentation. Risk factors are detailed, including smoking, diabetes, and periodontitis, with supporting study data. Finally, the text addresses aesthetic results and patient satisfaction, emphasizing the importance of proper implant position, soft tissue support, and natural appearance.

nodes.title: Aesthetic Results and Patient Satisfaction
nodes.summary: This text discusses risk factors affecting dental implant outcomes, focusing on smoking, diabetes, and periodontitis. Smoking clearly reduces implant survival and success. The impact of diabetes is uncertain, with controlled diabetics achieving similar success to healthy patients. A history of periodontitis does not greatly reduce implant survival, but long-term biologic complications such as peri-implantitis are more common. The text also covers aesthetic results and patient satisfaction, noting that factors like high smile line, thin soft tissues, and compromised bone increase aesthetic risk, and that most patients report high satisfaction with implant treatment. It concludes that implant therapy is highly predictable overall, but outcomes are difficult to compare across studies due to varying designs and patient factors.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: The text discusses aesthetic outcomes and patient satisfaction in implant therapy. It highlights that dissatisfaction arises when results do not meet expectations, with higher risks for patients having high aesthetic demands, high smile lines, thin soft tissues, or compromised bone. Aesthetic evaluation uses objective indices such as white, pink, and combined aesthetic scores. Multiple surveys show high long-term patient satisfaction with implant function, aesthetics, hygiene, and cost, and a systematic review indicates greater satisfaction with implant overdentures than conventional dentures. The chapter concludes that implants are highly predictable and beneficial, though comparing studies is difficult due to varying criteria, protocols, and populations, and understanding reported outcomes is important for clinicians and patients.

nodes.title: References

It reports specific satisfaction percentages for function, aesthetics, hygiene, cost, chewing comfort, and edentulous patients, and notes that implant overdentures are more satisfying than conventional dentures. The chapter concludes that implants are predictable but success definitions vary and risk factors can reduce success. It also includes a clinical correlation, a satisfaction table, a case scenario with a question and answer about replacing a failing anterior tooth with an implant, and a list of references.

nodes.title: Causes of Periodontal Diseases

It includes CO2 laser treatment for melanin pigmentation; causes such as microbial plaque, calculus, one-sided chewing, malocclusion, and mouth breathing; numerous examples of plaque, calculus, gingivitis, and periodontitis in varied patients, including implant cases and smokers; calculus formation at salivary gland duct openings and with tooth loss or malocclusion; effects of crowding and class III malocclusion; mouth breathing-related gingival enlargement; a radiograph of calculus; improvement after debridement and oral hygiene instruction; and mention of systemic and endocrine factors, including puberty gingivitis.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Modified by Systemic Factors
nodes.summary: The text is a section from an atlas of periodontal diseases illustrating various gingival conditions. It covers plaque-induced gingival inflammation associated with crowding, supernumerary teeth, and mouth breathing in young patients, as well as the effects of debridement and oral hygiene. It then discusses gingival diseases modified by systemic factors, focusing on endocrine influences and sex hormones, with examples of puberty gingivitis, menstruation-related gingival color changes, and pregnancy-associated gingival enlargement documented over time. Finally, it addresses gingival diseases associated with blood dyscrasias, including leukemia in several patients and anemia, demonstrating gingival hyperplasia, bleeding, inflammation, and pale gingiva.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases Associated With Blood Dyscrasias
nodes.summary: The text covers an atlas of periodontal diseases focusing on gingival diseases associated with blood dyscrasias and drug-induced gingival diseases. It describes clinical presentations such as gingival hyperplasia, spontaneous bleeding, inflammation, enlargement, recession, and pallor in conditions including leukemia, various anemias, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, hemophilia A, and von Willebrand disease. It also documents gingival enlargement caused by phenytoin, amlodipine, and cyclosporine, with accompanying clinical figures.

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Gingival Diseases
nodes.summary: The text is from an atlas of periodontal diseases and covers clinical cases of bleeding/clot formation in von Willebrand disease, drug-induced gingival enlargement from phenytoin, amlodipine, and cyclosporine, including surgical management and outcomes, and non-plaque-induced gingival lesions due to Streptococcus infections, including a steroid-related hyperplasia case and acute streptococcal gingivostomatitis in a child.

nodes.title: Non–Plaque-Induced Gingival Lesions
Streptococcus Species Infections
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal disease atlas content, including cyclosporine-associated gingival enlargement with clinical and post-treatment images, followed by non–plaque-induced gingival lesions such as streptococcal infections and herpesvirus infections. It describes specific cases: steroid-related gingival hyperplasia in a bodybuilder, acute streptococcal gingivostomatitis in a child, herpetic gingivostomatitis with vesicles in a young man, and recurrent aphthous ulcers in a woman.

nodes.title: Herpesvirus Infections
nodes.summary: The text describes and illustrates herpesvirus infections and fungal-origin gingival diseases. It includes cases of herpetic gingivostomatitis, recurrent aphthous ulcers, severe chemotherapy-related mucositis prone to candidal infection, oral candidiasis, and mucormycosis with tissue destruction in patients, several of whom had acute myelogenous leukemia.

nodes.title: Gingival Diseases of Fungal Origin
nodes.summary: The text covers two categories of gingival diseases: fungal origin and genetic origin. Fungal diseases include candidal infections and mucormycosis in pediatric patients with acute myelogenous leukemia, often following chemotherapy, with mucormycosis causing rapid gingival and alveolar bone destruction and confirmed by fungal hyphae on Gomori methenamine silver staining. The genetic section presents hereditary gingival fibromatosis in a family, with longitudinal intraoral views of the father from 2000, 2003, and 2005.

The section covers non–plaque-induced gingival lesions of infectious, fungal, and genetic origin. It presents periodontal disease atlas images, including cyclosporine-associated gingival enlargement with clinical and post-treatment images and steroid-related gingival hyperplasia in a bodybuilder. Infectious cases include acute streptococcal gingivostomatitis, herpetic gingivostomatitis with vesicles, and recurrent aphthous ulcers. Fungal conditions include oral candidiasis, chemotherapy-related mucositis prone to candidal infection, and mucormycosis causing rapid gingival and alveolar bone destruction in immunocompromised patients, often pediatric with acute myelogenous leukemia. The genetic component describes hereditary gingival fibromatosis in a family, with longitudinal images of the father over several years.

nodes.title: Gingival Lesions of Genetic Origin
nodes.summary: The text covers hereditary gingival fibromatosis as a genetic gingival lesion, illustrated by a family: the father's progressive enlargement over several years and the younger son's condition in infancy and early childhood. It also covers gingival manifestations of systemic conditions, specifically mucocutaneous lesions, including severe desquamative lichen planus with a positive Nikolsky sign and reticular lichen planus causing a burning sensation.

nodes.title: Gingival Manifestations of Systemic Conditions
Mucocutaneous Lesions

nodes.title: Other Systemic Diseases

It covers scleroderma, juvenile hyaline fibromatosis, atopic dermatitis, fibrous dysplasia, Sturge-Weber syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, and Behçet disease, each illustrated with patient age, sex, and characteristic oral/gingival findings. It also includes a case of gingival allergy to apples diagnosed by oral challenge test.

nodes.title: Allergies

It covers recurrent aphthous lesions in Behçet disease, allergic gingival reactions diagnosed via oral challenge testing, and traumatic lesions that are factitious, iatrogenic, or accidental. Specific examples include gingival inflammation from restorations violating biologic width, injury from overhanging margins and acrylic, and trauma from calculus deposits and ill-fitting restorations.

The section covers gingival manifestations of systemic conditions as illustrated in an atlas of periodontal diseases. It describes mucocutaneous lesions such as hereditary gingival fibromatosis, lichen planus variants, pemphigus vulgaris, scleroderma, and juvenile hyaline fibromatosis. It also addresses other systemic diseases including atopic dermatitis, fibrous dysplasia, Sturge-Weber syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, and Behçet disease. Additionally, it includes allergic gingival reactions diagnosed by oral challenge testing, recurrent aphthous lesions in Behçet disease, and traumatic gingival lesions that are factitious, iatrogenic, or accidental, with examples such as restorations violating biologic width, overhanging margins, acrylic injury, calculus deposits, and ill-fitting restorations.

nodes.title: Traumatic Lesions: Factitious, Iatrogenic, and Accidental

The traumatic lesion figures show gingival inflammation, recession, desquamation, burns, trauma, hyperkeratosis, and calculus-related soft-tissue injury caused by faulty or ill-fitting restorations, orthodontic brackets/ligature wire, chemical irritants (ferric sulfate, bonding agent, cologne, raki, garlic, plant seeds), oral hygiene/cleansing habits (vigorous brushing, soap, tissue, nail scratching), and smokeless tobacco. The cyst/tumor figures illustrate fibromas and papillomas, including palatal location.

It also describes a case of chronic periodontitis in a 42-year-old man caused by plaque and calculus, with generalized radiographic bone loss.

Additionally, it covers chronic periodontitis modified by systemic factors, particularly diabetes mellitus, with complications such as abscesses, severe bone loss, tooth loss, and osteomyelitis, and includes a case of aggressive periodontitis in a child affecting deciduous teeth.

It also covers periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, presenting a case of granulocytic sarcoma of the gingiva in a 12-year-old girl that preceded acute myelogenous leukemia, with clinical, radiographic, histologic findings and response to chemotherapy.

nodes.title: O
nodes.summary: The text is a book index of dental and periodontal topics spanning entries from 'Needle anatomy' to 'Partially edentulous patients.' It covers periodontal anatomy, microbiology, immunology, disease classification, diagnostic methods, systemic health interactions, pharmacology, nonsurgical and surgical periodontal treatment, dental implants, orthodontics, occlusion, oral medicine, halitosis, and geriatric dentistry. It also lists instruments, surgical procedures, regenerative materials, and companion website references for e-pages.

nodes.title: P
nodes.summary: This text is an index from a periodontal textbook covering orthodontic-implant relationships; osseointegration and implant surgery; osseous and regenerative surgical procedures; outpatient periodontal surgery; periodontal examination, diagnosis, prognosis, and risk assessment; microbiology and host immune responses; classifications and clinical forms of periodontal and peri-implant diseases; surgical, nonsurgical, and laser therapies; systemic links to periodontal disease; dental implants and prosthetics; oral pathology and oral medicine; evidence-based dentistry and epidemiology; pharmacology; instrumentation; and historical figures in periodontology.

nodes.title: Q
nodes.summary: This is an alphabetized index excerpt from a dental/periodontology textbook, listing entries from Protozoa through Relative risk. It covers prosthodontic, occlusal, periodontal, endodontic, microbiologic, radiologic, surgical, implant, research-methodology, and patient-maintenance topics, each with page or e-page locators. A closing instruction explains that entries containing an 'e' in the page number are available on the companion website at www.expertconsult.com.

nodes.title: R
nodes.summary: The text is an index section from a dental/periodontology textbook, listing alphabetically arranged terms and their page numbers, including online-only 'e' page references. It covers a broad range of topics: periodontal microbiology, immunology, disease classification and diagnosis, nonsurgical and surgical periodontal therapy, dental implants, ridge augmentation, restorative and occlusal considerations, oral pathology, systemic and psychologic conditions, radiographic assessment, research methodology, and historical figures in periodontology.

nodes.title: S
nodes.summary: This text is a dental/periodontal index covering entries from 'Remote incision' through 'Titanium temporary abutment'. It includes periodontal surgical techniques, implant placement and restoration, nonsurgical instrumentation, disease etiology and microbiology, diagnosis and risk assessment, systemic medical conditions affecting the oral cavity, restorative and occlusal considerations, supportive maintenance therapy, tissue engineering and regenerative materials, pharmacology, oral pathology, historical references, and research methodology, with page numbers and companion website e-page references.

nodes.title: T
nodes.summary: This is an index excerpt from a dental/periodontology textbook containing alphabetized entries from 'Systemic lupus erythematosus' to 'Ulcerative stomatitis'. It covers systemic diseases and medications, oral anatomy and examination, periodontal microbiology and immunology, oral hygiene practices, periodontal pathology, TMJ and occlusion, dental implants and surgical techniques, tissue engineering, pharmacology, research/statistics, and historical references. Each entry includes page numbers, with 'e' page numbers indicating companion website content.

nodes.title: U
nodes.summary: This text is an alphabetically arranged index excerpt from a dental/periodontology reference, covering terms from T to Z. It includes topics spanning periodontology, implantology, oral pathology, microbiology, immunology, pharmacology, oral hygiene, surgical techniques, systemic diseases, and historical figures. It also notes that entries with 'e' page numbers can be found on the companion website.

nodes.title: Dental Index Entries from V to Z (Ultrasonic to Zygomatic)
nodes.summary: This is an index page from a dental/periodontology text covering terms alphabetically from V through Z. It includes clinical procedures, surgical techniques, implantology, ultrasonic instruments, curettes/scalers, bone grafting and augmentation, periodontal defects and abscesses, infections, vitamin deficiencies, medications, biomaterials, historical figures, and a companion-website note for e-page references.

nodes.title: Z
nodes.summary: This text is the tail end of an index from a dental/periodontology book, listing topics from U to Z. It covers ultrasonic and surgical techniques, periodontal instrumentation, bone defects and augmentation, implant-related topics, vitamin deficiencies, viral and bacterial conditions, drug entries, anatomical structures, and notable historical figures. It also includes a note directing readers to the companion website for e-page entries, and ends with blank pages and an advertisement for Elsevier's clinical search engine.

structure.summary: The section is the comprehensive alphabetical index of a periodontology textbook. It covers the full scope of periodontology and related dental/medical topics, including anatomy, microbiology, immunology, disease classification and diagnosis, clinical and radiographic evaluation, nonsurgical and surgical treatments, regenerative and implant procedures, orthodontics, occlusion, pharmacology, systemic health interactions, oral pathology, oral hygiene, maintenance care, prosthodontics, endodontics, evidence-based practice, and historical references. It also includes cross-references and companion-website e-page locators.
